#2. The separation and expansion of powers between Congress and the president

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

This is the fourth and final part in a series for SCOTUSblog recounting two decades of constitutional change through the five editions of our casebook, the first published in 2008 and the latest to be published this December.

The late 1990s and early 2000s ushered in the Rehnquist federalism revolution, which appeared to place limits on Congress’ powers and expand those of the states. Then came Sept. 11, 2001, and the global war on terror, which seemed poised to expand the president’s powers. Yet, by 2008, Congress’ powers seemed without meaningful limits and the president’s efforts to expand his own powers had failed. And the separation of powers remained, well, separate. Nevertheless, the next two decades would vastly enlarge the president’s powers as Congress’ authority over the executive branch would be greatly diminished.

Late-breaking changes for the legislative power

Most of the chapter on legislative powers has remained the same since our textbook’s first edition was published in 2008. The Rehnquist court’s federalism revolution hit a roadblock three years earlier. Gonzales v. Raich, which Barnett argued, halted the progress made by United States v. Lopez and United States v. Morrison. Those cases found limits on Congress’ powers to regulate guns in school zones and domestic violence through the commerce clause. But Raich upheld Congress’ powers to regulate locally grown marijuana. The second edition from 2013 ushered in NFIB v. Sebelius. This case held that the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate exceeds Congress’ powers under the commerce and necessary and proper clauses, but the penalty enforcing the mandate could be saved as a constitutional tax.

No further changes were made in the following editions. Indeed, it seemed to both of us that the justices were unwilling to look more closely at the scope of federal enumerated powers. But this year’s edition introduces two unexpected enumerated powers cases. Landor v. Louisiana Department of Public Safety and Corrections clarified the relationship between the spending power and the necessary and proper clause. As a general matter, Congress can only make state officials subject to suits for money damages if the law complies with the necessary and proper clause. Landor ruled that the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act does not provide a private cause of action for monetary damages against state officials who did not consent to suit, as such a law is not a “proper” exercise of federal power. We also included Justice Clarence Thomas’s concurrence in United States v. Hemani, which proposed tightening the so-called “jurisdictional hook” analysis. He would require a closer fit between interstate commerce and a regulated activity.

The future looks promising for a reconsideration of enumerated powers.

The contracting and expanding executive power

In March 2008, when the first edition of our casebook was published, the Supreme Court was primarily occupied by President George W. Bush’s global war on terror. The first edition of the casebook included Hamdi v. Rumsfeld and Hamdan v. Rumsfeld. These cases rejected early challenges to the detention of suspected terrorists at Guantanamo Bay. In June 2008, the court would conclude the trilogy with Boumediene v. Bush, which held that the writ of habeas corpus runs to that prison facility.

But that case would be a fleeting flash, as the global war on terror faded from relevance – at least jurisprudentially. Moreover, most first-year law students were born after Sept. 11, 2001, and have no living memory of the events that gave rise to the conflict in Afghanistan. What seemed so critical in the decade after 9/11 has waned significantly in prominence before the court.

The realignment of the separation of powers

Perhaps the most significant revisions across five editions of the casebook came in the context of the separation of powers. Labeling these cases is tricky. Cases not only move in and out of the canon but also shift in how they are perceived. Many cases started out under the label of separation of powers – as the court enforced the balance of authority between the branches – but now might be considered executive power cases.

Only three separation-of-powers cases have survived all five editions. First, United States v. Nixon required the president to comply with a subpoena for the Watergate tapes. Second, Morrison v. Olson rejected a challenge to the independent counsel statute. And third, Clinton v. Jones held that a sitting president is subject to a civil suit for conduct that arose before his term began. We pondered at some length whether to retain Morrison, as it has largely been supplanted by Trump v. Slaughter. This 2026 decision formally overruled 1935’s Humphrey’s Executor v. United States and allowed the president to remove members of certain independent agencies.

Three Burger court staples were dropped. Dames & Moore v. Regan upheld the president’s suspension of claims arising from the Iran hostage crisis. Nixon v. Fitzgerald ruled that former President Richard Nixon was immune from suit for certain actions taken while in office. INS v. Chadha rejected the so-called “one house” veto, or the ability of either chamber of Congress to prevent an action by the executive branch. In the 1980s, these cases were landmark decisions. Over time, however, their relevance faded. Still, as reflected in Justice Neil Gorsuch’s concurrence in Learning Resources v. Trump, the 2026 tariffs case, Chadha’s effect has been magnified as the court has ceded more power to the president over executive branch agencies, even as those delegations were originally enacted with legislative vetoes.

Three decisions from the early Roberts court quickly entered and left the chat. Trump v. Slaughter replaced Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB and Seila Law v. CFPB. These cases, which rejected attempts to limit the president’s removal powers, simply lost relevance. NLRB v. Noel Canning was an important case about the original meaning of the recess appointments clause, but it has become largely obsolete as the past three presidents have used other means to make short-term appointments.

President Donald Trump has been the most consequential president for the Supreme Court’s separation-of-powers jurisprudence since Franklin D. Roosevelt. Five cases bearing his name now appear in the separation-of-powers chapter. Trump v. Vance, which concerned the president’s tax returns, was added before the fourth edition went to press. The fifth edition now provides a Trump quartet. Trump v. United States expanded the scope of presidential immunity from the Nixon era. Trump v. Slaughter, as noted, at last overruled Humphrey’s Executor, as Morrison v. Olson remains in a zone of twilight. Trump v. Cook reaffirmed the Federal Reserve's independence. And Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump invalidated the president’s tariffs. These cases, Slaughter in particular, will likely trigger an entire generation of new cases concerning the separation of powers. Who knows what the sixth edition will bring?

For easy reference, this table illustrates which cases were added and dropped across the five editions of our casebook. A checkmark indicates continued coverage.

Up to the fourth edition of our casebook in 2022, constitutional law followed a somewhat predictable arc. To be sure, there were shifts to the left and to the right, but the doctrine could be explained by a coherent narrative: the New Deal settlement on federal power was untouchable; the court would offer only modest protections for federalism; the administrative state was beyond reproach; attempts to single out unpopular groups would be halted; “benign” racial classifications were permitted; and church and state were strictly separated. Now, each aspect of this narrative has been reconceived. The five years since that edition appeared have brought the most changes to constitutional law since the Warren court.

We began this series by observing that lawyers tend to internalize the constitutional law that existed when they attended law school. The same is true of law professors. Virtually all law professors today came of age in a time of stasis. They could safely assume that the trajectory of the Warren court would continue indefinitely. But the jurisprudence of the Burger and Rehnquist courts was primed for a reversal, just as the Warren court reversed so many precedents from before. Ultimately, the Roberts court continues to chip away at precedents from the 1970s and 1980s, even if the precedents from the 1960s and before remain.

Many of these professors have struggled to cope with sudden changes in the doctrine. Some have voiced their despair of teaching constitutional law at all. Unsurprisingly, their students also struggle to cope with these developments. This trend is regrettable. Our role as casebook editors, and constitutional law professors, is to guide students through the entire corpus of constitutional law, from the framing to the present day, without any nostalgia for, or bias against, times gone by.

Josh Blackman is a professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston. He holds the Centennial Chair of Constitutional Law. Josh is also an Adjunct Fellow at the Manhattan Institute.

Randy E. Barnett is the Patrick Hotung Professor of Constitutional Law at the Georgetown University Law Center, where he founded the Georgetown Center for the Constitution.

#4. US: Order ‘No ICE’ Zones during Election Period

Click to expand Image A voter carries a ballot during early voting in the New York City mayoral elections on October 25, 2025. © 2025 Olga Fedorova/AP Photo

(Washington, DC) – The United States government should order federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers not to operate in the vicinity of polling places, early voting locations, or drop boxes during the midterm electoral period, Human Rights Watch said today. The presence of these federal agents could deter people from voting. 

“ICE officers’ abuses have already seriously affected US citizens who have been stopped, beaten, detained, deported, and even killed,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director at Human Rights Watch. “Voters should not have to fear being caught in an ICE dragnet when they head to the polls.”

In-person early voting is already taking place in the majority of states. In a nationwide September poll, 40 percent of respondents said they expect some kind of ICE presence at polls, with even higher percentages among non-white respondents expecting to see ICE agents in places people vote. 

Federal law generally prohibits federal officials from sending “troops or armed men” to voting sites. Several state laws prohibit any armed officers, including police, from engaging in acts that could interfere with the elections or intimidate voters by their presence near polling places. Some states bar law enforcement officers, including police, from being in close proximity to polling places at all unless they are responding to a specific incident.

Despite these robust prohibitions, neither President Donald Trump nor the heads of the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation have been willing to rule out the possibility that federal agents, including ICE, may be at places where people vote.

In March, then-Deputy Attorney General and now-Attorney General Todd Blanche said, “Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations? ... Illegals can’t vote. It doesn’t make any sense.” In February, Karoline Leavitt, who was White House press secretary at the time, said she could not “guarantee” that ICE agents won’t be around a polling location in November.

In early September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there were no plans to station ICE agents at polling places but left the door open for them to be there if “serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down” or if “there is a threat to that polling place.”

Three lawsuits are pending in federal courts to prevent ICE from operating at the polls, with an additional court case seeking to require the government to disclose its plans regarding ICE agents at polling places. In Washington, DC, the Board of Elections in October asked the National Guard to limit their presence near drop box locations for the midterm election following complaints that troops had been spotted near a drop box in Foggy Bottom. 

The Trump administration has long touted the idea that large numbers of noncitizens unlawfully cast ballots in US elections but has not produced any evidence suggesting that the problem exists at a scale that would have affected the result of any election, anywhere in the country. Multiple research studies, including from the Fair Elections Center, Bipartisan Policy Center, Brennan Center, and the Cato Institute, have found no evidence of mass voting by noncitizens and concluded that the problem is insignificant in electoral outcomes.

ProPublica found that federal immigration officers have detained at least 500 US citizens since the start of Trump’s second term, including 36 incidents in which detained US citizens were prevented from contacting their family or lawyers for 24 hours or more. The same study also found that agents who questioned their claims of citizenship detained more than 100 US citizens, nearly all of them people of color.

In Minnesota, Human Rights Watch found that ICE’s Operation Metro Surge abuses terrified many people, causing them to stay home and miss work, school, and even essential health care appointments. US citizens of color whom Human Rights Watch interviewed at the time said they were so fearful of racial profiling that they began carrying their passports everywhere. 

Human Rights Watch analysis also suggests that in 2025, ICE used race and ethnicity in Los Angeles as a crude proxy for identifying a person’s nationality, and detained people on that basis. Perceptions of the risks associated with an encounter with ICE may well be higher among non-white communities.  

The notoriety of those incidents and of ICE’s widespread abuses over the last two years risks dissuading some people from voting if they feel they are likely to encounter ICE agents near polling places, Human Rights Watch said. 

“ICE agents should be publicly ordered to stay away from the polls and anywhere ballots are being cast,” Bolopion said.

#5. Kagan diagnoses American democracy with a Supreme Court problem

#6. The Supreme Court’s next major case on the free exercise of religion

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Nov. 3, the Supreme Court will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. This case raises important questions about how far the court will go in expanding the Constitution’s protections of the free exercise of religion. One of the most dramatic changes in constitutional law in recent years has concerned the religion clauses of the First Amendment. For decades, the Supreme Court took a robust approach to the establishment clause, seeing it as best described by Thomas Jefferson’s metaphor of a wall separating church and state. At the same time, the court took a much weaker approach to the free exercise clause, as embodied in its decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which held that the First Amendment does not provide a basis for religious exemptions from general laws.

But, in recent years, the court has completely reversed this. It has greatly lessened the protections of the establishment clause; a majority of the current justices reject the idea of a wall separating church and state. In its most recent case about that provision, 2022’s Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, the court declared: “‘[T]he line’ that courts and governments ‘must draw between the permissible and the impermissible’ has to ‘accor[d] with history and faithfully reflec[t] the understanding of the Founding Fathers.’” Given this, it is likely that only government coercion to worship or adhere to a particular religion will be found to violate the establishment clause.

By contrast, the Supreme Court has aggressively expanded the protections of the free exercise clause. In 2021’s Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, the court held that it violates the free exercise of religion for the city, in contracting with private entities to place children in foster care, to insist that contractors not discriminate based on sexual orientation when they had a religious reason for doing so. In 2022’s Carson v. Makin, as well as 2018’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer and 2020’s Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, the court ruled that it violates the free exercise of religion for the state to provide aid to private secular schools that it denies to religious schools. And in 2025’s Mahmoud v. Taylor, the court held that it violates the free exercise of religion for a school system to fail to give parents of elementary school students notice and a chance to opt their children out of a curriculum that presented “LGBTQ+- inclusive” storybooks.

Colorado’s universal preschool program funds preschools – public, private, and religious alike – that sign an agreement to give children an “equal opportunity to enroll” regardless of, among other things, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, or gender identity. Two Catholic parish preschools and the Archdiocese of Denver say that they have a religious belief that they must consider a family’s sexual orientation and gender identity in admissions, and they sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for an injunction against the preschool requirement.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10 Circuit upheld the Colorado law, applying Employment Division v. Smith and explaining that the Colorado law is a neutral law of general applicability; it was not motivated by a desire to apply to religion and applies equally to all. The court also explained that Colorado was not denying funding to religious schools that it provides to secular institutions: No preschool taking state money can refuse to admit children because of the race, religion, sexual orientation, or gender identity of the parents.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari on two questions: (1) Whether proving a lack of general applicability under Smith requires showing unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct; and (2) whether Carson v. Makin (that the government violates the free exercise clause if it denies funds to religious schools that it provides to private secular schools) displaces the rule of Smith only when the government explicitly excludes religious people and institutions.

There are many underlying issues that could make the case enormously important. First, will the court overrule Employment Division v. Smith and, if so, what will replace it? The court did not grant review on this question, but it certainly underlies the case. Five years ago, in Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Justice Samuel Alito wrote a lengthy opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, urging the overruling of Smith. Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote a concurring opinion, joined in full by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in which she said that she agreed with much of Alito’s opinion, but that overruling Smith would raise many difficult questions and there was no need for the court to resolve them in the case before it.

Petitioner St. Mary Catholic Parish clearly is urging the court to jettison Smith. The first argument in its brief is that the “Court rarely applies Smith.” It says: “Out of the eighteen free exercise cases this Court has resolved since Smith in 1990, this Court has relied on Smith only twice to rule against the religious objector,” and one of these was Smith itself. But the brief says that lower courts, like the 10th in this case, constantly rely on Smith.

The ideological shift on the court with regard to free exercise claims has been dramatic. The majority opinion in Smith was written by Justice Antonin Scalia and it was liberals at the time that were critical of this holding. Now, it is the most conservative justices who are urging Smith’s overruling and it is the liberal justices who are defending it. Smith was about whether Native Americans should have a constitutional right to a religious exemption from a law prohibiting consumption of peyote – a hallucinogenic substance. Now, the cases are about Christians, such as the Catholic Church in St. Mary Catholic Parish, that are seeking religious exemptions.

Second, there is the question of when religion is infringed. If the court overrules Smith, this issue will become much more salient, as will the court’s need to define what is “religion” and a “religious belief.” Under Smith, with no exemptions for any religion, there is far less need to face these questions.

For instance, in St. Mary Catholic Parish, there is a question of whether the Colorado law infringes the church’s religious beliefs. The Colorado statute does not limit the ability of the Catholic schools to teach whatever they choose. The law simply says that a school receiving government funds should not discriminate against children, including based on the sexual orientation or the gender identity of the parents. The Catholic Church certainly may say that its teachings condemn same-sex sexual activity and gender transitions. But their contention in the present case is that their religion requires that they discriminate against children because of their parents being gay, lesbian, or transgender. This seems a much more difficult argument unless the court is going to accord considerable deference to religious claims in applying the free exercise clause.

Third, even if the court overrules Smith, does the government have a compelling interest in preventing discrimination against children on account of the sexual orientation or gender identity of their parents? In 2018’s Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission, the court considered the question of whether a baker had a right under the free exercise clause to violate a Colorado civil rights statute by refusing to design and bake a wedding cake for a gay couple. The court ruled narrowly, holding that members of the Colorado Civil Rights Commission had expressed impermissible animus towards religion. In 2023’s 303 Creative v. Elenis, the court held that it would violate the freedom of speech to apply a civil rights statute to force a website designer to provide her wedding services for same-sex couples. The court did not consider her claim based on the free exercise of religion.

There always is a tension between liberty and equality. Any law that prohibits discrimination limits the freedom to discriminate. For decades, the Supreme Court was clear that prohibiting discrimination was more important than protecting the right to discriminate. In 1968’s Newman v. Piggy Park Enterprises, Inc., the court summarily rejected a claim that a person’s religious beliefs were a basis to discriminate in violation of civil rights statutes. If the court overrules Smith, or says that strict scrutiny should be used under Smith, the question will need to be addressed: should the free exercise of religion provide a right to harm others by discriminating against them?

Fourth, if the government provides funding for schools, may it deny funding to schools that discriminate based on their religious beliefs? In a series of cases culminating most recently in Carson v. Makin, the court has held that the government violates the free exercise clause if it denies funds to religious schools that it provides to private secular schools. St. Mary Catholic Parish argues that Colorado is doing just that: denying it funding because of its exercising its religious beliefs and excluding children whose parents are gay, lesbian, or transgender.

But Colorado argues that its law does not discriminate based on religion. It will pay for children to attend preschools that are religious so long as they do not discriminate against children based on their parents’ sexual orientation or gender identity. In Carson, the Maine statute paid for children in areas without public schools to attend private schools but denied funding for children attending religious schools. Colorado says that its law is different because it does not exclude such institutions.

The Supreme Court could rule in favor of Colorado by applying Employment Division v. Smith. But the conservative majority – and especially Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett – want to expand the protections of the free exercise of religion. St. Mary’s Catholic Parish v. Roy could provide them the opportunity to do so and thereby dramatically change the law.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

#8. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#9. Update on Canada's Two Secession Movements

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Alberta secessionists lost a referendum by a large margin. Quebec secessionists are in better shape, but still facing an uphill struggle.

Back in June, I wrote a post about Canada's two active secession movements: one in Alberta and one in Quebec. Since then, there have been some important developments. Alberta secessionists suffered a major defeat. Quebec secessionists are in better shape, but the odds are still against them succeeding anytime soon. That said, both movements may well persist for a long time to come.

Yesterday, Alberta secessionists lost a referendum on secession by a massive 75-25 margin. Pollsters expected a blowout, but this margin is close to the outer edge of expectations. Moreover, the result may actually understate the true extent of opposition to secession in the province. As noted in my earlier post, the question put to the voters was not directly about secession, but rather on whether "the Government of Alberta [should] commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada." Essentially, it was a referendum on whether to hold another referendum. Some "yes" voters might have been confused about what it meant or wanted to hold a second referendum, while planning to vote "no."

United Conservative Party Alberta Premier Danielle Smith (who played a key role in arranging yesterday's vote, despite opposing secession herself) has pledged not to hold any further referenda on secession. She may well be happy to sideline an issue that divides her party (Alberta secessionists are overwhelmingly right-of-center UCP voters).

All of this is bleak news for Alberta secessionists. But it's too early to say their movement is dead. As noted in my previous post, secession movements often persist for many years, even in the face of defeats in referenda and other political setbacks. Scotland, Quebec, and Catalonia are all examples of this phenomenon. And some 25% of Alberta voters did express support for secession, despite opposition from the leaders of all major political parties. That's a minority, but far from an insignificant one.

Meanwhile, in Quebec, on October 5, the secessionist Parti Quebecois (PQ) won the provincial election. But they got only 28% of the vote (the lowest percentage for any winning party in the history of Canadian provincial elections). That translated to a "minority" government that has 59 seats in Quebec's National Assembly (the provincial legislature), 5 short of a majority. And, as discussed in my previous post, secession remains unpopular, with polls showing opposition by a margin of 2-1 or more. For much more detailed discussions of the Quebec election and its ramifications, see analyses by Canadian election/polling experts Eric Grenier and Philippe Fournier.

As Fournier emphasizes, PQ leader Paul St. Pierre Plamondon (known as "PSPP") remains committed to holding a secession referendum. But the minority nature of his governments makes it unclear whether the PQ can find the votes to enact legislation to hold one. The left-wing Quebec Solidaire party (which holds 9 seats) is also pro-independence. But they may not be willing to work with the PQ. In addition, PSPP has promised not to hold a referendum so long as Donald Trump remains president of the United States, claiming it would be too dangerous to do so while Trump continues his trade war with Canada and otherwise threatens the country. Unless Trump dies or gets impeached and removed (both relatively unlikely), he will remain in office until January 2029. Canadian minority governments generally don't last more than two years. So PSPP may not be in power long enough to outlast Trump.

While Quebec secessionists seem unlikely to prevail in the near future, the fact that they managed to return to power is still a sign of the movement's persistence. And they have survived referendum defeats in 1980 and 1995. Thus, the movement is likely to continue to be a thorn in the side of Canadian federal governments, perhaps for many years to come. It has demonstrated its staying power over many years, much more so than Alberta secessionists.

Many Canadians believe Trump's threats against their country have weakened secessionists in both Alberta and Quebec. PSPP's stance is just part of the evidence for this conclusion. Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the "51st state" have bolstered national unity and made the Liberal Party government of Prime Minister Mark Carney much more popular than might otherwise be the case. Trump is making Canadian national unity - and the Canadian Liberal Party - great again! But for him, the Liberals would likely have lost last year's Canadian federal election to the Conservatives.

Perhaps, all along, Trump has been trying to help the Liberals and stymie secessionists. If that's the true objective of his Canada policy, then maybe it's not quite as evil and stupid as otherwise seems to be the case. On a more serious note, Trump's policies have illegally usurped congressional authority over trade,  damaged our economy, and alienated a crucial ally - all for no good reason.

In my June post, I outlined reasons why I am more sympathetic to Alberta's secession movement (motivated by conservative economic ideology and grievances about federal fiscal transfers and energy policies), than Quebec's (motivated by Francophone ethno-nationalism). Although I think the Alberta movement has greater merit than Quebec's, for reasons also summarized in the earlier post, I remain skeptical that Alberta secession would accomplish more good than harm. I also explained why these movements may be of interest to many non-Canadians and why I (an American) comment on them them:

[T]hese events are… of interest to students of federalism and secession, and to anyone who cares about the future of America's northern neighbor and one of our most important allies. And history shows that secession movements often persist even after defeat in a referendum….

From a US perspective, I worry that a successful secession movement would make Canada a weaker and less effective ally. Unlike our current president, I think a strong Western alliance is essential….

Some might find it inappropriate for an American to comment on Canadian politics. I disagree. Canadians and other non-Americans often express views on US politics. And they have every right to do so. Political analysis should be judged on its substance, not on the background of the author. In addition,… Canadian secessionism potentially impacts the US in various ways, and raises broader issues about the morality of secession movements that Americans and others have reason to take an interest in…. I am a longtime academic expert on federalism and secession-related issues, and I know French, as well as English. Thus, I think have the necessary qualifications to write about these issues. Whether the commentary is any good or not, is for others to judge.

City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#10. The Real Sherlock Holmes: How an Edinburgh Doctor Inspired Doyle’s Detective

The following is an excerpt from Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes.

Joe Bell was a man who liked to keep busy. In addition to his hospital and police work, he gradually built one of the largest private practices in Edinburgh, sustaining it throughout his career. Each day he made up to twenty house calls, trundling from appointment to appointment in his elegant barouche.

On one occasion, he called on Hugh Black—a minister at St. George’s United Free Church, where Bell was an elder. Black’s wife, who had summoned Bell, was concerned that her husband was coming down with a cold. The minister dismissed his wife’s worries, insisting that he would be well enough to deliver his sermon the next morning.

When Bell arrived at the house, he stepped into Black’s study, took a seat opposite him, and began telling him a joke. When the minister laughed heartily at the punchline, Bell shot to his feet and pointed a stern finger at his patient, as if he had caught him in a lie. “Ye’ll no preach the morrow,” Bell said. He knew by the sound of the minister’s rattling laugh that the cold was deep-seated, and the only remedy was rest.

Bell also secured a fourth revenue stream for a time by working as a medical examiner for an insurance company. The nineteenth century witnessed a surge in the number of people taking out life insurance policies. This was driven in part by concern over the prevalence of diseases such as smallpox, tuberculosis, and cholera.

It was a system, however, that was open to abuse. The most egregious perpetrators of fraud in the industry were corrupt doctors who were paid by patients to send insurance companies medical examination reports that omit-ted unfavorable findings. So common was this practice that by the middle of the century, insurance companies were regularly employing their own medical referees to submit thorough and unbiased reports for review.

Bell’s talents were especially suited to this role. He once correctly identified a man sent to him by insurers as a former soldier. Poking the subject in his bare ribs after he had stripped to the waist, Bell declared, “You have belonged to the volunteers.” The man confirmed this, but said that his military service had ended some years before. Though Bell knew the man was not in the army, his musculature still betrayed to Bell his previous career. Bell’s clients, the insurers, must have been delighted to have such a keen pair of eyes on their side.

While Bell split his time between this sideline, his private practice, his collaborations with Henry Duncan Littlejohn, and his duties on the wards of the Royal Hospital for Sick Children, he also continued to monitor Conan Doyle’s success. The interview in The Bookman had inaugurated what turned into a flurry of correspondence with his old clerk in the spring of 1892.

In one letter, Conan Doyle thanked Bell for further story suggestions. “Your letters are really of great value to me and I am exceedingly obliged to you for the details which you so kindly furnished. The deserter-cobbler is admirable, and I wish I had a dozen more such cases.” In the same letter, Conan Doyle also told Bell that he was “insatiable for material,” as he had committed to writing twelve more stories for The Strand.

“Your sketch too of the crime is capital,” he continued. “It wants a sort of second plot to run parallel with the first, and to drag some other red herring across the scent besides the ex-soldier. But there is the nucleus—and indeed much more than the nucleus, of something very good. I shall certainly—with your kind permission—avail myself of the idea.” He ended the letter by saying that he had asked the bookseller to send Bell a “complete edition of my little yarns,” and thanked him “once more very heartily for the ‘tips.'”

That Bell was the inspiration for Sherlock Holmes was still known to only a handful of people, including Robert Louis Stevenson, who had by then guessed the truth. Since the publication of the interview in The Bookman, however, interest in the identity of the unnamed “professor of medicine at Edinburgh University” had been growing.

Harry How, who had been working as a features writer for The Strand Magazine since its inception, was determined to get the scoop. After all, what better place to reveal the mysterious professor’s identity than in the very magazine responsible for making the fictional detective an international sensation? And so, How appeared on Conan Doyle’s doorstep one afternoon in the summer of 1892, seeking an audience with the acclaimed author.

“I found him totally different from the man I expected to see; but that is always the case,” How wrote in the article he soon published. “There was nothing lynx-eyed, nothing ‘detective’ about him—not even the regulation walk of our modern solver of mysteries.” Instead, he was greeted by a “happy, genial, homely man” who grasped his hand heartily and welcomed him to his house.

After a tour of Conan Doyle’s “prettily-built and modest-looking red-brick residence” at 12 Tennison Road in South Norwood, the two men availed themselves of the author’s luxuriantly wallpapered study. They lit cigars, and settled into their chairs to discuss Conan Doyle’s childhood and his early steps into adulthood. Before long, the conversation turned to his time as a medical student at the University of Edinburgh.

“There I met the man who suggested Sherlock Holmes to me—here is a portrait of him as he was in those days, and he is strong and hearty, and still in Edinburgh now,” Conan Doyle told the journalist, handing him a photograph. “I was clerk in Mr. Bell’s ward,” he continued. “A clerk’s duties are to note down all the patients to be seen, and muster them together. Often I would have seventy or eighty. When everything was ready, I would show them in to Mr. Bell, who would have the students gathered round him. His intuitive powers were simply marvelous.”

Conan Doyle then regaled How with several stories of Bell’s observational sorcery: the man whose alcoholism was revealed by a flask hidden in his breast pocket; the cobbler whose trade was betrayed by wear on the inside of his trousers where he rested his leg against the lapstone.

“He was continually before me—his sharp, piercing grey eyes, eagle nose, and striking features,” he said, puffing on his cigar. “He was most kind and painstaking with the students—a real good friend—and when I took my degree and went to Africa the remark-able individuality and discriminating tact of my old master made a deep and lasting impression on me, though I had not the faintest idea that it would one day lead me to forsake medicine for story writing.”

Conan Doyle realized that he had provided enough details to pique How’s curiosity about the Edinburgh professor. Shortly after the interview, he penned a slightly panicked letter to Bell.

I am afraid that my little sketches have had the effect of setting a newspaper man on your trail with as great per-sistence as even Holmes showed to any of his criminals. Mr Harry How…was out here yesterday, and on my mentioning in the course of the interview about the influence which your teaching had in making us observe, de-duce [sic] he departed with all intentions of writing to you and getting all he could from you to embellish his article with. I thought that I would write to you independently to say that I have nothing to do with the matter, and that I hope you won’t consider me in the least in deciding whether to give him what he wants or not. I should be so sorry if you were bothered in any way in consequence of my having made use of your teachings.

Bell replied in his usual jovial manner, agreeing to the reproduction of his photo in the forthcoming article. He also told his former stu-dent that he’d be happy to answer any further questions the journalist might have. “Your permission will rejoice the cockles of Mr Harry How’s heart,” Conan Doyle replied.

Not long after this exchange, Bell wrote a lengthy letter to Harry How in which he downplayed any influence he may have had on the creation of Sherlock Holmes.

“Dr. Conan Doyle has, by his imaginative genius, made a great deal out of very little, and his warm remembrance of one of his old teachers has colored the picture,” he wrote, with characteristic modesty. “In teaching the treatment of disease and accident, all careful teachers have first to show the student how to recognize accurately the case. The recognition depends in great measure on the accurate and rapid appreciation of small points in which the diseased differs from the healthy state.”

Sharing some of Sherlock Holmes’s bafflement at those who failed to notice a world of detail in apparent trifles, Bell went on to explain his method to the journalist:

The soldier and the sailor differ in gait, though last month I had to tell a man who said he was a soldier that he had been a sailor in his boyhood. The subject is endless: the tattoo marks on hand or arm will tell their own tale as to voyages; the ornaments on the watch chain of the success-ful settler will tell you where he made his money. A New Zealand squatter will not wear a gold mohur, nor an engi-neer on an Indian railway a Maori stone. Carry the same idea of using one’s senses accurately and constantly, and you will see that many a surgical case will bring his past history, national, social, and medical, into the consulting-room as he walks in. Dr. Conan Doyle’s genius and intense imagination has on this slender basis made his detective stories a distinctly new departure, but he owes much less than he thinks to yours truly Joseph Bell.

Captivated by Bell’s letter, Harry How asked if he could reproduce it verbatim in the article that was scheduled to appear in The Strand’s August issue. Bell consented.

A short while later, Conan Doyle wrote to Bell with another warning. Holmes’s popularity had brought the author many inconveniences, and he worried about the effect How’s interview would have when published. “I fear that one effect of your identity being revealed to the readers of the ‘Strand’ will be that you have ample opportunity for studying lunatic letters, and that part at least of the stream which pours upon me will be diverted to you,” he wrote.

By then, Conan Doyle was receiving dozens of inquiries addressed to Sherlock Holmes each month—requests for autographs, advice, even locks of hair.

You will hear alas from the youth in the South of Portugal, from the American lady with the curved spine, from the Liverpool merchant who burns to know who Jack the Ripper is, from many folks who believe that their neighbours are starving maiden aunts to death in hermetically sealed attics, and in short you will bless me and my yarns when you look at your postbox.

As yet, and in spite of his former student’s prescience, Bell could not imagine the enormity of what would follow. The next month, The Strand ran a feature entitled “A Day with Dr. Conan Doyle,” profil-ing the author and, for the first time in print, naming Joseph Bell as the real Sherlock Holmes. What Conan Doyle had most feared was about to be unleashed upon his old professor.

Lindsey Fitzharris is a New-York-Times-bestselling author whose books include The Butchering Art, Sleuth-Hound, and The Facemaker. Along with her husband, Adrian Teal, she also writes children’s nonfiction, including Dead Ends! Flukes, Flops, and Failures That Sparked Medical Marvels and Plague-Busters! Medicine’s Battles with History’s Deadliest Diseases. She holds a PhD in the history of science and medicine from the University of Oxford and has written for The Wall Street Journal, Scientific American, The Guardian, The Lancet, and other major publications.

#11. Guatemala: Prominent Anti-Corruption Lawyer Fatally Shot

Click to expand Image People stand near a framed photo of Guatemalan lawyer and anti-corruption figure Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa, who died after being shot by unknown assailants on Saturday while visiting a sports center, during his wake at a funeral home in Guatemala City, Guatemala, October 19, 2026. © 2026 Cristina Chiquin/Reuters

(Washington, DC) – Guatemalan authorities should carry out a thorough, prompt, and credible investigation into the killing of Juan Francisco Solórzano Foppa, a prominent anti-corruption lawyer, former prosecutor, and former head of Guatemala’s tax agency, Human Rights Watch said today.

On October 17, 2026, armed assailants shot and killed Solórzano Foppa at the Campo Marte sports complex in Guatemala City. Another man, identified by authorities as Gustavo Adolfo Aguilar Gamarro, was also killed in the attack. Guatemalan authorities arrested two men in connection with the crime, but prosecutors said there was no evidence linking them to the attack and a judge ordered their release. 

“The killing of Juan Francisco Solórzano Foppa is a shocking attack against a lawyer who played a prominent role in some of Guatemala’s most important anti-corruption efforts,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “Guatemalan authorities should ensure a thorough, prompt, and credible investigation capable of identifying not only the gunmen, but also anyone who planned, ordered, or facilitated this crime.”

Armed attackers opened fire on Solórzano Foppa while he was at the sports complex coaching a football team, killing him at the scene, media reported. President Bernardo Arévalo condemned the killing and called for those responsible, including any who played a role in planning the crime, to be brought to justice.

Solórzano Foppa, 43, was widely known for his anti-corruption work in Guatemala. He served as director of criminal analysis within the attorney general’s office and later led Guatemala’s Superintendency of Tax Administration, from 2016 to 2018. He helped advance investigations into high-level corruption and tax evasion, contributing to efforts to recover millions in unpaid taxes and supporting major corruption cases, including work related to the criminal case known as “La Línea” (“The Line”), which led to the resignation of President Otto Pérez Molina in 2015.

After leaving public office, Solórzano Foppa continued to work as a lawyer and public commentator. He was known for denouncing corruption and links between criminal groups, politicians, and authorities. 

In 2023, he briefly joined the legal defense team of the well-known journalist José Rubén Zamora, who has faced arbitrary criminal prosecution since 2022. During Attorney General Consuelo Porras’s tenure, a campaign of arbitrary criminal prosecutions against critics included the detention of Solórzano Foppa, who was accused of “hindering criminal investigations” in connection with his defense of Zamora. Solórzano Foppa said the prosecution was arbitrary and pleaded guilty to obtain an early release.

“Solórzano Foppa’s killing is a chilling reminder of Guatemala’s long history of political murders,” Goebertus said. “Those responsible should be held accountable.”

#12. Corporate Alignment with the Human Rights Campaign: Legal, Financial, and Reputational Risks for Shareholders

In 2024, Bowyer Research conducted two coordinated shareholder engagement campaigns targeting more than 400 publicly traded U.S. companies, focusing on potential risks related to corporate alignment with the Human Rights Campaign (HRC)—particularly through participation in the HRC’s Corporate Equality Index (CEI)—and from extensive Pride Month messaging. This Backgrounder summarizes the substance and scale of those engagements and documents the legal, financial, reputational, and moral concerns raised by shareholders, with particular attention to policies and communications involving children.

The Corporate Equality Index has served as the primary mechanism through which the HRC exerts its influence on corporate governance, employment policy, and public messaging. Participation is nominally voluntary, but companies that achieve a perfect score of 100 are required to satisfy a set of criteria that, because it is ever-evolving and regularly expanded, creates more and more compliance obligations with no defined endpoint. These criteria now include coverage of sex-rejecting procedures for minors as employee health benefits, mandatory identity-based training programs, and public corporate endorsement of contested social positions.[REF]

Shareholders represented by Bowyer Research, most notably The Heritage Foundation, engaged these companies to identify legal vulnerabilities, financial risks, and the structural incompatibility of CEI participation with sound, long-term fiduciary governance.

The Corporate Equality Index: Structure and Escalating Demands

The Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index is a benchmarking tool that scores corporations on their compliance with a defined set of employment, benefits, and public-messaging criteria. First introduced in 2002, the CEI has expanded steadily in scope, and its criteria are revised fairly frequently.

Bowyer Research’s engagement database, compiled in collaboration with the 1792 Exchange, focused on 160 companies that publicly promote perfect CEI scores of 100. These companies span a variety of sectors, including technology, finance, health care, retail, energy, and consumer goods, and reflect the broad reach of the HRC’s influence across America’s capital markets.[REF]

Companies frequently present perfect CEI scores as evidence of commendable corporate citizenship, but shareholders represented by Bowyer Research take a contrary view: A score of 100 is evidence not of sound governance, but rather of deep structural entanglement with a controversial external activist organization’s ideological compliance demands. Because the HRC revises its criteria frequently, companies committed to maintaining a perfect score face escalating requirements with no defined endpoint. This process is incompatible with sensible risk management and long-term shareholder value creation.

More to the point, current CEI requirements extend well beyond foundational anti-discrimination policies. They include or have included, among other criteria, employee health benefit coverage for sex-rejecting transition procedures (including for minor dependents); mandatory participation in identity-based employee training programs (prior to this year); and a demonstrated pattern of “outreach” to the LGBTQ community, often involving support for contested social and political positions. Each of these creates distinct legal, financial, and reputational risks.

Legal and Regulatory Exposure

CEI participation creates legal vulnerability across several distinct areas of law. The 1792 Exchange has documented these risks in its Corporate Bias Ratings analysis, noting that the CEI “promotes policies that may violate existing civil rights laws” and that participation exposes companies to “unnecessary legal risks.”[REF]

  • Employment Discrimination. Policies that prioritize gender identity over biological sex in employment have generated litigation under the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and similar state statutes. The case of Activision illustrates how these policies can generate claims from multiple directions simultaneously—from allegations of discriminatory treatment on the basis of gender identity to allegations of discrimination arising from the company’s CEI policies that infringe on the well-grounded rights of others.[REF]
  • Religious Discrimination. Mandatory participation in gender-affirming or identity-based training programs has produced religious discrimination claims in federal courts. A lawsuit involving Alaska Airlines, in which employees alleged that mandatory diversity training conflicted with sincerely held religious beliefs, illustrates the risk companies face when compliance with external advocacy frameworks meets statutory protections for religious belief.[REF]
  • State-Level Legislative Risk. Benefits policies that include coverage for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and irreversible sex-rejecting surgical procedures for minor dependents are increasingly subject to state restrictions. As more states limit or prohibit procedures for minors—including treating such procedures as child abuse[REF]—companies that include them as standard employee health benefits may find themselves in conflict with state law, creating complex compliance obligations and potential liability exposure.[REF]

Financial and Brand Risk: Lessons from High-Profile Cases

The financial consequences of activist-aligned corporate messaging are notably well documented. Several high-profile cases provide clear evidence of material harm to shareholders.

  • Bud Light. Anheuser-Busch InBev's 2023 promotional partnership with transgender social media influencer Dylan Mulvaney resulted in a consumer boycott that produced an estimated $1 billion or more in lost sales and a sustained, multi-quarter decline in Bud Light’s market share, dropping from the number-one brand overall to number three.[REF]
  • Target. Target Corporation’s introduction of a controversial Pride merchandise collection that included “tuck-friendly” swimsuits in 2023 generated significant consumer backlash that had a measurable adverse impact on the company’s revenues and share price. Target scaled back its 2024 Pride Month campaign significantly—a widely noted signal that even companies with historically strong activist-alignment track records need to be open to reassessing risks.[REF]
  • Disney. Disney’s public positioning against Florida’s Parental Rights in Education legislation resulted in the loss of the company’s Reedy Creek special tax district, significant negative media coverage, and a period of brand and financial turbulence.[REF] The episode demonstrated that corporate activism on politically contested issues can result in unwanted regulatory and legislative attention.

These cases illustrate a consistent pattern: Activist-aligned corporate messaging that extends beyond non-discrimination into overt participation in polarized cultural debates creates consumer division, brand damage, and measurable financial losses. The 1792 Exchange’s analysis concludes that such alignment “divides employees, alienates customers, and distracts businesses from making good products and services.”[REF]

Child-Related Concerns: Medical, Moral, and Reputational Dimensions

A central and especially sensitive element of both engagement campaigns involved corporate policies and messaging that affect or appear to target children. Shareholders characterized this domain as a moral and reputational red line—one with consequences that extend well beyond standard brand-risk frameworks.

  • Health Benefits for Minors. The CEI’s rating criteria encourage or require companies to include coverage for puberty blockers, sterilizing cross-sex hormones, and sex-rejecting surgeries for minor dependents as part of standard employee benefits packages.[REF] State-level restrictions create growing compliance complexity. Additionally, studies on the long-term medical effects of puberty suppression and cross-sex hormone administration on minors have shown that the risks and harms substantially outweigh any known benefits. In fact, several American and European health authorities have recently restricted such interventions pending further evidence.[REF] Offering benefits that facilitate irreversible medical procedures for minors creates significant exposure with a substantial segment of the consumer population.
  • Marketing and Messaging Involving Children. Pride Month engagement placed particular emphasis on the intersection of sexualized content and children in corporate marketing, in-store displays, and digital communications. Consumer research consistently demonstrates that parents are highly protective of their children, as a result of which they desire to prevent their exposure to sexualized content, and that brands perceived as targeting children with such messaging suffer long-term reputational harm.

Coerced Speech, Workplace Risk, and Employee Relations

Beyond benefits and public-facing messaging, the Bowyer/Heritage engagement campaigns addressed the internal workplace implications of HRC-driven compliance frameworks. Three categories of concern were identified.

  • Compelled Expression of Ideological Positions. Requiring employees to display ideological symbols such as pride flags or related insignia on uniforms or company-affiliated digital profiles constitutes compelled speech. This practice raises both moral and potential legal concerns and risks alienating employees who have sincere scientific, ethical, and religious beliefs that differ from the positions they are required to endorse.
  • Mandatory Identity-Based Training (prior to 2026). Unconscious bias and privilege-acknowledgment training programs that require employees to segregate or make affirmations based on race, sex, or gender identity create both discrimination exposure and workforce morale risks. As documented above, mandatory participation in such programs has already produced federal litigation.
  • Selective Inclusion Policies. Genuine inclusion requires protection for all employees, including those whose views differ from those of activist organizations. Companies that apply inclusion principles selectively risk discrimination claims and undermine the internal cohesion that drives long-term organizational success. The CEI’s “Responsible Citizenship” rating criterion penalizes companies up to 25 points for irresponsible citizenship, including donating to “anti-LGBT” non-religious groups.[REF]

The Scale and Scope of Shareholder Concern

The scope of the Bowyer Research/Heritage Foundation 2024 engagement efforts reflects the breadth of shareholder concern about these issues.[REF]

The CEI-focused engagement letter was distributed to 160 corporate contacts spanning technology, finance, health care, retail, energy, and consumer goods.[REF] Recipients included Amazon, Disney, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Johnson & Johnson, McDonald’s, Bank of America, BlackRock, Visa, Mastercard, Microsoft, and many others, demonstrating that shareholder concern about HRC influence is far-reaching and distributed broadly across the U.S. economy.

Pride Month messaging engagement was distributed to nearly 400 companies.[REF] In both engagement campaigns, shareholders communicated that they hold sufficient share positions to qualify to submit a proxy resolution at the next annual meeting but also expressed a preference for constructive direct dialogue before resorting to formal shareholder mechanisms.

A Gallup survey cited in the engagement materials found that a majority of U.S. adults do not want companies to speak publicly on political and social issues—confirming that the concerns raised by these shareholders reflect a significant segment of the consumer and investor base.[REF]

Recommendations for Action

Based on the evidence developed in the Bowyer Research/Heritage Foundation engagement campaigns as outlined in this analysis, it is recommended that corporate boards, investors, and policymakers seriously consider the following specific actions.

  • End or limit CEI participation. Participation in the CEI by Fortune 500 companies has declined by 65 percent in 2026. This serves as evidence that efforts to eliminate overt politicization of corporations can have a significant impact. The boards of corporations that maintain their participation in the HRC’s Corporate Equality Index should evaluate whether ongoing participation serves the long-term interests of shareholders, employees, and customers. Given the continually escalating nature of CEI requirements and their attendant, documented legal and reputational risks, companies should conduct a structured risk review before seeking renewal of participation or actions that would result in a “perfect score.”
  • Review benefits policies affecting minors. Companies should conduct a thorough legal and risk review of health benefit policies that include coverage for sex-rejecting procedures or treatments for minor dependents, accounting for evolving state law, current medical evidence, and potential litigation exposure. It should be noted in this connection that on October 22, 2025, the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi issued an order vacating provisions of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ “Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities” final rule relating to gender-identity discrimination. Consequently, the provision of health coverage for sex-rejecting procedures is no longer required under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act.[REF]
  • End sponsorship of the Human Rights Campaign and the HRC Foundation.[REF] Companies should limit sponsorships and partnerships to organizations that advance the interests of shareholders. Sponsorships and partnerships that are not business-related draw unnecessary scrutiny to the company and waste shareholder resources.
  • Limit public communications to core business. Companies should resist external pressure to engage in overt cultural advocacy and focus public communications instead on products, services, and business performance. In other words, businesses should focus on business.
  • Adopt viewpoint-neutral inclusion frameworks. Rather than pursuing scores on advocacy-affiliated benchmarks, companies should adopt more viewpoint-neutral inclusion frameworks—such as the Alliance Defending Freedom’s Viewpoint Diversity Score—that protect all employees regardless of their political, cultural, or religious perspectives.[REF]
  • Establish explicit protections for content that involves children. Companies should adopt clear policies prohibiting sexualized imagery or messaging in connection with children in marketing, in-store displays, or digital communications.
  • Ensure voluntary participation in training programs. Companies should review mandatory training programs for potential legal exposure under civil rights and religious freedom statutes and ensure that no employee is segregated or required to make affirmations that conflict with his or her sincerely held beliefs.

Conclusion

Corporate alignment with the Human Rights Campaign—particularly through participation in the Corporate Equality Index—creates a set of escalating legal, financial, reputational, and moral risks that fiduciary-minded companies can no longer treat as cost-free. The evidence from Bud Light, Target, and Disney demonstrates that activist-aligned messaging often leads to real financial harm. The structure of the CEI ensures that today’s compliance threshold becomes tomorrow’s minimum with no natural endpoint.

The concerns raised in the Bowyer Research/Heritage Foundation 2024 engagement campaigns—spanning more than 400 publicly traded companies—are backed by logic and evidence. They reflect the views of a broad and growing segment of the investor community and are supported by legal precedent, consumer research, and cautionary lessons from companies that have already paid a significant price for over-alignment with external activist agendas.

Corporate boards have both the authority and the fiduciary obligation to evaluate these risks clearly. Genuine inclusion—of all employees, customers, and shareholders—requires resistance to selective ideological capture, not capitulation to it. Companies that refocus on core business performance, protect employees of all viewpoints, and resist activist pressure will be better positioned to deliver long-term value to the shareholders they serve.

Stephen R. Soukup is a Visiting Fellow in the Free Enterprise Initiative at The Heritage Foundation. Jerry Bowyer is CEO of Bowyer Research, a proxy voting and corporate engagement consulting firm specializing in shareholder advocacy on issues of corporate governance, risk management, and fiduciary responsibility.

Appendix A: CEI Shareholder Engagement Letter

The following is the verbatim text of the engagement letter distributed to 160 companies regarding their participation in the Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index.

Bowyer Research is a proxy voting and corporate engagement consulting firm. Our clients, who are your shareholders, are extremely concerned about the company embroiling itself in non-core business advocacy of some of the most divisive issues in American life. A prime example would be the Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index. Our data indicates that you participate in this survey and have a score of 100. It is important that you understand that for many shareholders, a 100 is not an A plus, it is an F minus, especially when some of the specific demands of the HRC are factored in, such as paying for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and (irreversible) surgeries for minors as a health benefit.

We represent X investors who hold Y shares in COMPANY.

It is always our preference to begin with a request for dialogue before moving ahead with shareholder proposals.

We share the concerns of the 1792 Exchange, whose analysis of the CEI and its risks is as follows:

Participation in the Human Rights Campaign’s (HRC) Corporate Equality Index (CEI) exposes corporations to unnecessary legal risks by promoting policies that may violate existing civil rights laws. For example, the CEI encourages companies to adopt controversial stances on gender identity, which can lead to litigation under the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and similar state laws. For instance, prioritizing gender identity over biological sex in employment practices has led to discrimination lawsuits, as seen with Activision. Additionally, mandating employees to attend gender-affirming training could result in religious discrimination claims, as evidenced by the lawsuit involving Alaska Airlines. Furthermore, companies open themselves up to financial risks and brand harm by adopting the policies of the CEI. High-profile cases, such as Bud Light’s collaboration with a transgender activist and Target’s controversial ‘Pride’ collection, resulted in consumer boycotts that led to financial losses of billions of dollars. Aligning with the CEI divides employees, alienates customers, and distracts businesses from making good products and services. Prioritizing shareholder interests and consumer satisfaction over the demands of radical activist groups is a better path to long-term success.

You can view the 1792 Exchange’s evaluation of your company in their Corporate Bias Ratings database (https://1792exchange.com/spotlight-reports/corporate-bias-ratings). We note that under the influence of journalist Robby Starbuck, many companies have been, wisely, rethinking their relationship with the Human Rights Campaign. If a company participates in HRC’s survey but not in surveys such as the Alliance Defending Freedom’s viewpoint-neutral Viewpoint Diversity Survey, we are well justified in thinking of that company as taking sides in a culture war with shareholders’ dollars.

Appendix B: Pride Month Shareholder Engagement Letter

The following is the verbatim text of the engagement letter distributed to approximately 400 companies regarding Pride Month messaging practices.

We know that you are under constant pressure from outside activist groups and well-organized subsectors of your employees to go full-in this June on Pride Month. We urge you to remember that they do not represent the voices of everyone. Many of your shareholders, including the ones we represent, are concerned that June messaging goes beyond the commonsense acknowledgement that all customers and employees should be treated equally and with dignity and tips into taking sides in a deeply polarizing culture war. We think you want to avoid this, and we want you to know that we will back you when you do.

We see Disney, Target and Bud Light as cautionary tales of ways in which companies have been cajoled into brand-destructive messaging. We note that even Target is pulling back this year. That should speak volumes to those who have ears to hear.

We especially want the company to be aware of the extreme sensitivity that the majority of your customers have regarding the mixing of highly sexualized content and minors. Parents are naturally highly protective of their children and do not want them targeted with sexual messaging. This is a red line, morally and reputationally. Don’t cross it. Customers have long memories where kids are concerned.

We also urge you not to force sexual identity flair and paraphernalia onto the uniforms of service employees, nor onto their business-related websites. Coerced speech is morally unjustifiable and legally actionable. If an employee doesn’t want to be forced to fly the rainbow flag, they should not be forced to.

The same is true for ‘unconscious bias training’ sessions in which employees are forced to confess to various privileges inherent in having a sexual identity that is not among the current ideologically protected classes. You should let every employee bring their whole self to work, and employees who are not ‘allies’ should have their viewpoints protected against discrimination.

Of course, employees should be evaluated based solely on merit. LGBTQ employees should not be discriminated against, but neither should employees who dissent from the political or cultural views of that interest group. Inclusion is for everybody, otherwise it isn’t inclusion at all—it’s just taking sides. And it is not in your or your shareholders’ interests for the company to be taking sides.

A slim majority of Americans do not want companies speaking publicly on political and social issues (Gallup, 2024). The shareholders we represent possess sufficient shares to easily qualify to propose resolutions for the proxy statement of the next annual meeting, but we believe the proposal system is a fallback for companies that are not responsive to shareholder concerns, not a first resort. We hope this is something you are willing to genuinely discuss.

Researchers found that more than two-thirds of voters believe noncitizens will be stopped if they try to cast ballots, but Democrats are more confident than Republicans.

(CN) â As Republican lawmakers raise the specter of illegal voting, Pew Research finds in a new poll that a majority of voters have confidence noncitizens will be prevented from voting in the midterms.

Researchers surveyed 5,062 U.S. adults, including 3,917 registered voters, from Sept. 28-Oct. 4 and found that 68% of voters are at least somewhat confident that noncitizens will be blocked from casting ballots if they try to do so, with 34% saying they are very confident. However, that confidence varies by party: 45% of Republicans say they are confident noncitizens won’t be able to vote, compared with 90% of Democrats.

Voters are also somewhat divided on whether all legally qualified voters can cast a ballot if they want to, with 72% of Democrats saying they are at least somewhat confident all eligible voters will be able to vote, compared to 90% of Republicans.

This comes as legal battles over voter citizenship verification rage at both the state and national levels. Some red states have passed laws requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, and Republicans in Congress have been trying to implement similar requirements at the federal level through the SAVE America Act.

Meanwhile, in late September, the U.S. Supreme Court’s conservative majority voted 6-3 to stay a lower court ruling blocking Trump administration efforts to develop a national database to verify the citizenship status of registered voters, and on Monday the Justice Department announced it was charging 28 foreign nationals in California with election-related crimes.

Critics of citizenship verification efforts claim such measures are unnecessary, as it is already illegal for noncitizens to vote and documented instances of noncitizens voting are rare. They also argue that requirements for voters to prove their citizenship are unfairly burdensome and that errors in citizenship-verification databases could block eligible citizens from voting.

Pew also asked voters about other election-related concerns. Sixty-seven percent of voters said they were at least somewhat confident that attempts to intimidate voters at polling places will be stopped, and 52% of voters were confident U.S. election systems are safe from hacking.

Fifty-three percent of voters said they’re confident mail-in ballots will be counted accurately. Confidence in mail-in voting was higher among Democrats than Republicans â 64% versus 42% â but Democratic confidence in mail ballots was down from the 85% it was at in 2024. This drop in trust is also reflected in a dip in the amount of Democratic voters who say they have voted or plan to vote by mail, from 22% in 2022 to 15% this year.

This comes amid Republican efforts to restrict mail-in voting. Since 2020, many Republican-led states have enacted laws that tighten mail-in voting, including adding identification requirements, shortening deadlines, restricting eligibility for mail-in voting and limiting who can collect mail ballots.

Meanwhile, at the federal level, the Trump administration has sought to enforce an executive order requiring the U.S. Postal Service to work with states to create pre-approved lists of mail-in voters and deliver mail ballots only to voters on those lists, but the U.S. Supreme Court has blocked it.

#14. Book deals leave Supreme Court without quorum in music copyright fight

The U.S. Supreme Court failed recently to muster a quorum to hear a high-profile music copyright appeal, thanks to several justices’ book deals. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)

The U.S. Supreme Court failed recently to muster a quorum to hear a high-profile music copyright appeal, thanks to several justices’ book deals.

Courthouse News Service reported Monday that Justice Sonia Sotomayor, Justice Neil Gorsuch, Justice Amy Coney Barrett and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson had to recuse themselves from considering a petition brought by record label BMG Rights Management because they each have book deals with Penguin Random House, which shares a parent company with BMG Rights Management.

With only five justices left, the court lacked the six required for a quorum, meaning that the lower court’s decision granting songwriter Cyril Vetter full ownership of the 1962 song “Double Shot (Of My Baby’s Love)” will stand.

According to Courthouse News Service, the dispute began in 2022, when ABC sought permission to use the song on international broadcasts and streaming platforms. Two lower courts sided with Vetter, allowing him to reclaim the song’s copyright in the United States and abroad.

BMG Rights Management argued that the rulings upset long-standing industry norms on publishing rights and would create confusion.

The episode drew criticism from Fix the Court, a watchdog group, which said the justices have earned more than $13 million combined from book deals.

“Today’s recusals make clear that the Supreme Court’s current disqualification standards need review,” said Gabe Roth, Fix the Court’s executive director, in a statement, adding that “where the lack of a quorum means a lower court’s judgment is affirmed, and the Supreme Court is no longer supreme.”
