#17. Saudi Arabia: Man Executed for Childhood Offenses

Click to expand Image Riyadh's general court, Saudi Arabia, October 20, 2008. © 2008 Fahad Shadeed/Reuters

(Beirut) – Saudi authorities announced on October 17, 2026, that they had executed Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, who was convicted of crimes allegedly committed when he was a 14-year-old boy, Human Rights Watch said today. 

The Supreme Court has also apparently upheld the death sentence of another man, Yousef al-Manasif, who was convicted of crimes allegedly committed when he was 15 and 16, putting him at risk of imminent execution. At least three other men convicted of alleged crimes committed as children are on death row, despite allegations of torture, forced confessions, and prolonged solitary confinement.

“The execution of Hassan al-Faraj is unconscionable compounded by alleged torture-tainted evidence and a well-documented record of unfair trials,” said Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “With the Supreme Court’s recent decision, Yousef al-Manasif is also at serious risk of execution.”

The death sentence for al-Manasif was recently upheld by the Supreme Court, the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR) reported. In October and November 2022, Saudi Arabia’s notorious Specialized Criminal Court handed down death sentences to al-Manasif and al-Faraj, as well as Ali al-Mabyook, Jawad Qureiris, Ali al-Subaiti, and Mahdi al-Mohsen for alleged terrorism crimes they committed as children, according to a report by the ESOHR and court documents. 

Saudi authorities arrested al-Faraj on November 27, 2017, held him in solitary confinement for six months, and charged him with various counterterrorism offenses, including one allegedly committed when he was 14, which relates to meeting and developing friendships with other detained and wanted individuals, based on the charge sheet and court documents. The Specialized Criminal Court sentenced him to death on November 3, 2022, despite allegations that he had been tortured and forced to sign the confession on which the conviction was based, his defense said. 

Court documents reviewed by Human Rights Watch show that authorities arrested al-Manasif on April 6, 2017, and al-Mabyook on January 29, 2018. Al-Manasif was arrested for protesting Saudi authorities’ treatment of its Shia minority and attending funeral processions in 2011 and 2012 when he was 15 and 16, according to the ESOHR and United Nations experts. Al-Mabyook was arrested for attending funeral processions before he turned 18, ESOHR and court documents said.  

The court convicted and sentenced them to death on November 2, 2022, under broad and vague counterterrorism laws based almost exclusively on confessions that their defense alleges were obtained under torture, the documents showed. The authorities did not inform al-Manasif of his charges until months after his arrest or provide him with legal representation during his interrogation and held him in pretrial detention for over two years, including six months in solitary confinement, the documents show. 

Both al-Manasif and al-Mabyook appealed to the Appellate Chamber of the Specialized Criminal Court on March 19, 2025. The appeals were based on them both having been under 18 when the alleged offenses were committed, the court documents said. On August 26, 2025, the appellate court rejected that defense, referring to the dates in their confessions, despite allegations that the confession was obtained under torture.

Saudi authorities arrested Qureiris on December 31, 2020, court documents say. Saudi authorities charged him under the counterterrorism law for alleged offenses at the ages of 15 and 17. The Specialized Criminal Court convicted and sentenced him to death on November 5, 2022, despite allegations of severe beatings during interrogation to make him sign a confession, the documents say. Qureiris was also held in solitary confinement for 270 days to force the confession, according to the documents.

The decision was submitted to the same court for review on November 12, 2025, where Qureiris stated that he did not commit any of the alleged offenses except participating in a protest in 2010 when he was 15, court documents showed. The court approved his death sentence on March 2, 2025. 

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention concluded in November 2024 that the detentions of al-Manasif, al-Faraj, and Qureiris were arbitrary and based on the men’s exercise of their right to free speech when they participated in protests against Saudi Arabia’s treatment of the country’s Shia minority. 

On April 9, 2026, Saudi authorities executed Ali al-Subaiti for alleged crimes committed when he was 12, according to the Saudi Press Agency. On October 23, 2017, Saudi authorities arrested al-Subaiti, who was then 19, and charged him under counterterrorism provisions including joining and financing a terrorist organization and attempting to undermine the social fabric and national security by inciting protests, according to the charge sheet. The charges included participating in a demonstration when he was 12 and “covering up for terrorists” when he was 17. The court sentenced al-Subaiti to death on October 17, 2022, according to the ESOHR.

Saudi Arabia’s Juvenile Law of 2018 and a 2020 executive order ended the use of the death penalty against individuals who were under 18 when the crime was committed, in cases that do not involve the 2017 counterterrorism law. In non-terrorism cases, the death penalty is replaced with a maximum 10-year prison sentence. Human Rights Watch has documented Saudi Arabia’s long-standing misuse of counterterrorism provisions to silence dissent.

In 2025, Saudi Arabia executed Jalal al-Labbad and Abdullah al-Derazi, both accused of committing crimes as children, as part of the country’s unprecedented execution spree, despite calls from UN experts and rights groups to halt the executions. 

Human Rights Watch has documented long-standing due process violations in Saudi Arabia’s criminal justice system, including restricted or denied access to legal representation and forced confessions, making it highly unlikely that any of the eight men received a fair trial. 

The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which Saudi Arabia is a party, strictly prohibits the use of the death penalty for offenses committed by individuals under 18. Article 6(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and article 6 of the Arab Charter on Human Rights oblige countries that use capital punishment to use it only for the “most serious crimes.” Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all countries and circumstances due to its inherent cruelty and irreversibility. 

“Saudi Arabia’s execution spree, particularly for offenses by children, shows no signs of slowing down in 2026,” Shea said. “This underscores the urgent need for the international community to press the Saudi government to immediately halt executions and abolish the death penalty once and for all.”

#18. The Greenland Deal Is a Huge Success

Ignore the naysayers: President Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a huge win for the United States, and also one that will improve Danish, Greenlandic and, indeed, trans-Atlantic security.

This is a major diplomatic achievement. It expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits a non-NATO military presence, and protects critical parts of the Greenlandic economy that adversarial governments could otherwise use for dual-use purposes.

The agreement contains language clarifying the core U.S. interests at stake and the rationale behind increasing activities in the Arctic, recognizing “the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and that “the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”

Critics have said the deal is the same as the one we had before. Not true. The 2026 agreement augments, updates and improves the 1951 treaty, expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with two new bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig. It also prohibits Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and creates a mechanism for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk and Washington to veto investment in critical parts of the Greenlandic economy. Importantly, the new agreement and its provisions will continue to apply even if Greenland becomes independent.

The strategic rationale for the United States to maintain a military presence in Greenland and secure it from adversarial influence should be obvious. Greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland-Iceland-U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass. At more than 836,000 square miles, Greenland is a major geographic shaper of the Arctic region, and U.S. radars based in Greenland play an essential role in detecting and intercepting any hostile movements toward the U.S. mainland.

>>> Why America Should Take the Lead in Greenland—Before Our Adversaries Do

Indeed, the strategic rationale for American military presence in Greenland is strongest when considered in the context of great power competition. The Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles heading toward the United States, and Greenland in particular lies in the shortest and most likely path for these systems when fired from Russia. Pituffik Space Base, an existing U.S. military site in Greenland, supports American missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance.

Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, with significant self-rule but responsibility for defense resting with the Danish government in Copenhagen. Russia and China have consistently demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region, with Chinese investments in particular targeting Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.

To combat this, the deal also creates a mechanism for the three parties to deny Chinese or Russian investment in key Greenlandic sectors such as ports, airports and mines. Greenland is estimated to possess 1.5 million tons of critical mineral reserves. Denmark had already played a positive role in preventing malign investment in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy, but the new deal formalizes the need and mechanism for doing this and gives the United States a say.

>>> How Norway Can Do More To Forestall the Russian Threat

Denmark has long been a very strong and reliable ally of the United States. Danish troops served in combat roles alongside Americans in Afghanistan after the 9/11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates in the war among our NATO allies. Denmark is one of the highest spenders on defense within the NATO alliance, had already reached 3.2 percent of gross domestic product as of 2025, and is projected to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the near future — among the first NATO allies to do so.

Much of Denmark’s new spending is going into capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory. The successful conclusion of this agreement, of course, will create new avenues for Arctic security cooperation between the American and Danish militaries.

The American, Danish and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure Arctic where Russia is unable to threaten North America or Europe and where China (a non-Arctic state) is unable to meddle where it doesn’t belong.

This deal secures the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps cement trans-Atlantic security cooperation in the Arctic for decades to come.

#20. Liberty Justice Center Files First Lawsuit Challenging Trump's Section 338 Tariffs Against Canadian Imports

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The tariffs are illegal for multiple different reasons.

Today, the Liberty Justice Center (LJC) filed Gellert Global Group Corp. v. Trump, the first lawsuit challenging President Donald Trump's massive Section 338 tariffs against a variety of Canadian imports. The case was filed in the US Court of International Trade (which has jurisdiction over tariff-related cases); Gellert Global Group is an importer of Canadian cheese subject to the tariffs. LJC is the same public interest group that I worked with on the case challenging Trump's earlier IEEPA tariffs, which ultimate resulted in their invalidation by the Supreme Court. I am not directly involved in the present case. But I support it and believe it deserves to prevail.

LJC has also filed cases challenging Trump's massive Section 122 and Section 301 tariffs. They have become America's premier public interest law group standing up for free trade and enforcing constitutional constraints on executive power over trade restrictions.

Section 338 was part of the infamous Smoot-Hawley tariff act of 1930, which gravely exacerbated the Great Depression. It has never been used before, likely because it was superseded by later laws.

I have previously written about why Trump's Section 338 tariffs are harmful and illegal. See my recent Montreal Economic Institute paper on this topic, and earlier pieces here, here, and here. To briefly summarize, the tariffs on Canada are illegal because 1) Section 338 has been superseded by later legislation, 2) even if Section 338 is still operative, Trump's tariffs do not meet its requirements because the Canadian actions they supposedly respond to do not "discriminate" against US goods, as the law requires, 3) Trump's tariffs do not "offset" the Canadian actions (as Section 338 also requires), but go far beyond that, 4) the administration's interpretation of Section 338 runs afoul of the "major questions" doctrine, and 5) if Section 338 is operative and does authorize the Trump actions, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine (which restricts delegation of legislative power to the executive).

The LJC complaint advances all five of these arguments. To prevail, they need win on only one. They also add a few more technical points that I will not try to cover here. LJC further seeks a class action certification for a class of all those importers subject to the Section 338 tariffs. If this succeeds, it would block all enforcement of Section 338 tariffs, not just those paid by Gellert.

This lawsuit does not directly challenge Trump's extension of the Section 338 action to categorically ban some Canadian imports, in addition to imposing tariffs. As far as I can tell, Gellert does not import goods subject to the ban (as opposed to the tariffs). However, as I explained here and here, the legality of the bans is dependent on that of the initial tariffs. In a recent Lawfare article, I outline the reasons why executive-imposed import bans are subject to most of the same legal constraints as executive-imposed tariffs.

Like the IEEPA, Section 122, and Section 301 tariffs, Trump's use of Section 338 is an attempt to convert a limited delegation of authority into a blank check enabling the president to impose tariffs whenever he wants. Courts should reject all of these power grabs.

I commend LJC for bringing this important case. And I hope and expect it may not be the last lawsuit challenging the Section 338 measures. Future cases might well challenge the import bans directly, as well as the tariffs.

#21. Peter Swanson: 7 Great Stories of Suspense in a House by the Sea

The trope of a house being a character in and of itself, especially in gothic fiction, is well-known, and well earned. Old dark houses can anchor even the flimsiest stories. They have secrets or their own: locked closets; musty basements; dusty attics; and sometimes even ghosts, literal or figural. Most of the time they have names. Thornfield Hall. Hill House. Bly Manor. And sometimes these houses are perched by the sea, like Grey Gables, situated on the dunes of Truro, on Cape Cod, the house I invented for my new Christmas novella, Do You See What I See?

I have a particular love of the seaside house, both in real life and in books and movies. Here are seven of them from the worlds of fiction (primarily mystery fiction), that grabbed my attention and didn’t let go.

There’s a more famous novel by Christie that involves a large house on a small island, but I thought I’d go with this Hercule Poirot mystery, in which the house is named right in the title. Set along the coast of Cornwall, End House is the primary setting for an ingenious but pretty convoluted mystery. Poirot and his sidekick Hastings are pulled into it when they witness a near murder outside of their seaside hotel. It’s a good puzzle, with lots of dropping bodies, and the atmospheric appeal of the Cornwall coast.

I suspect that there are people who have never read the famous novel by DuMaurier or seen the Alfred Hitchcock movie version who could still correctly identify the house at the center of this story as Manderley. DuMaurier makes full use of the seaside manor house in the south of England, in her story of the second wife of Max deWinter being brought to her new home, where she can’t escape the shadow of Rebecca, Max’s first wife. There are many moody walks along the seaside cliffs, a startling twist, and one of the more famous endings in gothic history.

A flawed novel, for sure, but not boring. Tim Madden wakes up in his seaside house in Provincetown, deeply hungover, sporting a new tattoo he can’t remember getting, and finds that the interior of his car is soaked in blood. He decides to find out what happened during his lost hours. Some of the best parts of this pulpy book (apparently written by Mailer in two months) are his descriptions of Cape Cod and Provincetown. The opening line (certainly not as famous as the one from Rebecca) has the narrator say how he wakes to the chatter of gulls, and how on certain mornings he felt they were feeding on his heart.

The Talented Mr. Ripley by Patricia Highsmith

I don’t think this book is commonly thought of as a classic house-by-the-sea novel. But the whole first half of this timeless novel has Tom Ripley insinuating himself into the life of Dickie Greenleaf, who is currently idling away at his summer home in the imagined village of Mongibello on the Italian coast. I love the details of the small villa, the martini lunches, the steep walk down to the beach. And from all that sunlight and bliss Highsmith moves the story into her typically dark, murderous territory.

Another book in which the ideal house by the sea (this time on the Gulf Coast of Florida) hides multiple secrets and marital disfunction. This standalone novel by one of my all-time favorite writers has the perfect set-up. Widower Mike Rodenska is invited by his oldest friend to visit him and his wife at their mid-century beach house in Florida. Once there, Rodenska naturally discovers that all is not well. But between the twists and violence MacDonald paints such a perfect picture of beach-side living, with its constant crashing waves and near-constant cocktail parties.

Set on a fake island (modeled after Fire Island, probably) off the coast of New York, this is easily the most chilling novel on this list. Four teenagers, basically unsupervised for the summer, slip into a violent imaginary realm with real consequences. In between their clandestine meetings on the sun-baked dunes, they dip in and out of the summer homes that populate the island, where their parents, oblivious to what their children are doing, host get togethers and ignore the teenagers and their childhood cruelties.

Well, I’m cheating with this one because a) it’s a short story, not a novel and b) it’s not really a mystery story. That said, I return to this mesmerizing, chilling tale often. It’s narrated by a husband and father describing his family’s annual beach house rental, and how the house itself, and its previous occupants, begin to infest the interior world of the renter. It’s a psychological study of a marriage breaking down, but it reads like a horror movie, in which the primary ghost is a residence.

Peter Swanson is the New York Times bestselling author of The Kind Worth Killing, winner of the New England Society Book Award and finalist for the CWA Ian Fleming Steel Dagger; Her Every Fear, an NPR book of the year; and Eight Perfect Murders, a New York Times bestseller, among others. His books have been translated into 30 languages. He lives on the North Shore of Massachusetts, where he is at work on his next novel.

#22. Did ‘corporate speak’ and PowerPoint lead to complacency at GM?

General Motors headquarters in Detroit. Jonathan Weiss Shutterstock.com

General Motors employees were taught to be careful when writing about safety issues.

A 2008 Power Point presentation had some helpful suggestions, according to a report by Jenner & Block chairman Anton Valukas on the automaker’s failure to respond to defective ignition switches.

A “problem” should be described as an “issue, condition, matter.” The word “safety” should be replaced with “potential safety implications.” The word “defect” should be nixed in favor of “does not perform to design.”

A defective ignition switch in Chevy Cobalts that could switch to the accessory or off position? GM personnel didn’t make the connection between the low-torque switch, which required less force to turn, and airbags that wouldn’t deploy when the switch changed out of the run position. They saw stalls caused by the switch as a “customer convenience” problem, rather than a safety problem, according to the report (PDF).

The Washington Post notes the proliferation of “corporate speak” at GM. “Idioms and corporate cliches are more than just buzzwords that threaten our linguistic sanity,” the story says. “At GM they stood to mask real meaning, obscured leaders’ responsibilities, and created labels that hindered the critical thinking needed to keep real problems from getting worse.”

The story cites another instance where words got in the way. A top GM lawyer asked a vice president of global quality to be a “champion” in the probe of the switch “nondeployment” problem. The executive believed he was supposed to be a person who helps the team remove roadblocks and obtain resources. After that executive’s retirement, a new executive stepped in who also did not understand the urgency of the safety issue.

A Wall Street Journal article says PowerPoint presentations were a substitute for meaningful communications at GM. In one instance in 2009, then GM CEO Rick Wagoner “may have viewed” a PowerPoint presentation that included a “back-up” slide about a change in design to the Cobalt’s key. The change was described as a move to reduce warranty costs as a result of customer complaints about the ignition switching out of the run position because of a heavy key chain swinging in a wide slot.

“What if someone had simply stood up,” the Wall Street Journal asks, “without a visual prop, and said: ‘People are dying’?”

#23. What businesses should know about consent rules when calling consumers

Rules around obtaining consumer consent before calling or texting are in a state of legal and regulatory uncertainty – and companies should remain cautious.

Senosiain is an associate and Rollins is a shareholder at Gunster. Views are the authors’ own.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act governs calls and text messages sent by businesses to consumers. One such rule is that businesses must obtain express written consent prior to sending text messages to consumers, if they are using an automated telephone dialing system or making calls using an artificial or pre-recorded voice, including the use of AI bots.

The TCPA also provides that businesses may not call or text consumers on the federal Do Not Call List unless prior express consent is given. Even basic telemarketing calls and text messages require prior express consent. Violation of the statute can trigger liability for up to $1,500 per call or text message sent.

Additionally, many states have their own version of the TCPA, deemed “mini-TCPAs,” that require compliance for all businesses who make calls to consumer-residents in that state, regardless of where the business is domiciled.

Many companies use lead generators which gather consumer consents for multiple businesses and then provide the companies with consent and contact information for those potential consumers. Lead generators who obtain proper written consent can be a very useful tool for companies. This was generally permissible under the TCPA.

However, in 2023, the Federal Communications Commission updated its TCPA rules requiring “one-to-one consent” which was to become effective Jan. 27, 2025.

The one-to-one consent rule provides that if a business uses an ATDS, artificial or prerecorded voice, the business must obtain prior express consent, one seller at a time.

Thus, it prevents lead generators from using a single consumer’s consent for multiple businesses. Additionally, the one-to-one consent rule provides that the consent must be clear and conspicuous, and the calls and texts initiated pursuant to the consent must be logically and topically associated with the interaction that prompted the consent. This rule applies to both text messages and phone calls.

On Jan. 24, 2025, the FCC postponed the 2023 order by a year, until Jan. 26, 2026. Later that same day the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the 2023 Order, thus eliminating the one-to-one consent rule.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held “that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority under the TCPA because the 2023 Order’s new consent restrictions impermissibly conflict[ed] with the ordinary statutory meaning of prior express consent.”

Notably, the court ruled that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority at the outset, when it created the one-to-one consent rule. The court held that the 2023 Order’s one-to-one prior express consent restriction impermissibly conflicted with the ordinary statutory meaning of “prior express consent.” Thus, the Court vacated application of the 2023 Order, and remanded for further proceedings.

As a result, it is very likely that we will see other cases challenging TCPA regulations, especially as to the consent required before making a telemarketing call or text message using an ATDS.

It is unclear whether the FCC will revise its 2023 Order to comply with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision. In order to be prepared for this rule to come into effect, and in an abundance of caution, businesses who use lead generators to source potential consumers’ consent should ascertain that the lead generators are obtaining individual, one-to-one consent.

Businesses should also only contact consumers who provide this consent for telemarketing that is logically and topically associated with that which the consent was provided. Further, in addition to storing consumer contact information, businesses must retain the consent forms, information as to when consent was given, and through whom. Even businesses that do not use lead generators to obtain consent should continue to review their consent practices to ensure strict compliance with the TCPA and mini-TCPAs.

The TCPA requires prior express consent, and in many cases, prior express written consent, for calls and text messages made to prospective consumers. Regardless of any changes to the TCPA, the FTSA still requires that businesses obtain prior express written consent when making unsolicited telephone calls (including sending text messages) using an automated system. And lastly, to further protect your business, the consent form should have robust terms of service, including a class action waiver.

We continue to recommend that businesses ensure compliance with the TCPA, FTSA, and any other state regulations by always obtaining express written consent prior to contacting potential consumers via calls or text messages.

#25. Lebanon: Amend Media Law to Protect Free Expression

Click to expand Image Lebanese lawmakers at the parliament building in downtown Beirut, January 9, 2025. © 2025 Hussein Malla/AP Photo

(Beirut) – Lebanon’s parliament should amend the recently-adopted media law to fully remove all provisions in Lebanese law that restrict the right to free expression, Human Rights Watch said today. Parliament passed the law on August 11, 2026, but a new draft law introduced by 10 members of parliament on October 5 offers amendments to the law that would resolve its key problematic provisions.

“Given the history of public officials and powerful individuals abusing Lebanon’s laws to clamp down on journalists, activists, and artists, parliament should act to prevent further abuse,” said Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch. “No one should face abusive retaliation for peacefully expressing their views, and parliament has a chance to end these abuses right here and now.”

The media law, which parliament adopted after 16 years of deliberation, includes significant improvements. Some of the key advances include ending pretrial detention for free expression-related crimes committed online or through media-related means. The law establishes individuals’ right to create online media platforms or issue publications without prior state authorization and limits the military court’s jurisdiction over expression-related crimes committed online or through media-related means. It also decriminalizes defamation and insult in certain cases, transferring them to civil court jurisdiction.

The law also includes provisions that would promote media independence, including by prohibiting undue interference in journalists’ work, promoting media workers’ rights to unionize, protecting sources’ anonymity, and limiting the ability of security services to search and seize journalists’ electronic equipment and documents.

The adopted media law, however, includes a provision, article 104(b), which criminalizes the “intentional fabrication of falsehoods and dissemination of false and harmful news” providing for a sentence of up to three years in prison. For decades, Lebanese journalists, artists, media organizations, and civil society groups have repeatedly faced lawsuits based on criminal defamation charges and other vague legal provisions in retaliation for their work.

This provision, which includes vague and undefined terms such as “harmful news,” risks enabling continued threats of criminal proceedings against journalists as well as such lawsuits.

While the adopted media law decriminalizes defamation and insult in some cases, provisions found in Lebanon’s Penal Code, which the law does not mention, annul, or make inapplicable, would continue to criminalize libel, slander, and insult directed against a foreign state or its president, representatives, army, flag, or emblems. 

Such provisions also criminalize defamation against Lebanon’s president, state institutions, and army, among others, imposing prison sentences of up to two years. Provisions of the Lebanon Military Justice Code, which also remain in effect, include the criminalization of “publicly disparaging the flag or the army or infringing upon its dignity, reputation or morale,” imposing a prison sentence of up to three years.

The amendments sought in the October 5 draft law would annul article 104(b) of the media law and make these articles, in both Lebanon’s Penal Code and Military Justice Code, inapplicable to cases covered by the media law, including for both media-related or online forms of expression. 

The amendments would also limit security forces’ ability to interrogate and investigate media professionals for expression-related crimes, limiting these powers solely to the public prosecution’s jurisdiction. Human Rights Watch has repeatedly documented violations, including, physical and psychological interrogation tactics and bias by Lebanese security agencies in enforcing criminal defamation laws against journalists and activists. 

Since Lebanon’s media law only applies to acts of media-related and online forms of expression, Lebanon’s parliament should fully repeal all provisions, including in Lebanon’s Penal Code and Military Justice Code, related to criminal defamation or insult, Human Rights Watch said. It should make any such cases, including offline and non-media related expression, subject to civil court jurisdiction, in accordance with international human rights standards.

“For years Lebanese civil society has fought for increased protections to the right to freedom of expression and the press,” Kaiss said. “Passing the proposed amendments to the media law would be a breakthrough.”

#26. The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall Street

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has confirmed what conservatives have said for years. The OCC's 47-page report, released Wednesday after reviewing 100,000 complaints and 50,000 internal bank records, found that between 2020 and 2025 the nation’s nine largest national banks denied service to Americans because of their political, social, or religious beliefs.

The details are ugly. JPMorgan’s WePay payment unit closed the account of a merchant selling “MAGA” themed merchandise, and its screening system flagged phrases like “America First.” It shut down a religious non-profit because the Southern Poverty Law Center, since indicted on federal fraud charges, had branded it a hate group.

PNC refused a line of credit to a media company because one owner’s foundation had funded Christian conservative groups. Banks also choked off financing to entire lawful industries like firearms, coal, Arctic oil and gas, private prisons, tobacco, etc. While the instinct is to blame the banks, a different culprit emerges in the report’s details.

Banks feared negative press, protests, and organized activist criticism. But the greatest fear was reprisals from regulators and politicians, because those can actually shut down a financial institution.

>>> Regions Financial’s Reasonable Retreat From Ideology

A Wells Fargo review of a prospective firearms client was blunt: under the Biden administration, banks could face “greater supervisory pressure to move away from lending to the firearms industry.” Another bank dropped private-prison clients citing “changing policymaker attitudes,” then tried to win one back just months into the Trump administration. 

Those aren’t the actions of institutions pursuing an ideological crusade but of businesses reading the weather in Washington. That’s the real scandal in the OCC report.

Banks don’t operate in a free market so much as under the permanent supervision of federal examiners who can downgrade their ratings, initiate expensive investigations, and impose costly enforcement actions.

For years, those examiners graded banks on “reputational risk,” a category with no financial definition or objective yardstick. While a loan defaulting is a pass-or-fail course, reputational risk is whatever a regulator wants it to be, with no financial impact required.

A deposit account for a pro-life ministry poses no inherent danger to a bank’s balance sheet. Neither does a loan to a firearms manufacturer or payment services for a conservative think tank. But when the regulators who effectively control your fate hate those groups, a threatening phone call from the government can result in debanking.

That’s how faceless bureaucrats circumnavigate the Constitution. Officials who could never lawfully seize a disfavored group’s money can simply make it costly for banks to hold it. The Supreme Court unanimously rejected that tactic in NRA v. Vullo in 2024, holding that regulators may not coerce the firms they oversee into punishing protected speech. Yet the practice persisted, because it rarely leaves fingerprints.

For those who believe in free markets and individual liberty, debanking was doubly offensive because it wasn’t a market failure but a regulatory distortion. Left to sound financial judgment, banks have every reason to serve profitable, lawful customers. It took government pressure to make turning away business look like the safe choice.

Fortunately, the Trump administration has acted. Its August 2025 executive order directed regulators to end politicized debanking, and the OCC has stopped using reputational risk in examinations. But executive orders and agency guidance can be reversed on the first day of the next administration. Another far-left White House could revive reputational risk, restore the quiet phone calls, and start the cycle over.

>>> Elizabeth Warren’s Big Government Power Grab Will Make Depositors Pay

Congress ought to step up and make that impossible by enshrining into law protections for bank customers and the banks themselves so that the latter cannot be unconstitutionally coerced by regulators. Federal law should prohibit non-financial and nonsensical metrics like reputational risk from supervision and forbid officials from pressuring institutions to drop lawful customers without a documented, quantifiable financial reason.

Rules like that don’t expand government but restrain it, keeping regulators focused on safety and soundness, not their private political preferences.

Furthermore, whatever standards must apply evenly. Fintechs, payment processors, and other non-bank firms are increasingly providing the deposit and payment services Americans use every day. It’s no accident that WePay, a payment platform, produced some of the report’s worst examples.

If those firms are exempt, politicized gatekeeping just migrates to the less-regulated, and fast-growing, corner of the market. Firms offering the same services must play by the same rules.

Americans should never have to wonder whether their bank account depends on their politics. The debanking pressure came from Washington, and the fix has to come from Washington too, written into law where the next administration can’t quietly undo it.

MANASSAS, Va. (CN) â In the days following Mamta Kafle Bhatt’s disappearance, prosecutors say her husband tossed heavy-duty bags containing her dismembered remains in trash compactors around northern Virginia.

#28. Supreme Court declines to take up cases on vehicle seizures in Chicago, 9/11 plea disputes, and the president’s removal of National Labor Relations Board members

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

For the second week in a row, Justice Sonia Sotomayor penned a statement regarding the denial of review that was joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch. Sotomayor’s opinion in O’Donnell v. City of Chicago, a challenge to the city’s policy of seizing and selling (without any compensation to the owners) cars owned by drivers with as few as two unpaid parking tickets, was part of a list of orders from the Supreme Court’s Oct. 16 conference released on Monday morning. (The two cases in which the justices granted review are covered in separate stories.)

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit rejected the challenge to the policy, calling it “an exercise of the City’s police power to enforce its traffic code.” Ryan O’Donnell and Michael Goree, two motorists whose cars the city sold, then came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to weigh in.

In a brief order, the court denied review. In her statement, Sotomayor expressed “serious concerns about” the 7th Circuit’s decision, but she emphasized that the court should not take up the question until more courts of appeals have had a chance to consider it. Moreover, she suggested, O’Donnell and Goree’s case was not necessarily an appropriate one in which to consider the constitutionality of such a scheme, because they had challenged the entire ordinance, “which might require this Court to invalidate even those features of the law that have nothing to do with vehicle forfeiture.”

The justices turned down, without comment, petitions for review in several high-profile cases, including two – Mohammad v. United States and bin ‘Atash v. United States – filed by (among others) Khalid Sheikh Mohammad, who is considered to be the “mastermind” behind the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and others involved in the planning of those attacks. As Kelsey Dallas explained last month, the men had sought to reinstate plea agreements that they entered into more than two years ago, after spending nearly two decades in Guantanamo Bay, that would allow them to plead guilty but avoid the death penalty in exchange for life sentences. Following this, however, Lloyd Austin, then the Secretary of Defense, announced that he had the ultimate power to decide whether such agreements were appropriate, and sought to withdraw the government’s consent. When the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit agreed with the government that it could do so, and that the agreements were not binding, the men came to the Supreme Court, which on Monday denied their requests to weigh in.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in Mohammad’s case.

The court also denied a petition for review filed by Gwynne Wilcox, who served on the National Labor Relations Board until President Donald Trump attempted to fire her shortly after his second inauguration. Under the federal law governing the removal of NLRB members, Trump could only fire her for “neglect of duty or malfeasance in office” – neither of which Trump alleged had occurred. The lower courts initially ordered the Trump administration to reinstate Wilcox, but in May 2025, the Supreme Court paused those rulings and cleared the way for Wilcox’s removal while litigation continued.

In December 2025, the D.C. Circuit held that the for-cause removal provision violates the Constitution’s separation of powers. “Congress,” Judge Gregory Katsas wrote for the majority, “cannot restrict the President’s ability to remove NLRB … members” because they “wield substantial executive power.”

Wilcox came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up her case, but on Monday they declined to do so.

Citing the lack of a quorum – that is, the minimum number of members required to vote – the justices left in place a ruling in a copyright dispute between several major music companies and a songwriter. Four justices – Sotomayor, Gorsuch, and Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Ketanji Brown Jackson – recused themselves from the dispute, presumably because one of the companies involved is owned by the parent company of Penguin Random House, which has published books by each of those justices.

The Supreme Court sought the views of the U.S. solicitor general in Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, in which that state’s attorney general has asked the justices to weigh in on a challenge to the constitutionality of an Iowa law that makes it a crime to be present in the state after having illegally reentered the United States. There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his brief, although he is likely to do so sometime next year.

The justices did not act on a group of redistricting cases out of Alabama; they also did not rule on a petition for review asking them to decide whether a car is always a tool of interstate commerce, so that its use in a kidnapping automatically makes the crime a federal one.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#29. Natalie Kikic on Croatian Folklore, Female Rage, and Writing a Gothic Novel

When I first started working on The Haunting of Lavender House, I didn’t set out to write a Croatian gothic novel. But that is what it became.

The story started with a protagonist like me: A Croatian American woman who didn’t feel like she belonged in her parents’ homeland. Because even though both my parents are Croatian, I’ve never really felt at home there.

I attribute this disconnection mainly to my lack of fluency in Croatian—my parents were more focused on assimilating into American culture, and therefore did not teach my sisters and me Croatian growing up. Yet I was intensely curious about my heritage: the breathtaking Adriatic coastline, the complex history, and the mix of cultures.

So much so, that after I visited Croatia for the first time when I was twenty years old, I decided to change my major in university from English to Slavic Languages and Literatures with a focus on Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian.

When I first started crafting the story that would become The Haunting of Lavender House, things weren’t clicking. Something was missing, but I wasn’t sure what. And so, on one of my breaks from the project, I began to research Croatian folklore. I had taken a Slavic folklore class in university and was especially drawn to it as a subject. I liked the idea of stories passed down through generations; stories I may have missed out on by growing up in the U.S.

That’s when I came upon the concept of a mora.

A mora is a supernatural female spirit said to cause nightmares and paralysis by sitting on the chest of a sleeping person. The idea immediately intrigued me. Though I’ve never experienced sleep paralysis, I often become lucid during my nightmares, resulting in half-conscious attempts to scream that inevitably wake my husband. A being that caused nightmares and paralysis seemed especially frightening, and because my story didn’t have a strong antagonist, my mind leapt with ideas on how a mora could add tension and dread to my plot.

As I did more research, I discovered that concepts of sleep paralysis demons or spirits actually exist in several cultures. For example, in Newfoundland, where my husband is from, there are folklore beliefs in the “Old Hag,” a frightening old woman who causes sleep paralysis in a similar way. (Fans of the show Widow’s Bay will find several similarities between this hag and the sea hag in the show).

But one of the core features of a Croatian mora that differentiates it from other interpretations is that this spirit is a young woman. A beautiful one.

To learn more about moras, I relied heavily on the research of Dr. Luka Šešo, primarily his works, “Which Woman is a Witch? The Stereotypic Notions about Witches in Croatian Traditional Beliefs” and Živjeti s Nadnaravnim Bićima: Vukodlaci, Vile i Vještice Hrvatskih Tradicijskih Vjerovanja (Living with Supernatural Beings: Werewolves, Fairies and Witches of Croatian Traditional Beliefs). From him, I learned that in the patriarchal society of Dalmatia (the central coastal region of Croatia), women who defied societal norms in some way were labeled as witches or moras (with the difference being if they were married or widowed; the title of mora was given to unmarried women).

For example, if a young woman was particularly beautiful or forward with men, she was called a mora, as these traits often spurred envy or dislike. Furthermore, women were believed to reveal themselves as moras after experiencing unrequited love or jealousy. A man turned the woman down, or refused to marry her, and so he claimed that she was harassing him supernaturally.

On the other hand, women were also accused of being moras after having sexual relations with a man who later wanted to distance himself from her. He could simply say that she had “bewitched” him, and be free of all responsibility (while the woman was then ostracized). Additionally, labeling a woman as a mora or witch turned them into scapegoats when a troublesome or unexplainable event occurred.

All these findings were naturally a bit infuriating. Women who were labeled as moras were made into monsters simply because they stood out, or because they weren’t behaving as men thought they should, or because society needed someone to blame.

At first, I was fascinated by the mora because of all the haunting elements she could bring to my story. But my motivation to include one began to grow and shift—I didn’t only want to feature a mora as a scary supernatural villain—I also wanted to give the women behind the label justice.

And so I asked myself, who is the person behind this “monster?” And what if she fought back? What if she embraced her label of monstrosity and sought revenge for the stigmatization she faced? Thus the mora in The Haunting of Lavender House took shape. She is not only a villain, but a character in her own right, with a history that unveils itself throughout the novel.

In the end, I realized that her story fits gothic themes very well. After all, gothic heroines often struggle with isolation, anxieties, and the fight for autonomy. All things that defiant women in historical Dalmatia likely faced themselves. By the end of the novel, I want readers to understand where all the mora’s rage and villainy comes from—and to also question if a peculiar or defiant woman is truly the monster when she’s not the master of her own tale.

Though I didn’t set out to write a Croatian gothic novel, I am very proud that it has become that. By incorporating Croatian folklore into my writing, I feel that I have reclaimed something that I missed out on through my life in the U.S. I hope that The Haunting of Lavender House and its mora figure cast some light on the hardships women faced (and continue to face) in patriarchal societies.

And finally, even though the mora brings fear and dread, I also hope it makes readers think, “Good for her.”

Natalie Kikic is a Croatian American who grew up on stories of her parents' lives in the former Yugoslavia. She holds a Bachelor's in Slavic Languages & Literatures from the University of California, Berkeley and her work explores Balkan folklore, belonging, and hauntings, both ghostly and romantic. Originally from California, she currently resides in Massachusetts with her husband and two polydactyl cats. She is the author of The Haunting of Lavender House.

#30. New in SCOTUSBlog: "The separation and expansion of powers between Congress and the president"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Our final installment to track the changes in constitutional law.

SCOTUSBlog has published the final installment in our series on recent changes in constitutional law. This essay focuses on the separation of powers. It begins:

The late 1990s and early 2000s ushered in the Rehnquist federalism revolution, which appeared to place limits on Congress' powers and expand those of the states. Then came Sept. 11, 2001, and the global war on terror, which seemed poised to expand the president's powers. Yet, by 2008, Congress' powers seemed without meaningful limits and the president's efforts to expand his own powers had failed. And the separation of powers remained, well, separate. Nevertheless, the next two decades would vastly enlarge the president's powers as Congress' authority over the executive branch would be greatly diminished.

Here is a chart that shows the shift in cases:

Up to the fourth edition of our casebook in 2022, constitutional law followed a somewhat predictable arc. To be sure, there were shifts to the left and to the right, but the doctrine could be explained by a coherent narrative: the New Deal settlement on federal power was untouchable; the court would offer only modest protections for federalism; the administrative state was beyond reproach; attempts to single out unpopular groups would be halted; "benign" racial classifications were permitted; and church and state were strictly separated. Now, each aspect of this narrative has been reconceived. The five years since that edition appeared have brought the most changes to constitutional law since the Warren court.

We began this series by observing that lawyers tend to internalize the constitutional law that existed when they attended law school. The same is true of law professors. Virtually all law professors today came of age in a time of stasis. They could safely assume that the trajectory of the Warren court would continue indefinitely. But the jurisprudence of the Burger and Rehnquist courts was primed for a reversal, just as the Warren court reversed so many precedents from before. Ultimately, the Roberts court continues to chip away at precedents from the 1970s and 1980s, even if the precedents from the 1960s and before remain.

Many of these professors have struggled to cope with sudden changes in the doctrine. Some have voiced their despair of teaching constitutional law at all. Unsurprisingly, their students also struggle to cope with these developments. This trend is regrettable. Our role as casebook editors, and constitutional law professors, is to guide students through the entire corpus of constitutional law, from the framing to the present day, without any nostalgia for, or bias against, times gone by.

This is my last planned post with SCOTUSBlog. I'm sure there will be more to come.

#31. SCOTUS allows Hastings name change to remain at University of California law school

The University of California College of the Law at San Francisco can retain its new name, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday. (Photo illustration by Sara Wadford/ABAJournal/Shutterstock)

The University of California College of the Law at San Francisco can retain its new name, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday, rejecting a challenge by its former namesake’s descendants after revelations that Serranus C. Hastings ordered troops to slaughter thousands of Native Americans in the 1860s.

The San Francisco Chronicle via MSN.com has coverage.

When the San Franscisco-based school was founded 148 years ago, a state law declared that it “shall forever be known” as the University of California Hastings College of the Law in San Francisco.

It committed Hastings to paying the state $100,000 to found the school, which claims alumni such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and former San Francisco Mayor and Assembly Speaker Willie Brown.

Hastings, a former California Supreme Court chief justice and a state attorney general, was also a rancher. He blamed tribes for attacking his cattle. But in the last decade, evidence emerged proving that he sent the militia to Native Americans in Mendocino County, California.

The state legislature passed a law, effective in 2023, changing the school’s name to the University of California College of the Law at San Francisco, leading six of Hastings’ descendants along with alumni to file a lawsuit against the state for violating a binding contract and seeking return of the $100,000 plus interest for a total of $1.7 million.

After the California courts ruled that the 1878 law was not a contract but a law that could be repealed, a state appeals court later agreed.

On Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in a one-sentence order with no indication of dissents.

State supreme court lets stand decision to ax Hastings name from University of California law school

#33. EU, Belgium, Denmark: Raise Rights With Vietnam’s Leader

Click to expand Image Vietnam’s leader To Lam meeting President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen during United Nations General Assembly meetings, September 24, 2024. © 2024 Pool Union Europe/Agence Hans Lucas via Reuters

(Brussels) – Leaders of the European Union, Belgium, and Denmark should urge Vietnam to make concrete progress in improving its human rights record during Vietnamese President To Lam’s visit to Copenhagen and Brussels the week of October 19-24, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today.

Human Rights Watch wrote to the prime ministers of Denmark and Belgium and, jointly with other groups, to the European Council and European Commission presidents, expressing concerns about Vietnam’s intensifying crackdown on human rights, which violates several obligations and commitments it made to the EU in a 2020 free trade agreement.

“The Vietnamese government has broken its pledges of reform and continues to crack down on basic freedoms,” said Patricia Gossman, senior associate Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “European leaders should communicate clearly and publicly to President To Lam that human rights and labor rights violations will no longer be tolerated.”

Human Rights Watch, in its letters, highlighted that the Vietnamese government has sharply intensified its repression of basic freedoms over the past 10 years. To Lam served as Vietnam’s minister of public security from 2016 to 2024—the head of its police force—and since then as general secretary of the Vietnamese Communist Party and later president.

On To Lam’s watch, Vietnamese police initiated a far-reaching crackdown that decimated the country’s civil society, stepped up transnational repression, and expanded the scope and use of draconian laws that criminalize the exercise of freedom of expression in contravention of Vietnam’s international human rights obligations.

Vietnam currently has at least 160 political prisoners imprisoned under draconian laws that violate their rights to free expression and peaceful activism for human rights and democracy. These include: Pham Doan Trang, a writer and human rights advocate; Can Thi Theu, a land rights activist; Pham Chi Dung and Nguyen Tuong Thuy, independent journalists; Hoang Duc Binh, a labor activist; and Le Dinh Luong, Nguyen Van Tuc, Tran Duc Thach, Tran Van Bang, and Nguyen Trung Ton, democracy campaigners.

During the first 9 months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 28 activists, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan, to long prison terms. Police arrested at least 39 other people for allegedly criticizing the government or being affiliated with disfavored religious or political groups.

The Vietnamese government has failed to implement legal reforms it pledged to undertake in its free trade and partnership agreements, including commitments to ratify International Labour Organization Convention No. 87 on Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise, and continues to thwart the establishment of independent trade unions.

Despite Vietnam’s failure to meet its pledges, the EU in January upgraded bilateral relations with Vietnam to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. Concerns continue to be raised in yearly human rights dialogues that have largely failed to yield concrete results.

“The EU and its member states should stop giving Vietnam a free pass on repression,” Gossman said. “To Lam needs to hear loud and clear that unless his crackdown ends and reforms are adopted, there will be consequences for political and trade relations with Europe.”

#34. Pactiv Evergreen settles for $6.25M over 2023 North Carolina mill closure

The restitution amount is more than half of what Pactiv Evergreen received from the state in economic development grants for the site.

The paper mill in Canton had been in operation for more than 100 years prior to then-owner Pactiv shutting it down in 2023, according to the state of North Carolina. Blue Ridge Paper Products operated the facility since 1999, and in 2007 that company became Evergreen Packaging through a merger. Pactiv Evergreen formed in 2020 through the combination of Evergreen Packaging and Pactiv, both of which were previously acquired by Reynolds Group Holdings.

At the time of the Canton mill’s closure, many people expressed surprise at Pactiv Evergreen’s decision. The company made the announcement in March 2023 along with other closure and restructuring disclosures, and CEO Mike King noted a “challenging market environment” for Pactiv’s beverage merchandising business. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper said in a statement last week that the Canton closure came as a “gut punch" to the local and state economies.

Upon introducing the lawsuit in May 2024, then-Attorney General Josh Stein noted that taxpayers “invested in Pactiv Evergreen to bolster our state’s economy,” but Pactiv didn’t hold up its end of the bargain. He said at the time that his office had tried working with Pactiv for a year to address the company’s obligations, but it had “become clear that legal action was necessary to hold Pactiv accountable.” The initial lawsuit sought repayment of the full $12 million in economic incentives that Pactiv had received.

The settlement should not be viewed as an admission to wrongdoing, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

“Pactiv broke its promise to the state and the people of Canton, and today’s settlement holds it accountable for violating its agreement,” Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who was elected in November and took office last month, said of the new settlement. “This settlement will allow the people of Canton and Haywood County to immediately put millions back into rebuilding their economy after the mill’s closure, and it will shield them from future litigation from Pactiv.”

The candidates for state attorney general repeatedly brought up the mill issues on the campaign trail prior to November’s election. Both candidates expressed a desire to hold Pactiv accountable.

Pactiv had filed a motion to dismiss the complaint in July 2024. But a judge denied that motion in October, allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

“We are pleased to have resolved with the State of North Carolina all outstanding matters relating to the closure and sale of our former Canton mill site. We thank our employees for their contributions to our company and wish the Canton community well in this next chapter for the Town,” said Pactiv Evergreen Tuesday in an emailed statement.

This wasn’t Pactiv’s first legal battle over the Canton site.

In autumn 2023, the company reached a settlement worth more than $2 million with the U.S. EPA over Clean Air Act violations at Canton. Earlier that year, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the site violated water quality requirements; the company denied the allegations. In 2021 and 2022, the mill faced state air quality violations.

Novolex is in the process of acquiring Pactiv Evergreen for $6.7 billion. The deal, which would take Pactiv private, is expected to close during the first half of this year.

#35. Stop the Blame Game: Time To Restore Bipartisanship in Foreign Aid

Last year saw the lowest number of people dying of AIDS around the world in over 30 years. This should be big news, given the millions the disease has killed and the billions the United States government has spent to combat it. Yet it isn’t. Why?

It’s not just the media’s natural aversion to reporting good news. The real problem is when that good news undercuts the foreign aid industry’s narrative that President Donald Trump’s dismantling of the U.S. foreign aid apparatus has been an unmitigated global catastrophe.

The U.S. Agency for International Development’s demise last year prompted severe criticism. For thousands of people that lost their jobs and careers it is understandable. But one should expect more calibrated responses from prominent foreign aid advocates.

It was the opposite. U2 frontman Bono cited an estimate suggesting that as many as 300,000 people may already have died as a result of the cuts, while acknowledging that the figure was unproven. Bill Gates warned that millions could die if cuts are not reversed. UNAIDS warned that the collapse of U.S.-supported HIV services could lead to around 4 million additional AIDS-related deaths between 2025 and 2029. A Lancet study projected that continued USAID defunding could result in more than 14 million additional deaths from all causes by 2030.

Missed amid the histrionics was that according to UNAIDS, 570,000 people died of AIDS worldwide in 2025, the lowest in years and a 73% decline from a peak of over 2.1 million in 2004. While still too high, the vast improvement is a testament to America’s unique and durable ability to mobilize massive resources—particularly through the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR, and taxpayer generosity—to respond to any global crisis anywhere. The predicted mass death did not happen last year, nor so far this year, and the industry looks unserious.

>>> Response to Venezuela’s Crisis Proves That America Can Still Help in Substantial Ways—Even Without USAID

It is over 18 months since Trump ordered a review and suspension of U.S. foreign assistance, leading to USAID’s subsequent dismantling, and the reimagining of foreign aid as an unapologetic tool of national security. This was the basis for USAID’s establishment during the Cold War.

We can now better assess the impact. Emerging is a picture not of death and doom but, rather, a growing self-reliance from once aid-dependent countries where social services were regularly outsourced to foreign groups. They are now stepping up.

An accelerated journey to self-reliance

As the Democratic Republic of Congo struggles to contain its 17th Ebola outbreak—amid concerns about reduced U.S. assistance—in a region beset by armed conflict, neighboring Uganda was declared free of the Ebola virus by the World Health Organization in August.

Kenya, meanwhile, has mobilized testing, contact tracing, and surveillance after confirming its first imported Ebola case in October. As of Oct. 11, authorities had reported no additional infections.

Both prove Africa’s growing competence to handle serious epidemics.

Ghana responded to its aid funding gap by removing a cap on the National Health Insurance Fund, freeing up an estimated $300 million, to “take our destinies into our own hands.”

African leaders are mobilizing continentwide to develop new financial models not with donor agencies but with the private sector. They rightly see local manufacturing of medicines as “central to health sovereignty and long-term development.” Africa CDC estimates that the continent imports around 70%-90% of its medicines and medical devices and 99% of its vaccines.

Kenya’s President William Ruto, one of the continent’s vocal advocates of a shift away from dependence on foreign assistance, sums up Africa's reaction to U.S and Europewide foreign aid cuts: “Africa wants investment and equal partnership, not aid.”

Aid cuts are not just a MAGA obsession. European socialist and conservative governments alike are also reducing aid budgets amid fiscal pressures and changing priorities, and questions of aid effectiveness.

The new U.S. bilateral health agreements

In part, the African continent’s accelerated move to self-reliance springs from the U.S. administration’s restructuring of its global health programs. It has struck 36 government-to-government agreements. The administration says that countries will receive predictable multiyear financing and technical support to transition to full financial ownership of these lifesaving programs. I understand this is designed to cut out international NGOs, U.N. agencies, and contractors in favor of direct engagement with the private drug producers, and is this not what was needed?

Corruption and the legacy of foreign aid

For years, open-ended foreign aid subsidized African budgets that, in many cases, fostered a culture of corruption and rewarded bad economic policies. Meanwhile, aid diversion risks undercutting congressional and popular support for foreign aid.

>>> PEPFAR: From AIDS Relief to Leftwing Funding Apparatus

If the new approach creates stronger incentives for accountability and domestic ownership, that would be a welcome change.

Also, fears that placing America’s global disaster response capacity under the State Department proved misplaced, as shown by the U.S. response to Venezuela’s earthquakes.

Nevertheless, the sector’s condescending dismissal of foreign aid critics continues. The administration’s approach to foreign aid is based on working oneself out of a job by transitioning from traditional grants-based aid to what we all know creates wealth: foreign investment and trade.

This was the core of USAID’s Journey to Self-Reliance during the first Trump administration. Throughout the decades, foreign aid achieved much in advancing American interests and doing good, but it went on too long without a credible and sustainable pathway to self-reliance.

Still, much of the media coverage focuses on the disruption caused by the dismantling of USAID, covering views of former aid officials and defunded partners. Without an honest accounting of both the costs of the cuts and the results of the new approach, rebuilding bipartisan confidence in foreign aid will remain difficult.

HONOLULU (CN) â More than a dozen lawyers for the worldâs largest oil companies and their trade group crowded into a Honolulu courtroom Tuesday to argue Hawaiiâs climate change lawsuit against them belongs in the Legislature, not a courtroom.

The state says BP, Chevron, Exxon and others spent decades misleading the public about what burning their products would do to the planet. The companies told First Circuit Judge Jordon Kimura the state is really asking a court to decide how much fossil fuel the world should have burned.

âIt sounds like the defendants are trying to hit a home run on the idea of political questions,â Kimura told Theodore Boutrous, the Chevron attorney arguing for all the defendants.

Kimura asked how deciding whether an advertisement was misleading, or whether the companies had a duty to warn, would require the court to set emissions targets.

Boutrous conceded it would not. But he said the stateâs theory would force a court to decide whether global emissions were too high and what governments around the world would have done without the companiesâ statements.

Climate policy belongs to the Legislature and the governor, Boutrous argued, who he said have balanced the stateâs need for fuel against climate concerns since the 1980s. He also pointed out the state itself argued climate change was a political question when young people sued it in the Navahine case.

âThey want this court to become the climate change czar under state law, at the expense of these defendants,â Boutrous said. âWhat theyâre really saying is: political question doctrine for me, but not for thee.â

Kimura appeared skeptical. He said Hawaiiâs liberal pleading standard allows a complaint to survive if the state can prove any set of facts supporting it.

When Boutrous said no one could trace where the emissions harming Hawaii came from, he pushed back.

âWeâre in the middle of the Pacific, with no adjoining states or countries for thousands and thousands of miles,â Kimura said.

Victor Sher, representing the state, said the case is about deceptive marketing, not emissions limits. He read at length from the Hawaii Supreme Courtâs 2023 ruling in Honoluluâs nearly identical lawsuit, which held that the cityâs claims do not seek to regulate emissions.

âThe emissions, itâs true, Your Honor, are the vehicle of the injury,â Sher said. âTheyâre not the source of the liability.â

The state must prove the difference between the world as it is and the world as it would have been without the companiesâ conduct, Sher said. If a jury finds no deception or that it made no difference, âthen we lose.â

Kimura pressed Sher, too. He noted the Hawaii Supreme Courtâs Honolulu ruling addressed only federal preemption, not the political question doctrine.

He also questioned whether the stateâs proposed abatement fund would put the court in the business of climate policy and whether the state had identified a legal basis for imposing a standalone public trust duty on the companies.

Scott Janoe, representing Sunoco and its Aloha Petroleum subsidiaries, argued separately that the complaint is a fraud case in disguise and should have to meet a stricter pleading standard. He said the complaint uses terms such as deceive, mislead and greenwash about 430 times.

âA rose by any other name, Your Honor,â Janoe said.

The American Petroleum Institute is also seeking dismissal under Hawaiiâs anti-SLAPP law, arguing the stateâs claims violate its First Amendment rights.

Kimura questioned how the law applies to multiparty cases, saying it âleaves us guessing a lot.â

The state sued BP, Chevron, Exxon Mobil, Shell, ConocoPhillips, Phillips 66, Sunoco and other companies, along with the American Petroleum Institute, in May 2025. It seeks damages, civil penalties and a fund to help pay for sea-level rise, wildfires and other climate harms.

Kimura took the motions under advisement and did not say when he would rule.

#37. Justices take up case on race and school admissions

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument early next year in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a challenge to the process that a Maryland county uses to determine who will be admitted to a group of highly selective public magnet schools. The challengers, a group of mostly Asian-American parents in Montgomery County, Maryland, which is located just outside Washington, D.C., argue that although the policy does not on its face take race into account, it is nonetheless unconstitutional because it was intended to reduce the number of Asian-American students in those schools. The announcement came on a list of orders from the justices’ Oct. 16 conference and two years after the court turned down similar challenges, one involving Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in northern Virginia, which is regarded as one of the country’s top high schools, and another involving three of Boston’s elite public high schools.

The lawsuit was first filed in 2020 by the Association for Education Fairness, an organization of “concerned Asian-American parents in Montgomery County.” It alleged that the admissions process recently put into place, which was intended in part to increase enrollment of Black and Hispanic students at four highly selected magnet middle schools, violated the constitutional rights of Asian-American students. That policy, among other things, involved screening all fifth graders for possible admission (rather than only those whose parents asked for them to be included), eliminating teacher recommendations, and comparing students with their peers at their local schools.

Beginning in 2021-22, the county adopted a new policy. All fifth graders who met a series of criteria – including grades, reading level, and standardized test scores – were placed in a pool, from which students were selected by lottery for admission to magnet programs. The parent association then amended its complaint to argue that the new policy, sometimes nicknamed the Pandemic Plan because of when it was adopted, intentionally discriminates against Asian-American students.

The school board filed a motion to dismiss the case, which U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis granted. The parent association and the school board, she said, agree that, on its face, the Pandemic Plan is a “neutral admissions process that MCPS has applied evenhandedly.” Moreover, she continued, the parent association “does not meaningfully contest that the Pandemic Plan is rationally related to MCPS’ legitimate purposes.” The parent group’s claim can only go forward, she wrote, if the facts of its complaint “make plausible that the Pandemic Plan both” had a disproportionate effect on Asian-American students and “was motivated by discriminatory intent.” But she could not, she concluded, “see how the Pandemic Plan visited a disproportionate burden on Asian American students when the percentage of admitted Asian American students so substantially outpaces the percentage representation among all applicants.”

In a brief opinion in February, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld Xinis’ ruling. The parent association then came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to weigh in. It contended that the courts of appeals are divided (a key factor that the justices consider in deciding whether to grant review) over whether a case, like theirs, alleging intentional discrimination in violation of the Constitution’s guarantee of fair treatment can go forward without allegations that the admissions policy has a disproportionate effect on students of a particular race. Citing the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, in which the majority held the use of affirmative action in college admissions to be unconstitutional, the parent group argued that “[i]f ‘[e]liminating racial discrimination means eliminating all of it,’ this cannot stand.”

The school board urged the Supreme Court to deny review. It portrayed the dispute as “unremarkable and of little significance,” emphasizing that it “involves a race-neutral lottery adopted in response to a global pandemic” and that “the proportion of Asian Americans among selected students actually increased at the two other magnet schools in the same year, under the same policy.”

In a brief order on Monday morning, the justices agreed to take up the case and to decide “[w]hether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.
