#38. Did Oregon Man Who Shot the School Shooter Violate Oregon Law in Carrying Gun onto School Property?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I've seen some say yes as to that—as an objection to gun control laws, not as an objection to the man's actions—but I don't think it's quite right.

It's true that Oregon law generally criminalizes gun possession on school property, including by people with concealed carry licenses, if the school board adopts such a no-guns-allowed policy. And apparently the Bend school in which the shooting took place indeed has such a policy.

But Oregon law recognizes a so-called "choice of evils" defense, often called a "necessity" defense, that allows people to violate a wide range of laws if it's genuinely necessary in an emergency:

(1) Unless inconsistent with other provisions of chapter 743, Oregon Laws 1971, defining justifiable use of physical force, or with some other provision of law, conduct which would otherwise constitute an offense is justifiable and not criminal when:

(a) That conduct is necessary as an emergency measure to avoid an imminent public or private injury; and

(b) The threatened injury is of such gravity that, according to ordinary standards of intelligence and morality, the desirability and urgency of avoiding the injury clearly outweigh the desirability of avoiding the injury sought to be prevented by the statute defining the offense in issue.

(2) The necessity and justifiability of conduct under subsection (1) of this section shall not rest upon considerations pertaining only to the morality and advisability of the statute, either in its general application or with respect to its application to a particular class of cases arising thereunder.

That means that, even when gun possession is otherwise criminal, it is "not criminal" when it's necessary to avoid imminent serious harm. Indeed, even felons, who are generally barred from possessing guns, may pick up a gun that's physically available to them when it's necessary for imminent self-defense:

We think that the trial judge's conclusion that ORS 161.200 [the choice of evils statute] is inapplicable to the offense of being an ex convict in possession of a firearm is incorrect. The statute contains no such express exception, and we see no justification for implying one. To the contrary, one who has been previously convicted of a felony is just as entitled to defend himself from an imminent threat of injury as is any other private citizen. We hold that the defense is available to those who have been previously convicted of a felony and, in appropriate circumstances, may justify their resort to a weapon which it would otherwise be unlawful for them to possess.

Likewise, a law-abiding gun owner may go into a school where gun possession is otherwise criminal when it's necessary to try to stop a school shooting. (Even in jurisdictions that don't formally recognize a choice-of-evils / necessity defense, the separate doctrines of self-defense or defense of others may provide a defense as to bringing a gun onto school property in such a situation, just as they provide a defense as to using the gun to kill the shooter.) And while in some situations the balancing test in the necessity defense can be vaguer than the somewhat more precise terms of the self-defense defense, carrying a gun into a no-guns zone in order to stop an apparent in-progress school shooting makes for an extraordinarily clear case for the defense.

Nor is this just a matter of prosecutorial discretion. If a prosecutor does file charges in such a situation, the gun owner can raise the defense. And if the evidence is sufficient to potentially trigger the defense (e.g., if the defendant or a witness testifies to facts that a reasonable jury may interpret as sufficing for the defense), then "the state must negate [the defense] beyond a reasonable doubt."

In this respect, the choice-of-evils defense is much like the defense-of-others defense. Killing someone is generally a crime; but the law recognizes that sometimes it's justifiable (in particular, to defend yourself or others against death or other very serious harms), and thus provides a defense-of-others affirmative defense.

Likewise, carrying a gun onto school property in Oregon is a crime when the school district forbids it. But the law recognizes that sometimes it's justifiable (in particular, to defend people against a school shooting), and thus provides a choice-of-evils affirmative defense.

Naturally, the operation of the defense depends on the good sense of prosecutors, judges, and juries—just as the operation of the self-defense and defense-of-others defense do. But it's the way our legal system deals, even if at times imperfectly, with situations where an emergency need warrants what would otherwise be illegal action (whether that otherwise illegal action would be murder, as to the shooting itself, or a weapons offense, as to the carrying of a gun onto school property).

Of course, the choice-of-evils defense doesn't work for people who want to carry guns in forbidden places simply to be prepared in case the gun is needed (the usual reason most people who carry guns do so). One can certainly debate whether schools should allow at least some people, such as teachers or other school staff who are trained and licensed, to keep guns on their persons in school.

But even if you think the Oregon law (coupled with Bend's policy) is foolish in generally criminalizing gun licensees' carrying a gun onto school property, it's not so foolish as to criminalizing their carrying a gun onto school property when necessary to stop an in-progress school shooting.

NEXT: Children May Proceed Pseudonymously; May Their Parents?

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. #39. ‘A Killer Story’: When everyone knows who did it, nobody knows anything

Convicted murderer Dana Chandler at her 2022 retrial. (Story Syndicate via AP, Pool)

I get quite a few online inquiries about old convictions people want me to investigate. I’ve learned over my career that it isn’t always about the merits of the case; sometimes, people just want closure.

That’s why the first few minutes of the HBO original documentary series, A Killer Story, drew me in so quickly. As investigative journalist Joe Sexton explained how Eileen Umbehr banged on his digital door for months before he finally listened to her about Dana Chandler’s conviction for the 2002 shooting murders of her ex-husband and his then-girlfriend, I understood the skepticism of Sexton, a Pulitzer Prize winner who had worked for the New York Times and ProPublica.

The difference, though? Eileen Umbehr ultimately contacted Sexton with a Kansas appellate reversal of the conviction in question. That’s rare, but so is a case that offers nearly every other procedural complication you could imagine: a near-absence of direct evidence, prosecutorial misconduct, a hung jury, competing suspect theories, the hazards of witness credibility and a pro se defendant.

Most murder prosecutions hope to establish motive, means and opportunity at a bare minimum. The prosecutors in Chandler’s first trial, however, were simply content with the first angle. In my last column, we touched on the problem of establishing motive and intent after the fact. Means and opportunity, though, should be easier to prove. By relying on Chandler’s hostility and hatred for her ex-husband, Mike Sisco, and his girlfriend, Karen Harkness, the prosecution was certain they had the right person, even though almost a decade passed before she was charged—charges that seemed more the result of a 48 Hours television investigation than law enforcement intervention.

When all the evidence is circumstantial, it leaves plenty of room for the defense to argue. Sadly, it also gives the prosecution space to exaggerate the strength of its evidence. In Chandler’s case, even though the prosecution ultimately achieved a conviction the first time around, their misconduct in misstating—and at times outright lying about—the evidence ultimately led the Kansas Supreme Court to reverse the conviction and remand for a new trial.

Who pushed that appeal process? No one other than Eileen Umbehr, who initially contacted Sexton; and Umbehr’s husband, Keen, a garbageman who later became an attorney. So not only were the Umbehrs actively engaged in Chandler’s defense when they reached out, they were also stalwarts of her appeal. That’s some heavy lifting for seasoned defense firms, let alone a husband-and-wife team.

I got to thinking: Could the Umbehrs occupy an interesting category in true-crime lore? Could they separate themselves as truly objective citizen sleuths? True-crime fans with not only the gumption and diligence to gather the evidence, but also the knowledge and the experience to do something with it in a court of law?

Over the next two episodes, I saw that possibility play out for both better and worse. Both the defense and prosecution theories of their evidence changed along with the procedural posture of Chandler’s case. For each side, new witnesses and suspects appeared, and attempts to manufacture proof after the fact ended up more like ill-fated interceptions than last-second Hail Mary touchdowns.

Obviously, the couple weren’t out of their depth. While working in sanitation, Keen Umbehr had an agreement with the courthouse janitor to receive sensitive documents in a separate trash container. Prior to becoming an attorney, he used those documents and the information he gained to write a newspaper column criticizing and exposing various county officials, such as Jeff Sutton, a former prosecutor in the area.

Sutton was also Karen Harkness’ son-in-law, and the Umbehrs were certain he had committed the shootings. The couple went so far as to utilize a Kansas law that allows private citizens to present an affidavit of probable cause to a judge to open an investigation into Sutton.

It seemed their certainty about his guilt and Chandler’s innocence would be rewarded until DNA evidence gathered during the investigation cleared Sutton in law enforcement’s eyes. Keen Umbehr was left with a bit of egg on his face once the former feud and bad blood between the two came to light.

Chandler proceeded to her second jury trial, where, days in, the prosecution solicited testimony from a never-before-seen witness who was certain she’d seen Chandler in the area of the murders on the night in question. But once the defense attorney thoroughly dismantled that theory and testimony, the prosecution was also left eating crow: The jury deadlocked, and the judge declared a mistrial.

Not to be outdone, Chandler raised the stakes of certainty on her own behalf. When the prosecution decided to try her a third time for the murders, Chandler fired her attorneys on the morning of trial, thinking she knew the case better than anyone else. Chandler was ultimately convicted of both counts.

Sexton, through his narration, put it best: “Knowing your case really well and arguing it effectively are two different things.” Honestly, that goes for licensed attorneys too.

Certainty, as A Killer Story shows, is often more harmful than beneficial.

Certainty doesn’t really fit into criminal litigation. The prosecution carries the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, but it isn’t required to eliminate every conceivable argument for innocence. A defense attorney may insist those arguments for innocence should cast significant doubt, all the while reminding the jury they have no obligation to prove an alternative explanation.

Arguably, uncertainty is the backbone of the criminal justice system. Very rarely should anyone feel certain during trial. After all, the only way to be certain is to have been there yourself.

A juror who believes a defendant probably committed a crime, but is uncertain, may be required to acquit. A defense attorney who believes their client is guilty, but is uncertain, still carries the obligation to zealously represent them. And a prosecutor who wholeheartedly believes in the defendant’s guilt, but is uncertain, still has the ethical obligation to turn over exculpatory evidence.

The system breaks down when certainty becomes a substitute for scrutiny.

A prosecutor who is certain may refuse to listen to exonerating evidence during plea negotiations, pushing a case to trial and wasting taxpayers’ time and money. A defense attorney who is certain may overlook a weakness in their case and fail to counsel their client against risking more time by going to trial. A juror who is certain may fail to look at all of the evidence in the grand scheme of the case and fail to honestly and truthfully engage in open deliberations.

Verdicts bring legal resolutions to a case; they do not resolve every historical or moral uncertainty.

A Killer Story accomplishes something I’ve rarely seen while writing this column: It effectively navigates many true-crime tropes while also presenting a story with all the hallmarks of a judicial landscape that constantly reminds me Murphy’s law is real—and rampant as well.

For attorneys, the documentary offers an exposé on trial strategies, witness credibility, attorney-client dynamics and prosecutorial responsibility. For true-crime fans, it offers an opportunity to look inward and ask why and how we become so attached to the plights of someone we’ve never known—even though we can’t be certain as to their ethical, moral and legal culpability.

The ultimate takeaway? The most dangerous person in a jury trial isn’t the one who acted wrongfully; it’s the one incapable of believing they might be wrong from the get-go.

Adam R. Banner is the founder and lead attorney of the Oklahoma Legal Group, a criminal defense law firm in Oklahoma City. His practice focuses solely on state and federal criminal defense. He represents the accused against allegations of sex crimes, violent crimes, drug crimes and white-collar crimes.

The study of law isn’t for everyone, yet its practice and procedure seem to permeate pop culture at an increasing rate. This column is about the intersection of law and pop culture in an attempt to separate the real from the ridiculous.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#40. Matthew Gavin Frank on Kim Wall and the Ethics of Sensationalistic True Crime

In August 2017, the Swedish journalist, Kim Wall, was brutally assaulted and murdered by the amateur submersible builder, Peter Madsen, while onboard his sub, UC3 Nautilus, off the coast of Copenhagen, Denmark.

In my book, Submersed, I did not want to write about the murder of Kim Wall. I did not plan on writing about this. I wanted to engage the eccentric micro-community of DIY submersible folks, and to scratch at their obsessions and their actions for some kind of larger—if elusive or illusory—meaning; some kind of sly microcosmic comment on the human condition and on human longing.

I wanted to write about the flights of fancy and motivations of the PSUBS (or “personal submersibles”) collective—a group of self-proclaimed free spirits, who identify first and foremost as “amateur submarine builders and underwater explorers.” I wanted to write about coral beds, and about bioluminescence.

But, in my research, I kept bumping up against violence, misogyny, the murder of Kim Wall. What is it with my own malign and fraught compulsion to sink to these depths, the ethics of inquiring into and interacting with—in book form and other art forms—real-life atrocity?

“As news organizations grapple with shrinking budgets, they increasingly rely on freelancers [like Wall],” says journalist Sruthi Gottipati, “who cost less and are often willing to take on the attendant risks reporting in places they wouldn’t send their staff to.  Even against this backdrop, the competition is fierce to place stories and female freelancers work hard to ensure their gender isn’t calculated as a liability. So they clam up about the dangers they face…”

And I realize that, even before the details of Wall’s murder began attending, like metal flakes to a magnet, my investigations into, and obsessions with the personal submersible community, my particular cage of skin lent me the sort of privilege that mitigated the sorts of dangers that Wall and Gottipati had to consider, negotiate, face.  I had the privilege to be less complicatedly excited about diving to depth with one of these PSUBS guys, who is, in part I suppose, a guy like Peter Madsen, or a guy akin to who a journalist may have thought Peter Madsen was—a hobbyist eccentric—before the murder occurred.  An admission: I revised this previous sentence.  It once ended, “…a hobbyist eccentric—before the unthinkable occurred.”  To whom, I had to ask, was the threat of murder unthinkable?  To me, I’m both privileged and ashamed to admit.  In this world, such an outcome may have been quite thinkable to Kim Wall.  It must now be devastatingly thinkable to Gottipati, and most likely every female journalist.

“[T]he world has a way of knocking down women who are sharp, funny and bold,” Gottipati says, “It has a habit of strangling the voices who dare to speak up, of humiliating the women who step outside their comfort zones, of crushing the ones who break the rules.  After traveling and reporting in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean, it was in her native Scandinavia, a supposed bastion of gender parity, in which Kim has disappeared. It’s a chilling reminder that women’s safety can’t be shrugged off as a problem specific to developing countries, as if the west is immune to misogyny.”

I can only hope—however inadequately, and perhaps in moments even infuriatingly—to draw inspiration from Wall’s own work as I negotiate the threads of my own. “As the empathetic reporter she is,” Gottipati says of Wall, “she writes with nuance and gives her characters, however downtrodden or peculiar or disenfranchised, agency. I wish we lived in a world that does the same for her.”

I share this wish, but also recognize the shortcomings of my own attempts to empathize with experiences that are not, and can not be my own, as such attempts are bound up in my very particular network of experiences moving through this world, in the ferment and fracas of the chemicals in my brain, which sometimes fools itself into thinking it is righteous, as if the way I wish to see myself is what I actually am.

The fact may very well be that my unbridled chasing of my own obsessions into the personal submersible world, and the seemingly ancillary threads that attend that chase, is itself an ethically unsound act. I am sinking through, at great speed, with blinders on, alternately attracted to and repelled by the subjects with which I collide, but, regardless, I can’t stop moving forward, or down.

I’m not sure what this tells me about myself as a writer, or about my ability to truly empathize with my subjects, lend them the agency they deserve. What is it then to engage this thread of “true crime” from this vantage? To realize that an engagement is ethically unsound, but to be unable to stop oneself from pursuing it, is to acknowledge that (to simplify) I’m not a very good person.

And even if one attempts to de-sensationalize the gristly (which, of course, is not innately sensational, but only becomes so if passed through the lurid portal of a particular breed of reportage), is one’s initial draw to the subject matter rooted in part in the sensational?  If one strips the varnish off a doorknob, the thing that compelled them to do so is often the varnish itself.

In pursuing this story, I haven’t been eating well. I’ve been sleeping poorly, and when I when I do sleep, it’s ornamented with nightmares. I’ve been waking up screaming. My heart seems to be racing all the time. I’m worried I’m doing more harm than good. The ghosts seem to be warning me away, but I’m stubbornly ignoring them. This is hokey, sure: but I feel as if I’ve sunk too deep. And still, I can’t stop until I’ve found out where the crush depth is.

Is this draw to the true crime story “bad for us?” wonders journalist Phoebe Lett.  No matter the answer, it seems such a draw has been with us for quite some time, prompting some to debate whether such an attraction is innate or learned.

In seventeenth-century England, the masses flocked to theaters to watch the performances of “conjurors”—early magicians and jugglers who, it was widely believed, achieved their powers of trickery by making deals with the Devil. They represented manifestations of evil in human form, and the more evil a conjuror was perceived to be, the more popular they were, the more tickets they sold. The masses couldn’t look away, and, as ever, they continually sought a darker, more devilish show.

One of the more popular conjurors was a man who took the stage name Hocus-Pocus, a bastardization of the Latin phrase, Hoc est corpus (“This is the body”), the very phrase a priest would intone during Mass at the moment of transubstantiation. Hocus-Pocus, in adopting this name, was blasphemously implying that the changing of the bread and the wine into the body and blood of Christ was yet another conjuring trick—rhetoric that was seen to have come straight from the Devil itself. (The word hoax shares this derivation).

And so, establishing himself as the greatest blasphemer on Conjurors Row, he filled his theater seats with the greatest number of butts. People couldn’t resist, even as they cringed.

“Before the Enlightenment, many thought human nature was inherently depraved,” says historian Joy Wiltenburg, “and the most sinister threat was the devil inside you, not an assailant around the corner. But there has long been a thrill to witness morally transgressive behavior and a desire to protect oneself from harm.”

But the “thrill to witness” eventually dovetails with elements of fear—the sort of which affect the ways in which we move through the world. The writer (and stabbing survivor) Emma Berquist argues that the popularity of the genre has made us—especially women—”inappropriately paranoid,” compelling us into a “state of hyper-awareness” and distrustfulness that can become unhealthy, unsustainable. Such “hypervigilance,” as aggravated by the ubiquity of so-called true-crime entertainment, Berquist says, “is a common symptom of PTSD, a trauma response that constantly puts your body into fight-or-flight mode.”

Conversely, professor of criminology Dawn Cecil, believes that the genre can help people “deal with their trauma…[and] live in a society that is still violently misogynistic.” But, Berquist says, “So many true-crime shows advise women to trust their instincts, but how can we trust instincts that have been hijacked by [the] anxiety…induced [by the shows themselves]?”

The popularity of the genre has also inspired a greater vigilantism among the public, wherein viewers can feel empowered to self-deputize, cast aside any notion of due process, and sometimes perpetuate crimes of their own in the name of virtue. “We’re a nation of crime experts now,” says Jean Murley, a true-crime scholar at Queensborough Community College. In some cases, when a person is convicted of a crime in the court of public opinion, that person has turned up dead, only to have evidence exonerate them posthumously.

Law professor Lindsey Webb also believes that the true-crime genre often perpetuates stories that serve to entrench white people’s fear of people of color and of immigrants, and further enshrine the racism inherent in our criminal justice systems. “We can both see the power of the narrative and get why this is compelling… and also say, ‘Wait a second, what are we perpetuating here?'” Webb says.

“Crime stories are a fundamentally conservative way of looking at the world,” Berquist seconds.

Suburban crime paranoia is as old as the suburbs themselves—hell, it’s why they exist to begin with….I see women on Twitter…instructing others to rip out strands of hair to leave in cabs for DNA evidence in case the driver murders you….Be aware of your surroundings and don’t trust strangers is not particularly helpful advice for avoiding the one scenario in which women are most likely to actually be murdered: by their partner. It’s victim blaming dressed up in empowerment.

I can’t help but think of Kim Wall’s parents; Ingrid and Joachim Wall’s tireless campaign to launch systems to empower female journalists in the aftermath of their daughter’s death, rather than sow fear, no matter how appropriate that fear may be.

The true-crime genre, historically, has depended on turning up the heat and the light on that fear, not only fostering an imbalance within a particular story, but swallowing entire aspects of it for making the fear splashier, addictive in its technicolor and the arousal of noradrenaline, norepinephrine, dopamine, and phenylethylamine—yes: those very same chemicals elicited when we fall, and fall in love, and go mad.

As the genre evolves, perhaps it can do better than this.  The writer Elon Green feels that the genre has finally opened itself up to telling stories in new ways, highlighting voices that have been traditionally subsumed. In Green’s view, true crime has potential in its increasing willingness to de-lionize the police and other investigators, and to focus on overarching systems that have allowed violence to be perpetuated onto the bodies of marginalized factions of our populace. “The fact that people are even asking these questions,” he says, “is new.”

In spite of this newness, I worry about the fabric of the genre within which I find myself drifting, its mercurial nature, and what it needs to tell itself in order to sustain itself.

What I need to tell myself….Even if I scrupulously try to avoid the ugly luridness of much of the coverage of the Wall/Madsen case, even if I try to highlight new truths about it by focusing on the peripheral ephemera dancing around it, drawing a chalk outline around it, I am still likely doing some kind of harm to the victims—to Wall’s family—in simply refusing to not engage it, stitched to a rabid and pathological sort of curiosity that I’m convinced makes me a bad person—not only capable of doing harm, but continuing to do harm, even when I come to recognize that what I’m doing may be harmful.

Tucking this kind of hedonism into the confines of the essay does not excuse the rottenness of the hedonism itself. I cannot excuse myself, I cannot sleep, but I also cannot stop. I have this need to explore how things seem to attend one another—how the story of Wall’s murder kept linking itself to my investigation into the amateur submersible community; and how one can tell us something about the other, help to contextualize the other—again, however implicitly, inadequately, elusively.

Knowledge of the probable and malign side-effects of this exploration are speed-bumps that I find myself speeding over.  I am complicit in perpetuating these side-effects of true crime.  I didn’t want to write about this.  I don’t want to write about this.  I am writing about this.  I don’t know where the surface is.  I’m afraid that when I find it, I won’t emerge the same as when I sunk.  Fuck me for being afraid.  Fuck my particular fear.  It’s nothing in the face of the sea.  Fuck me for writing that too.

I can’t shirk this: The act of engaging—perhaps even artfully—a real-life murder is ethically unsound. To do so involves an act of conjuring, of making the wind and weather and clouds that obliviously encase horror.

Good god, why is it so difficult to stop fixating on the sky, the horizon, the temperature of the air and the things visible and invisible threading through it? Gnats and birds, cumulus and cirrus, breeze and calm, the waves, the waves. What good are any of these things? How can they be anything but inadequate lenses through which to examine the act of one person’s body harming another person’s body?

What good are the paper plates once heaped with food at Kim Wall’s final dinner party with her friends along the Copenhagen quayside? Why is it so difficult to stop fixating on the plates, the thin smears of ketchup and barbecue sauce soaked into the Styrofoam, some of which were smeared by the forefingers of the guests, the friends, the people who did not yet know what was to come, who were about to have their capacities for surprise and despair stretched out into, perhaps, something that resembled—however ephemerally—another translucent circle?

Matthew Gavin Frank is the author of the nonfiction books Flight of the Diamond Smugglers, The Mad Feast, Preparing the Ghost, Pot Farm, Submersed, and Barolo, as well as the poetry books The Morrow Plots, Warranty in Zulu, and Sagittarius Agitprop. His work has appeared in The Kenyon Review, The Paris Review, Guernica, The New Republic, Iowa Review, Salon, Conjunctions, The Believer, and The Best Travel Writing and Best Food Writing anthologies. He’s a professor of creative writing in the Masters of Fine Arts Program at Northern Michigan University, where he is also the Nonfiction/Hybrids Editor of the literary magazine, Passages North.

#42. Mali: Military Attacks on Civilians, Insurgent Abuses

Click to expand Image Screenshot of a video posted online and analyzed by Human Rights Watch showing the destruction of a health center following an apparent Malian military drone strike in Talahandak village in the northern Kidal region, Mali, on July 29, 2026.   © Private Malian armed forces and their allies have since July 2026 responded to mounting attacks by Islamist and separatist armed groups with abusive counterinsurgency operations in central and northern Mali.The Malian military, armed groups, and insurgent forces are committing grave laws-of-war violations while international organizations and governments largely stand by.The AU Peace and Security Council should undertake sustained scrutiny of all parties to Mali’s conflict by convening a dedicated session on civilian protection and accountability and pressing them to halt abuses.

(Nairobi) – Malian armed forces and their allies have since July 2026 responded to mounting attacks by Islamist and separatist armed groups with abusive counterinsurgency operations in central and northern Mali, Human Rights Watch said today. 

Mali’s military and the allied Russia-controlled Africa Corps (formally the Wagner Group) have killed and wounded scores of civilians in attacks and in custody in violation of international humanitarian law. Islamist and separatist fighters have also violated the laws-of-war, including torturing and executing captured Malian soldiers. The African Union Peace and Security Council should urgently take action to prevent further atrocities in Mali. 

“The Malian military, armed groups, and insurgent forces are committing grave laws-of-war violations while international organizations and governments largely stand by,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The AU Peace and Security Council should undertake sustained scrutiny of all parties to Mali’s conflict by convening a dedicated session on civilian protection and accountability and pressing them to halt abuses.”

Between July 30 and September 20, 2026, Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed 30 people, including 16 witnesses to abuses, human rights defenders, community leaders, journalists, and a Malian soldier. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated two videos posted online showing the aftermath of an apparent drone strike and analyzed 12 photographs of the drone’s debris. Human Rights Watch also reviewed photographs and videos of casualties from other incidents documented. Human Rights Watch sent a letter to Mali’s defense minister on August 5 with findings and questions but received no response. 

Human Rights Watch documented two apparently indiscriminate Malian military drone attacks: a strike on July 29 in Talahandak village, in the northern Kidal region, that partially destroyed a health facility; and another one on August 19 at a market in Tombonkore village, in the central Bandiagara region, that killed six civilians and injured at least 20 others. Human Rights Watch also documented that on July 12 Malian soldiers shot and killed five girls during a counterinsurgency operation in the central Ségou region, and that on July 27 and 28, allied Dozo militia killed three civilians in the central Mopti region, all with impunity. 

The Al-Qaeda-linked Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM) and allied separatist fighters of the Azawad Liberation Front (Front de libération de l’Azawad, or FLA) attacked a military convoy on July 18 in Gao region and then tortured and executed at least 19 Malian troops taken prisoner.

These incidents occurred amid renewed fighting in Mali. On April 25, JNIM carried out coordinated attacks across the country alongside FLA fighters seeking to overthrow the military junta led by Gen. Assimi Goïta and backed by the Africa Corps. Malian armed forces and their allies responded with airstrikes that killed civilians and with reprisals against ethnic communities accused of collaborating with the insurgents.

“I found myself on the ground, propelled by the blast, stuck between a cart and a tree more than 15 meters from where I had been,” said a 24-year-old man who survived the August 19 attack. “Everyone started running. I tried to get up and saw that my right leg was completely shredded. Blood was dripping from my pants.”

Since their coordinated attacks in April, JNIM and the FLA have captured and detained increasing numbers of Malian security personnel. Concerns over their treatment intensified after the two armed groups claimed responsibility for a July 18 attack against a Malian military and Africa Corps convoy in Tabrichat, Gao region, in which at least 19 Malian troops who had surrendered were tortured and executed.

Human Rights Watch reviewed videos posted online, also previously analyzed by Amnesty International, showing armed men beating and shooting surrendering soldiers. Human Rights Watch could not determine whether the armed men were JNIM or FLA fighters. However, in one of the videos, credible sources and international media identified one of the men as the son of JNIM’s leader, Iyad Ag Ghali. In at least two videos, as Amnesty International highlighted, a white flag with black writing, characteristic of JNIM, is visible on the front of the attackers’ vehicles.

“Once [we made it to] Gao, over 50 military personnel were missing,” a soldier who survived the attack said. “At least 19 were executed – we saw them in the videos. The others? Dead? Captured? We don’t know. We can’t ask questions and we have been prohibited from watching the videos in the camp.”

JNIM’s Sharia Committee, in a September 30 response (English, Arabic) to Human Rights Watch, wrote that “although the killing of captives in Tabrichat … did in fact take place, we did not give the order for it, not because it is not permitted in our religion, but because we considered it a matter of interest to leave this alone.” JNIM added that Islam “grants Muslim leaders four choices with respect to captives: release, ransom, enslavement, and execution … even though we did not order our troops to commit that incident and it is not our policy to do such things, what they did does not violate our Sharia such that we see it necessary to hold them accountable or punish them.”

In a September 20 response to Human Rights Watch, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, FLA’s spokesperson, wrote that “[t]he FLA acknowledges that armed clashes took place between its forces and those of the Malian army and its Russian allies of the Africa Corps in Tabrichat on July 18, … However, the FLA categorically rejects any allegation that its forces carried out the execution” of Malian soldiers. He added that “the FLA has carried out and will continue to carry out … internal checks about any … violations of international humanitarian law by some of its members … especially those from Tabrichat.”

All parties to Mali’s armed conflict are bound by international humanitarian law, notably Common Article 3, Protocol Additional of 1977 to the 1949 Geneva Conventions relating to the Protection of Victims of Non-International Armed Conflicts (Protocol II),  and customary laws-of-war. Deliberate or indiscriminate attacks on civilians or civilian property, including medical facilities, are prohibited. Indiscriminate attacks include those that do not target a specific military objective. Common Article 3 and Protocol II also provide that anyone deprived of their liberty must be treated humanely in all circumstances. In particular, they are protected against murder, torture, and cruel, humiliating, and degrading treatment. Individuals who commit serious violations of the laws-of-war with criminal intent or are responsible as a matter of command responsibility may be prosecuted for war crimes.

At its April 28 session on Mali, the AU Peace and Security Council called for protecting civilians and regular briefings and requested increased AU support for Mali’s security sector in compliance with international human rights and humanitarian law. The council should follow through by adopting a communiqué condemning abuses by all parties to the conflict and requesting an urgent report on civilian protection measures and investigations, Human Rights Watch said.

“The AU Peace and Security Council should follow up its commitments to protect civilians in Mali with concrete measures and regular public reporting,” Allegrozzi said. “It should press the Malian authorities to conduct independent investigations into abuses by the Malian military and its allies as well as opposition forces, and offer support in such investigations from AU human rights experts.” 

Abuses by Malian Armed Forces and Allied Militias

Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a nongovernmental organization that monitors, collects, and analyzes conflict-related data globally, reported that between April and August 2026, Malian forces and the Africa Corps carried out 49 airstrikes, killing 89 civilians, more than double the 22 strikes and 44 civilian deaths reported during the same period in 2025. ACLED data also show that between April and August, the Malian armed forces killed 268 civilians. JNIM forces killed 134 civilians over the same period.

Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali’s junta has increasingly used airstrikes in its operations against armed groups. Mali has acquired and used Turkish-made Bayraktar TB2 drones since 2022 and Turkish-made Akinci drones since 2024. Russia has since 2022 also provided drones and fighter jets to Africa Corps personnel in Mali. Human Rights Watch, as well as other human rights groups and several media and investigative organizations, have repeatedly documented unlawfully indiscriminate or disproportionate airstrikes that caused civilian casualties. 

Apparent Indiscriminate Drone Strikes

Tombonkore, Bandiagara Region, August 19

On the morning of August 19, an apparent military drone released munition on civilians gathered at the cattle market in the village of Tombonkore, Kilimpo area, Bandiagara region, killing six men and injuring at least 20 others. The strike also killed several animals and destroyed market stalls and motorbikes. 

Five witnesses, including three injured in the strike, said that JNIM forces controlled the Tombonkore vicinity, but that no JNIM fighters were at the market or in the village at the time of the strike. They said the drone flew over the village for an extended period before releasing its munition, suggesting that the area was being surveilled.

“It [the drone] was gray and slowly flew above us from east to west and back for about 30 minutes before it bombed us,” said a cattle trader, 48, who was at the market.

Human Rights Watch could not identify the specific drone or munition used. However, the Malian military and allied Africa Corps are the only known forces in Mali to possess the large drones described by witnesses.

A 43-year-old witness said:

When the drone dropped the bomb on the market, I was thrown to the ground, blood gushing from my body. I saw my right arm was almost severed, held together only by a tiny piece of flesh. The blood was flowing profusely. A man … dragged me toward a small house nearby. I felt excruciating pain, and lay in a pool of blood. I saw people running, I heard screams. I got up after 40 minutes like that, and … looked for help. A man I didn’t know rescued me, took my turban and tied it around my arm securely to stop the bleeding.

The man’s arm was later amputated at the hospital in Sévaré. 

A 24-year-old man injured in the strike was interviewed hours before doctors amputated his right leg at the Sévaré hospital. He said he saw the drone repeatedly fly over the village, first eastward and later westward at increasingly lower altitude, until it approached the village more directly and dropped its munition. He said:

I saw people lying down, screaming and asking for help. It was at least an hour later that the villagers came to rescue us. I was rescued by a [ethnic] Dogon [man] who took me to his home next to the market, where I found my wife and other wounded people.… The motorcycle that my friend and I had come with to the market had caught fire. We had no means of transportation.… My foot was wrapped with a big cloth, and the pain was so severe. I spent the night with this Dogon family.… The next day, my foot looked like an elephant’s leg…. They took me to the hospital, and I am waiting for doctors to amputate my leg.

A 29-year-old butcher said he was at the market when the drone dropped its munition:

I fell and tried to get up, but I couldn’t. I saw blood running from my clothes, but I didn’t feel any pain. I then crawled to take cover under a cart to avoid a second strike. I looked at my leg; it was red with blood and twisted. From there, I saw several people on the ground, some screaming and others not moving. People were running everywhere. Motorcycles parked near my butcher shop caught fire. I was screaming for help, but people were running around, and no one was listening to me. After an hour and a half like that, calm returned, the market was empty, and villagers came to help the injured. I had lost a lot of blood. Friends and a cousin … tied my leg with a cloth before lifting me. I couldn’t breathe; I felt nauseated.

The man said that his cousin took him to the hospital in Bandiagara and then to the Sévaré hospital, where his right leg was treated for a fracture. 

The 48-year-old man said he helped evacuate the injured by putting them on carts and motorcycles and buried the bodies of those killed. He said five civilian men died on the spot, while a sixth died of his injuries at the Sévaré hospital:

Around 3 p.m. we buried the dead at the village cemetery, each in his grave.... There were no JNIM fighters among the dead. The bodies of those killed … had deep wounds in the abdomen and back.… The bodies were almost all at the same place, at the market, a few meters one from the other. Fourteen were seriously injured and were taken to either Bandiagara or Sévaré hospitals. Others, with less serious wounds, were treated in the village – they did not want to go to the hospital because they feared reprisals from the FAMA [Malian armed forces]. Among the injured, I saw one who had almost lost an arm, another had both legs in tatters, and others had open wounds on their abdomen, back, and head.

Witnesses shared with Human Rights Watch a video showing the aftermath of the strike. Although Human Rights Watch was not able to independently geolocate it, the footage includes an on-screen narration identifying the location and date of the attack consistent with witness accounts. The video shows the bodies of at least two men and blood on the ground.

Human Rights Watch also reviewed 10 photographs from witnesses showing one of the bodies visible in the video, another dead man, dead animals, and other people that witnesses said were injured in the strike. One of the photographs shows a man whose right arm is severely damaged; a forensic expert who reviewed the image said that injuries to the arm were highly consistent with a blast injury. Three other photographs show three injured men, with wounds to their legs and arms, including one who sustained a traumatic amputation. 

The chief of staff of the Malian armed forces issued a statement on August 20 that on the previous day Malian forces and their partners successfully struck a “terrorist hideout” in the Kilimpo area after long monitoring it. He added that about 20 “terrorists” were “neutralized,” and military equipment destroyed.

Human Rights Watch reviewed a list provided by witnesses with the names of the six men, ages 21 to 54, killed in the strike. 

“They [JNIM fighters] weren’t there that day, and still they are often around the village and also visit it,” said the 24-year-old man. “They preach and, above all, they make a lot of purchases at the market, buying fuel, pasta, spices, cereals, especially on Fridays. They also come during the week to make sure everyone follows the rules.”

Talahandak, Kidal Region, July 29 

On July 29 at about 4 a.m., an apparent one-way (“kamikaze”) attack drone hit and partially destroyed a health center in Talahandak, a village in a JNIM and FLA-controlled area near the Algerian border. 

Two men, including a 45-year-old health worker who witnessed the explosion, said that no JNIM or FLA fighters were in or around the health facility at the time of the strike and that the health center did not store anything other than medicines and medical equipment. 

The health worker said:

At the health center, we took care of men, women, children, and elderly people suffering from, among other things, malaria. Under no circumstances was this facility used by armed groups.… Only civilians received care here. Today, the center is destroyed.… Women and children, already deprived of basic health services, are going to suffer from this situation, not the armed groups. There were never any munitions or armed vehicles on site, even in the days before the attack. The fighters never came here. No terrorist or armed man was ever treated here; we don’t even have the medical means to treat war injuries.

The witnesses said they recovered the drone’s debris. They provided 12 photographs they said were taken at the site after the strike. The photographs analyzed by Human Rights Watch show components and remnants consistent with a Shahed-type delta wing drone, including control surfaces, brackets, bolt patterns, and internal construction. In a July 24 report, Bellingcat and Jeune Afrique geolocated footage showing Shahed-136 type one-way attack drones in operation in Mali. They verified two strikes, including one in Talahandak on July 17 that destroyed a truck carrying cooking oil and killed one civilian.

A 35-year-old resident of Talahandak said:

The health center was hit. The pharmacy and the room where the patients used to get treated were destroyed, as well as the patients’ beds, the lab equipment, and the pharmaceutical products. It’s completely in ruins and can’t be used for anything anymore. I can’t accurately describe the drone because it was dark. But I heard it and saw the strike, the explosion, the flames, and the fire coming from the health center. The drone sounded like a motorcycle, came at full speed, and crashed straight into its target. The next day, we went to see the ruins of the health center. We saw the drone’s engine as well as its propeller, which were not too damaged.

Human Rights Watch also verified and geolocated two videos posted to X on July 29 showing the interior and exterior of the Talahandak health center. The footage shows extensive damage to several rooms identified as the men’s and women’s treatment rooms, the laboratory, the pharmacy, and a consultation and ultrasound room. Damaged medical equipment and supplies are visible throughout the facility. 

The room marked as the men’s treatment room appears to be the most damaged, with a large hole in its exterior wall where a window had been. Debris is scattered through the room, and numerous fragmentation impacts are visible on the walls, along with signs of fire damage, and a charred stretcher. The videos also show structural damage to at least two of the building’s facades and its roof. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery from August 6 that showed severe damage to the roof’s northwestern corner.

Under international humanitarian law, all medical facilities are protected from attack, including facilities that treat members of belligerent armed forces or armed groups. This protection ceases only when medical facilities are used to commit hostile acts outside their humanitarian function, and then only after a warning that goes unheeded. 

Abuses During Counterinsurgency Operations

Djenné, Mopti Region, July 27 and 28

On July 27 around noon, a militia member from a group of dozens of Dozo militiamen wearing traditional clothing and armed with Kalashnikov-style assault rifles shot and killed a 50-year-old ethnic Fulani man near the main mosque in Djenné. Minutes later, the militiamen fatally shot another Fulani man, 43, at the same location. 

A 45-year-old resident said:

During the attack, I was with my friend [the 43-year-old man]. We were together when we heard a gunshot. I immediately told him, ‘Let’s take cover, it’s right next to us.’ He hesitated while I ran without waiting. The Dozo then shot him. In fact, the very first gunshot we heard was aimed at another friend of mine [the 50-year-old man]. The Dozo killed him, and we saw him collapse. When I turned my head, I saw a large group of Dozo, armed with Kalashnikovs, heading toward us. I personally know them because we all live in Djenné. To save myself, I had to run and leave my friend behind. That’s when they shot him.

Another witness provided a similar description of the incident.

On July 28, four Dozo militiamen, believed to be members of the same group who entered Djenné the previous day, forced their way into a house in Sankore neighborhood. They dragged out a 42-year-old Fulani man, tied his hands behind his back, blindfolded him, and drove away with him. His relatives found his body the next day, about two kilometers away, with three gunshot wounds to the head and chest.

Human Rights Watch spoke to two witnesses to the abduction, including the victim’s 32-year-old wife. She said that on the day the Dozo shot and killed the two men near the mosque, fear spread throughout Djenné’s Fulani community, prompting many to flee. She said she urged her husband to flee, but he refused, saying that he had spoken with the military based in town to report the incident and seek protection. 

The wife said:

The next day, on July 28, around 10 a.m., four Dozo armed with Kalashnikovs, dressed in their traditional outfits and horned hats, surrounded our house.... Two of them broke inside the house and forcibly took him [the husband] out. They grabbed his turban to blindfold him, tied his hands behind his back, put him on a motorcycle, and drove off with him. That’s the last time I saw him alive.

The other witness, a 39-year-old man, was among the people who found the victim’s body, “under a tree [with] a bullet wound in the head and two in his chest.”

Residents said that there were no JNIM fighters in Djenné on the days of the killings and the abduction. They said the victims were targeted because they were Fulani. Islamist armed groups, including JNIM, have long recruited from Fulani communities in the area. Malian authorities and allied ethnic militias have repeatedly equated Fulani civilians with Islamist fighters to justify killings and other serious abuses.

Niono, Ségou Region, July 12

On July 12 at about 3 p.m., Malian soldiers shot and killed five girls, ages 10 to 13, who were harvesting rice in a field about three kilometers from Niono town.

The soldiers took the victims’ bodies to the morgue at Niono hospital and later apologized to their families, acknowledging that they had made a mistake. They said that earlier that day, around midday, they had come under attack approximately nine kilometers away. When they later saw heads emerging from the rice fields, they mistakenly believed they were the attackers and opened fire.

The father of three of the victims, a 46-year-old Fulani man, said: 

When I arrived, the hospital was cordoned off by soldiers. I went inside and a nurse told me, ‘The soldiers brought the children’s bodies here.’ … The nurse confirmed the children had been shot by the army […] and then he led me to the morgue. That’s where I found my three children lying, their bodies riddled with bullets. Devastated, I asked the nurse, “What happened to them? They were just kids going to work in the fields, they weren’t fighting in any war! Why are they coming back like this?”

“An army captain came all the way to our home in person to apologize to us,” said the father of the two other victims, a 59-year-old ethnic Dogon man. “He told us that they were completely sorry and that their intention was never to kill children.” The other father said he received a similar explanation from the soldiers.

It is evident that the soldiers did not do everything feasible to verify that the targets of the attack were combatants, resulting in the killing of civilians in violation of the laws-of-war. 

As of mid-September, the government had not, to Human Rights Watch’s knowledge, opened an investigation into this incident, nor had the families been offered any reparations. 

Abuses by JNIM and FLA Armed Groups

Tabrichat, Gao Region, July 18

On July 18, JNIM and FLA fighters attacked a Malian military and Africa Corps convoy traveling from Anefis to the city of Gao near Tabrichat village in the Gao region. Both armed groups claimed responsibility for the attack, with JNIM noting “heavy casualties and significant material damage to the enemy,” and the FLA stating there were “heavy losses on the enemy side, several dead left on the battlefield, dozens of injured as well as prisoners.” 

International media and human rights organizations reported that the armed groups captured dozens of Malian soldiers, tortured several, and then executed many. Radio France Internationale reported that JNIM and FLA fighters “summarily executed Malian soldiers who had surrendered.” Amnesty International documented the beating and abuse of the captured soldiers by alleged JNIM and FLA fighters and the execution of at least 19.

Human Rights Watch spoke to a Malian soldier who was in the convoy and with two victims’ relatives and reviewed videos posted on social media previously analyzed by Amnesty International. The videos show surrendering soldiers with their hands in the air or clasped behind their heads walking in the desert surrounded by armed men and their vehicles. Armed men can be seen beating and shooting at the captured soldiers. 

On July 23, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the torture and killing of surrendered soldiers in Tabrichat and called for accountability.

The Malian soldier said the convoy left Anefis at about 10 p.m. on July 17, bound for Gao. Africa Corps fighters, he said, led the convoy, followed by soldiers from the Aguelhokcamp. Soldiers from the Anefis base were at the rear. He said that right from the convoy’s departure, he was worried by “the huge lack of coordination between the Africa Corps, the Anefis units, and the few units that came from Aguelhok.” 

The soldier said: 

Breakdowns and flat tires were too frequent, while FLA and JNIM fighters were following us since we left the camp. We were intercepting their communications. They clearly intended to attack the convoy before the morning. The terrorists had surveillance drones and launched rockets at the convoy…. Near Tabrichat, everyone understood that the convoy would be attacked and that when the attack happened, nobody would be able to counter it because we were slowed down by the breakdowns and flat tires and lacked any real coordination. We didn’t know who was where, who was doing what, who was on defense, and who was dealing with the broken-down and stuck vehicles.

He said that JNIM and FLA fighters attacked the convoy at about 7 a.m. in Tabrichat, in a sandy area where vehicles could easily get stuck. The insurgents began surrounding the convoy and split it into two groups. He said Africa Corps fighters in front did not turn back to help, escaping instead. Malian soldiers at the middle and rear of the convoy were overwhelmed despite returning fire. “Some managed to escape, others were captured and executed,” he said. “The number of soldiers we counted as missing after the ambush is over 50. Among these 50 soldiers, 19 were executed.”

A 32-year-old woman said she learned that her husband, an army sergeant who had been deployed to Anefis since 2023, was killed in the ambush by watching videos that circulated online soon after the attack.

She said:

I began struggling to breathe. I immediately left the hairdresser—who had shown me the images—to go to the military camp [in Gao].… I asked a soldier if he knew about the ambush and he replied: ‘Yes, but the situation is under control.’ … I told him I identified my husband in the videos … but he told me not to pay attention to fake videos produced by the JNIM and FLA’s propaganda [outlets], which are ‘aimed at discouraging and demoralizing the military.’ He told me to go back home and wait for an official military communication.

The woman said the following day she spoke to her husband’s brother who told her he had also gone to see the military in Gao but had received the same answers. They then decided to seek more information from an FLA commander. 

She said:

We wrote him the following message: ‘Was our military relative among the soldiers who were attacked in Tabrichat? Can you verify if he’s still alive?’ The rebel commander immediately responded that the FLA did not execute any soldiers but only took them prisoner and brought them to a safe place [but] a military drone bombed the place and all prisoners died. He added that if our relative was among those taken prisoner, we should not assume that he would come back home.… It was at this moment that I began mourning.

In response to Human Rights Watch’s query, the FLA’s spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, also suggested that drone strikes had killed the soldiers in the custody of the rebel groups: “[S]everal military personnel under the control of or near FLA forces were killed following drone strikes carried out by the Malian armed forces and their Russian Africa Corps allies after the clashes.”

In a July 18 statement, the chief of staff of the Malian armed forces said that “alongside the air and ground response launched to support the convoy attacked in Tabrichat by the JNIM/FLA terrorist coalition, the Malian armed forces are continuing their operations ... across the country.”

The media reported that the public prosecutor at the judicial unit specializing in terrorism cases and organized transnational crime announced on August 1 the opening of an investigation into the summary executions at Tabrichat.

As of mid-September, the Malian army had not contacted the families of the soldiers killed or missing to provide information or support.

A carpenter whose brother, a 37-year-old soldier, has been missing since the Tabrichat attack, said that he had identified him in one of the videos that circulated online:

The day after the ambush, we watched the videos and we identified him. He and his comrades can be seen with their hands up, one after the other, surrounded by the armed groups.… Any attempt to get more information from the army was in vain. His surviving comrades refused to tell us more about what happened that day. So, we have to mourn and leave it in God’s hands.

He added that no authorities contacted him or his family to provide information about Tabrichat:

I learned that the government has opened an investigation, but ... no government official has come to ask us anything.... The government has never reached out to us. Neither to offer condolences nor to talk to us about the investigation.… Authorities have shut themselves off in silence about this incident, and in this specific situation where soldiers are captured, executed, and filmed, relatives deserve answers.

Human Rights Watch reviewed a list, shared by the soldier and victims’ relatives, with the names of five soldiers believed killed in the attack, ages 37 to 52.

#43. The Public School System Has Failed American Kids. Now What?

Writing in the London Times on Sept. 29, author Evan Barker wrote a sobering account about her experience in a Kansas City, Missouri, school two decades ago:

Every day is a fight for survival, not a place to get an education. During passing periods, I’d hurry as fast as I could to avoid being 'jumped.’ I’d walk down the hallways seeing fights break out with alarms blaring and the school’s lone police officer running through masses of pupils after a kid had been beaten up. It’s impossible to learn when you’re constantly in survival mode.

The next day, the Daily Mail published a piece headlined “Huge room full of distraught children confront school district over violent behavior at chaotic New York school.” This was not a troubled New York City school, but a high school in upstate Henrietta, south of Rochester. Students “claim the entire student body has been desensitized to fights, substance use and physical threats.”

This is useful context for Nicole Hannah-Jones’ recent reentry into the national conversation. In her article “In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?” she discusses her daughter’s experience in a New York City school. In brief: absent or incompetent teachers; misbehaving and violent students; kids who can’t read or write.

>>> France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America

Ms. Hannah-Jones deliberately placed her daughter in New York’s Public School 307, hoping the presence of enlightened parents such as herself would make them better. It didn’t. Neither will more money. Her daughter’s elementary school spends $52,000 per pupil, so each classroom costs taxpayers more than a million bucks a year.

For that, they should expect teachers who show up, grade papers and keep kids under control. They also could hope for better than 17% proficiency in math and 28% in reading at a school with a ratio of only nine pupils per teacher.

Harvard economists Will Dobbie and Roland Fryer found that class size, per-pupil expenditure, teacher certifications and advanced degrees are not correlated with school effectiveness. What is? “Frequent teacher feedback, the use of data to guide instruction, high-dosage tutoring, increased instructional time and high expectations.” The proof of this concept is in the field.

In New York, charter schools—where discipline and accountability are possible—outperform regular city schools in reading and math. These are not bastions of “white privilege,” but highly diverse schools with 95% non-white students. In London, Katherine Birbalsingh’s Michaela School continually churns out top exam results, with a student body that is mostly non-White and non-wealthy.

As a former teacher, my heart sinks for the millions of American kids held captive to left-wing ideology. Their teachers no doubt read Paulo Freire’s “Pedagogy of the Oppressed” in teacher college, because research shows it is one of the most often assigned books in colleges of education. There, they learned not so much how to teach but how to foment activism.

Many of the good teachers move to better schools or simply give up teaching. The worst stay, protected by their labor unions from ever being fired.

>>> Stop Writing Blank Checks to Campuses That Protect Hate

The national teachers’ unions want lifetime employment with no accountability. They spend millions to elect politicians who will pay them more and expect less. They resist efforts to fire teachers for poor work or conduct, implement performance pay, or test teachers’ competence and knowledge. And of course, they most bitterly resist charter schools, school choice, or other attempts to give parents a choice to escape failed schools in the public K-12 system.

Meanwhile, the National Assessment of Educational Progress reveals that students have made no gains since they began tracking performance 30 years ago. iPads, PCs and now artificial intelligence are not magic bullets that can replace study and discipline. Faddish nonsense such as Critical Race Theory, equitable grading, emotional and social learning, ethnic studies, and multicultural awareness takes valuable, limited time away from reading, writing, math and science.

We owe it to our children to end this expensive failure and resume what works. As I wrote in “The Ten Woke Commandments (You Must Not Obey)”, the solutions are obvious, but the teachers’ unions will fight them to the death: no phones in class, student discipline, testing, teacher competency, longer hours, more homework and parental responsibility.

It’s not rocket science. But if we fix K-12, maybe we’ll get some more rocket scientists out of the wasted talent stagnating in schools such as P.S. 307.

#44. Bernie Sanders stirs up progressive support in Houston rally

Sanders rallied alongside Congressman Greg Casar, former congressman Beto OâRourke and others for Medicare for All and campaign finance reform.

HOUSTON (CN) â Senator Bernie Sanders brought his Fighting Oligarchy rally series to Houston on Tuesday to garner support for Democratic candidates in Texas, as part of a bid for a Democratic majority in Congress and progressive policies like Medicare for All.

While the heated Senate race between Democratic state representative James Talarico and Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has grabbed headlines, Sanders reminded the audience the fight is much larger than one candidate, one majority flip or one election.

âTo my mind, at the top of the agenda when Democrats win the House and the Senate, is campaign finance reform,â Sanders said. âYou want to disagree with me? You want to disagree with me? Go for it. But you cannot be allowed to spend tens of millions of dollars in that election.â

Congressman Greg Casar, chair of the House Progressive Caucus, echoed Sanders’ appeal towards the big picture.

“This election is not just about beating [Governor Greg] Abbott and Paxton and Trump,” Casar said. “It’s about winning Medicare for All. It’s about saying we don’t need money to bomb kids in Gaza, we need that money here for our schools here in Texas. This election is about loving who you wanna love, about restoring reproductive freedom for everybody here in our state and across our country.”

“And here is something you don’t often times hear from the establishment but needs to be said. It is time to fix the rigged system that brought us this in the first place. It’s time to ban super-PACs, get corporate money out of politics, end gerrymandering once and for all, and make it illegal for politicians to trade stocks. They should be working for you, not enriching themselves,” he added.

“This must be a workersâ wave,” he said. “Because this election is not about political parties; itâs not about changing the color of the jerseys of the people in charge from red to blue. This is about fundamentally changing who has power in America.â

Dr. Reverend Angela Ravin-Anderson, one of the leaders at the Wheeler Avenue Baptist Church, the long-established Black church in Houston’s Third Ward where the rally was hosted, said democracy requires the continued participation of individuals and the community.

âWill we be spectators to history, or participants in shaping it? Will we simply invoke the legacy of those who fought for freedom, or will we have the courage to continue that work? My prayer and my challenge is that we choose to act, and that we demonstrate that we, the people, remain the most powerful force in this nation,â she said.

Former congressman Beto OâRourke, a longtime Democratic organizer and multi-time candidate for Texas governor, balanced the sense of optimism in the room with a very direct anger at President Donald Trumpâs policies in the past two years.

#45. Trump order tightens White House grip on Fed, SEC

Under the order, independent agencies must submit for review “significant” regulations to a unit within the Office of Management and Budget, and OMB Director Russ Vought has power over agency budgets.

Agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Federal Trade Commission – which Congress established as independent from the White House – would also be affected by the order.

The carve-out for the Fed on monetary policy “seems directed toward preventing a negative market reaction to the order,” said Jeff Naimon, a Washington, D.C.-based partner at law firm Orrick.

The agencies also have to employ a White House liaison, and consult regularly on policy and priorities with the OMB, the White House Domestic Policy Council and the White House National Economic Council, according to the order.  The OMB will “adjust so-called independent agencies’ apportionments to ensure tax dollars are spent wisely,” according to a fact sheet that accompanied the executive order.

“These regulatory agencies currently exercise substantial executive authority without sufficient accountability to the President, and through him, to the American people,” the order said. “Moreover, these regulatory agencies have been permitted to promulgate significant regulations without review by the President.”

The move to expand Trump’s authority is the latest by an administration that’s sought to concentrate power under the executive branch. It also reflects the influence of Vought, one of the architects of conservative blueprint Project 2025, and broadens his supervisory powers. In addition to leading OMB, Vought also is acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

“For the Federal Government to be truly accountable to the American people, officials who wield vast executive power must be supervised and controlled by the people’s elected President,” the order continued.

Naimon noted there was strong coordination between independent agencies and the White House during Trump’s prior administration, but the executive order would now require that coordination.

Legal challenges to the order are “almost certain,” Kathryn Judge, a Columbia University professor of law, said in an email.

The outcome of any litigation is less clear, however, since the judiciary has embraced a more unitary view of the executive branch and a more expansive view of executive authority, she added.

The order “represents the largest single assertion over executive power over the administrative state that I can recall, not only in my lifetime but through history,” Peter Conti-Brown, a professor of financial regulation at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, said in an email. “Some aspects of this control represent departures from long-standing norms. Others are in apparent contravention of statute and will be challenged legally.”

“How much of the modern independent regulatory system survives the Trump Administration’s efforts at consolidation is anyone’s guess,” Conti-Brown said, noting that the Supreme Court has repeatedly expressed skepticism of independent agencies. SCOTUS did, however, uphold the funding structure of the CFPB.

Banks may welcome the development in the near term, since the Trump administration is widely expected to usher in an era of reduced regulatory burden. But “those shifts would be far less enduring than if implemented in other ways,” Judge said.

“Longer term, the result may be a whipsaw in regulatory and supervisory expectations,” she said. “That will make it harder for banks to make operational and other decisions that are core to their business.”

#46. Supreme Court agrees to consider federal ban on home distilleries

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court has agreed to weigh in on the constitutionality of an 1868 federal law that imposes a tax on distilled spirits but also bans home distilleries – that is, the at-home production of spirits like bourbon and whiskey. The penalties for violating the law include fines of up to $10,000, five years in prison, or both. In a list of orders from the justices’ Oct. 16 conference, the court announced that it had granted review in Department of Justice v. McNutt.

The justices will likely hear oral argument in the case early next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

The lawsuit was filed in 2023 by a nonprofit, the Hobby Distillers Association, and some of its individual members, who want to be able to operate home distilleries. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit ruled that the ban on home distilleries violates two different provisions of the Constitution: the taxation clause, which gives Congress the power to “lay and collect Taxes … to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States”; and the necessary and proper clause, which gives Congress the power to “make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution” its listed powers.

The Constitution gives Congress the power to impose a tax on distilled spirits, the 5th Circuit determined, but it concluded that the ban on home distilleries exceeds that power. Not only does the ban not raise revenue, the court of appeals wrote, it prevents the production of spirits that could generate revenue. The court of appeals similarly rejected the government’s contention that the ban guards against tax evasion, explaining that “preventing activity lest it give rise to tax evasion places no limit whatsoever on Congress’s power under the taxation clause.”

The federal government came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. It contended that “[a] law is necessary and proper if it is ‘convenient’ or ‘useful’ for carrying an enumerated power into effect, and ‘plainly adapted’ to that legitimate end.” That is precisely what the ban on home distilleries does, the government argued. “Congress restricted home distilling because a distiller can more easily conceal a distilling operation or thwart necessary inspections—thereby evading the requisite tax—if the still is located in” a house or a structure attached to that house.

The challengers agreed that the court should grant review, although they urged the justices to leave the 5th Circuit’s ruling in place. The case, they said, “presents fundamental questions of the extent of federal power and the powers reserved to the states and the people.”

In a separate case, Ream v. Department of the Treasury, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit reached the opposite conclusion from the 5th Circuit, holding that the ban on home distilleries is a necessary and proper exercise of Congress’s power to collect the federal tax on distilled spirits. John Ream, a retired aerospace engineer and the owner of a brewery who wants to be able to distill his own spirits, then came to the Supreme Court in July, asking the justices to weigh in on the legality of the ban and on the broader question of Congress’ power to regulate “local, noncommercial conduct.”

The federal government agreed that the justices should take up the question at the center of Ream’s petition for review, but it urged the court to grant its own petition, in McNutt, instead. On Monday, the justices did just that.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.
