#47. Children May Proceed Pseudonymously; May Their Parents?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From L.R. v. Bd. of Ed. of Jennings School Dist., decided Wednesday by Judge Joshua Divine (E.D. Mo.):

L.R. and her mother, R.S., alleged that after an incident involving L.R.'s father at end-of-school pickup, employees of Jennings School District placed L.R. in an out-of-school virtual learning program that was inferior to regular schooling. According to their complaint, the district employees did not provide L.R. with an explanation of how her conduct justified the suspension, a timeline or consistent standards for returning to in-person classes, or an opportunity to be heard or appeal. Those shortcomings, they argued, violated L.R.'s rights to constitutional and statutory due process as well as a free public education.

Since then, the parties have reached a settlement…. As to the settlement, the Court intends to approve it provided that the plaintiffs file an amended complaint that discloses R.S.'s identity.

[R.S.] argues that disclosing her identity "will effectively disclose L.R.'s identity" too. True, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure presumptively require anonymizing minors by their initials, but there is no similar requirement for parents. Compare Fed. R. Civ. P. 5.2(a)(3) (stating that filings must replace "the name of an individual known to be a minor" with "the minor's initials"), with id. 10(a) ("The title of the complaint must name all the parties."). Instead, Rule 10 creates a "strong presumption against allowing parties to use a pseudonym." A party may overcome that presumption "only in those limited circumstances where [the] need for anonymity outweighs countervailing interests in full disclosure."

This case is not one of them. R.S. and L.R. do not share a last name, and R.S. has not established that third parties necessarily will infer L.R.'s identity from her mother's.

Even if third parties would discern L.R.'s identity, the fact that she was suspended from in-person classes after a vaguely described "incident" involving her father is not particularly sensitive…. [O]ne factor to consider [in pseudonymity cases is] whether identifying a party "threaten[s] to reveal information of a sensitive and highly personal nature" …. "[S]ome cases allow parents who are suing on behalf of their minor children to proceed pseudonymously, at least when the case involves highly personal information about the children" …. This case does not involve, for example, sexual assault or coercion of a minor to use drugs.

If anything, there are weighty interests in full disclosure because knowing the identities of the people involved in this case could help third parties assess the reasonableness or unreasonableness of a school policy that has become a topic of public debate across the nation. The school district in this case has been featured in national media on the topic of discipline at issue. See, e.g., Carly Graf, The newest form of school discipline: Kicking kids out of class and into virtual learning, Washington State Standard (Aug. 7, 2023) (explaining how "[s]chool districts across the country, including in Missouri, have begun punishing students by forcing them into online classes"); id. (quoting the "superintendent of Jennings School District in Missouri"). R.S.'s own complaint invokes the surrounding policy debate about virtual learning, including what critics say is a negative effect on students of certain races. Therefore, the Court will deny her motion for leave to proceed anonymously.

The settlement, by the way, was that "[a]lthough the defendants are not required to admit liability, they must remove any mention of the suspension from L.R.'s records, promote her to 8th grade, pay her $40,000 dollars plus $20,000 to her attorneys, and make available a policy that "clearly enshrines due process protections for all students prior to any transfer to virtual learning."

#48. Supreme Court agrees to review federal home distilling ban

The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Monday to consider whether Congress had the constitutional authority to impose a ban on home distilling more than 150 years ago. (Photo from Shutterstock)

The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Monday to consider whether Congress had the constitutional authority to impose a ban on home distilling more than 150 years ago.

The federal ban was passed as part of Reconstruction-era efforts to discourage liquor tax evasion.

The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at New Orleans ruled April 10 that the ban on home distilling was unconstitutional because it allowed Congress to improperly use its taxing authority. But 11 days later, the 6th Circuit at Cincinnati upheld the ban.

The Supreme Court agreed to review the 5th Circuit’s case in which the Texas-based Hobby Distillers Association argues that people should be able to make liquor at home for personal consumption, including an apple-pie-vodka recipe.

Government attorneys said Congress properly restricted where spirits can be distilled, and that lifting the ban would go against Supreme Court precedent and erode congressional powers, according to a story by the Associated Press.

Under the federal ban, violators faced up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

#49. Indonesian Author Faces Blasphemy Probe for Short Stories

Indonesian police in September began investigating Feby Indirani, the author of the short story collection Memburu Muhammad (Hunting for Muhammad), for alleged blasphemy after an Islamist group allegedly intervened with the organizers of a literary festival at which Indirani was to appear.

Click to expand Image Feby Indirani. © Private

Bogor Literary Week organized an event featuring Indirani that was scheduled for September 20 but cancelled it days after the Front Persaudaraan Islam (Islamic Brotherhood Front, FPI) threatened to disrupt the discussion.

In response to a Human Rights Watch query, an Islamic Brotherhood Front representative neither confirmed nor denied the organization’s role in the cancellation of the event, stating: “In principle, FPI respects every citizen's right to express opinions and carry out activities guaranteed by the constitution. However, this right must also be exercised while respecting religious values, public beliefs, and the constitutional rights of others as regulated in the applicable laws.”

Indirani is a prominent author whose work often focuses on Islam, women’s rights issues, and marginalized groups. After the organizers cancelled her event, she faced a wave of sexualized and gendered online harassment, as did women who spoke up online to support her. Indirani told Human Rights Watch that these attacks sought “to silence women’s freedom to read, write, and express their opinions safely.”

The Jakarta Metropolitan Police said on September 24 that they would investigate Indirani after social media users alleged Memburu Muhammad was blasphemous. The Ministry of Religious Affairs said on September 25 that the book contained “sensitive material” that could “offend the beliefs of religious people.”

Prominent religious leaders have also called for a blasphemy investigation, including Amirsyah Tambunan, secretary general of the Indonesian Ulema Council (MUI), an umbrella body for Islamic organizations and scholars in Indonesia, Anwar Abbas, chairman of the Muslim social organization Muhammadiyah, and Saifullah Yusuf, the social affairs minister and a Nahdlatul Ulama figure.

Under Indonesia’s new Criminal Code, the term “blasphemy” was replaced with a reformulated category of criminal offenses that outlaw acts or expressions of hostility against the religion or beliefs of other people or groups. It is punishable by up to five years in prison.

Indonesian authorities have an obligation to protect the right to freedom of expression, including from unlawful interference by non-state actors. The police should investigate harassment of the event organizers and Indirani—including online gendered harassment—rather than probing alleged blasphemy in a work of fiction.

#51. France’s Riots Echo 1968. But Macron Is No de Gaulle

On March 29, 1968, at the height of leftist protests crippling France, President Charles de Gaulle boarded a secret flight to a French military base in Germany. France was teetering on chaos, and the iconic French leader wanted to know whether the army would remain loyal.

There are strong similarities but also differences with the present situation in France, whose streets are now engulfed daily in violent riots that are spreading to other European countries.

Clement Liebard, president of La Cocarde Etudiante, a conservative student group fighting the Left to keep schools open, emailed me one difference with ’68: Trade unions are less engaged now than they were back then. That reflects the trend of industrial workers being less and less interested in pursuing societal change.

But some elements of today’s protests are integral to France. The French character can be explosive, which means that France periodically succumbs to massive street violence, and this violence can topple not just governments but entire societal systems.

>>> France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America

De Gaulle was despondent when he landed at the base in Baden-Baden. According to Gen. Jacques Massu, the commander of French forces in Germany, de Gaulle said to him, “Everything is ruined, the communists have caused a total paralysis of the country. I command nothing anymore. I’m going to quit.”

Massu, who revealed this exchange years later, well after de Gaulle’s death from a heart attack in 1970, said he reassured his president that the military was behind him in case he needed to use it to quell the unrest. He urged him to return to Paris.

That de Gaulle did. The next day, back in Paris, de Gaulle resolutely told his countrymen: “I will not resign.” He dissolved the National Assembly and called for snap elections. A massive demonstration in his favor took place on the Champs-Elysees, and weeks later the Gaullists triumphed in the elections, re-establishing de Gaulle’s authority.

President Emmanuel Macron, however, is no Charles de Gaulle. The former is a weak man leaving behind him a failed economy and a country gripped by riots; the latter led the Free French during World War II.

Another difference in today’s riots is the participation of Islamic demonstrators, who can be seen waving Palestinian and Algerian flags and who have forged a “red-green alliance” with communists, also coordinating the riots. We see this alliance here in the U.S. as well.

France in the 1960s had a Muslim population of just over 1%, nowhere near the 10% of today. And today they are highly concentrated in the urban areas where the riots are taking place. In Paris it is close to 20%, and in Marseille, just under 30%.

But when you hear today’s rioters chant slogans from ’68, you realize that the similarities are numerous, too.

De Gaulle was well aware back then that street violence could lead to change in France, having himself returned to power in 1958 after demonstrations over the war in Algeria shook France, and he was asked to form a government.

The turmoil proved fatal for the Fourth Republic, with its unstable coalitions, and led to today’s Fifth Republic with its strong presidential system, initially under de Gaulle.

The ’58 crisis is not called “the Algiers putsch” for nothing; constitutional niceties were kept as the National Assembly invested de Gaulle as president and authorized him to write a new constitution. But it was street violence that delivered the death blow. Massu himself seized government buildings in Algiers and formed a “Committee of Public Safety.”

And then there was that other massive street uprising, the French Revolution, which ended Europe’s old order and rewrote borders, politics, and society, and the street rebellions of the 19th century. Baron Georges-Eugene Haussmann, Napoleon III’s prefect, had parts of Paris demolished and ordered the construction of the wide, straight boulevards we admire today—to make it easier for troops to shoot protesters.

>>> Why This Legacy Newspaper Is Siding With Illegal Aliens Over American Citizens

Today, street violence is helping the Right electorally, just like the Revolution led to Napoleon and ’58 to de Gaulle. Marine Le Pen, leader of Rassemblement National, is poised to win the upcoming presidential elections, defeating by a 67-33 margin Jean-Luc Melenchon, the communist leader of La France Insoumise. Melenchon is expected to face Le Pen in the second round of voting in May.

RN is described in the media as “far right,” but this is wrong. It is a strong supporter of French identity, and Le Pen has responded to the riots by saying, “I will immediately conduct mass deportations. Mass immigration has been a disaster to France.” Liebard tells me that the riots and LFI’s involvement give Le Pen “the perfect arguments.”

However, Liebard adds that the riots help Melenchon mobilize his electorate and train his activists. “He will have the largest activist striking force to occupy the field during the weeks leading up to the election,” he wrote to me.

Melenchon has already promised to install a Sixth Republic with a new Marxist constitution if he is elected. Let’s hope France finds a way to save herself and not export her revolution to the rest of Europe—as it did during the period known as “the Terror” in the 1790s.

#52. Paige Shelton on What Bones Can and Can’t Reveal in Mysteries

There are several “bone sciences,” but those of us who read a lot of crime fiction are probably most familiar with forensic anthropology. Remains of a skeleton are found, and investigators test and measure them to look for answers as to what happened to the person who used to be. I love all parts of a good mystery, but the bones have always been my favorite clues; the things they reveal, the secrets they uncover.

Of course, bones can’t tell us everything.

They might help us understand the age of a person when they died, uncover their diet or daily activities, or possible diseases they long suffered. But unless the appropriate DNA is there to test, they can’t tell us things like eye or hair color. We can’t know if the person was recently poisoned or had a heart attack. They can’t tell us about personality traits or freckles or tattoos. Bones can’t tell us everything about facial features.

Reconstructions are possible, but still, we can’t be sure they’re accurate. And time of death is not easy to pinpoint with just bones.

They can’t tell us about mental health or how a victim chose to be in the place they were when their life ended or was taken. Who they might have been afraid of, or who was afraid of them.

The good news though is they can sometimes point in the right direction to uncover those answers. We begin with bones, but it’s the scars and stories that ultimately give them a voice. It’s always good to have a place to start. It takes some deep digging (figuratively and sometimes literally) to bring together the whole story.

In my new book, The Bone Woman (October 27,2026, Crooked Lane), the protagonist, Hazel Dylan knows bones. As a forensic consultant, she’s often brought in to a crime scene or an anthropological discovery because she understands the stories bones tell.

Her talent was sparked by her time as a child watching her taxidermist father at work. There might not have been anything cooler to the young Hazel than a mountain lion’s femur.

But Hazel’s talents stretch beyond the obvious, past the facts that bones can illuminate. To solve a mystery, she “reads” the bones, sure, but she’s always going to dig deeper. Her talent is in her insight and curiosity, sometimes uncovering secrets the other investigators can’t see.

Bones prove a person once existed, but forensic science ensures they did not die in silence. Everyone leaves a record behind, and every person deserves to have it read. Hazel thinks that bones make a perfect Chapter One. She lives for writing the rest.

Thanks to CrimeReads for the chance to stop by today. And, as always, thank you, readers!

Paige Shelton had a nomadic childhood as her father’s job as a football coach took the family to seven different towns before she was even twelve years old. After college at Drake University in Des Moines, Iowa, she moved to Salt Lake City where she thought she’d only stay a few years, but she fell in love with the mountains and a great guy who became her husband. After a couple of decades in Utah, she and her family recently moved to Arizona. She writes the Scottish Bookshop Mystery series, which begins with The Cracked Spine. Thin Ice is the first in a new series.

#54. Where the Supreme Court favors Trump on the emergency docket – and where it doesn’t

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In August 2024, the Biden administration asked the Supreme Court to partially lift lower-court injunctions blocking its new Title IX regulations, which expanded protections against sex discrimination in education. The justices refused. Less than eight months later, the Trump administration asked the same court to intervene after a federal judge ordered the Department of Education to continue funding grants that it had terminated. This time, the government prevailed.

Both applications came from the Department of Education, both sought emergency relief from lower-court orders, and both were decided by the same nine justices. But their outcomes differed entirely.

The comparison raises a broader question about the Supreme Court’s treatment of presidential power: Has the court given Donald Trump a more favorable reception than Joe Biden? The two cases might seem to suggest yes, but they illustrate why answering that question is difficult. They concerned different policies, legal claims, and procedural circumstances, each of which could influence how the justices responded.

Across the emergency applications examined, Trump has an apparent advantage when his administration seeks relief. During his first term, the government prevailed in 28 of 36 substantively decided applications, or 78%, in the published full-term tally. During his second term, the figure rises to 27 of 33, or 82%. Under Biden, it was 10 of 15, or 67%. But that difference becomes considerably smaller when the comparison expands to include cases in which the government was defending its actions against applications filed by others (rather than bringing the application itself). At the level of distinct controversies, executive success was approximately 75% under Trump I, 74% under Biden, and 77% under Trump II.

Part of the explanation is visible in the composition of the docket. Immigration accounts for 12 identified government-applicant applications during Trump’s first term and 14 during his second, compared with four under Biden. Trump’s second-term docket also includes 10 personnel and removal applications involving presidential control over executive-branch officials and operations. Biden’s affirmative applications were more concentrated in education and public health, while Trump’s first-term docket featured a larger share of immigration, federal execution litigation, foreign-affairs, and census disputes. Comparing the administrations therefore also means comparing different mixtures of executive actions, legal disputes, and lower-court interventions.

To separate these relationships, I examined Supreme Court emergency applications involving general federal executive actions from January 20, 2017, through October 12, 2026. The primary dataset contains 165 identified applications grouped into 109 distinct controversies, with 93 controversies producing determinate outcomes. Applications are classified by administration, whether the federal government sought or opposed emergency relief, substantive issues, policy direction, lower-court circumstances, and disposition. Related applications are grouped into controversies so that repeated litigation over a single executive policy does not disproportionately influence the aggregate results. Applications withdrawn, dismissed as moot, deferred, or otherwise unresolved are excluded from the success-rate calculations. Individual justice positions are reconstructed from the court’s orders, treating justices who did not actively dissent as joining the court’s ruling.

The key question is how much of Trump’s advantage survives closer comparisons. Does the difference persist when the government is the party requesting relief, when the same substantive issue is involved, or when the court confronts similar lower-court restrictions? Do particular policies receive greater support regardless of who occupies the White House? And do individual justices consistently favor presidential authority, or does their support change with the administration and the substance of its actions? Examining these distinctions provides a more precise account of presidential success on the emergency docket than simply the overall win rates.

A presidential advantage that depends on who is asking

The first important distinction in comparing Trump and Biden is the position each administration occupied when its disputes reached the Supreme Court. During both Trump presidencies, the federal government overwhelmingly appeared as the applicant, asking the justices to intervene after a lower-court ruling had restricted an executive action. Under Biden, the pattern was nearly reversed. His administration was much more frequently defending an existing policy against an emergency application brought by someone else.

The difference is substantial. Of the 39 core applications involving Trump’s first administration, the government was the applicant in 34 (that is, 87% of these). Under Trump II, it was the applicant in 42 of 45 (93%). Under Biden, the government brought only 18 of 81 applications (22%); the other 63 were brought by challengers to federal executive action.

That difference changes what an executive victory means. When the government files an emergency application, success generally requires persuading the justices to alter a lower-court ruling. When the government is the respondent, success may mean convincing the court to deny the challenger’s application, allowing the existing policy or lower-court arrangement to remain in place.

As noted earlier, the difference becomes apparent in the outcomes. Among applications in which the federal government sought relief and the court issued a substantive disposition, Trump prevailed in 25 of 33 identified applications during his first term (76%), and in 28 of 36 (78%) under the published full-term tally, which includes three additional favorable rulings. He prevailed in 27 of 33 during his second term (82%). Biden prevailed in 10 of 15 (67%). The Trump administrations therefore had a higher success rate when seeking emergency intervention, with the difference especially pronounced during Trump’s second term (at least so far). The relatively small number of Biden applications, however, limits how precisely the extent of that advantage can be estimated.

The comparison looks different when every distinct executive-action controversy receives equal weight, regardless of which side requested relief or how many applications the controversy generated. The executive prevailed in 18 of 24 determinate Trump I controversies (75%), 29 of 39 Biden controversies (74%), and 23 of 30 Trump II controversies (77%). At this level, the three administrations look remarkably similar. Biden’s overall record is considerably stronger than his applicant-only record because his administration frequently prevailed when challengers sought to interfere with its policies. Indeed, among the resolved Biden controversies initiated by challengers, the president prevailed in 21 of 27, or 78% of them.

This paints different portraits of the court’s rulings. Trump enjoyed greater success securing affirmative emergency relief, while Biden’s frequent success defending executive actions brought his overall record close to those of both Trump administrations. The distinction is important, although it leaves the central explanation unresolved. The presidents did not arrive with interchangeable applications, and the legal burden of obtaining emergency intervention depends on more than the identity of the applicant. The next question is therefore what kinds of executive actions each administration was bringing before the justices.

Three administrations, three different emergency dockets

The presidential comparison becomes more revealing when the applications are separated by subject matter. Unsurprisingly, Trump and Biden approached the same Supreme Court with substantially different kinds of disputes, reflecting differences in executive policy, the lower court challenges those policies encountered, and the kinds of relief each administration sought.

Across the 94 identified core applications filed by the federal government, immigration is the largest recurring category under both Trump administrations. During Trump’s first term, 12 of 34 (35%) government applications concerned immigration, citizenship, or border policy. Eight more involved federal execution litigation, with seven favorable dispositions for the government, while foreign-affairs and elections/census disputes accounted for four applications each. The first Trump administration’s emergency docket was thus heavily concentrated in questions involving entry restrictions, immigration enforcement, federal executions, and other exercises of federal authority.

That composition changes during Trump’s second term. Immigration remains prominent, accounting for 14 of 42 (33%) government applications, but personnel and removal disputes emerge as a second major category, with 10 applications. Together, those two areas comprise nearly 60% of Trump II’s government-applicant docket. The personnel matters include disputes over presidential authority to remove officials serving on independent federal agencies and the ability of lower courts to reinstate those officials while litigation proceeds. These cases place questions about presidential control of the executive branch more directly before the justices than much of the first-term docket.

Biden’s applicant docket looks different. Of the 18 core applications brought by his administration, five concerned education and five involved health or public-health policy. Those 10 applications account for more than half of the government’s affirmative emergency requests. Biden’s education disputes included protecting student-loan programs and Title IX (sex discrimination) regulations, while his health-related applications included federal vaccination requirements and FDA regulation. Immigration appears in four applications, but the policies at issue frequently differ in direction from Trump’s. Two additional applications concerned federal firearms regulation, rather than capital punishment. The relative prominence of these categories means that comparing presidential success also means comparing very different statutory frameworks and substantive policy choices.

The contrast becomes even more pronounced when the applications filed against each administration are considered. Of the 63 applications in which Biden’s government was the respondent, 25 (40%) concerned health or public health and 23 (37%) involved environmental or energy regulation. Together, those categories account for approximately three-quarters of the applications challenging Biden-era executive actions. Many also arose from repeated challenges to the same policies. The OSHA vaccination-or-testing standard alone generated 15 applications, while several EPA regulations produced additional clusters of related filings.

The administrations’ different portfolios provide a plausible explanation for part of the presidential disparity, but they also raise a more precise question. If Trump wins more frequently because his emergency applications involve policies more compatible with the court’s preferences, we should expect the presidential gap to vary across issue areas. Immigration provides one test, although the administrations often sought opposite policy outcomes. Health, education, and other overlapping categories offer additional comparisons. Examining those differences helps distinguish the court’s response to a particular president from its response to the legal policies the president asks it to protect.

The differences are clearer where the cases overlap

The different composition of each administration’s emergency docket makes the presidential comparison difficult, but, as noted, it also provides an opportunity to examine the areas where their cases overlap. If the justices were simply inclined to favor one president over another, we would expect a relatively consistent difference across subject areas. Instead, the size and direction of the presidential advantage change considerably depending on the issue.

Immigration provides the most pronounced contrast. Among substantively decided government-applicant applications, Trump prevailed in 11 of 12 immigration matters during his first term, or 92%. His second administration has prevailed in 11 of 12, also 92%. Biden, by comparison, succeeded in two of four, or 50%. These are application-level figures, and related cases sometimes concern the same underlying policy. Nevertheless, they identify immigration as an area in which the Trump administrations achieved considerably greater success than Biden when seeking emergency intervention.

One of the closest comparisons involves the Migrant Protection Protocols, better known as Remain in Mexico – which required non-Mexican asylum seeks to stay in Mexico while their case was processed. In March 2020, the first Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stay a lower-court injunction restricting the program. The justices granted the application, allowing the policy to remain operative while litigation continued. Justice Sonia Sotomayor would have denied the request. In Aug. 2021, the Biden administration sought emergency relief from a different injunction requiring continued implementation of the same program after Biden had attempted to terminate it. This time, the court denied the government’s application, with Justices Stephen Breyer, Sotomayor, and Elena Kagan indicating that they would have granted relief.

In denying Biden’s application, the court specifically questioned whether his administration was likely to succeed in defending the explanation it had supplied for rescinding the program under federal law. The later merits proceedings further complicate the comparison. In June 2022, the Supreme Court reversed the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit’s judgment and held that federal immigration law did not require the administration to continue Remain in Mexico. The earlier emergency denial therefore cannot be treated as a final judicial endorsement of Trump’s policy over Biden’s.

Other issue areas produce different patterns. Biden prevailed in all four substantively decided health and public-health applications, including challenges involving federal vaccination requirements and FDA regulation. Trump I won one of two such applications, while Trump II won its single substantively decided application in this category. Biden’s success in health disputes stands in contrast to the immigration results and suggests that a general presidential ranking conceals areas in which a Democratic administration received substantial emergency relief.

Education points in the opposite direction. Biden lost all three substantively decided education applications in the core sample, while Trump II won both of its applications. The Biden cases included Title IX and student-loan repayment disputes; Trump’s concerned education grants and executive-branch restructuring. The outcomes differ sharply, although, once again, the underlying legal questions provide limited grounds for a direct comparison.

Federal execution litigation and firearms regulation offer a different contrast: Biden prevailed in both applications involving the federal ghost-gun rule, while Trump I prevailed in seven of eight applications concerning federal executions. These results arose from substantially different uses of federal authority rather than comparable criminal-law disputes.

The results then reveal a pattern more complicated than a uniform preference for Trump. His immigration success is significant, particularly during his first term, but Biden also achieved consistent victories in certain health and firearms disputes. Moreover, the number of genuinely comparable controversies is smaller than the number of applications suggests. Multiple travel-ban applications contribute to the Trump I immigration total, three birthright-citizenship applications contribute to Trump II, and repeated challenges to the same vaccination or firearms rule affect the other categories.

The strongest conclusion from these comparisons is that subject matter makes a notable difference, although it operates alongside the substantive direction of the policy and the particular relief being requested. The presidential averages combine cases involving different statutes, different lower-court orders, and sometimes opposing positions on the same federal program. To determine whether these differences reflect a general attitude toward executive authority or preferences concerning particular policies, it is also necessary to examine how the individual justices respond as the administration changes.

The presidential comparisons look different when examined justice by justice. A general preference for executive authority would suggest that at least some justices consistently support the federal government, regardless of which president occupies the White House. Yet again, the voting patterns reveal something more complicated. Several justices shift dramatically between administrations, while others display considerably more stable support for executive action.

Justice Clarence Thomas provides one of the clearest examples. He supported the Trump administration’s position in 83% of the substantively decided applications examined from Trump’s first term and 94% during his second, compared with 41% under Biden. Alito’s corresponding rates were 83%, 94%, and 57%. Sotomayor shows almost the reverse pattern, supporting Biden’s executive position in 93% of applications but Trump’s in 27% during his first term and 11% during his second. Kagan’s support similarly rises to 93% under Biden, compared with 43% under Trump I and 17% under Trump II. Jackson supported the Biden executive position in 89% of her eligible observations, compared with 6% under Trump II.

These differences are considerably smaller for some of the conservative justices. Roberts supported the executive position in 76% of Trump I applications, 73% under Biden, and 78% under Trump II. Kavanaugh’s corresponding figures were 79%, 70%, and 78%. Gorsuch occupied an intermediate position, supporting Trump in 83% of first-term applications and 83% during his second term, compared with 62% under Biden. Barrett’s record is also comparatively balanced, with 75% support under Biden and 78% under Trump II. (The four emergency applications she heard under Trump I provide too little evidence for a meaningful comparison.)

These patterns complicate the proposition that the justices are simply divided between supporters and opponents of strong presidential power. Thomas, Alito, Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson exhibit substantial differences depending on the administration whose position is before them. Roberts and Kavanaugh, by comparison, are relatively consistent across presidents. The broader finding is then that presidential identity alone tells relatively little about aggregate executive success, but it is strongly associated with how several individual justices respond.

The Supreme Court’s emergency docket provides evidence of an advantage for Trump, but a more qualified one than the raw outcomes might suggest. Both Trump administrations were more successful than Biden when the federal government requested emergency intervention. Yet when applications are grouped into underlying controversies and cases brought against the government are included, the administrations’ overall success rates are similar. Much of the apparent difference depends on whether the president is asking the justices to intervene or defending an action already taken.

The differences also depend substantially on not just the administration itself, but what that administration is trying to accomplish. Trump’s immigration victories contrast with Biden’s success in health-related disputes, while the same justices frequently change their support for executive action across presidencies. Some, particularly Roberts and Kavanaugh, show relatively consistent support for executive positions. Others display sharp differences that align more closely with the administrations and policies before them.

These findings complicate the notion of a Supreme Court uniformly committed to Trump on the emergency docket or simply strong presidential power. Executive authority receives substantial protection, but that protection varies with the legal issue, the government’s procedural position, and the particular justices. The more revealing question may therefore be which exercises of presidential power command the court’s support, and which justices are willing to depart from their usual alignments when those powers are tested.

Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

Recommended Citation: Adam Feldman, Where the Supreme Court favors Trump on the emergency docket – and where it doesn’t, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 19, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/where-the-supreme-court-favors-trump-on-the-emergency-docket-and-where-it-doesnt/

#55. In broad sweep, EEOC moves to abandon its pending gender identity bias lawsuits

In its motions to dismiss, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and guidance from the Office of Personnel Management.

The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has requested dismissal of nearly every lawsuit it filed in the previous year alleging discrimination against a transgender worker or workers, less than one month after Acting Chair Andrea Lucas announced the agency would focus on “rolling back the Biden administration’s gender identity agenda.”

According to court filings viewed by HR Dive, EEOC last week filed motions to dismiss at least six pending lawsuits. These include cases against a Holiday Inn Express owner; the owner of a Home2 Suites by Hilton hotel in Alabama; an Illinois hog farm; a pizzeria located in Chicago O’Hare International Airport; a Wendy’s operator based in southern Illinois; and a Lush location based in California’s Bay Area.

The complaints included a range of charges, including employers’ tolerance of deadnaming, misgendering, “outing,” and harassing and invasive comments from co-workers. Multiple lawsuits alleged retaliation, with workers reporting they had been fired after coming to their supervisors with complaints about the conduct.

EEOC filed the lawsuits under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which the U.S. Supreme Court determined to include employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation in the landmark 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County, Ga. case.

In its motions to dismiss, the majority of which were filed Friday and used largely the same language, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and to guidance from the Office of Personnel Management requiring all federal employees to comply with the order.

“The EEOC’s continued litigation of the claim in this action may be inconsistent with the Order and the OPM Guidance,” the agency stated in each motion.

“This dereliction of EEOC’s duty under its legal mandate requires immediate judicial intervention,” Equal Rights Advocates, a legal group that advocates for “gender justice in workplaces,” said in a statement Tuesday on the move. “Transgender and gender non-conforming employees deserve the full protection of our civil rights laws, as established by Congress and the Supreme Court, not selective enforcement based on political whims and hastily issued executive orders.”

EEOC told HR Dive it would not comment on litigation.

#56. Syria: Women Barred from Defense, Security Colleges

Click to expand Image Officials from the Syrian Ministry of Defense hold a press conference announcing the launch of the National Defense Sciences University in Damascus, Syria, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Rami Alsayed/NurPhoto via AP Photo

(Beirut, October 16, 2026) – Syrian authorities have imposed admissions rules that bar women from most programs at two new state universities focused on defense and security, with applications closing on October 19, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria’s international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women’s role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes. 

The Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research announced on September 30 that admission to programs in law, economics and management, and social sciences at the National University of Defense Sciences is reserved for men. At the Syrian University for Security Sciences, women can only apply to cybersecurity programs. Elsewhere, programs on kindergarten teaching at public universities, some midwifery programs, and the nursing schools in Damascus and Aleppo are reserved for women. 

“Syria’s authorities are rebuilding the army without women,” said Hiba Zayadin, senior Syria advisor at Human Rights Watch. “Women can’t train as officers, and they can’t even study to be the army’s lawyers or administrators. This is discrimination, plain and simple.” 

A former higher education ministry official told Agence France-Presse in early October that some of the men-only rules predate the transition, and Damascus University, the country’s largest, still admits women to all programs. But the defense and security universities are admitting students through the general university admissions process for the first time this year and shutting women out of most tracks. 

At the National University of Defense Sciences, at which a mandatory commitment to serve in the military is required, only men can enter the land, naval, and air force military colleges, which teach engineering, and the College of Humanities and Administrative Sciences. The only part of the university open to women, the Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology, involves no commitment to military service. 

At the Syrian University for Security Sciences, the College of Security Sciences, and the Technical Institute of Security Sciences admit men only. Graduates of the university must serve with the Internal Security Forces or another competent body for 20 years after completing college or 10 years after completing an institute program.  

Women can study law, economics, and social sciences at other public and private universities and can join the police through a separate Women’s Police Institute, which graduated its first class in September 2026. But these new policies effectively deny women a path into the army. The exclusion is already playing out in northeast Syria, where the authorities refused in August to let the Women’s Protection Units, or YPJ, the all-female component of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, join the army alongside its male fighters.  

Men-only rules also apply at the state oil and gas and railways technical institutes, whose graduates must work for the relevant ministries, and in the radio and television directing department of Idlib University’s media institute. 

The restrictions contradict the transitional authorities’ own commitments. The Constitutional Declaration, which President Ahmed al-Sharaa signed into force on March 13, 2025, guarantees equality without discrimination based on gender, and women’s right to education and work, along with their social, political, and economic rights. Al-Sharaa has also publicly pledged to respect women’s rights.  

Syria is also party to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. CEDAW guarantees women equal access to education (article 10), the right to hold public office and perform all public functions (article 7), and equal employment opportunities (article 11). Syria has entered no reservations to articles 7, 10, or 11.  

Reserving professions involving care for women while keeping military, security, and some industrial programs for men also entrenches and enforces the gender stereotypes that Syria is obliged under CEDAW to eliminate (articles 5 and 10(c)). 

Shutting women out of these programs also undermines Syria’s transition. United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 and the CEDAW Committee’s General Recommendation No. 30 call for women’s full participation in all post-conflict reconstruction, including security sector reform. 

Since December 2024, women have been sidelined across Syria’s public institutions. In the October 2025 indirect parliamentary elections, women won 6 of the 119 elected seats in the People’s Assembly, about 5 percent. The UN deputy special envoy for Syria said that women were consistently underrepresented throughout the process. 

Senior Syrian officials have publicly questioned or openly disparaged women’s place in public office. In December 2024, the government spokesperson suggested women may be biologically unsuited for some political roles and said their ability to serve as judges “could be an area of study and research for specialists.” 

Women working in some public sector roles face new rules about their physical appearance. In January 2026, the governor of Latakia, a central government appointee, issued a directive banning female public employees, including school staff, from wearing “excessive” makeup at work, under threat of “legal accountability.” The directive does not explicitly define what counts as excessive makeup or outline specific punishment details.  

On the other hand, in December 2024, the education minister, Nazir al-Qadri, said the right to education is not limited to one gender. The authorities should honor that commitment, Human Rights Watch said.  

The Ministry of Higher Education should open the security and defense university programs to women on equal terms before applications close on October 19, 2026, and rescind all other gender-based admissions restrictions. The transitional authorities should revoke the Latakia makeup ban and adopt concrete measures to ensure full, equal, safe, and meaningful participation by diverse women in all public institutions, including the People’s Assembly.  

Governments and donors supporting Syria should prioritize ending all forms of discrimination, including in the security sector. All Syrian authorities should uphold the Constitutional Declaration and Syria’s international commitments and remove any provision or policy that discriminates against women.  

“Women are underrepresented in parliament, the police, and some public offices, and are now shut out of the army," Zayadin said. “The authorities have promised to respect women’s rights, but their actions directly contradict those promises. Women’s full participation, in all roles and sectors, is essential to building a brighter future for Syria.”

#59. Time Bought, Leverage Preserved: Outcomes of the Trump–Xi Summit in Washington

From September 23 to 25, 2026, Chinese General Secretary Xi Jinping visited Washington, DC, for a summit with President Donald Trump. A previous Heritage Foundation analysis expected the summit to be limited to tactical agreements rather than transformative breakthroughs.[REF] The outcomes largely matched those expectations. This Issue Brief reviews the Washington Summit’s deliverables, assesses its outcomes, and looks ahead at the U.S.–China relationship’s trajectory.

Outcomes

The Washington Summit marked the second series of in-person meetings between President Trump and General Secretary Xi in 2026. Shortly before the summit began, the United States and China announced that the Busan trade truce, which was reached in 2025 to stabilize tariff rates and the flow of rare earths, was extended from November 10, 2026, to January 10, 2027.[REF]

On September 25, the White House published a fact sheet detailing the summit’s outcomes.[REF] The outcomes include:

  • The United States welcomed Chinese progress on cracking down on fentanyl precursor chemicals while “strongly encouraging” additional actions, including the “permanent scheduling” of morphine and the imposition of “maximum sentences, including the death penalty where applicable,” for 21 Chinese citizens arrested for illicit drug production.
  • The United States welcomed two pandas destined for the Atlanta Zoo.
  • The two countries operationalized the Board of Trade by reaching a consensus for “more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction.”
  • China committed to importing “at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the United States in 2027 and again [in] 2028.”
  • The two countries “established” the Board of Investment but provided no additional operational details.
  • The two countries “continue to work on U.S. concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths and other critical minerals, with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels.”
  • President Trump will visit China in November for the meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum while General Secretary Xi will visit the United States in December for the G20.
  • The leaders “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon and no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways.”
  • While stating that the United States and China were “allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war,” the fact sheet immediately follows up by stating that the United States’ “forward military presence has preserved a Free and Open Indo–Pacific contributing to generations of American prosperity.”
  • The leaders also discussed Russia, North Korea, “trilateral arms control,” and “super intelligence.”
  • The two countries “established the U.S.–China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits related to SI,” which includes a “bilateral communication channel for SI incidents.”

On September 26, the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs published its own readout outlining eight outcomes:[REF]

  1. The two countries agreed to build “a constructive China–U.S. relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity.”
  2. The two heads of state intend to attend each other’s hosting of APEC and the G20.
  3. Both leaders agreed that Iran “should honor its commitment to not developing nuclear weapons, and no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways.”
  4. Both leaders “recall that China and the U.S. were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war.”
  5. The two countries reached an agreement on reciprocal tariff reductions on $30 billion worth of goods.
  6. The two countries highlighted cooperation on counter-narcotics and law enforcement operations.
  7. Both sides agreed to establish the “China–U.S. AI Dialogue” and “establish a bilateral communication channel for AI [artificial intelligence] incidents.”
  8. The United States welcomed two pandas arriving at the Atlanta Zoo.

Interestingly, the Chinese readout also claimed that the United States and China agreed to “conclude a memorandum of understanding on crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible.”[REF] The United States fact sheet did not include this reference, and a U.S. official has since stated that the claim “is not accurate and was not even discussed.”[REF] One issue not included in the White House fact sheet was addressing wrongfully detained Americans and other political prisoners, such as Min Zin, who was detained shortly after the May summit, and Jimmy Lai. President Trump has since confirmed to reporters that “I did” raise their cases during his meetings with General Secretary Xi.[REF]

Combined, the White House fact sheet and Chinese readout show that the U.S.–China relationship’s “floor” remains steady, but the “ceiling” remains constrained to short-term agreements that do not address the most contentious issues that underlie the bilateral relationship.

Analysis

The Washington Summit produced three main takeaways:

  1. The United States Did Not Concede on Strategic Policy Issues. Ultimately, this is perhaps the best U.S. outcome from the summit. Based on the agreements announced, the United States did not alter its policy positions on Taiwan, export controls, and strategic economic sectors. General Secretary Xi’s most recent attempt to have the United States oppose Taiwanese independence did not succeed.[REF] Unlike the May summit, President Trump has kept to a stricter script when discussing Taiwan policy publicly, only telling reporters that Xi “understands very much how I feel.”[REF] This should reduce some anxieties across the Indo–Pacific, including in Taiwan. Furthermore, through the Board of Trade, China is expected to import “agricultural goods, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics, and medical devices,” while the United States will import “primarily consumer products, including appliances, toys, holiday decorations, and car seats.”[REF]

    This list is important because the goods with reduced tariffs are non-sensitive, with few national security implications. The Trump Administration rightly kept export controls “off the table.”[REF] Ultimately, the United States reached agreements that support its economic interests without sacrificing strategically significant policy positions or sectors to get an agreement across the finish line. That is a desirable and defensible outcome.

  2. Time Was Bought, But Structural Issues Are No Closer to Being Resolved. One of the summit’s most important outcomes is the two-month extension of the U.S.–China trade truce, which extends the deadline from November 10, 2026, to January 10, 2027.[REF] Initially, the United States reportedly preferred a six-month extension.[REF] By contrast, some analysts believe that the Chinese side was seeking a longer extension, perhaps up to a two-year extension, to the end of President Trump’s second term.[REF] The Administration was right to prefer a shorter extension because it allows the United States to regularly assess China’s compliance, and the Administration’s messaging suggests China has not been entirely upholding its end of the bargain. At the same time, this extension will not fundamentally alter U.S.–China relations. Both sides will continue to compete while “buying time” to strengthen their advantages and reduce external vulnerabilities. While the truce extension incentivizes compliance, it is unlikely to result in any breakthroughs.

  3. Optics Mattered, But They Were More Complicated Than Perceived. Much attention has been paid to General Secretary Xi’s reception in Washington. On the surface, many have criticized President Trump’s willingness to, literally, roll out the red carpet for the Chinese leader. This summit served as the first state visit for a Chinese leader in more than 10 years and an unusual instance of President Trump personally greeting a visiting foreign leader on the tarmac. A closer review, however, reveals that the optics may have been more mixed than some have perceived.

    As General Secretary Xi was welcomed by President Trump at Joint Base Andrews, two B-1B Lancer bombers flew over both leaders,[REF] sending a very different message than President Trump’s greeting in Beijing by dozens of children waving flags and singing songs. The next day, a B-2 Spirit bomber and four F-22 Raptors flew over the White House as President Trump and Xi participated in a military ceremony.[REF] Then, during the state dinner, performances included selections from Les Misérables, including “Do You Hear the People Sing?” which was censored in China following 2019 pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong.[REF] At the National Archives, President Trump showed General Secretary Xi America’s founding documents.

    A “last minute” change was made, however, to remove a display of Chinese artifacts after Beijing became “irate” over the planned inclusion of the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco, because “the U.S. and Japan signed it, but not China.”[REF] Notably, the treaty “leaves the status of Taiwan undetermined and does not state that the island belongs to Beijing.”[REF] The United States also reportedly considered showcasing the Six Assurances and the Three Communiqués, but the documents were “ultimately not included.”[REF] Overall, while it will not fundamentally alter the trajectory of U.S.–China relations, the summit’s pageantry carried different messages and symbolism designed to demonstrate American strength while potentially pressing into Chinese sensitivities, even as some actions may be perceived as unnecessary.

Looking Ahead

With the trade truce sustained and future meetings expected to occur in only two months, policy analysts should track five primary issues through the start of 2027.

  1. The Trade Truce. While it is possible for the truce to be extended further in 2027, analysts should also consider under which conditions the truce will not be extended. Both sides are emphasizing a “reciprocal” nature to “constructive strategic stability,” with rare earths, fentanyl, Taiwan, and trade already known to be potential flashpoints. Before the summit, the United States believed that China was only “fulfilling two-thirds of [its rare earth commitments].”[REF] Almost immediately after the summit, U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue warned that “it’s going to be a bumpy road over the next year” as the United States seeks to “establish independence again on rare earth elements, pharmaceuticals, [and] commercial shipbuilding.”[REF] These statements raise the question of whether the United States will determine that extending the truce is no longer in its interest. China could also make the same decision if it believes it could extract U.S. concessions by reimposing significant export controls on rare earths. China could also reassess its position following the U.S. midterm elections. Therefore, while both sides currently have incentives to continue the truce, analysts should not automatically assume this will be the case, especially if evidence grows of Chinese noncompliance.
  2. APEC and the G20. It is possible for the leaders’ APEC and G20 meetings to result in additional deliverables, but if the September summit itself produced few unexpected outcomes, these two meetings will likely have even fewer outcomes. Instead, the purpose of these meetings will likely be to sustain a floor in the relationship, maintain leader-to-leader interactions, serve as a “safety valve” to address any immediate disputes, and lay the groundwork for 2027 interactions, including a potential trade truce extension. One emerging issue, however, could be establishing “reciprocal nuclear site visits” following “US concerns about China’s rapidly growing nuclear weapons program and after the last remaining arms control agreement between the US and Russia expired earlier this year.”[REF] If the reporting is accurate, the discussions demonstrate the issue’s increased importance to the Trump Administration, even if potential visits would provide only limited visibility into China’s broader and rapidly expanding nuclear arsenal.
  3. Taiwan Policy. On one hand, the Trump Administration did not offer any concessions on Taiwan. On the other hand, questions about a stalled $14 billion arms package for Taiwan remain. The additional planned meetings may complicate the timing of the package, potentially pushing action into early 2027, which is another reason why the two-month truce extension matters. To be clear: The Trump Administration approved nearly 40 percent more arms sales to Taiwan in 2025 alone than the Biden Administration did in its full four years.[REF] In fact, no U.S. President has approved more arms sales to Taiwan in American history than President Trump.[REF] Still, it is in America’s security and economic interests to approve the currently stalled arms sale package as soon as reasonably possible because it supports deterrence across the Taiwan Strait and helps to sustain a free and open Indo–Pacific. It is also important to avoid setting the precedent that Taiwan arms packages are negotiable.
  4. AI Policy. Debates within the United States about AI safety, namely about the potential need to “slow down” AI development or “pace the frontier,” are increasingly relevant to the U.S.–China relationship. China engages in widespread distillation attacks on U.S. large language models, such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini.[REF] This means that Chinese developers can generate large volumes of outputs from U.S. models and use those outputs to train Chinese models to replicate aspects of the U.S. models’ capabilities.[REF] In other words, China’s AI “advancements” are linked in important, though not exclusive, respects to U.S. AI advancements. The Trump Administration has in recent months grown more vocal in condemning these practices.[REF] Furthermore, as AI-related security incidents continue to occur, including breaking out of digital sandboxes and conducting autonomous hacking,[REF] the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) must tackle a significant challenge: How can China advance AI without potentially compromising the CCP’s grasp on power?[REF] Thus, the establishment of a U.S.–China Super Intelligence Dialogue is a reasonable starting point to address shared interests and concerns about AI developments, but it should be viewed as merely the starting point for bilateral conversations regarding AI. Additionally, as with other issues, a “dialogue” will not solve significant and ongoing policy challenges about AI, and mistrust between the two countries will severely restrict cooperation. To this point, the United States should be wary of Chinese AI commitments and operate under the assumption that China will seek to gain advantages while protecting the CCP’s legitimacy in any cooperative arrangement.
  5. Wrongfully Detained Americans. While it is good news that President Trump raised Min Zin’s case directly with General Secretary Xi, it is unfortunate that no additional breakthrough has yet been announced. It did take multiple weeks following the May summit to secure and announce Pastor Ezra Jin’s release, however, so it is possible that discussions are ongoing through diplomatic channels. More broadly, it is important that “hostage diplomacy” does not become a routine part of China’s playbook as a means of extracting concessions from the United States. If a suitable deal, in accordance with U.S. national security interests, cannot be reached to secure Min Zin and Dr. Youlin Chen, the United States should consider imposing costs in response to Beijing’s unjust actions against American citizens.

Conclusion

The Washington Summit met expectations. While diplomatic interactions will continue, the United States and China remain locked in a state of competition, and meetings can only hide so much of the deep mistrust between them. In a highly competitive relationship, avoiding bad outcomes and limiting the escalation of tensions can be a meaningful success. Even within a narrow operating lane, the Trump Administration’s China policy should continue to prioritize holding China accountable to its commitments, safeguarding U.S. advantages, and putting the American people first.

Andrew J. Harding is Policy Analyst for National Security and Indo–Pacific Affairs in the Asian Studies Center at The Heritage Foundation.

ST. PAUL, Minn. (CN) â A legal battle over digital asset mining in Arkansas landed before the Eighth Circuit Tuesday, as state officials urged the court to lift an injunction blocking state law limiting foreign ownership.

At the heart of the debate is Arkansasâ Act 174, passed in 2024 to create a permitting scheme for electricity-consuming digital asset mining operations, a type of data center.

The Arkansas Cryptomining Association â a trade group representing crypto mining companies â sued the state last year over a section of the act prohibiting certain foreign parties from owning an interest in such operations.

Prohibited parties include citizens and businesses from or belonging to countries subject to federal arms export restrictions, like China, Iran, North Korea and Venezuela.

Arguing against âgovernment overreach,â the association claimed Arkansas has no right to set its own foreign affairs and national security policies, let alone discriminate against would-be investors based on national origin.

Arkansas, however, argued control over property ownership within a stateâs borders is a power long held by states â adding federal foreign oversight law is not an all-encompassing scheme meant to crowd out state control.

âRegulating property ownership and protecting public well-being goes to the very heart of state police powers,â Joseph Nelson, Arkansasâ attorney, said. âThese laws ensure that crypto mining facilities will not strain local utilities.â

A lower court in 2025 sided with the association, blocking the entire act after finding the ownership section was likely preempted by federal law and in conflict with foreign policy.

The injunction’s massive scope became a major roadblock for the group Tuesday, as U.S. Circuit Judge James Loken criticized the lower courtâs ruling, calling the sweeping injunction âway overbroad.â

âYouâre saying, âwe asked for a slice of bread, and the district court gave us the full loaf,ââ the George H.W. Bush appointee said, scoffing at a request that the court affirm the injunction and let litigation handle the specifics.

âIf the injunction is overbroad, it shouldnât stay in effect,â Loken added. âI donât care if there are one or two issues that should stay in effect; itâs an affront on separation of powers.â

Nelson shared Lokenâs concerns, noting facial challenges like this one âshort-circuit the democratic process," arguing a blanket injunction against the act â which largely deals with regulations, noise limits and utility protections â is improper, and any ruling should be tailored to the actual plaintiffs before the court.

Beyond challenging the scope, Arkansas argued the lower court misapplied preemption.

The state maintained federal foreign investment laws are inherently restrictive â designed to block bad actors for national security â and therefore states should not be prevented from enacting similar safeguards.

U.S. Circuit Judge David Stras played devilâs advocate against that logic, suggesting the federal government may have limited investment to some sort of âideal amount.â

âIf so, then going further than what the federal government would want as a matter of foreign policy arguably at least frustrates the objectives of the federal system,â the Donald Trump appointee said.

If that were true, Nelson countered, the state would have already faced government interference.

âThe federal government has been silent,â he said. âIt has never protested or suggested itâs somehow lessening the federal governmentâs ability to conduct foreign policy.â

The association, meanwhile, said Arkansasâ law risks leaving the federal government with less power and fewer âbargaining chipsâ to use when deciding foreign policy.

It also noted the act triggers at any foreign investment amount, capturing minor investments that would never warrant federal review.

Stras challenged that framing, noting federal law governing foreign investments likely prioritizes national security over actual investment objectives â which would leave plenty of room for states to step in and regulate property ownership.

âItâs a twin goal. It is promoting good economics, which itself can enhance national security,â the associationâs attorney, Alexander Jones, said, referencing policy language encouraging the U.S. to âenthusiastically welcomeâ and support foreign investment.

Stras, admitting that may be a goal shared by federal officials, noted foreign investment committees are not explicitly told to weigh the benefits of that investment against security concerns.

âYou may be right about the purpose, but it doesnât really show up anywhere,â he said.

One of the associationâs members, Jones Eagle LLC, similarly sued the state in 2024 over the law â later obtaining an injunction enjoining enforcement while the case played out.

Both injunctions now face Eighth Circuit review, though Tuesdayâs case targets the statute on a sweeping, statewide scale rather than for a single firm.

U.S. Circuit Judge Bobby Shepherd, a George W. Bush appointee, rounded out the Eighth Circuit panel.

#62. There’s a “true crime concert documentary” about David Byrne

I love the work of documentarian John Wilson, the wildly observational filmmaker who specializes in discovering strange, whimsical, and poignant aspects of everyday life via capturing the mundane. His beloved series How To with John Wilson, which ran on HBO for three seasons, emulated instructional videos to probe topics like “small talk” and “building scaffolding” and “plastic seat covers.” He “yes-and”s with his subjects, allowing his initial inquiry to sidetrack him on paths of exploration that bring him to strange places and introduces him to wild people—experiences that help him refine his initial inquiries in unexpected ways. If I might attempt to ascribe a unifying thesis to his approach: his work is about the surreal, and often surprising, things that lurk beneath the quotidian, the perennial, and the forgettable aspects of modern human life.

Wilson, whose canvas is usually the city of New York, has just released a delightful documentary called The History of Concrete, which is about how he is trying to make a documentary about the history of concrete. It is his first feature, and it was met with critical acclaim. Personally, I enjoyed it. Following my viewing of the film, I looked into Wilson’s filmography. It was early in the morning (much earlier than I normally wake, but my baby is teething and was screaming all night before settling down at 5:30 am and leaving me feeling like this), which is when I normally can’t think of anything else to do besides go down Wikipedia rabbit holes, which is why I now know everything there is to (reasonably) know about Phineas Gage, Stendhal syndrome, and the Battle of Zutphen.

Anyway, it turns out, John Wilson made a documentary short in 2015 featuring the filmmaker David Byrne. Wilson was hired by the filmmakers Bill and Turner Ross to help them in their capture of Byrne’s multimedia arena tour, Contemporary Color. But Wilson made his own short about the experience, Temporary Color, which is about how he was hired by the filmmakers Bill and Turner Ross to help them in their capture of Byrne’s multimedia arena tour, Contemporary Color, but ultimately doesn’t have too much work much to do, and gets sidetracked when he realizes that Byrne’s tour destinations correspond with the escape route of two convicts on the lam, and begins to tell their story, turning the concert video into a true-crime doc, instead.

It’s funny, it’s strange, it is both very Byrne-ian and very Wilson-ian.

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. #64. Federal judge sides with Biden Labor Dept. on ESG fiduciary rule

A Texas Northern District Court judge said the rule is still valid under Loper Bright and does not violate the Employment Retirement Income Security Act of 1974.

The Labor Department rule in question, “Prudence and Loyalty in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights,” was finalized in 2022 and has been in effect since January 2023. The rule was designed to overturn guidance the agency issued in 2020 under the first Trump administration that forbade fiduciaries from utilizing “non-pecuniary” factors in investment decisions.

The 2022 rule was designed to overturn a “chilling effect” that the Biden administration’s Labor Department said was witnessed under the 2020 rule. The guidance revised the agency’s tiebreaker standard to allow for consideration of collateral benefits like ESG in the event that two or more investments would equally serve the plan’s best interests but it would be imprudent to invest in both or all options.

The DOL rule has been repeatedly challenged by a coalition of 26 Republican-led states, who argued it runs afoul of ERISA and exceeded the agency’s statutory authority. However, Kacsmaryk disagreed in his Feb. 14 ruling and said such a reading of the law “embodies the wooden textualism that courts should endeavor to avoid.”

“Under the rule, a fiduciary faced with choosing between investment options — that all equally serve the beneficiaries' financial interests — does not advance the interests of nonbeneficiaries nor act for a purpose other than their financial benefit when he chooses based on collateral factors,” the judge ruled. “Plaintiffs' interpretation of ERISA would demand arbitrary randomness to choose between such investment options.”

The Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo case — which determined the fate of the Chevron doctrine — was decided in the time between Kacsmaryk’s initial dismissal of the case and when the plaintiffs and the Biden administration’s Labor Department argued before the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court’s decision in June 2024 overturned the Chevron doctrine, which previously directed courts to give agencies deference in their interpretations of ambiguous law statutes.

While the parties had opposing views on how Chevron’s demise affected the case at hand, the Fifth Circuit refused to rule on the case, but vacated the initial dismissal and asked Kacsmaryk whether the rule can be squared with ERISA or the Administrative Procedure Act in light of Loper Bright.

Kacsmaryk said Loper Bright “did not disturb how courts evaluate a rule under the APA's arbitrary and capricious standard,” in his ruling Friday. He said the overturn of the Chevron doctrine should change how courts should interpret statutes, but not how they review the reasonableness of agency decisions.

The judge said that the tiebreaker standard in the 2022 rule does not violate ERISA’s duty of loyalty nor its requirement that fiduciaries act “solely” and for the “exclusive” benefit of the plan’s financial interests. Kacsmaryk said ERISA defines “whose interest the fiduciary must protect” and what their purpose is, but “says nothing of what they may consider.”

“Just as a driver, duty-bound to choose the fastest route to his destination, may choose the most scenic of two routes that each bring him to his destination at the same time, so too can a fiduciary choose a preferable investment option between two that will equally satisfy his duty of loyalty,” the judge wrote.

The coalition of Republican-led states were also joined in their lawsuit by public oilfield services company Liberty Energy, where Energy Secretary Chris Wright served as CEO at the time. The plaintiffs have previously signaled a willingness to fight the case all the way to the Supreme Court, but first it will return to the Fifth Circuit panel that initially heard the arguments.

However, it remains to be seen how the Trump administration’s Labor Department will handle the case. Experts have previously expressed concerns about the DOL’s rule being one of the Biden administration’s ESG-related regulations likely to be put on the chopping block under Trump.

#65. F1’s Rwanda Race Could Be Bad News for Rights

Click to expand Image Rwanda's President Paul Kagame delivers remarks during the announcement of the Formula 1 African Grand Prix at BK Arena in Kigali on October 13, 2026. © 2026 Jean Baptiste Nkurunziza/AFP via Getty Images

Formula One’s decision this week to bring a Grand Prix to Rwanda in the early 2030s could be an important moment for Africa. The continent deserves more prominence on the global sporting calendar.

But the 10-year agreement between Formula One and Rwanda also brings significant human rights risks.

The Rwandan government’s repression means journalists and others who challenge the government’s relentlessly positive image of the country may be at risk prior to, during, and after race weekends. The Rwandan government has long targeted independent media and political opponents both within Rwandan and abroad, including through torture, unlawful military detention, enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.

Human Rights Watch has also documented how Rwanda’s authorities routinely round up and detain homeless people and street venders before large events. People detained in the capital Kigali are held in a large warehouse—labeled a “transit center”—until foreign visitors have left. For example, some of the city’s poorest and most marginalized people were locked up prior to an international conference in 2021.

Rwanda, like other countries, has also used past high-profile sports deals and races to distract from its abysmal human rights record, a tactic known as “sportswashing.” Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement, large-scale forced recruitment and arbitrary detention campaigns, and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law.

Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One on February 24 to ask how it is addressing the risks of sportswashing and of human rights abuses connected to its events, including regarding Rwanda’s bid to host an F1 Grand Prix. We’ve yet to receive a response.

Prior to giving the green light to racing in Rwanda, Formula One should conduct an in-depth assessment of human rights risks, including by consulting with civil society groups inside and outside the country. Formula One’s agreement with the Rwandan government should include commitments, with measurable benchmarks, to protect national and international journalists covering the sport. Formula One should also address the risk of the Rwandan government using motorsport to sportswash its record.

Bringing Formula One back to Africa is good for the sport and for the continent. But the Rwandan government’s repression—at home and abroad—means Formula One can’t cut corners on human rights.
