#66. Preventing the Next World War

It’s clear from the increasingly bellicose actions of the People’s Republic of China that the PRC seeks to return to its self-appointed role as the “Middle Kingdom” at the center of the world. To do this it must supplant the United States, both economically and militarily, by becoming the preeminent power on the world stage—at which point it will be able to rewrite the rules of the existing world order established by America after World War II.

The first step to overturning that order (and replacing it with a world order dominated by Beijing) is for China to become the world’s largest economy. The second and most threatening step is for China to make itself the dominant military power in the Western Pacific and expel American forces from the region while ending the long-standing system of alliances that the United States has maintained in the Indo-Pacific for the past several decades. The most decisive way for the PRC could do this would be to defeat U.S. forces in a large-scale military conflict.

China today is a threat in a way that the Soviet Union, even at the height of its power, never was. At its strongest, the Soviet Union’s economy was only one-half that of the United States and was handicapped by not having a population large enough to fully support the necessary economic growth of a world power. Today, the PRC economy is slightly more than two-thirds as large as the U.S. economy. China has the world’s largest navy and largest concentration of missiles, is building the largest fleet of fifth-generation aircraft, and is the world’s most rapidly growing military power.

Admittedly, the United States maintains military technological superiority over China, but quantity has a quality all its own, and China’s military expansion is impressive. The PRC regularly threatens its neighbors with economic punitive action, uses its military to carry out hostile actions against them, and even questions the legitimacy of elected governments. And it does all this while exporting its population around the world under the guise of economic support to smaller countries but actually to create economic dependence and situations for coercion.

>>> Securing and Defending America’s Interests in the Pacific: A Strategy to Prevent the Next World War

For these and other reasons, the United States—across both Republican and Democrat administrations—has prioritized China as its primary foreign military adversary. The United States Department of War has embarked upon a massive modernization effort to field a force that can credibly deter and, if necessary, decisively defeat Chinese aggression across the Indo-Pacific theater.

And we do mean massive. This revitalization includes investments in shipyards, missile production lines, next-generation fighters and bombers, more strategic airlift and sealift capabilities, air refueling tankers, the Golden Dome missile defense system, and a strategic deterrent to carry the United States through most of the 21st century.

Given American commitments to and responsibilities in parts of the world beyond the Indo-Pacific—including the Western Hemisphere, Europe, and the Middle East—the United States must and will work with allies and partners to deter aggression from the Beijing-led axis while other U.S. allies and partners that are threatened by Russia and Iran assume a larger share of the burden for their own security.

Everyone will have to step up. Such an axis is designed to overturn the existing U.S.-led world order, which ensures much of the stability so many rely on today. Working with allies and partners to deter aggression from such an axis means identifying which capabilities, provided by which countries, are needed in the world’s theaters to deter aggression and so avoid conflict from a position of strength.

Should deterrence fail, however, the United States and its allies and partners must field the forces and capabilities—and maintain the political will—to defeat decisively any aggressive action from the PRC or its vassal, North Korea. There are positive trends that indicate this strategy would be successful. They include especially the U.S.’s military modernization plans, which include new systems such as the B-21 that will provide a credible deterrent to Chinese military planners, and the seriousness with which American allies and partners like Japan, Australia, the Philippines, and Taiwan are taking the threat from China as exemplified by their expanded defense budgets and security cooperation.

>>> Reintroduce Nuclear Weapons to the Pacific To Reduce the Chances of War With China

Yet while building U.S. military capability and capacity while working with regional partners and allies as a means to deter adversary aggression is critically important, it should be remembered that the most credible (and therefore the most effective) deterrence posture is the one that can achieve victory on the battlefield. There is essentially no difference between the fielding of capabilities that can best deter aggression and the fielding of those that can decisively defeat an adversary.

To secure peace, deter aggression, and if necessary, decisively defeat the authoritarians in Beijing, the United States should:

  • Support a peaceful and free Pacific with the United States as the status quo power against an aggressive PRC that seeks to overturn the regional balance of power and order in its favor.
  • Encourage U.S. allies in the Indo-Pacific to adopt the NATO 5 percent spending model.
  • Expand U.S. airpower across the region.
  • Proliferate air and missile defenses across the theater.
  • Forward deploy ground-based long-range precision fires across the theater.
  • Create a U.S. anti-access/aerial denial (A2/AD) zone within China’s A2/AD zone before a conflict erupts.
  • Finance and sell inexpensive, asymmetric capabilities for Taiwan and the Philippines.
  • Forward deploy non-strategic nuclear weapons to Guam and Korea.
  • Expand maritime presence within the theater, to include destroyer and submarine operations.

“To be prepared for war is one of the most effectual means of preserving peace,” President George Washington said in his first annual address to Congress. Only by heeding his advice can we prevent China from achieving complete hegemony over the United States.

#71. Ex-state deputy attorney general accused of making AI-generated child porn

Prosecutors in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, have alleged that a since-fired New Jersey deputy attorney general used artificial intelligence software to produce sexually explicit images of children and circulated them through the communication platform Discord. (Image from Shutterstock)

Prosecutors in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, have alleged that a since-fired New Jersey deputy attorney general used artificial intelligence software to produce sexually explicit images of children and circulated them through the communication platform Discord.

Law360 reported Friday that Brian Richard Fitzgerald, 51, of the Lower Makefield Township in Pennsylvania, is accused of and faces charges of possessing child sexual abuse material, disseminating depictions of sex acts involving children, and misusing a communication facility.

According to Law360, the case began in August, when the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children passed along a tip about a Discord account that had shared an image of a nude prepubescent girl. Records from Discord led investigators to an IP address and email accounts they say they connected to Fitzgerald through a backup email address and payment details tied to it.

In Discord chats, the account holder said he only had AI-generated images, and he had made nearly all of them, according to the affidavit. When officers searched Fitzgerald’s home Thursday, he told them that he used an online generator to create the images, shared them on Discord, and gathered pictures of real children from the internet, according to the affidavit. He said he erased his material after Discord shut down his account, but investigators say they found his text prompts saved in a notes app on his phone.

Fitzgerald joined the New Jersey attorney general’s office in May 2016 and mostly handled insurance fraud matters, according to his LinkedIn page. A spokesperson told Law360 that the office fired him effective Oct. 15 and is assisting in the investigation.

Bucks County District Attorney Joe Khan said in a statement his office will vigorously pursue these cases regardless of the defendant’s profession or position.

A preliminary hearing is set for Oct. 27. No defense attorney is listed, according to Law360.

#72. Trump administration asks justices to determine courts’ ability to vacate federal agency actions

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether and when a federal court can throw out an agency’s action or rule in its entirety. In a 29-page filing docketed on Wednesday, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer urged the court to set limits on the authority of federal courts, telling the justices that nothing in the “text, context, or history” of the federal law governing administrative agencies “suggests that the statute vests courts with that ‘new and far-reaching remedial power.’”

The question comes to the court in a case that began as challenges (that were later combined) to rules issued by the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Labor, and the Department of the Treasury to implement parts of the No Surprises Act, a 2022 law that was intended to protect patients from surprise healthcare bills, particularly in emergencies or from out-of-network providers. A federal district court in Texas ruled for the challengers – the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies – but a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed that ruling in part.

The case then went to the full 5th Circuit, which vacated some of the challenged provisions. In an opinion joined by nine judges, the court of appeals rejected the government’s argument that doing so would “create a host of practical problems” – for example, that patients might lose some of the protections provided by the law while the rules are reformulated.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Oct. 14, asking the justices to review the 5th Circuit’s decision. It pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA, in which the justices held that federal courts do not have the authority to enter so-called universal or nationwide injunctions, which prohibit the government from enforcing a policy anywhere in the country. The court in that case reasoned, Sauer said, that such injunctions were inconsistent with “the ‘equitable tradition,’ under which courts can grant ‘complete relief’ to parties before the court but cannot, as a rule, reach beyond them.” The same logic applies here, Sauer suggested. Under the 5th Circuit’s decision, “at the behest of a handful of plaintiffs, those regulations are erased from the books as to everyone.”

Moreover, Sauer continued, like universal injunctions, a practice of vacating agency action as to everyone will create incentives for forum shopping and give district court orders “the type of nationwide effect usually reserved for the precedents of the court of last resort.” The practice also “has harmful consequences for the courts themselves,” Sauer said, because when an action or a rule is vacated nationwide, the government will often have to seek emergency relief, which “’forces courts to resolve significant and difficult questions of law on a highly expedited basis and without full briefing.’”

The challengers’ response is currently due on Nov. 13, although that deadline may be extended.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#73. Abusive Care Facility in Thailand Raises Broader Concerns

Click to expand Image A person lies in bed at a nursing home in Ayutthaya, Thailand, April 9, 2016. © 2016 Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters

A care facility in Kanchanaburi, Thailand made headlines in early October when photos of conditions in the facility went viral, including images allegedly depicting metal cages that confine residents to their beds. Further investigation by the country’s Department of Health Service Support uncovered unsanitary conditions and overcrowding, as well as evidence that the facility had been treating residents with psychosocial disabilities (mental health conditions) without an appropriate license.

The whistleblower, known as “Mae Phat,” appeared on television to recount her experiences at Sothornchai Nursing Home as a former resident, describing how she was involuntarily committed, forced to take medication, and physically restrained, often for hours at a time.

Thai officials promptly ordered the facility’s closure as well as inspections of 1,203 facilities for older people nationwide. While the authorities have taken appropriate first steps, conditions at the facility have raised broader concerns about institutionalization, shackling, and the treatment of older people in Thailand.

The United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs predicts that 28 percent of Thailand's population will be 65 or older within the next decade. Though Thailand has launched a community-based long-term care program for older people, responsibility for care falls under several government ministries. Ongoing shortages of qualified care and support workers as well as budgetary constraints leave many older people reliant on family care, which not all families can adequately provide.

The Thai government should take this opportunity to reconsider its fragmented policies and commit to ensuring older people are treated with dignity and empowered to make decisions about their care and support. The government should develop and implement a comprehensive, time-bound deinstitutionalization plan for older people and people with disabilities, ensuring full access to community-based services and individualized support that would enable them to live independently and participate fully in their communities.

The government should also establish a task force to conduct regular, unannounced visits to public and private institutions housing older people and people with psychosocial disabilities, assessing living conditions and conducting confidential interviews with residents and staff. This task force should also establish a hotline to receive and investigate reports of abuse and ensure accountability.

Thailand should move beyond institutional care and guarantee everyone the support required to live independently in the community.

#74. Childhood Vaccine Schedules Across Countries

There is a wide disparity across the globe when it comes to childhood vaccination policies. American kids receive up to 75 vaccines; twice as many as kids in other countries. That is why if Dr. Heidi Overton is confirmed as the next director of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), one of her top priorities should be helping to drive President Trump’s mandate to study the safety and comparative outcomes current vaccine schedule to that of other countries. 

High on her list of priorities will surely be the two executive orders President Trump signed this year to promote the health of American children, especially since there doesn’t appear to be any movement on either. 

He issued Executive Order 14407 on May 29, 2026, directing the federal government to realign US childhood vaccine recommendations with best practices from peer nations. Section 3 of the order directs HHS, through the Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, to present plans within 90 days to assess timing and sequencing, as well as “improve vaccine safety monitoring, transparency, and research.” 

Next, on August 10, the president signed Executive Order 14420 to reduce immunization recommendations from 17–18 diseases down to 11, spacing out shots across more doctor visits, and splitting the combined MMR vaccine into three separate injections. 

The president is fulfilling his commitment to vaccination study and reform, but it doesn’t appear that anyone is listening. Ninety days have passed and the task force, chaired by NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, just recently resurrected in August 2025 after 27 years dormant, still hasn’t shared the names of anyone (other than the always present HHS heads) who have been appointed to take charge of designing the study, along with statistical plans, according to a rudimentary internet search. 

>>> Parents, Not Bureaucrats, Should Call the Shots

To date, there has not been any publicly proposed draft study design, outline, list of experts needed, proposed safety endpoints, request for public comment, or even a single primary or secondary safety or efficacy study objective shared. 

The Task Force does not owe Congress a report until 2027. 

Comparing Childhood Vaccination Schedules to Peer Countries 

The inaction on this priority is concerning because the president has good reason to scrutinize the current vaccine schedule. A cursory review of international vaccine standards reveals that no two countries are quite the same when it comes to the number of vaccines or recommendations versus mandates. 

For example, by age 18, a child in the United States will receive roughly 30 to 75 total vaccine doses depending on the state. All 50 states mandate a robust set of childhood vaccines. On top of CDC requirements, some states follow American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines and recommend even more. 

Various peer countries have a mixture of mandated or recommended schedules when it comes to their childhood schedules. For example, Denmark recommends 30 to 38 vaccines. Bulgaria recommends 56 to 61. France and Italy mandate most of their vaccines in kids. Norway, Sweden, and Spain mandate none. 

Here is a breakdown of the various countries I looked up: 

United Kingdom:

19 injections, 44 different vaccines by age 14

Australia (NSW):

As many as 26 total vaccines by the age of 10, with recommendations varying for aboriginal versus the European populations. 

China:

Up to age 7, there are 26-29 total vaccines, depending on if the live versus inactivated strains are used. There are no vaccine mandates in China, and there are “no punishments associated with noncompliance.” 

Yes, you read that correctly. 

After Chinese citizens contended that the mandate violated the principles of “informed consent and voluntariness” the government withdrew its Covid mandates after just one day. And Chinese children aren’t mandated to take any other vaccines either. 

Despite the fact that China is a one-party authoritarian government run by the ruling Chinese Communist Party, Chinese citizens face less pressure to obey vaccine mandates. Yet American citizens had Covid shot and vaccine mandates before they could attend schools, restaurants, or even go to work. 

Japan: 

By the age 16 in Japan, 14 injections total, 29-32 total vaccines, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. 

Norway: 

Through the age of 15 years, Norway has 37-44 total vaccines/boosters recommended, depending on the population and/or vaccine regimen used. In Norway, no vaccine is mandatory. 

Sweden:

Through the age of 18 years, Sweden has 41-50 vaccines/boosters recommended, depending on the population and/or vaccine regimen used. In Sweden, no vaccine is mandatory. 

Austria:

Through the age of 18 years, Austria has 49-54 vaccines/boosters recommended, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. In Austria, no vaccine is mandatory.

Belgium:

Through the age of 18 years, in Belgium 49-57 vaccines/boosters are recommended or mandated, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. 

Bulgaria: 

Through the age of 18 years, in Bulgaria 56-61 vaccines/boosters are recommended, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. In Bulgaria, no vaccine is mandatory.

Czech Republic: 

Through the age of 18 years, in Czechia 46-59 vaccines/boosters are recommended or mandated, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. 

Denmark:

Through the age of 18 years, in Denmark 30-38 vaccines/boosters are recommended, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. In Denmark, no vaccine is mandated. 

France:

Through the age of 18 years, in France 46-53 vaccines/boosters are recommended or mandated, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. 

Italy: 

Through the age of 18 years, in Italy 45-50 vaccines/boosters are recommended or mandated, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. 

Spain:

Through the age of 18 years, in Spain 42-51 vaccines/boosters are recommended, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. In Spain, no vaccine is mandatory.

Germany: 

Through the age of 18 years, in Germany 49-53 vaccines/boosters are recommended or mandated, depending on the population and/or vaccine product used. 

As is clear, peer nations significantly differ from each other and the United States, when it comes to the number of vaccines they recommend and/or require. 

Buried in that variation are the questions Trump wants his HHS officials to answer. They include: Which country’s vaccine schedule produces the best short- and long-term overall health outcomes? With both severe and serious adverse events reported and important questions about safety, how far out would those safety evaluations take place after vaccine administration? What will be done to assure that those measurements will be accurately collected? 

No one has answered these or a multitude of other important questions, and the delays in appointing a team to ask, plus address these questions, make it seem like nobody’s even trying. 

Separate MMR Shots: Japan Got a “Yes”…Will Trump Get a “No?”  

Trump’s Executive Order 14420 separating vaccine combinations and spreading them out across doctor’s visits signed in August has both a regulatory and clinical precedence in the real word, rooted in bona fide drug-safety epidemiology findings. 

Japan withdrew its combined measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in 1993 because data showed that it had led to an unexpectedly high incidence of meningitis (an inflammation of the membrane surrounding the brain—a clinical emergency). When the government became aware of that, they requested that manufacturers split apart the triple combination MMR, allowing Japanese citizens the option to take separate components. While pharmaceutical manufacturers accommodated Japan’s request, no manufacturer has stepped up to accommodate Trump’s order. 

Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines

Trump’s executive order on childhood vaccines mandates to present plans within 90 days to assess timing and sequencing and “improve vaccine safety monitoring, transparency, and research.” 

Plans. Not studies. Ninety days to plan a study of a schedule that had already been rewritten by declaration. And we don’t even know any details about those planned studies. Are Trump’s executive orders being ignored? Are these childhood vaccine study plans confidential? When are they planning on their first meeting? How often will they meet? The task force still hasn’t shared the names of whom (if anyone) has been appointed to take charge of designing a study according to a rudimentary internet search. Are the task force members’ names a secret? 

In sum: It’s been two months following the second of two executive orders, and to date, there’s been no publicly proposed draft study design, study outline, list of experts, proposed safety endpoints, request for public comment, or even a single primary or secondary study objective. 

HHS Delays Needed Vaccines Studies for Over a Decade 

While the time it is taking to address this issue is disappointing, Trump’s HHS is not the only one to blame. Questions regarding vaccine safety go back much further. In 2013 the Institute of Medicine reported that “studies designed to examine the long-term effects of the cumulative number of vaccines or other aspects of the immunization schedule have not been conducted.” The Institute of Medicine authors recommended building that capacity into the Vaccine Safety Datalink. Will that be part of the testing methodology for Trump’s EO? 

Your guess is as good as mine. 

Thirteen years later, a Congressional report aptly calls our postmarket vaccine surveillance “limited” and “underutilized.” The same finding, twice, under both parties, with nothing built in between. 

The 18-disease schedule the courts restored following the reduction proposed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. in March 2026 was never tested as a whole or in comparison to peer-developed countries. And neither was the 11-disease schedule written to replace it. Washington has now rewritten the schedule twice without producing a single proposed study design for comparative outcomes measurement. 

Trump Ordered Childhood Vaccine Schedule Scrutiny for Good Reason 

The assessment that the FDA and CDC keep citing declares that manufacturers: “have inadequate incentives to study vaccine adverse effects” and that vaccine “safety and risks are therefore often poorly characterized, quantified, or understood.” The same Congressional report called for gold-standard, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. If manufacturers can’t or won’t conduct objective data, NIH officials are obligated to do so. Not immediately proceeding with studies is to surrender to the status quo on providing Americans answers vaccine safety and efficacy. 

The pattern held on August 21, 2026, when HHS sought input on whether its recommendation labels are the right ones and invited comment on: “The appropriate approach when randomized controlled trial evidence is limited or absent.” 

Did you catch that? 

You might want to read that sentence again: 

It appears that officials are on track to blow past their 90-day EO deadline. They have not publicly mentioned assembling a team of outside experts for input on how to design and generate better vaccine evidence to protect America’s kids…they appear to be asking for advice on how to proceed without it! 

Agency and Outside Experts Need to Do Their Jobs

Studying the childhood schedule doesn’t require new Congressional authority, novel theory, regulatory modification, or even special permission. The NIH, FDA and CDC already have that ability and discretionary funding—and have had so for decades—they just need to do their jobs to protect kids. 

First, they should build the study around the variation that already exists: our schedule against peer countries’ schedules, combination products against single—injection components, spaced administration versus concomitant. Create strict criteria to make sure that investigators diligently collect all safety and efficacy failures, and report their findings in real time. 

>>> Preparing Now for the Next Deadly Pandemic

Second, they should share the study protocol and publish it before a single child is enrolled. Ask for input from a multi-disciplinary group of experts to make sure important details are not omitted. After all, an essential dialectic of science is discussion and debate between experts on how to best answer a clinical question.

With that, design a study protocol with an independent, multi-disciplinary team, including experts in pharmacology, statistics, epidemiology, and clinical trial design—not manufacturers, not “sponsored” special-interest groups, not a biased panel hand-picked to ratify a premeditated conclusion. Carefully design primary and secondary endpoints, so it is done correctly the first time. Hold all overseers and career federal employees who design and author the trial accountable.

Third, they should convert passive adverse-event reporting into active surveillance and fund it permanently. Demand complete ingredient transparency of all vaccine ingredients from manufacturers. After all, one cannot fully evaluate the safety or efficacy of any type of vaccine unless the exact vaccine ingredients are known (which they aren’t). 

Finally, they must finish what was proposed in 2013. Prominently publish all data, positive or negative, and have the HHS scientists who designed and conducted the studies hold public town halls and press conferences to discuss those findings and give careful and measured answers to all questions, perpetually as dose rollouts and data rolls in. 

In sum, Americans have had questions about their vaccines for many years now, and that number has only exploded with mRNA development. Americans are desperate for answers, but are instead getting even more mRNA FDA approvals. 

Trump appointees and career employees at the CDC, NIH, and FDA now have the chance to provide Americans with answers and be transparent, if they choose. Under Trump, we finally have the opportunity to study and learn about the risks and benefits of the childhood vaccine schedule. 

DISCLAIMER: This article is NOT medical advice. Do not start or discontinue any drug without first discussing it with a pharmacist or physician you know and trust.

#76. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.

#77. Atlanta’s ‘Urban Cowboy’ returns to federal court in battle over seized horses

The 11th Circuitâs revival of a yearslong legal battle between Atlantaâs âUrban Cowboyâ and officials who seized his horses could set a new precedent for how federal courts look at the Fifth Amendment.

ATLANTA (CN) â Atlantaâs âUrban Cowboyâ on Tuesday asked the full bench of the 11th Circuit to take the reins in his lengthy legal battle with officials who seized his horses.

The case raises a novel constitutional question: If the government takes your property but no law passed by Congress applies to your case, can you still sue for compensation under the Fifth Amendment, which protects against government abuse during legal proceedings?

Attorneys for Brandon âBrannuâ Fulton, nicknamed Atlantaâs âUrban Cowboyâ for his tendency to ride through the city’s streets on horseback, say you can.

Seven of Fultonâs horses were seized in 2017 by police when he was arrested and charged with 12 counts of felony cruelty to animals. Although the charges were dismissed the following year, the horses were never returned. They were instead placed at rescues or sold at auction.

In the fight to secure payment for his horses, Fultonâs attorneys point to the takings clause of the Fifth Amendment, which bars private property from being taken for public use without “just compensation.â They argue the clause provides a direct cause of action under which plaintiffs can sue even if no statutory vehicle to do so exists.

âThe founders might find surprising some of our modern takings jurisprudence, but this would not be surprising to them: that when the government takes someoneâs horses, that person can go into court and ask the government to pay just compensation,â said attorney Brian Williams of Arnold Porter, representing Fulton.

Fulton has asked the appellate court to revive his case after it was dismissed by a lower court and let him amend his lawsuit to sue Fulton County officials under the Fifth Amendment directly.

The arguments drew mixed responses from the 13 judges of the en banc court. At least one judge appeared swayed by the idea that the takings clause could mandate a remedy on its own, while others, like U.S. Circuit Judge Kevin Newsom, seemed skeptical.

âIs it necessarily the case that every right vested by the Constitution brings with it a judicially enforceable right?â asked Newsom, an appointee of Donald Trump. âIs that, like, written in the stars?â

Fulton sued the Fulton County Board of Commissioners, former Atlanta District Attorney Paul Howard and Rebecca Guinn, the then-CEO of an animal welfare organization in charge of managing Fulton County Animal Services. He claimed his rights were violated when the value of the horses was not paid to him.

Cameron Norris of Consovoy McCarthy, an attorney representing the board of commissioners, agreed that the government has an obligation to pay just compensation when taking property for public use but called Williamsâ arguments extreme.

âThis case is easy,â Norris said. âMy friend concedes thereâs adequate alternative ways to get just compensation, he just didnât use them against the county under [Section] 1983 â¦ There is no explicit cause of action under the takings clause itself.â

Fulton initially sued under Section 1983, a federal law allowing plaintiffs to sue state and local governments when their official policies violate the Constitution. But a Georgia federal judge dismissed the case in 2021, ruling Fulton had not shown the county had a policy or practice in place that caused his constitutional injury.

An 11th Circuit panel sided with Fulton in a 2025 decision and overturned the dismissal. But that ruling was itself tossed out when a majority of the court’s judges voted to rehear the case.

On Tuesday, Newsom and U.S. Circuit Judge Robin Rosenbaum appeared at odds over whether the right to sue the federal government for just compensation under the Fifth Amendment had always existed.

âCongress never vested [federal courts] with federal question jurisdiction until 1875,â Newsom said. âThese claims proceeded in state court. To the extent that the federal government was involved at all, it was through Congress. So how can you say for 80 years everyone misunderstood this?â

Rosenbaum, an appointee of Barack Obama, noted there was a âdifferent model of enforcementâ at the time of the countryâs founding because Congress did not want to part with its authority.

âWhen that became unworkable, Congress created the court of federal claims and federal question jurisdiction,â Rosenbaum said. âWhy isnât it simply the case that the right was always there, the question was how it would be enforced?â

U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Luck suggested the appeals court may not even need to decide the issue. The Trump appointee insisted Fulton âhas other available avenuesâ to get the compensation to which heâs entitled.

Chief U.S. Circuit Judge William Pryor echoed Luckâs concerns. The George W. Bush appointee said if Fulton âfailed to take advantage of other available remedies,â it was not incumbent on the court to âembark on this expedition of recognizing a constitutional right of action.â

Tuesdayâs en banc panel included six Trump appointees, three Obama appointees, two Joe Biden appointees, one George W. Bush appointee and one Ford appointee. The court did not signal when it will issue a decision in the appeal.

#78. Second Amendment Roundup: Saving Lives at Silver Rail Elementary

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

After School District bans licensed pistols, license holder saves children.

On October 15, I published a post arguing that true "sensitive places" where guns are banned must have armed protection.  The same day, a murderer broke into a "gun-free-zone" school in Oregan and began shooting children and teachers.  A dad of two girls at the school just happened to be driving by and grabbed his pistol, rushed into the school, and "neutralized" the killer with several shots.  He was a concealed pistol licensee.

Silver Rail Elementary School is a public school in the Bend-La Pine Schools District with roughly 400 students, kindergarten through fifth grade, and approximately 40 staff members.  It is located in Bend, Oregon.  On October 15, a 16-year-old former special-needs student threw a shotgun over a fence outside the school and then scaled the fence.  A passerby verbally confronted the teenager, who fired three shots at his truck.  The driver called 911 at 12:59 p.m.

Kaylub Giamanco, a concealed pistol licensee, was also passing by when he saw the intruder shoot at the truck and then shoot the glass panes on two double doors to get inside the school.  He reached for his .40-caliber pistol and rushed in through the same door.  But the killer had already shot and killed three boys and a teacher and wounded another boy and a teacher.  Another teacher threw a phone at the suspect, tackled him, and attempted to disarm him.  As they struggled, Giamanco entered the room and shot the teen several times, killing him.

The killer fired as many as 15 rounds from a Maverick 88 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, which his mother had legally purchased.  He had 44 more shotshells on his person and in his backpack.  His devastation would have been far worse had not Giamanco intervened.

Besides a round in the chamber, the Maverick 88 shotgun holds either five or seven rounds in the magazine, depending on the model.  Manufactured by Mossberg, the shotgun is typically used for protection and for hunting.  It would not be an "assault weapon" under any of the laws that ban them, which exempt pump-action firearms.

Police arrived on the scene at 1:02 p.m. after being advised that the suspect had already been shot by a community member who had pursued the gunman.  An armed citizen had ended the tragedy minutes before police could arrive.  For the above, see ABC news account here.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek reacted to the event as follows: "To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well."

Just last year, Governor Kotek signed S.B. 243, the Community Safety Firearms Act, which her press release said "will help prevent mass shooting events in Oregon."  "This matters to every parent dropping their kid off at school," in her words.

As revised by S.B. 243, Oregon law makes it a felony to possess a firearm in a public building, but if the building is a school, it is an affirmative defense that the person has a concealed handgun license, in which case it is a misdemeanor.  ORS 166.370(1), (3)(g).  However, a district school board "may adopt a policy providing that the affirmative defense … concerning persons licensed to carry a concealed handgun … does not apply to the possession of firearms on the grounds of the schools controlled by the board."  ORS 166.377(1).  A board that adopts the policy must "Post a clearly visible sign, at all normal points of entry to the school grounds subject to the policy…."  Id.

The only effect of this policy is to criminalize a concealed handgun licensee from possession of a handgun at a school.  It was already an offense for a member of the general public to possess a firearm at a school.  Given that murder was already illegal, one would not expect a person intent on homicide to be dissuaded by a sign.

Only 25 of the 197 school districts in Oregon have adopted this policy, one of them being the Bend-La Pine School District.  That policy prohibits school staff members, such as the teacher who threw her phone at the attacker, from being armed even if they are concealed pistol licensees.

It also means that the brave community member who entered the school and ended the carnage would have violated the law, but for a "choice-of-evils" justification defense.  It was an emergency measure to avoid an imminent injury of such gravity that the desirability and urgency of avoiding the injury outweighed the desirability of avoiding the injury sought to be prevented by the statute defining the offense (ORS 161.200).  Likewise, his use of deadly force was justified as the defense of third persons from what he reasonably believed to be the use of unlawful physical force (ORS 161.209).  Those two provisions were held to warrant an adequate jury instruction in State v. Taylor (Ore. App. 1993), which was a self-defense case.

The lessons to be learned here are timeless.  Thomas Jefferson and other of our Founders recognized the wisdom of Cesare Beccaria, who wrote in On Crimes and Punishments (1764):

The laws that forbid the carrying of arms … disarm those only who are neither inclined nor determined to commit crimes.  Can it be supposed that those who have the courage to violate the most sacred laws of humanity … will respect the less important and arbitrary ones, which can be violated with ease and impunity…. Such laws make things worse for the assaulted and better for the assailants; they serve rather to encourage than to prevent homicides, for an unarmed man may be attacked with greater confidence than an armed man.

NEXT: "The Court Requires Me to Warn You That I Pose a Risk of Stalking and Harassment to Intimate Partners"

Stephen Halbrook is a Senior Fellow with the Independent Institute. His latest books are America's Rifle: The Case for the AR-15 and The Right to Bear Arms: A Constitutional Right of the People or a Privilege of the Ruling Class? He is also author of The Founders' Second Amendment, Securing Civil Rights, Gun Control in the Third Reich, and Gun Control in Nazi-Occupied France. He has written over 30 law review articles and has testified in Congressional hearings on firearm law bills. He has also litigated extensively in the field, often representing groups such as the NRA, National African American Gun Association, Western States Sheriffs' Association, Congress of Racial Equality, National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, and more. He has argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in Castillo v. U.S. (2000), Printz v. U.S. (1997), and U.S. v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. (1992), as well as in front of many other courts.  In D.C. v. Heller, he filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of a majority of members of Congress.

#79. New murder trial ordered over juror’s mental health crisis in 9th Circuit

A man’s convictions for a killing on the waters off California’s coast were vacated by the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at San Francisco on Thursday. (Photo by Jason Doiy/Getty Images)

A man’s convictions for a killing on the waters off California’s coast were vacated by the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at San Francisco on Thursday, declaring that a mistrial should have been called after a juror experiencing a mental health crisis during deliberations was dismissed.

After disagreements with fellow jurors in the 12-day trial with three days of deliberations, the juror reported that she was in a mental health crisis.

Because the dismissal was tied to her views on the merits of the case regarding defendant Hoang Xuan Le on charges of first-degree murder, conspiracy and gun possession, the dismissal was allowed, 9th Circuit Judge Michelle Friedland wrote.

“The alternative—permitting dismissal when a majority’s pressure eventually succeeds in incapacitating a dissenting juror—would give jurors perverse incentives and undermine the jury right enshrined in our Constitution,” Friedland wrote in the court’s opinion.

#80. J.H. Markert on the Cult Leaders That Inspired His New Novel

I wasn’t scared easily as a child, but I watched two things early on in my life that certainly managed to do the trick. And they weren’t just “scares” that came and went; they lingered. One was watching the movie, The Exorcist, at the age of twelve. Too young, for sure, and to this day, I’ve never been able to finish the book, despite trying on three separate occasions to do so. The other was watching the 1987 TODAY Show/NBC interview with Charles Manson.

I was a young teen at that point, and didn’t even know what cults were, but believe me in saying I’ve been intrigued by cults ever since—not to the point of ever wanting to join one, of course, because that could never happen to me, right? —and I’ve been especially terrified of Manson to this day. (Yeah, I know he’s dead, but even so.)

That interview, back then, made me instantly feel uneasy, first because he simply freaked me out—those eyes, his intensity, his quirky movements, bizarre mannerisms, and outlandish beliefs—but then, the true unease came after learning about how cults formed and with how easily people were swayed by the often-times charismatic yet diabolical leaders of them.

I knew I would at some point write my Cult Book, which became my latest novel, The Chain House, and create my own cult leader in Sal Batise, who was heavily influenced by Charles Manson.

But while Manson’s influence was always there in the background and foreground and in every creative nuance in between—especially the high-profile murder of Sharon Tate in 1969—I did, in my research, come across other cult leaders who were equally as bad, if not worse. Once I went down that rabbit hole, it was hard to come back up for air, and even harder to pick only five cult leaders for this article.

In no real order of importance—they were all maniacal, controlling, manipulative, narcissistic experts at brainwashing, and I’d rather not rank them—I’ll start with Jim Jones.

Jim Jones founded a religious organization based on racial equality and social awareness in Indiana in the 1950s called the Peoples Temple. He pressured members into giving their homes and money to the church and, in an attempt at total control, began punishing those who attempted to associate with anyone he deemed an “outsider.” His organization quickly grew, and after preaching to them about the vision he’d had of a nuclear apocalypse, he convinced them all to move to California, where they’d be safe from a nuclear attack.

As he became more controlling and manipulative and protective of his flock, Jones relocated again, this time to a settlement in Guyana that he infamously named Jonestown. Not very arrogant of him, right?

In 1978, a U.S. Representative and several others were killed after investigating reports of abuse on the settlement. Later that day, over 900 members of his Jonestown cult died by cyanide, while Jones was found dead by a gunshot.

Marshall Applewhite’s cult, Heaven’s Gate, which he co-founded with Bonnie Nettles in the 1970s, was based on the belief that they were meant to witness apocalypse from the Book of Revelations. In my mind, Heaven’s Gate—which believed an alien spacecraft was hiding behind a comet called Hale-Bopp, and said spacecraft was set to take them to a higher level of existence—was about as bizarre as a cult can get, but at the same time hammered home how thoroughly brainwashed some people can get when desperate and gullible and lost and looking for answers.

Applewhite, known as Do to his members, convinced them that they could leave their human bodies to reach extraterrestrial levels of existence, and this spacecraft would take them where they needed to go. Unfortunately for them, the spacecraft never arrived, and in 1997, Applewhite and 38 of his followers were found dead in a California home after committing mass suicide.

Gary Heidnik leans more toward serial killer than cult leader, but with the way he used his pseudo-church he called the United Church of the Ministers of God in the mid-1980s to lure his victims into his evil embrace, he could be considered very cultlike. Using his fake church as a tax shelter to get rich, Heidnik, a self-proclaimed bishop, dug a pit beneath his house—the same house inside which he held his “church” gatherings—and imprisoned, abused, and tortured women there until he was arrested in 1987.

Heidnik, who was executed by lethal injection in 1999, was believed to be an inspiration for the Buffalo Bill character in The Silence of the Lambs.

As the most recent from this short list of cult leaders, David Koresh (real name Vernon Howell), the leader of the Branch Davidians religious group near Waco, Texas, was most well-known for the gunfight and fifty-one-day standoff with federal agents, after they attempted to execute search and arrest warrants at his Mount Carmel Center compound in February of 1993.

On a visit to Israel, Koresh—as many cult leaders did before him—claimed to have seen a vision. His vision (according to…him) revealed him as the modern-day incarnation of the prophet Cyrus. He legally changed his name to David Koresh, with the first name referencing King David and his last name being that of Cyrus’s biblical name.

Koresh preached of sick “spiritual weddings,” which, in his mind, made it legal to bed female followers, no matter the age, if God had chosen them for him. He, of course, played the part of God in these decisions, and it was believed he had as many as twenty wives and at least twelve children when his compound burned in April of 1993, killing dozens of Branch Davidians, as well as Koresh.

There’s a popular saying, truth is stranger than fiction, and it fits perfectly with most cults and their leaders, because how could someone create such as thing and still sleep at night?

Well, these particular leaders believed they could, and then did it, although not without failing a time or two; so I wrote my novel, The Chain House, with the hope that it could be just as strange and frightening as the truth, and here’s to it one day gathering a nice cult following of its own.

J. H. Markert is a producer, screenwriter, husband, and father of two from Louisville, Kentucky, where he was also a tennis pro for twenty-five years, before hanging up the rackets for good in 2020. He graduated with a degree in history from the University of Louisville in 1997 and has been writing ever since.

#81. Court unlikely to alter deference to sentencing guidelines commentary

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In Beaird v. United States, argued on Tuesday, Oct. 13, the Supreme Court considered when courts should defer to the U.S. Sentencing Commission’s commentary interpreting the federal sentencing guidelines. More specifically, the question presented in Beaird is whether the court’s 1993 decision in Stinson v. United States still correctly describes the appropriate deference required. Under Stinson, commentary that “interprets or explains a guideline is authoritative unless it violates the Constitution or a federal statute, or is inconsistent with, or a plainly erroneous reading of, that guideline.” By a wide margin, the justices appeared disinclined to upset how Stinson and lower courts have traditionally approached deference to the commission’s guidelines commentary.

The legal backdrop of the arguments in Beaird

In recent years, lower courts began questioning Stinson’s continuing validity after the court decided Kisor v. Wilkie in 2019. Kisor revisited deference to agencies’ interpretations of their regulations and emphasized several limitations on that deference, including that the regulation must be genuinely ambiguous.

Because the government agreed that Kisor limited Stinson to some extent and advocated for a remand, the court appointed an amicus, Anthony Dick, to defend the judgment. The amicus argued that, as a general matter, agency deference should be viewed as subject to even more stringent limitations than Kisor endorsed. Dick maintained that 2024’s Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which discarded the court’s prior doctrine deferring to agencies’ interpretations of statutes they administer, further limits deference to agencies’ interpretations of their own statutes and undercuts Kisor. But despite his challenges to Kisor, the amicus maintained that, principally because the guidelines are now advisory, deference to the commentary under Stinson falls entirely of outside the framework that limits deference to agency interpretations.

Kevin Page, the attorney for Kendrick Jarrell Beaird, squarely rejected the amicus’ view that advisory guidelines are not subject to the general rules governing agency deference, and contended that the commentary is entitled to no deference at all.

Although whether Loper Bright limited or undermined Kisor featured in a few questions, particularly from Justice Neil Gorsuch, the justices conveyed little interest in using this case to revisit Kisor. Chief Justice John Roberts, the author of Loper Bright, said to Page that “I just don’t see” how deferring to commentary from “an agency in the judicial branch [that] issues non-binding advice, really has much to do with Loper Bright at all.” Justice Brett Kavanaugh echoed that sentiment.

Along those lines, many of the justices’ questions zeroed in on the advisory nature of the guidelines, which to them took the case out of the ordinary context of agency deference. As noted, near the beginning of Page’s argument, Roberts remarked that “the guidelines are advisory,” and that the question of deference to the commentary therefore “str[uck him] as an academic exercise.” Why shouldn’t courts “just look at what the commission meant in the guidelines” and then exercise their discretion?

As a number of justices similarly noted, when a court defers to the commission’s interpretation of the guidelines through the commentary, the sole effect of that deference is to determine what the commission’s recommendation is. A federal court is not obliged to follow that recommendation. Near the end of nearly two hours of argument, Dick recapped this point in response to a question from Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a former vice chair of the Sentencing Commission. Dick agreed that the commentary is “binding on what the commission’s advice means. It's not binding in the sense that courts have to follow it.”

Justice Amy Coney Barrett raised another point at argument, that the commission frequently sends its commentary through the same notice-and-comment process as the text of the guidelines. She asked Page whether it was his “sense that the commission, by calling this commentary, is somehow pulling a fast one, getting things into the commentary that it might not be able to put into the guideline itself?” Page denied that the commission was engaging in such a ploy and emphasized that his central arguments rested on whether Congress had expressly authorized the commission to issue its commentary. He argued that Congress had not.

Turning to workability concerns, Justice Sonia Sotomayor addressed the guideline at issue in Beaird’s specific case. For his firearm offense, the applicable guideline, Section 2K2.1, increases the commission’s recommended guideline range when the defendant’s offense involved a “semiautomatic firearm that is capable of accepting a large capacity magazine.” A broad reading of “capable,” Sotomayor noted, would mean that the sentencing enhancement could apply if a defendant’s gun merely were able to accept such a magazine, even though the defendant did not have one. Sotomayor noted that “it’s only by reading the application note do I know that the magazine has to be attached to” the defendant’s gun or in close proximity to it to fit under Section 2K2.1. “Without the application note,” she remarked, “you’re creating a sea of confusion for district judges to fill in the blanks.”

Justice Samuel Alito echoed Sotomayor’s point and asked Page how a district judge would decide what the phrase “large capacity magazine” means without the commentary explaining that. Page responded that you “use… the text and structure of the guidelines.” Page continued that the word “large” means “large for a semi-automatic firearm” and that a magazine that held 17 rounds “is the average” and shouldn’t be deemed large. Alito followed up that his “methodology would be to examine all semi-automatic weapons and see what is the average,” and “whatever is above the average that … would be the large capacity magazine?” Page rejected “that something that’s just above the median would necessarily qualify.” Alito remained skeptical: “I just don’t see how this could possibly work without some degree of deference to what is essentially a policy call by the Sentencing Commission.”

Addressing a consideration relevant to stare decisis, Justice Elena Kagan and Sotomayor both pressed Page about whether under his view a court would be required to overrule Williams v. United States, which, in Kagan’s words, indicated that “the commission needs to defer to the commission's policy statements.” Page argued that Williams should be viewed as limiting deference only to certain policy statements that Congress expressly referenced in various statutes. Kagan and Sotomayor seemed unpersuaded that Williams could be properly read in that way.

Only Gorsuch appeared open to revisiting Kisor. As he remarked at one point, “Stinson relied on silence being enough to be an implicit delegation … of interpretive authority and that their ambiguity is the appropriate trigger, both of which we've since rejected in Loper Bright.” But none of the other justices seemed particularly interested in adopting such a position.

Eric J. Feigin, arguing on behalf of the government, defended the view that Stinson’s rule must be understood in light of Kisor, explaining that the government believed that approach best fit the court’s precedent. Nevertheless, Feigin made clear that “if the court wants to say that the guidelines don’t need to follow Kisor,” the government would “be very happy with that.”

Exactly how the court will ultimately describe the outer limits of deference to the commentary is unclear. But there seemed little doubt that the court would leave Stinson essentially as it has been understood since it was decided in 1993 and that the court’s ruling would be strictly limited to the context of advisory sentencing guidelines.

Richard D. Cooke worked for the U.S. Department of Justice for 23 years, first at the Antitrust Division for 5 years and then as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia for 18 years.

#82. Cambodian Supreme Court Maximizes Sentence for Opposition Activist

Click to expand Image Cambodia’s Supreme Court, Phnom Penh, June 25, 2026. © 2026 Sopheng Cheang/AP Photo

Cambodia’s Supreme Court on October 14 denied opposition activist Voeung Samnang’s request to serve his two sentences concurrently, meaning he will spend 11 years in prison. Samnang had been convicted on charges of “plotting an attack on the state” and received sentences of five and six years.

The case illustrates the Cambodian government’s increased use of vague plotting charges to prosecute opposition activists and social media users and sentence them to long prison terms.

Samnang had been a local commune official for the Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP), the opposition party dissolved by the government-controlled Supreme Court in 2017. He fled to Thailand in 2020 after charges were filed against him. In 2021, Thai police arrested him and forcibly returned him to Cambodia, alongside opposition activist Veourn Veasna, despite both being recognized as refugees by the United Nations refugee agency.

Samnang was charged with plotting, convicted and sentenced to five years in prison in 2022 as part of a mass trial of 36 former CNRP leaders and supporters. While incarcerated, he was tried and convicted again in 2023 on additional plotting charges and sentenced to six years in prison. The ostensible evidence against him in both cases was Facebook posts related to the CNRP and his criticism of the government.

Samnang’s wife, Teang Chenda, joined the “Friday Women,” a group of Cambodian women who held regular protests in the capital, Phnom Penh, to call for the release of their imprisoned husbands and sons. The Friday Women have faced harassment from Cambodian authorities during their public protests.

Samnang’s case highlights the government’s unrelenting persecution of the political opposition ahead of next year’s local elections. Veasna, the man arrested alongside Samnang, was charged and convicted in a separate case. He later apologized to then-Prime Minister Hun Sen, joined the ruling Cambodian People’s Party, and was released from prison – part of the government’s systematic use of coerced confessions to discredit political opposition members and activists. Veasna later fled Cambodia and disavowed his defection to the ruling party.

#83. When Union Leaders Are Not Working for Their Workers

Last month, a House hearing exposed eight years of America’s industrial unions spending members’ money on union leaders’ personal priorities rather than on members.

The findings should change the way Washington hears union leaders when they claim to speak for workers.

First are political donations. The railroad brotherhoods’ PACs sent 95% to 99% of their party committee dollars to Democrats, and the conductors’ union made far-left EMILY’s List its single largest recipient.

Yet when the Teamsters, parent of some rail unions, polled its members in 2024, roughly 60% backed President Trump.

Then there are questionable expenditures. These include the Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers—Transportation Division, the largest railroad labor union in North America, spending $3.9 million at Caesars Entertainment in 2024—part of nearly $10 million on casinos and resorts over eight years.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Convention Exposes the Teachers’ Union as a Political Machine

Meanwhile, its president earned more than five times the median pay of a railroad worker. Apparently, it is wrong only when management does it.

Similarly, two former United Auto Workers presidents went to prison for spending members’ dues on golf, cigars and Palm Springs villas.

The same divide appears in the policies that union leaders push, such as the Faster Labor Contracts Act, which passed the House in June. Under the act, if a union and an employer cannot agree on a first contract within roughly four months, a three-member arbitration panel would impose one, binding for two years, without workers themselves being able to vote on it.

It guarantees that union leadership collects dues without risking members’ rejection of the terms. It short-circuits a process by which members have a basic check on those allegedly bargaining in their name.

Union leaders have also spent years pushing to replace secret-ballot elections with public card signings, letting organizers know how members vote and thereby exposing those members to pressure and even retaliation.

The rail unions’ latest top priority, the Railway Safety Act, fits the pattern. Recently attached to the House transportation bill, its centerpiece is a federal mandate to increase freight crew sizes. Leadership loves it because every additional crew seat written into federal law is a stream of dues that cannot be bargained away for things members might actually want, such as higher pay or better schedules.

Although union leaders claim this is about crew safety and cite the East Palestine, Ohio, derailment as their motivation, they have been pushing for enlarged crews for years before the Ohio disaster. Furthermore, the East Palestine crash train crew had an extra crew member on board, and that practice did not prevent the accident.

Likewise, federal regulators have repeatedly conceded they lack data showing that an additional crew member prevents accidents. The industry reports that 2025 was its safest year on record across several measures, largely thanks to technology. These are advancements that the bill threatens.

When BNSF Railway tested automated track inspection, its track geometry cars found 64,657 defects while covering 97% fewer miles than human inspectors, who found only 4,796.

Rail unions fought that shift at every turn, and now they want the Railway Safety Act to undo this technological progress, expanding manual inspection mandates and freezing detector rules just as better monitoring arrives.

>>> The Anti-ICE Campaign Protecting Mexico’s Train-Robbing Cartels

These moves would not only make the rails less safe by catching fewer defects but also expose inspectors to greater danger.

Sadly, union leadership keeps rejecting railroads’ better offers to members. Union Pacific proposed piloting ground-based conductor jobs with regular shifts and the chance for workers to sleep in their own beds every night, a real improvement over the unpredictable, days-away-from-home schedules widely considered the worst part of the job. SMART-TD agreed to the pilot only on the condition that Union Pacific maintain current crew sizes and drop negotiations to reduce crew size.

Rank-and-file railroaders could have regular schedules, safer jobs and technology that makes their work less dangerous, but the Railway Safety Act delivers none of that. Union leadership prefers headcount and dues instead.

This failure of leadership will also harm families because the compliance costs of these draconian measures are in the tens of billions of dollars, costs that flow to farmers, manufacturers, energy producers—anyone who uses railroads—and to family budgets. Higher rail costs also shift freight to trucks, leading to more highway congestion and crashes.

Union leaders have a responsibility to do what is best for their members, not pad their own pockets or enrich their political cronies. Washington would do well to remember as much.
