#85. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#86. "The Court Requires Me to Warn You That I Pose a Risk of Stalking and Harassment to Intimate Partners"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Ted Stewart (D. Utah) in U.S. v. Wang, dated Sept. 9 but just docketed today:

Defendant objected to the condition that she notify any intimate partners "about the potential risk she poses" as vague. To avoid any vagueness, the Court imposed the following: "The court requires you to notify any intimate partners that you have been convicted of cyberstalking and pose a risk of stalking and harassment to intimate partners." The Court finds this condition is necessary to protect the public considering Defendant's history of cyberstalking and her relationships with her past victims.

I believe similar conditions are sometimes imposed as to sex offenders, but this is the first time I've seen something like this as to stalkers. (Note that, once a criminal defendant is convicted, the standard for evaluating probation conditions restricting or compelling speech becomes more much government-friendly than would be the case in the absence of such a conviction.) Here's the Justice Department's statement summarizing the case:

A Utah County woman was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment [and thee years of probation] today for cyberstalking two male victims she met on online dating platforms and became obsessed with them….

According to court documents and statements made at Wang's change of plea and sentencing hearings, Wang connected with the victims separately on online dating sites in 2017 and 2018 and became obsessed with each victim. Using multiple accounts, fake names, social media accounts, and phone numbers, she harassed and disparaged them publicly and privately, tagging their friends, family, and employers.

On three separate occasions, Wang reported the victims to the federal Internet Crimes Complaint Center (IC3) claiming she was being harassed and impersonated online by them. Wang reported that they did these things together, even though there is no evidence that the victims had any relation to each other. Wang admitted that she filed the IC3 complaints to get law enforcement to investigate the victims in order to harass and intimidate them.

Wang's crimes against victim 1 and victim 2 are not isolated incidents. Wang engaged in a pattern of stalking behavior in 2013 and was convicted in the state of New York.

#87. France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America

France spent the past three weeks watching its high schools burn. What originally began in late September at a suburban school outside Paris as a protest over missing teachers, overcrowded classrooms, and decaying buildings spread to hundreds of schools and quickly metastasized into riots that included Marxists, Antifa, and Islamists.

On the biggest day, the interior ministry counted more than 250,000 people in the streets. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called the casualties the heaviest toll on the school system in decades: at least 215 teenagers and 85 staff injured, plus more than 760 police officers. Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked.

The original grievances were actually real. The response is the predictable product of a state monopoly on education. France already spends more per upper-secondary student than the European Union average, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), yet the buildings still fall apart.

Parents in France have almost nowhere else to go. Since 2022, the country has essentially banned homeschooling for ordinary families. Raising your own children at home now requires government permission, granted only for narrow exemptions such as a disability, intensive sports or artistic training, geographic isolation, or a family that travels constantly. The default is the state school. When that school fails, the street is the remaining outlet.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Dirty Back-to-School War on Target

American parents should recognize the script. Our government-school cartel spends more per pupil than almost any country on earth and still leaves most children below proficiency. On the latest Nation’s Report Card, only about one in four eighth-graders is proficient in math. Union leaders respond to that failure with another political campaign.

At its Portland convention last summer, the National Education Association pledged to defend democracy against what it called President Trump’s “embrace of fascism,” and directed staff to use that label in union materials. This July in Washington, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) adopted a resolution to “mobilize for the 2026 elections,” casting the midterms as a “which side are you on” moment and committing the union to an unprecedented turnout machine.

The same convention heard Jeff Freitas, president of the California federation, tell delegates that “we need to be in the streets” to “fight back against this fascist regime.” His red shirt read “Solidarity is the Lesson Plan,” with “May Day” printed on the book in the graphic. A separate resolution turned May 1 into a day of civic action, complete with political education and with students used as political pawns in the marches and rallies.

Politics don’t stop at the ballot box. The AFT has been a major backer of the “No Kings” protests. Randi Weingarten, who is paid over half a million dollars per year to run the union, used her 2025 convention speech to call for people “in the streets” and to threaten lawmakers who refused to listen.

This week the union’s own social-media account posted her outside Delaney Hall, the immigration detention center in Newark, shouting that detainees “play by the rules” and “should not be detained or deported because we have a broken immigration system.” If Weingarten fought this hard for instruction, more than one in four American children might be able to do grade-level math.

The New York City affiliate, the United Federation of Teachers, endorsed Zohran Mamdani. Nationally, about 99 percent of the AFT’s campaign contributions in the last federal cycle went to Democrats. The same union urged members to skip Target for back-to-school shopping because the company had not denounced immigration enforcement, and Weingarten leaned on pension funds that directly hold about 6.8 million Target shares to try to force a political statement out of a retailer.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Convention Exposes the Teachers’ Union as a Political Machine

A Freedom Foundation review of the union’s own federal filings found at least $1.4 million in AFT resources tied to producing and promoting her book, “Why Fascists Fear Teachers.” Congress is now scrutinizing that spending. Members paid for the manifesto. She kept a cut of the proceeds.

Teachers who want to teach reading and algebra are financing a permanent political operation that marches their students, boycotts their stores, and labels half the country fascist. France shows where that model ends: a system that cannot staff a classroom, a law that keeps most families inside it, and children in the street when the adults fail them.

Two exits would break the pattern. Teachers who are not on board can resign from the government union and join an alternative such as the Teacher Freedom Alliance, which offers liability coverage and advocacy without the partisan machine. A real exodus would hit the bosses where the dues are and force them to represent members instead of a party.

Parents have the other lever. School choice lets a family take the education dollars assigned to a child and spend them elsewhere. The school that drills math and history gets the money. The school that treats May Day as the lesson plan loses it.

That escape valve does more than rescue one household from indoctrination. A monopoly that cannot hold its customers cannot keep marching the next generation into socialist politics. France is the control group. America still has time to save itself from teachers’ union tyranny.

#89. The Backlist: Sarah Weinman on a Classic Domestic Thriller, ‘The Hours Before Dawn’

The expression “so many books, so little time” doesn’t seem to apply to the writer and New York Times crime fiction columnist Sarah Weinman. Every time I’ve had the opportunity to talk with her about a specific book or specific writer, she ends up mentioning ten or twenty other novels that I immediately vow to add to my TBR. She has a truly encyclopedic knowledge of both crime fiction and true crime, one that’s evident not only in her reviews but also in her work as a writer and editor, which has included nonfiction like Without Consent and The Real Lolita, as well as several anthologies of true crime and domestic suspense. Her website describes her as a “writer, editor, crime lady,” and perhaps that’s the best description of one of the foremost authorities on the genre of our time. It was a pleasure to speak with her about one of the novels that first got her thinking about the development of domestic suspense, Celia Fremlin’s Edgar-winning classic The Hours Before Dawn.

Why did you choose The Hours Before Dawn by Celia Fremlin?

I first read it in 2011. I’d been solicited to write an essay for the magazine Tin House, which regrettably no longer exists. I was thinking about novels that didn’t quite fit in with Golden Age detective fiction, and also didn’t fit in with the hard-boiled and noir fiction that was predominantly American. These were novels that were primarily by women, and tended to be more on the domestic side. They tended to deal with the affairs of the home and the terror of marriage and motherhood. The examples that I used for the piece were Elizabeth Sanxay Holding’s The Blank Wall, which came out in 1944, and which I would late include in a two-volume set on women crime writers of the 40s and 50s that I edited for the Library of America, and the other one was The Hours Before Dawn.

I think I first found it because I was looking into past winners of the Edgar Award. I thought it looked interesting, and when I started reading, I thought, “Oh my God, this is amazing!” The first line just grabbed me: “I’d give anything—anything—for a good night’s sleep.” I’ve never been a mother, but I’ve been around enough mothers and children to know what it’s like when a kid is up and screaming and you can’t tell what’s wrong. All they can do is scream, and screaming can mean anything. The child in the novel is probably a perfectly happy baby, but he screams a lot and keeps his family awake. The mother is the one who’s expected to tend to him, so she’s extremely sleep-deprived, and as the story progresses, she begins to doubt her sanity.

The reader is immediately catapulted into an empathetic relationship with the mother, Louise, because the baby isn’t her only problem. Her elder daughter, Margery, is clearly very anxious, and the younger daughter, Harriet, is more mischievous and gets into trouble. She has these awful friends who keep dropping off their kids with her or showing up at her house and hanging out until midnight. On one level, we want to say to her, “Just assert yourself,” but it’s clear that she’s never been socialized to do that. Her husband has no interest in helping, and doesn’t seem to even understand what she’s going through. At one point, he comes home in the middle of the day just to see how she is, and then expects her to make his lunch. When the book opens, Louise has decided that they should take in a lodger to make extra money, and that’s how we get to Vera Brandon.

Vera Brandon is a schoolteacher, and at first glance, she seems independent and capable and not particularly suspicious, but from the reader’s perspective, she’s very much in the tradition of the mysterious stranger. Another novel that I’ve compared it to is The Lodger by Marie Belloc Lowndes, which became the basis for an early Hitchcock film. The conceit is that in 1888, when the Ripper is active in London, a mysterious male lodger shows up at the home of a couple who is in financial straits. They quickly become suspicious of him, but they also need his money. Fremlin doesn’t deal with financial necessity in quite such an overt way, but it’s clear that Vera is there to defray the costs of having an extra mouth to feed. Then the question is whether Vera is up to something, or is Louise so addled from lack of sleep that she’s basically in a state of hysteria? When I was rereading the novel for this interview, I remembered how clearly the characters were drawn, but I’d totally forgotten the twist, which made it kind of shocking and delightful when I got to the end.

Toward the beginning of the novel, the protagonist, Louise, thinks: “to neglect one’s own tastes was more labor-saving than any vacuum cleaner, and it was a form of neglect about which nobody would call you to account.” There’s definitely plenty of fiction from feminists of this period that looks at the drudgery of women’s lives–I think of the work of Tillie Olsen or (ugh) Alice Munro–but I wonder if Fremlin was the first to see how well this type of experience lends itself to the form of the thriller. Is that accurate?

I don’t know if she thought about that in those terms at all. The edition I have is a reissue that came out in the UK in 2017 from Faber and Faber, and there’s a really interesting afterword by Chris Simmons, who runs the site crimesquad.com. He quotes Fremlin in the introduction to an edition that came out in 1988: “The original inspiration for this book was my second baby, whose name was Geraldine. She was one of those babies who, perfectly content and happy all day, simply don’t sleep through the night. Soon after midnight, she would wake, and again at half past two, and again at four. As the months went by, I found myself quite distracted by lack of sleep. My eyes would fall shut while I peeled the potatoes or ironed shirts. I remember one night sitting on the bottom step of the stairs, my baby awake and lively in my arms. It dawned on me: this is a major human experience. Why hasn’t someone written about it? It seemed to me that a serious novel should be written with this experience at its center. Then it occurred to me, why don’t I write one?”

By my calculations, she would have had this realization sometime in the 1940s, during the war or just after, but by the time she had actual headspace to work on it, it was closer to the mid 1950s. Clearly this marinated in her mind for a very long time, and it wouldn’t surprise me if, as happens to many an author, it was only after the book was done and about to be published that someone said, “Oh, you’ve written a suspense novel.” I imagine this was news to her, because she probably thought she was writing a social novel.

How influential do you think this novel has been for other writers, and how does it fit into the timeline of what we now call domestic or psychological suspense?

I don’t know if it’s directly influential. I know that when I published the essay in Tin House, that was the first time it had been written about at any length for a while. That essay led to the first anthology I ever edited, titled Troubled Daughters, Twisted Wives, which was my attempt to put the term domestic suspense in a historical context. To me, the first wave of domestic suspense ends with the publication of Where Are the Children? by Mary Higgins Clark in 1975. That novel ushered in the next wave that both ended and restarted with Gone Girl, and it remains to be seen what the next inflection point is going to be.

It seems to me that a lot of contemporary domestic suspense has lost the focus on character that makes Fremlin’s work so compelling. I pick up a lot of novels that move from exciting plot point to exciting plot point without, it seems, much of an understanding of how a person would get from one to another. Do you agree, and if so, what went wrong?

A lot of contemporary writers may be missing what makes a great work of domestic suspense so great, but I’d put it down to the writing in general. Tony Scott wrote a piece for the Times where he did a close read of the opening paragraphs of Gone Girl, and you could see that Gillian Flynn is operating at a level that’s just so far above those who have tried to copy her. The authors that make a mark are those who work out from their own obsessions and compulsions, who care about character, who care about writing, who care about a real sense of place, who care about larger issues. Gone Girl is as much a marriage thriller as it is one of the best books about what it was like to deal with the recession. It’s a downward mobility novel. That second-half reveal is just so good, and what people forget is that you can’t copy something that essentially reinvented a genre. I don’t think it’s just a problem in psychological suspense, but there are definitely times when I’m reading a novel and I’ll think, “Oh, you’re not reading enough.” It’s really important to read as widely as possible, because you have to give your brain a chance to make connections between things that might not seem related on the surface. If you look at the books that I designate as the best of, what they have in common is the quality of the writing.

Speaking of reading a lot, one thing I loved about this novel is how it’s in conversation with the nineteenth-century novel. There’s a wonderful meta-moment about halfway through that I can’t stop thinking about. Louise senses a sympathetic response from her awful nosy neighbor, and Fremlin compares it to “the warm, genuine sorrow that an author can feel for his heroine when he is about to plunge her into yet worse disaster.” I don’t think I’d be brave enough to include a moment like this, but I love the way that it hearkens back to writers like Trollope, and there are definite Jane Eyre vibes in the ending.

Yes, and Greek tragedy is in there too. Throughout the novel, Vera Brandon keeps mentioning Medea, and you could say that in a way, Fremlin was trying to update Medea for the contemporary era. As I said, I don’t know if Fremlin was reading crime fiction when she wrote this book. I think she was just so interested in domestic life and figuring out the darkness that lay not so far beneath the surface, and that was what she was preoccupied with. I think at one point she said that her favorite things were gossip and what people were up to, and just the day-to-day vagaries of life. This was somebody who really drew a lot of inspiration from what we might characterize as “mundane,” but clearly she saw so much rich material to mine in those situations.

I can think of a lot of recent titles that have to do with the months of early motherhood and the hallucinatory strain it can put on the mind and body, but I assume that this novel was one of the first.

That’s true, but I think a lot of these narratives are expressed as horror now as much or more than psychological suspense. That genre has really experienced a boom in the last few years, and a boom that parallels with the cozy and romantasy. It’s a sense of “how do you choose your sense of escape from the real world when the real world makes no narrative sense?” We as humans are primed to create order out of chaos, and for some people horror fiction provides that order, because there’s a level of catharsis. I do wonder if a lot of writers who might have written psychological suspense twenty years ago are now writing female body horror. Look at the proliferation of cannibal narratives. Still, in a sense the kind of psychological suspense that Fremlin wrote is even more palpable and horrific, precisely because it tracks the mundane so well.

The novel won the Edgar Award in 1960, but in a blurb on my edition, Peter Swanson calls it “a lost masterpiece.” Do you have any thoughts on why it isn’t more widely read?

There are some novels, for better for worse, that keep having to be rediscovered for whatever new wave or generation. But this book still has a potent hold on anyone who will seek it out, and I think it’s always going to have a place because, first of all, it’s really good. Secondly, it was an inflection point of psychological suspense and domestic suspense. Ruth Rendell started moving towards psychological thrillers pretty early in her career, and P.D. James’s procedurals with Inspector Dalgleish are very acute psychologically. One could argue that Fremlin was an ancestor of that kind of British crime fiction, and not just by women. She might not have been a direct influence, but she was tapping into something that people could then channel, and that’s often the way that art and literature works.

Is there anything else we haven’t talked about that you’d like to get to?

One thing I was surprised and saddened to learn is that about ten years after The Hours Before Dawn was published, Fremlin suffered two terrible tragedies within a month of each other. Her youngest child died of suicide, and then a month later, her husband also died of suicide. I don’t think it’s an accident that after those tragedies, her work shifted. I bring this up because it’s an indication that much as we like to think that art is separate from life, I don’t think someone like Fremlin could fully divorce herself from whatever was going on in her home. Frankly, I would like to know more about her. I think possibly she found refuge in storytelling because it was better than the life she was actually living.

Polly Stewart is the author of The Good Ones. She grew up in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Virginia, where she still lives. Her short fiction has appeared in Best American Mystery Stories, and her nonfiction has appeared in the New York Times, Good Housekeeping, and other publications. She writes the monthly Backlist column for CrimeReads.

#90. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#91. Getting the Second Amendment right

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, the Supreme Court announced something that may seem technical, but has great importance to how the Second Amendment is to be enforced in courts. It gave courts a two-step test for adjudicating Second Amendment challenges. Step one: Decide whether “the Second Amendment’s plain text covers an individual’s conduct.” If so, courts should move on to step two: Decide whether the regulation of that conduct “is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”

The court’s most recent Second Amendment decision, Wolford v. Lopez, clarifies that step one is a narrow textual inquiry. Courts should ask who is claiming the right, whether weapons are involved, and whether the law restricts keeping and bearing such weapons. Then they should move to step two.

This post looks more closely at what is at stake and how Wolford's clarification is (and is not) reshaping lower court decisions.

Before Wolford, some lower courts and litigants improperly converted step two questions (whether the plain text covers the conduct at issue) into step one questions (whether regulating that conduct “is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation”). This matters because the burden shifts between steps one and two. The rights-claimant bears the burden of persuading the court that the text of the Second Amendment covers his or her conduct; the government party bears the burden of persuading the court that its regulation is historically justified. By addressing a question at the first step, rather than the second, a court makes it more difficult for the rights claimant to prevail.

Bringing historical practices into step one

The Bruen decision instructs lower courts to apply the “original meaning” of the Second Amendment, so the “plain text” of that provision bears its historical, rather than contemporary, meaning. If our usage of “arms” over the past 235 years changed its meaning – in the way that, say, our usage of “nice” has – courts would have to use the meaning the word was understood to bear at the time the Bill of Rights was ratified. That is why, in 2008’s landmark Second Amendment case District of Columbia v. Heller, the Supreme Court looked to dictionaries dating the 18th century to figure out what the plain text of the Second Amendment means. As it happens, the definitions of “arms” the court discovered accord with contemporary usage: e.g., “weapons of offence, or armour of defence.” (Of course, the weapons to which “arms” refers today differ from those of the 18th century, but it does not follow that the word’s meaning differs.)

Some lower courts have reasoned that, if they must look to history to ascertain the meaning of “arm,” then they ought to be able to consider historical evidence that the right to keep and bear arms was thought not to extend to conduct involving certain types of weapons. Specifically, Heller stated “that the sorts of weapons protected were those in common use at the time.” Citing that language, courts have insisted that “in common use for lawful purposes” is part of the historical meaning of “arms” in the Second Amendment. This would mean that a claimant must prove that the weapon at issue is in common use to get past step one of the Bruen analysis. (Courts have used similar reasoning to carve exceptions out of the word “people.”)

But that puts the inquiry in the wrong step. Weapons that are not “in common use for lawful purposes” are still “arms” within the meaning of the Second Amendment; Heller’s theory is that the government may regulate them consistent with what Heller described as the “historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of dangerous and unusual weapons.” Thus, the question whether an arm is “in common use” or is instead “dangerous and unusual” properly arises at Bruen’s second step, where the government bears the burden of showing that one’s conduct may be restricted.

Some courts have also increased the burden on claimants in step one by requiring them to prove that the regulation’s impact on their right is substantial enough to trigger a step two inquiry. These courts, for example, point out that selling firearms is neither “keeping” nor “bearing” them, or conclude that magazines are not “arms” because they cannot function independently as weapons. According to these courts, claimants who seek to sell arms or own magazines cannot rest at showing that sales restrictions or magazine bans burden conduct covered by the plain text of the Second Amendment, as they undoubtedly do. They must also show that the regulation meaningfully limits their ability to exercise their constitutional right.

This move, too, transfers questions from step two (where they took the form of, “does the burden the government imposes today resemble the burden in the historical regulatory tradition?”), to step one (where they take the form of, “does the regulation really burden the right enough for us to require a showing from the government?”). Indeed, that latter question is just the sort of “whether the right is really worth insisting upon” inquiry that the court rejected in Heller as untethered from an originalist understanding of the Second Amendment.

Wolford clarified that both of these moves are improper. That case involved a challenge to a Hawaii law that required permit-holders to obtain express permission from property owners before carrying a firearm onto private property held open to the public.

Wolford rejected Hawaii’s attempt to introduce “historical materials and precedents” into the “plain text” analysis. “[T]hey are out of place at Bruen’s first step,” the court pointed out. Rather, “the question is simply whether a challenged law falls within the Second Amendment’s plain text.”

Wolford explained that step one consists entirely of “three subsidiary questions” anchored in the text of the Second Amendment:

Guided by these questions, the step one burden was “easily met” because Hawaii’s law restricted a right protected by the text of the Second Amendment: namely, the right to carry arms in public. This was so even though the law did not directly forbid bearing arms and reached only property (private property) where one has no absolute right to bear arms. Property owners – even owners who hold their property open to the public – had and still have a right to exclude persons carrying firearms. But by making it more difficult to obtain consent, Hawaii had restricted the right to bear arms, and that was enough to shift the burden to the government to show that such a restriction was “consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”

Wolford is already changing the shape of step one analysis in lower courts.

In Association of New Jersey Rifle & Pistol Clubs v. Attorney General of New Jersey, for example, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit (sitting en banc) held that New Jersey laws banning semi-automatic rifles and magazines capable of holding more than 10 rounds of ammunition violate the Second Amendment. It correctly held that the “common use” inquiry occurs at step two. Allowing that the question “was a closer call” before Wolford, the en banc court considered that Wolford settled the question of what role history plays at step one – as an inquiry into the text’s meaning.

And in Elite Precision Customs LLC v. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held unconstitutional a federal ban on buying and selling handguns across state lines. It rejected the argument that the claim failed at step one because the ban “is only a minor infringement of the Second Amendment rights that still allows ample access to handguns by those who are permitted to possess and purchase them under state and local laws.” It held that, under Wolford, claimants need only demonstrate that the law restricts the keeping and bearing of arms, as a sales regulation does. “Once this showing has been made, the law in question is deemed presumptively unconstitutional, with no further need for argumentation and negotiation.”

Still, not all of Wolford’s lessons have registered. In particular, litigants continue to press lower courts to relocate questions from step two to step one by leaning on dicta in Heller listing “presumptively lawful regulatory measures.” As the court noted in Heller,

Although these regulatory measures have no textual hook, some courts have misunderstood the “presumptively lawful” label to exempt certain of them from the presumption of unconstitutionality that attaches at Bruen step one. Last month in United States v. Berger, for example, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit wrote that “[t]he best way to understand the Court’s presumptive endorsement of these rules is at Bruen’s step one, as a reading of the Second Amendment’s text” – specifically, as a gloss on “infringe.”

So understood, the language relieves the government of the burden to show that the regulatory measure is part of a historical regulatory tradition. In courts that have embraced this reading, claimants thus bear the burden to show not only that the plain text of the Second Amendment covers their conduct, but also that the government’s regulation falls outside the historical scope of these “presumptively lawful regulatory measures.”

This reasoning cannot be reconciled with Wolford, which enumerated the subsidiary questions comprising step one without mentioning the presumptively lawful regulatory measures, and relegated the question of what comprises such historical exceptions to step two. As Pete Patterson recently explained on SCOTUSblog, Heller’s presumptively lawful regulatory measures touch conduct falling within the plain text of the Second Amendment that Wolford comprehensively explicated. To the extent that they are lawful, it is because they are part of the nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. Nothing in Heller or Bruen relieves the government of its burden to prove that they are in step two.

Wolford has returned step one to its textual roots. But until it grants a case involving a “presumptively lawful regulatory measure” – several such petitions remain pending – the confusion around that category may persist.

Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

Recommended Citation: Haley Proctor, Getting the Second Amendment right, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 16, 2026, 12:30 PM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/getting-the-second-amendment-right/

#92. How India-Philippines Cooperation Reinforces America’s Interests in the South China Sea

With so much media focus in recent months on the war in Iran, it’s no surprise that Undersecretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby’s speech in Manila received so little coverage. That means very few know what the U.S. and its allies are doing to deter China from launching any hostilities of its own.

In April, Filipino marines undertook one of the most expansive iterations of Balikatan, the annual bilateral U.S. and Philippines military exercise. They took part in simulated firing of the BrahMos anti-ship missile during the joint maritime strike phase of the exercise. The BrahMos is an Indian missile, and while India was not a participant in Balikatan, it joined as an observer. The image of a U.S.-Philippine drill with an Indian weapons platform aptly captures India’s role in the South China Sea.

India is not explicitly present and may never put boots on the ground, and yet its presence is felt in how it strengthens the deterrence of Southeast Asian partners through hardware, intel sharing, and strategic diversification. This is not necessarily a case of policy alignment but of strategic convergence: India’s pursuit of its own interests produces outcomes that complement Washington’s regional objectives.

Washington’s strategy in the first island chain rests on a strategy of denial by making it too costly for China to strike against a partner nation. The Trump administration has emphasized burden sharing, pushing allies and partners do their part in ensuring that they can defend themselves. This was captured best and most recently by Elbridge Colby’s speech. He not only spoke about the importance of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific but also how partners are expected to do their part.

>>> Why Trump’s India Policy Is Working

“When we ask our allies and partners to step up, to invest more in their own defense,” he said, “we are not signaling abandonment.” Colby argued that deterrence along the first island chain cannot rest on American power alone but must also rely on capable partners able to defend their own territory.

The Philippines has been doing its part, despite a rather small budget of approximately $6.12 in 2024 and $6.7 billion in the proposed 2027 budget—some of its highest figures to date. Manila also adopted Comprehensive Archipelagic Defense Concept in 2024 to focus on territorial and maritime defense. And the Self Reliant Defense Posture Law hopes to build indigenous defense capabilities, reinforced by the Horizon I, II, and III plans.

India is playing its own role albeit for its own interests of expanding defense exports, deepening its Act East Policy, and perhaps even hedging against China—a known challenge for India as much as it is for the United States and the Philippines. India is doing so through three levers: hardware, intel sharing, and enabling a strategic diversification strategy; all of which allow Philippines to burden share and reinforce denial strategies.

Regarding hardware, India sold to the Philippines three shore-based batteries for $375 million in 2022. India even offered a $100 million line of credit for the sale, though Manila decided to finance it from its defense appropriations. The batteries arrived on time in April 2024 and the first became operational in November in Zambales (in West Luzon) under the Marine Corps coastal defense regiment, providing a strike capability of 290 km that reaches Scarborough Shoal. India has since also offered extended range variants of 400 km with future batteries reaching up to the Spratlys when deployed from Palawan.

Recently the Philippines Ambassador to India Ignacio remarked how the BrahMos missiles Manila imported from New Delhi are a game changer and provide the Philippines with “real credible deterrence” as territorial challenges continue to rise in the South China Sea. India has also offered Akash surface to air missiles, Tejas LCA fighter jets, helicopters, and submarines and naval vessels. The sale of these platforms is commercially useful to India, but its second-order effect is also to strengthen the same maritime denial architecture Washington is pursuing in the region.

>>> Can the U.S.-India Defense Partnership Keep Pace With AI?

Regarding intel, India invited the Philippines to the Information Fusion Center for the Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR) in 2025. The IFC-IOR is India’s maritime domain awareness hub which tracks activity in the Indian ocean region. The move builds on a 2023 coastal guard agreement and white shipping arrangement where the two navies are already collaborating on information sharing, maritime training, exchanges, joint search and rescue operations, and more. Greater maritime domain awareness improves Manila's ability to identify, track, and respond to Chinese activity, complementing the strike capabilities India is helping provide.

Last year, India and the Philippines also had their warships conduct their first joint maritime activity inside the Philippine exclusive zone and the South China Sea. Notably, Chinese vessels were shadowing them during the joint sail. India has also publicly backed Manila’s position in the South China Sea including the 2016 arbitral award in Philippines favor which China has ignored by continuing to extend its territorial claims through artificial islands and the nine dash line.

There are limitations. India is highly unlikely to ever put boots on the ground for the Philippines, but this may actually matter less. By providing strategic diversification, India strengthens the Philippine’s deterrence, making regional balancing look less like simply joining an American bloc. And that is the paradox here: the same strategic autonomy that limits how far India will pursue formal alliances also increases the value of what it does do.

Because New Delhi is neither a U.S. nor Philippine treaty ally, its cooperation is harder to portray simply as an extension of American alliance politics. By pursuing its own interests, India is in the process also reinforcing American interests.

#93. Federal appeals court rejects qualified immunity for judge who jailed 2 kids

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at St. Louis last week found that a Missouri judge who locked two children in jail cells was not shielded by qualified immunity. (Image from Shutterstock)

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at St. Louis last week found that a Missouri judge who locked two children in jail cells was not shielded by qualified immunity.

The appeals court panel found that Taney County, Missouri, Judge Eric Eighmy could be held liable for violating the children’s Fourth Amendment rights.

Eighmy put the children into holding cells after a 2019 hearing because he was frustrated by their resistance to a parental custody decision, according to a story by Reason.

“A reasonable judge should have known better,” 8th Circuit Judge David Stras wrote for the three judge panel.

The panel also noted that “judges do not do double duty as jailers.”

#94. Eternal Glow

The house remains dark, quiet, completely still, and my grip on the steering wheel tightens. This is how all those Netflix true crime docs start, I think, before the reality of the situation starts to sink in: I’ve driven into the foothills for a secret procedure I know nothing about. Nobody knows where I am. What am I doing?

Of course, I could turn around, tell Brayden that the meeting ended early, pretend none of this ever happened.

Another luncheon full of Lydia’s backhanded jabs? Where Sophie’s pity stings worse than her hot goss? Where I’m always worried I’ll be the target of the next round of whisper campaigns? Worried that I’m one wrong move away from total ostracization?

I finally cut the engine. The rain taps insistently on the roof, the only sound besides my breathing. The fog presses in. This is insane. Turn around. Go home.

But home won’t comfort me. Images flash through my head—Brayden cemented to the sofa, the bills piling higher on the kitchen table. I grab my purse and step out into the drizzle. It soaks through my trench coat immediately, cold rivulets trickling down my neck. My heels click on the front path.

Up close, the house is exactly as anonymous as it looked on Street View. No signage. No buzzer. Just a brass knocker and a doorbell glowing faintly in the dark. I press it. A chime sounds somewhere deep inside—melodic and almost churchlike.

A chill unrelated to the rain crawls up my spine. The invite said 8:00 sharp—don’t be late. My phone shows 7:58. Unlike Aspyn’s pickup today, I’m right on time.

Then I notice—the door isn’t fully latched. Before I can chicken out or second-guess myself, I push.

The pale wood door swings open with a soft click, and light explodes out, sterile and blinding, forcing me to shield my eyes. I stumble forward blindly, the door sighing shut behind me with a finality that I can feel in my chest.

Blinking away spots, the interior comes into focus—and steals my breath.

It’s not the dim, empty house I braced for. Whatever this place looked like before, it’s been transformed—but not into anything clinical. Into something almost beautiful. The kind of interior you’d screenshot from an Architectural Digest spread and send to your group chat with three flame emojis.

Gleaming hardwood floors giving way to thick white carpet. Crisp white walls. Sparse furniture. Bare walls. Nothing on the surfaces, nothing in the corners, nothing that says anyone has ever spent a single ordinary moment here—which is either the work of a phenomenal stager who hasn’t finished yet, or something else entirely that I can’t quite name.

The air is crisp, laced with lavender and eucalyptus, undercut by the same chemical, antiseptic bite as Skinsational. Here, the scent mingles with something metallic, like the tang of fresh pennies. Or blood.

And then, on the far wall—a painting. Large, maybe four feet across, in a heavy gold frame. An angel in flight, wings outstretched, feathers tipped in gold leaf, rendered in a style that sits somewhere between Renaissance devotional art and something you’d find in the lobby of a very expensive hotel. Underneath, in the same ornate script as the card:

It should look out of place. Somehow it doesn’t.

In the corner, a towering Moroni statue stands sentinel, trumpet raised to the heavens, painted entirely in gold leaf that gleams under the recessed lights. Angel Moroni—the heavenly messenger who appeared to Joseph Smith and revealed the golden plates that became the Book of Mormon, the very foundation of our faith. Every temple in the Church is crowned with his image, trumpet aloft, heralding the Restoration. I’ve looked up at him my entire life.

If the doctor put Moroni here—in this space—she isn’t just a scientist. She’s a woman of faith. She understands what it means to believe in something bigger than yourself, to trust in a higher purpose. The Church teaches that the body is a temple.

Maybe that’s why it feels different from anything I could find at Skinsational.

My shoulders relax. Something loosens within me.

I step closer to the statue. His eyes—black obsidian—catch the light at an odd angle, and for just a second they seem to shift, to track me across the room.

I look away quickly. It’s just the lighting.

#95. Supreme Court Will Hear Case on "Facially Neutral" Discrimination Against Asian Students in Admissions to Public Magnet Schools

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The case arises as both right and left favor various forms of anti-Asian discrimination.

Today, the Supreme Court decided to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a challenge to "facially neutral" discrimination against Asian applicants to selective public magnet schools in Montgomery County, Maryland. The admissions criteria are, on their face, racially neutral. But evidence indicates they were likely adopted for the purpose of reducing the percentage of Asian students in entering classes. More specifically, the case addresses the issue of "[w]hether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool." This issue is increasingly important since the Supreme Court banned most explicit racial discrimination in college admissions (and, by extension, school admissions) in SFFA v. Harvard (2023).

The lower court ruled that, even if there is evidence that a facially neutral admissions policy was enacted for the specific purpose of reducing the number of admitted students from a specific racial or ethnic group, it must still be upheld so long as the percentage of admitted students from that group is as high or higher than the percentage of applicants from that group.

The case is similar to (and based on) Fourth Circuit decision in Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County School Board, which the Supreme Court refused to take in 2024 (though three conservative justices indicated they did want to hear it) [my wife Alison was one of the attorneys representing the plaintiffs in that case]. The present case is also from the Fourth Circuit. In my view (see here and here), the earlier Fourth Circuit decision is badly wrong and would - if the same approach were adopted by the Supreme Court - license all kinds of invidious, unconstitutional discrimination against Asians and other minorities:

Longstanding Supreme Court precedent holds that evidence of unconstitutional motivation for "facially neutral" policies shifts the burden of proof to the government to show that they would have enacted the same policy even in the absence of illicit motives. If they fail to prove that, then the policy must be subjected to strict scrutiny, which it would be unlikely to survive. In the TJ case, the Fourth Circuit majority opinion by Judge Robert Bruce King holds that even the most blatant discriminatory motivations do not trigger strict scrutiny so long as the group being targeted for discrimination by "facially neutral" means  is still represented in proportion to its percentage of the relevant population (or more). Under the new admissions policy, Asians were still 54% of accepted applicants (as compared to 73% under the old one). Since that is still higher than the Asian percentage of the applicant pool, evidence of discriminatory intent becomes irrelevant….

I and others have previously compared today's anti-Asian discrimination in selective educational institutions to discrimination against Jewish applicants in earlier eras.  Under the Fourth Circuit's reasoning, old-time policies using facially neutral means to reduce the percentage of Jewish students at elite universities would be perfectly legal, so long as Jewish applicants were admitted in the same [or higher] percentages as other groups. And that would be true no matter how extensive the evidence that the new policy was motivated by anti-Semitic prejudices, or that Jewish applicants had to have stronger academic records to be admitted than those required of gentiles.

The same point applies to all kinds of discrimination against racial, ethnic, and religious minorities. So long as facially neutral means are used and the overall success rates of different groups are similar, this reasoning would allow even the most blatant discriminatorily motivated policies intended to reduce the participation of some groups for the benefit of others. There are many situations where members of some minority groups are "overrepresented" in educational institutions, government contracting, and elsewhere, relative to their percentage of the applicant pool or of the general population. Jews, Muslims, Asians, atheists, and Mormons are obvious examples of groups that fit that bill in a variety of educational and professional settings.

If a federal or state government adopted a seemingly neutral policy to try to reduce the percentage of blacks among professional football or basketball players, that too would pass muster, so long as the percentage of blacks in the the relevant pro sports leagues remained at least as high as the percentage of blacks among those seeking employment as players…. Progressives and others inclined to support today's decision should consider whether they are really willing to live with these troubling implications.

Since I wrote the above, the ideological valence of anti-Asian discrimination in education has shifted somewhat. For a long time, many left-wingers defended such discrimination (along with discrimination against white applicants) on the grounds that it is necessary to achieve "diversity" and compensate Blacks and Hispanics for the history of discrimination against those groups. Most conservatives condemned it because it violates principles of constitutional color-blindness.

During the second Trump Administration, however, right-wing nativists have increasingly defended discrimination against Asian immigrants on such ridiculous grounds as that they work too hard (thus making it too difficult for whites to compete with them), or even that they undermine the supposed value of racial "homogeneity." The political right actually has a long history of anti-Asian bigotry. But recently the problem has gotten much worse, after a period in which it was diminishing because conservatives (rightly) condemned such discrimination as a violation of color-blindness. The growing anti-Asian bigotry among right-wing nationalists is similar to and linked with their growing tendency towards anti-Semitism. Indeed, as many commentators have pointed out, the two prejudices are similar in many respects. Both Asians and Jews are condemned for supposedly working too hard, emphasizing academics too much relative to other activities, and supposedly dominating various business and intellectual fields.

The left-wing rationales for anti-Asian discrimination are little better than the right-wing ones. If you truly value diversity, it makes no sense to disfavor Asian applicants as a class. They add as much or more to diversity as any others. Indeed, as I have pointed out before, lumping all Asians in one category makes no sense, as this group includes a vast range of different ethnicities and cultures, covering more than half the world's population.

The compensatory justice rationale for anti-Asian discrimination collapses under the weight of the fact that many Asian groups have themselves faced extensive discrimination at various times in American history. Discrimination against Chinese and Japanese by federal and state governments has a long and sordid history, of which Japanese internment during World War II is just one particularly awful example.

It is important to recognize that "facially neutral" policies adopted for the specific purpose of excluding particular racial or ethnic groups differ from those that merely have an unintended disparate impact. The former are deliberate efforts to discriminate on the basis of race, whereas the latter are probably inevitable in a diverse society where groups differ from each other in various ways. For example, laws banning violent crime disproportionately affect any group which is, on average, younger than others, since young people (especially young men) have much higher crime rates than older ones.

The Constitution at least presumptively bars racial discrimination by government, whether motivated by left-wing objectives or right-wing ones. And such discrimination is forbidden even if cloaked in "facially neutral" garb. Otherwise, the government could easily discriminate against virtually any group simply by targeting some characteristic that correlates with group membership. Hopefully, the Supreme Court will recognize that and rule the right way in this case.

NOTE: The plaintiffs in this case are represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation, a public interest group that was my wife's employer until recently. As noted above, she helped represent the plaintiffs in a previous case (also litigated by PLF), on which the lower court ruling in this case was based. She is not one of the attorneys in this case, and is no longer with PLF.

NEXT: Supreme Court Will Hear Necessary and Proper Clause Case on Federal Law Banning Home Distilleries

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#96. Turkish Government Takes Over Independent TV News Channel

Click to expand Image Halk TV general news coordinator Serhan Asker gives an interview to media after the government takeover of the channel, a police raid on the premises, and the announcement of an arrest warrant against its owner and 16 others. Halk TV, Istanbul, October 14, 2026. © 2026 Adem Altan/AFP via Getty Images

Police in Türkiye carried out a dawn raid on the widely watched, independent news channel Halk TV on October 14, signaling its takeover by a government-appointed administrator who promptly ordered the station to end its live broadcast.

Halk TV is close to the main political opposition New Party (Yeni Parti). Its journalists have reported on the imprisonment and trial of Istanbul’s mayor, Ekrem İmamoğlu, government moves to split the opposition, and persistent allegations of corruption in the ruling party. The seizure of the channel is part of a wider effort by the government of Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to restrict Turkish citizens’ access to independent news sources that has involved pulling the plug on several TV news outlets, prosecuting and jailing journalists, and greatly escalating internet censorship.

The Istanbul prosecutor’s office ordered the arrest of Halk TV’s owner on accusations of bribery, money laundering, and rigging tenders, along with 16 other people. As with other takeovers of media outlets, the financial crimes investigation provides a pretext for censorship. Halk TV will now be managed by the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund, a state body attached to the presidency, which has been used over the past 10 years to manage companies under governmental administration that are subject to criminal investigations.

Halk TV continued to report on matters of pressing public interest until the last moment. An anchor was conducting an interview about an investment fund scandal implicating prominent figures in Erdoğan’s party moments before the administrators cut the live broadcast, leaving viewers instead with a scene from an old Turkish film.

The takeover of Halk TV came on the very day that İmamoğlu took to the stand to begin his defense in the main politically motivated trial against him.

The Turkish government’s steps to suppress and silence a TV station that broadcasts critical content violates not only the rights of the workers and journalists targeted, but the public’s right of access to information and to freedom of expression.

Most people in Türkiye rely on television over other media for news coverage. Halk TV has been a critical voice in a country where broadcast news is increasingly monotone and government-aligned. The Turkish authorities should take immediate steps to reverse the takeover of the channel. A free, pluralistic media offering varied views and opinions is a cornerstone of a democratic society.

#97. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”
