#98. Trump’s Census Proposal Is a Big Step in Restoring National Unity

The Trump administration has made bold moves in its attempt to rescue America from cultural balkanization, as its fights with the Smithsonian Institution and the educational establishment demonstrate. But no move is more vital than its proposal to eliminate race, ethnicity, and sexual preference from the U.S. Census.

Trump’s proposed rule states: “No question about race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation shall appear on the short form decennial census questionnaire or any questionnaire used for the enumeration of the population. . . . With the exception of questions about biological sex, date of birth, and household relationships, no person shall be obligated to furnish a response to any demographic question as part of the decennial census.” The rule would also exclude illegal aliens and temporary foreign workers, students, and visitors—none of whom can legally vote—from congressional apportionment.

These changes are significant and worthy of support. Dismantling the grievance industry, the oppressor-oppressed paradigm, identity politics, and other ideas that rend the national fabric is an essential cause. The Census is a frequently overlooked theater in that struggle.

>>> Lonnie Bunch’s Smithsonian Exit Is a Culture-War Win

The high stakes of these Census reforms may be news to many Americans, especially conservatives and nonactivists minding their own business and trying to make ends meet. No doubt many see the Census as a mundane task that happens at the start of every decade, undertaken to provide the necessary data for apportioning seats in the House of Representatives.

It’s considerably more than that. The Indo-European root of the word “census” means “to evoke in speech, almost to call a thing into existence by naming it,” in the words of the French classical historian Claude Nicolet. In the wrong hands, a census can change the character of a republic.

For nearly four decades, leftists have used the Census to do just that, fragmenting the U.S. into a nation of groups, some of them invented. Few know today, for example, the meaning of MENA—short for the Middle East and North Africa, a designation that encompasses peoples as diverse as Kurds, Arabs, Persians, and Berbers. If the Left’s plans to add MENA to the 2030 Census succeed, it may become the next official ethnicity in the public mind.

That’s how Hispanics and Asian-Americans became fixed categories in the public consciousness. Few used these terms before the Office of Management and Budget created them in 1977 and added them to the Census for the first time in 1980. I remember it happening: my uncle, a journalist, walked into our semi-detached home in Queens in the 1970s and announced, “They’re going to start calling us Hispanics.” We were dumbfounded.

Of course, the bureaucrats didn’t come up with the idea on their own. It was pressed on them by radical groups such as the National Council of La Raza (now called UnidosUS) and the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF), both founded with seed money from the Ford Foundation.

UCLA sociologist Cristina Mora, who is sympathetic to the creation of the Hispanic category, wrote in Making Hispanics, “U.S. Census Bureau records reveal that census officials were reluctant to create a Hispanic pan-ethnic category, in part because they judged that persons of Latin American descent were quite diverse and would eventually assimilate and identify as white.” Chicano activists couldn’t bear the idea of assimilation. “They used militant tactics and described Mexican-American communities as internal colonies that needed to shed the yoke of assimilation,” Mora writes. In the end, “Mexican American activists played an important role in pressuring hesitant state and census officials to institutionalize the Hispanic category.”

At the policy level, the Census reforms will help on fronts where the administration is already fighting elsewhere with other measures, eliminating several societal ills. Among these: the corrosive doctrine of disparate impact, which holds that group discrimination doesn’t have to be intentional to be illegal; racial preferences in university admissions and hiring; court holdings that the Voting Rights Act requires the creation of racial voting districts; and a society manipulated by interest groups.

The activists cloaked each of these actions in the rhetoric of noble intent. But America’s focus on race has unsurprisingly failed to produce the desired results. As the sociologist Nathan Glazer wrote in 2002, “As we follow this process further and further into the details that have shaped the census, the element of nobility declines.”

The Census’s racial questions are a betrayal of the vision of the American Founders, who wanted immigrants to “get assimilated to our customs, manners and laws: in a word, soon become one people,” as George Washington put it.

Trump’s Census proposal revives Washington’s vision by attacking the source of the problem: racial, ethnic, and sexual preference categories. As the proposal explains, the Census exists because of a constitutional mandate to count, for the apportionment of congressional seats, the “whole number of persons in each State” based on “usual residence.” This is “a process that factors in an element of allegiance but otherwise should be colorblind and should not be distorted in any way by questions about immaterial personal characteristics, such as race.” The proposal acknowledges that this step is of a “(potentially) sensitive nature” but hastens to add, “Substantial doubts about the meaning, significance, and impact of attempting to categorize persons by race and ethnicity, in particular, have featured prominently in our national discourse and have been reflected in shifts in the law.”

>>> People, Place, Principles: This Is America

The boldness of the proposal seems to have caught the Left off guard, but the Trump administration should hold the line against the inevitable blowback. The proposal is indispensable to the success of his overall project. It must, of course, be accompanied by a return to assimilation and a more rational immigration policy.

The proposal itself is not perfect. While it rightly aims to stop counting all transient or illegal aliens for apportioning House seats, it doesn’t specify how the Census Bureau should determine legal status. The Supreme Court has already held that the Constitution “lawfully permits the Census Bureau to at least inquire about citizenship on the census questionnaire,” and it should absolutely do so. The racial questions should also be eliminated from the much smaller American Community Survey. The best way to support the proposal is to go to the Federal Register, submit a comment supporting it, and then ask that a question on citizenship be added. There’s no time to waste, as the comment period ends on November 2.

In his seminal 2004 book, Who Are We?, Samuel Huntington worried that if the balkanization process continued much longer, whites would join the process rather than fight it. At that point, he warned, “the cultural divide in America will be formalized.”

The second Trump administration has made reuniting Americans one of its signature missions. It deserves our support in this effort.

#99. Federal judge accused of misconduct, abandoning her job

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas is facing a judicial misconduct proceeding. (Photo from Facebook/Judge Ada Brown for SCOTUS)

A federal judge in Dallas has been accused of refusing to take cases, making racial insults to judges and court staff and abandoning her role, judicial investigators have found.

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas is facing a judicial misconduct proceeding for allegedly mishandling her docket and treating other judges and court staff “in a demonstrably egregious and hostile manner,” Bloomberg Law reports.

A committee of judicial investigators recommended that she be temporarily stripped of her docket, according to internal court documents shared with Bloomberg Law. The investigators found a “reasonable basis” to think that Brown “suffers from a mental condition that currently interferes with her ability to perform the responsibilities of her office,” according to the documents.

Brown, appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term, faces two judicial misconduct complaints, according to the documents. One was submitted by an attorney who appeared before the judge, and the second was identified by Chief Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod of the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at New Orleans.

According to Bloomberg Law, Brown has declined to participate in the proceedings against her by the 5th Circuit’s judicial council.

#101. Kazakhstan Women Need Action on Domestic Violence

Click to expand Image Participants at the international Women's Day rally in Almaty, Kazakhstan, March 8, 2022. © 2022 Stanislav Beketov

During its October 6 review by the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), Kazakhstan pledged new legislation to make domestic violence a standalone crime – a timely commitment. Now the government should turn words into action.

On September 23, Zhazira Adauova, a mother of two, died after her ex-husband stabbed her 16 times in Astana, Kazakhstan’s capital. Zhazira’s family told the media she had repeatedly reported threats and violence to police. Four former police officers are under investigation for alleged negligence in handling her case. 

Elvira Erkebayeva, from western Kazakhstan, endured two decades of domestic violence, including having boiling water thrown in her face. Instead of protecting her and holding her former husband accountable, authorities prosecuted Elvira in 2025 for allegedly conspiring to murder him because she wanted to “find a firearm.” 

As in manyother cases, Kazakh authorities failed to protect women who sought protection against further violence, even when they had obtained multiple protection orders. Perpetrators are often held accountable only after killing their victims.

Kazakhstan no longer has a dedicated law on domestic violence, and the latest reforms still did not establish domestic violence as a standalone criminal offense. The 2009 Law on Prevention of Domestic Violence was repealed by the Law on Prevention of Offences, which entered into force in March addresses domestic violence within a broader prevention framework. 

The Kazakh delegation claimed during its CEDAW review that “enforcing zero tolerance for violence had become … the cornerstone of ongoing reforms,” and that in 2024 Kazakhstan had “intensified legal accountability for domestic … violence.” Yet CEDAW experts rightly questioned the effectiveness of existing measures, and the Committee’s Rapporteur for Kazakhstan underscored that domestic violence is still not a standalone criminal offence. 

Under CEDAW and the Committee’s General Recommendation No. 35, states must prevent, investigate, prosecute, and ensure accountability for gender-based violence. 

Kazakhstan should adopt reforms to make domestic violence a standalone offence, strengthen and improve enforcement of the protection order mechanism, ensure interventions are effective and perpetrators held accountable, and guarantee survivors’ access to justice and services. Kazakhstan’s international partners should press for these reforms. 

Accountability after a woman is dead is no substitute for timely protection and prevention. Kazakh authorities need to ensure that women in Kazakhstan receive meaningful protection and assistance before violence escalates or turns fatal.

#103. Advancing Abraham Accords 2.0: A Congressional Agenda

Introduction

September 2026 marks six years since the signing of the Abraham Accords on the White House lawn by Israel, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Bahrain. These historic peace and normalization agreements, brokered by President Donald Trump, produced a flourishing of diplomatic, economic, security, and cultural cooperation. Despite the multi-front war that followed Hamas’s October 7, 2023, terrorist attack, the Accords proved remarkably resilient. Diplomatic, trade, and security ties were largely preserved. At the same time, many of the people-to-people initiatives that had characterized the warm peace fostered by the Accords declined in scope and public profile.

In the wake of the U.S.-facilitated Gaza ceasefire and Operation Epic Fury, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region stands at a critical crossroads. Restoring the momentum of the Abraham Accords, building regional frameworks that advance U.S. interests, and expanding the circle of warm peace will require sustained American leadership. With the right commitment and support, the Abraham Accords can evolve into the foundation of a new U.S.-led regional architecture that promotes the vital national security interests of the United States and its allies. Congress can play a central role in providing that leadership and turning the potential of “Abraham Accords 2.0” into reality. There are five principal avenues through which Congress can advance this goal.

Evolution of Abraham Accords Ties

From September 2020 to October 2023, the Abraham Accords opened the door to the rapid development of ties among Israel, the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and (for a time) Sudan. Embassies were established; direct flights were launched; trade grew rapidly; and previously unimaginable commercial, technological, and civil society cooperation emerged. Partnerships were announced in artificial intelligence (AI), space, cybersecurity, water, precision agriculture, energy, health, financial technology (fintech), defense, and many other fields. The Accords also contributed positively to Israel’s ties with its traditional peace partners, Egypt and Jordan. More than 60 intergovernmental agreements, instruments, and memoranda of understanding (MOUs) were signed between Israel and its Abraham Accords and Arab peace partners.[REF]

This period also saw the emergence of Abraham Accords multilateral cooperation. In January 2021, the Trump Administration announced that Israel would be moved to the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility, enabling significantly enhanced cooperation with other American partners in the region. Under President Joseph Biden, the Israel–India–U.S.–UAE (I2U2) framework and Negev Forum were established.[REF] In September 2023, the United States, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the European Union, and other partners signed an MOU to establish the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC).[REF]

Iran, Hamas, and other radical actors understood the implications of this trend. They viewed the emergence of a U.S.-aligned regional architecture culminating in U.S.-mediated negotiations toward Saudi–Israeli normalization as a serious threat. While Hamas’s October 7 attack had been planned over a number of years, evidence indicates that the acceleration of this regional alignment was one of the factors that led Hamas to launch the attack in October 2023.[REF]

The attack and ensuing multi-front war generated far-reaching regional tensions and strain. Many questioned whether the Accords would survive. Nearly three years later, it is clear that the strategic foundations of the Accords are more resilient than many skeptics predicted. Despite the intense regional conflict, the framework of peace did not collapse.

This resilience found expression in at least four important ways.

  • Formal diplomatic relations remained in place.
  • Trade between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, Egypt, and Jordan continued to grow. According to data from Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics, combined trade between Israel and its Arab and Muslim peace partners increased by approximately 15.4 percent in 2024 compared to 2023. It increased a further 0.8 percent year-over-year in 2025, a modest rise that is nevertheless impressive given the regional tensions and disruptions. During the first five months of 2026, trade was approximately 7.7 percent higher than it was during the same period in 2025.[REF] In fact, Israel’s cumulative trade with its Arab peace partners has risen every year since the Accords were signed. Combined trade rose from approximately $1.97 billion in 2021 to approximately $4.56 billion in 2025, an increase of roughly 131 percent.[REF]
  • Air connectivity proved remarkably durable. Although international aviation to Israel faced severe disruption, Emirati airlines maintained service during periods when many Western airlines suspended flights. The UAE was the third most popular country for passengers traveling to and from Ben Gurion International Airport in 2025 and again during the first six months of 2026.[REF]
  • Defense integration advanced in the face of shared threats. In January 2026, CENTCOM announced the establishment of the Middle Eastern Air Defense–Combined Defense Operations Cell (MEAD-CDOC).[REF] The importance of this integration was demonstrated a month later with the launch of Operation Epic Fury. During the conflict, Israel deployed an Iron Dome battery and other military systems to assist in defending the UAE. This marked an extraordinary development made possible by the Abraham Accords: an Israeli defensive system, developed in close partnership with the United States, helping to protect an Arab partner under fire. Nor was military cooperation limited to Israel and the UAE. In January 2026, a senior Moroccan military delegation traveled to Tel Aviv and signed a strategic work plan with its Israeli counterparts.

It should also be noted that in November 2025, Kazakhstan joined the Abraham Accords, becoming the first Central Asian country to accede to the framework.

At the same time, the damage caused by the post–October 7 regional war and geopolitical tensions should not be minimized. Public support for normalization declined across much of the region. People-to-people initiatives suffered, business and technology partnerships were paused or canceled, academic and scientific cooperation decreased, multilateral forums lost momentum, and the expansion of normalization slowed.

As noted, the Middle East and North Africa region now stands at a critical juncture. The Abraham Accords have the potential to shape a new regional architecture that supports crucial U.S. national security interests. Realizing this potential and restoring positive momentum on the bilateral and multilateral levels will require American leadership, commitment, and focus.

Five Things Congress Can Do to Advance the Abraham Accords

While U.S. leadership on the Abraham Accords has traditionally been associated primarily with the executive branch, Congress can help to strengthen regional cooperation, integration, and warm peace, thereby deepening and expanding the Accords, by acting in five critical areas.

  • Advance concrete steps to realize the IMEC vision. IMEC could become one of the most consequential infrastructure initiatives of the 21st century. Such an overland route could shorten transit times for goods between India and Europe by 51 percent and between the UAE and Israel by 79 percent.[REF] However, IMEC’s potential extends far beyond freight. Energy infrastructure, digital connectivity, and data infrastructure could form part of the corridor.

    For the United States, IMEC is not simply a transportation project. It is an opportunity to strengthen supply-chain resilience, provide an alternative to China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and routes dominated by Russia and Iran, increase demand for American technology and services, connect close U.S. partners, and reinforce a Western-aligned economic corridor extending from India to Europe.

    Despite extensive diplomatic attention and rhetoric, there has been relatively little detailed analysis of IMEC’s likely economic benefits, costs, regulatory requirements, and commercially viable projects. Overcoming political, bureaucratic, and economic hurdles and attracting public and private investment will require a credible account of what the corridor could deliver for each of the countries involved; a detailed mapping of infrastructure needs and gaps; an analysis of the regulatory, customs, and security requirements for its success; and an assessment of the opportunities for public-sector and private-sector actors along the route.

    Congress should therefore pursue two complementary initiatives. Specifically, Congress should:

    1. Seek an independent U.S. International Trade Commission assessment of IMEC’s trade and economic implications.[REF] The assessment should examine potential employment, investment, trade, and growth effects for participating states and identify opportunities for American companies in engineering, logistics, cybersecurity, energy technology, and digital infrastructure.
    2. Call on the Department of Commerce, in coordination with the Departments of State, Treasury, Transportation, and Energy together with the U.S. Trade Representative, Trade and Development Agency, International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), and Export-Import Bank, to develop an actionable commercial road map that includes bankable projects, financing gaps, regulatory barriers, customs harmonization procedures, and investment opportunities.

    Congress should also encourage the Treasury Department and the U.S. Executive Director at the World Bank to support complementary analytical work. The World Bank has extensive experience modeling major transport corridors, including projects associated with China’s BRI. Comparable work on IMEC could add international credibility and help to identify the steps needed to make the corridor viable. In tandem with these studies, the United States should convene the IMEC signatories and the key transit and destination countries, including Israel and Jordan, to develop an implementation road map, measurable benchmarks, and a permanent secretariat for coordination, communication, and oversight.

    Progress need not wait for a complete regional railway network. Existing and expanded trucking routes can demonstrate commercial value as rail infrastructure is being developed. Congress should encourage engagement with Saudi Arabia and other partners on transit arrangements for goods originating from or destined for Israel. Where appropriate, U.S. financial support through the DFC and other mechanisms could be made available to qualifying regional partners for infrastructure projects. One potential project would be DFC-supported feasibility and project-development work for a national Jordanian railway connecting the country’s border crossings with Saudi Arabia and Israel.

    As noted, IMEC should be viewed not only through the lens of trade, but also through the lens of energy and digital connectivity. Saudi Arabia’s East–West oil pipeline has demonstrated the strategic value of energy infrastructure that is capable of bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. At this stage, IMEC’s energy component should focus on natural gas, including pipelines from the Arabian Gulf to Israel’s Mediterranean ports, from which the gas could then be transported to Europe through new pipelines in the Eastern Mediterranean.[REF]

  • Establish an Abraham Accords critical-technology partnership. Technological leadership will shape the global balance of power and the national security of states to an increasing degree. The United States, Israel, and key Arab and Muslim partners possess complementary capabilities that can strengthen U.S. and allied technological leadership.

    The State Department’s Pax Silica initiative provides a valuable global framework for cooperation with trusted partners on AI and technology supply chains.[REF] Congress should complement this global effort with an Abraham Accords critical-technology partnership that is focused specifically on regional projects and innovation ecosystems. This initiative could build on the United States–Israel Artificial Intelligence Center Act introduced by then-Senator and now Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2021 while expanding the concept to include Abraham Accords partners and additional fields such as quantum technologies, space, cybersecurity, and biotechnology.[REF] Such a partnership should leverage resources from all of its members to support joint research, shared test beds, pilot projects, standards cooperation, fellowships, commercialization partnerships, and deployment of emerging technologies that address shared regional challenges. Participation should depend on matching contributions and rigorous safeguards governing intellectual property, export controls, cybersecurity, and the exposure of sensitive technologies to adversarial nations.

  • Promote regional security integration. Congress has already advanced and in some cases has enacted important initiatives involving regional air and missile defense, maritime security, cybersecurity, space cooperation, and joint exercises. These efforts should be consolidated into a practical regional framework that encompasses planning, interoperability, resilience, research and development, and manufacturing. One realistic model is the Comprehensive Security Integration and Prosperity Agreement (C-SIPA) signed by the U.S. and Bahrain in September 2023. C-SIPA establishes mechanisms for high-level consultation and coordination in response to external aggression, strengthens defense cooperation, and integrates security with trade, technology, and investment.[REF]

    The United States should work to establish an Abraham Accords C-SIPA. Such a framework would not require an automatic commitment to use force. Rather, it could facilitate rapid senior-level consultations, shared threat assessments, and consideration of coordinated political, economic, and defensive responses whenever a participant faces external aggression or coercion. Standing working groups could deepen cooperation in integrated air defense, counter-drone systems, maritime security, cyber defense, and defense industrial cooperation. Particular attention should be devoted to protecting the infrastructure upon which regional integration and economic prosperity depend, including ports, energy installations, data centers, desalination facilities, airports, and logistics hubs.

    This architecture should be modular. Not every participant would take part in every aspect of the framework. The objective should be a flexible regional security platform that strengthens deterrence, enhances resilience, and enables partners to coordinate responses to common threats while respecting different constraints.

  • Invest in the human foundations of peace. Intergovernmental agreements and cooperation form the institutional basis for regional integration, but people-to-people relationships are this integration’s beating heart. Lasting peace will depend not only on agreements signed by officials, but also on entrepreneurs building businesses together, scientists conducting joint research, students studying side by side, and future leaders developing relationships of trust across borders.

    The post–October 7 period demonstrated the danger of failing to build extensive public constituencies that understand, value, and benefit from regional cooperation. If the Abraham Accords are to become a durable and lasting foundation, they must be rooted in sustained engagement among the peoples of the region. Fortunately, the United States already possesses highly effective tools for achieving this goal. Congress does not need to create new programs. Instead, it should adapt existing educational, scientific, and leadership programs by establishing dedicated Abraham Accords tracks that bring together participants from the United States, Israel, and regional partners.

    The State Department’s International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP)[REF] should establish recurring Abraham Accords cohorts that bring emerging leaders from Israel and Arab and Muslim partners to the United States as joint regional delegations. These cohorts could engage American counterparts while developing long-term professional networks focused on innovation, entrepreneurship, public administration, education, and economic integration. Similarly, the U.S.–Middle East Partnership Initiative (MEPI)[REF] should establish dedicated Abraham Accords groups within its existing leadership and entrepreneurship programs.

    Congress should support an Abraham Accords–focused track within the Stevens Initiative for Virtual Exchange,[REF] bringing American and Abraham Accords member countries’ classrooms, universities, and youth together for dialogue and shared projects. Finally, Congress should enhance the Middle East Regional Cooperation (MERC) Program[REF] by creating expanded funding opportunities for multilateral research consortia involving Israel, the United States, and Abraham Accords partners in such areas as water security, agriculture, health, and AI.

  • Appoint and confirm a Special Envoy for the Abraham Accords and develop country-specific strategies for expanding normalization. In the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Congress established within the Department of State the Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for the Abraham Accords, Negev Forum, and Related Integration and Normalization Fora and Agreements. The law provides for a Senate-confirmed envoy with the rank of ambassador who reports directly to the Secretary of State.[REF]

    This office should be filled, staffed, and empowered. The envoy should have the resources and access necessary to coordinate initiatives spanning the Departments of State, Defense, Commerce, and Treasury and other agencies while working closely with the White House and other special envoys. The envoy’s mandate should encompass both the deepening of existing agreements and expansion of the Abraham Accords. The United States, for example, should continue to work toward Saudi–Israeli normalization, but it should also be recalled that there are more than two dozen Arab and Muslim-majority countries that lack formal relations with Israel. Before October 7, 2023, progress reportedly had been made toward the establishment of formal relations with a number of these countries.

    The Special Envoy’s office should develop prioritized, country-specific strategies for a broad range of potential normalization partners. These strategies should begin with each country’s national priorities. For one country, the central issue might be defense cooperation. For another, it could be access to American technology, water and food security, energy, investment, or diplomatic and sovereignty-related issues. The United States should identify where American, Israeli, and regional capabilities can help to meet those needs, what mutually beneficial measures could pave the way for the expansion of ties, and what a road map toward gradual normalization would entail.[REF] There should also be a concerted effort to return Sudan to the Abraham Accords framework while countering the efforts of Iran and other hostile nations to expand their influence in Sudan and across the Sahel.

Conclusion

The Abraham Accords have demonstrated how bold and innovative American leadership can produce outcomes that few believed possible, but without concerted U.S.-led efforts, these agreements could fail to reach their full transformative potential.

The next phase will require active American leadership, commitment, and a strategy that treats regional integration as a central instrument and goal of U.S. policy. Congress can help to translate this vision into practical institutions and programs: a mutually beneficial IMEC, a trusted critical-technology partnership, a flexible regional security framework, stronger people-to-people networks, and a dedicated diplomatic effort to deepen and expand normalization.

Congress should also recognize that strengthening regional integration requires countering actors that seek to demonize Israel and undermine the Abraham Accords model of peace. The United Nations is today perhaps the most globally influential actor working to promote delegitimization and boycotts of Israel while whitewashing terrorism and rejectionism. The U.S. should not work to integrate Israel and Arab allies and at the same time provide funding to an institution that seeks to isolate Israel and undermine U.S. national interests.[REF] Similarly, some regional state-connected media platforms, such as Qatar’s Al Jazeera, have consistently promoted anti-normalization sentiments and a strongly negative framing of the Abraham Accords, thereby making the task of building warm peace more difficult. American policy should support institutions and initiatives that facilitate regional cooperation, recognition, and coexistence while opposing efforts to delegitimize the Abraham Accords.

The Middle East and North Africa region stands at a crossroads. Iran, the Muslim Brotherhood, rejectionist Palestinian factions, and others seek to steer the region down the path of extremism, instability, and terrorism. The Abraham Accords have provided an alternative path of tolerance, integration, and cooperation. Congress should lead the way in advancing regional peace, prosperity, and partnership in a manner that serves the vital interests of the American people.

Asher Fredman is a Visiting Fellow in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation.

#104. Supreme Court Will Hear Necessary and Proper Clause Case on Federal Law Banning Home Distilleries

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The case is likely to be the most important Necessary and Proper Clause case since 2012.

Today, the Supreme Court decided to review the case of Department of Justice v. McNutt, which challenges a federal law banning home distilleries. The key question in the case is whether the law in question is justified by the combination of the tax power and the Necessary and Proper Clause (which gives Congress the power to make laws "necessary and proper" for executing other powers granted to the federal government). This is likely to be most important Supreme Court Necessary and Proper Clause decision since at least NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), which ruled that a "proper" power permissible under the Clause is one that is "ancillary" to the implementation of an enumerated power; it cannot be a "great, substantive and independent" power. This case is likely to further clarify the meaning of "proper," perhaps by explicating in more detail what counts as a "great…and independent" power.

In the lower court decision in this case, the Fifth Circuit ruled that the law is not "proper" and even that it isn't "necessary." There is also a Sixth Circuit decision that went the other way, thereby creating a circuit split.

As explained in my earlier posts on the Fifth and Sixth Circuit decisions (linked above), I think this law is not "proper," and I hope the Supreme Court strikes it down. I summarize the reasons why in my post on the Fifth Circuit ruling:

The Fifth Circuit… concludes that the law in question exceeds Congress' authority under the Necessary and Proper Clause, which grants the power to makes laws "necessary and proper" for carrying into execution other federal powers. I think the court is right that the law in question is not "proper." The Supreme Court, in NFIB v. Sebelius(2012), ruled that a "proper" power permissible under the Clause is one that is "ancillary" to the implementation of an enumerated power. It cannot be a "great, substantive and independent" power. See my analysis in this article. The power claimed here is clearly "great and independent." As Judge [Edith] Jones notes, "[u]nder the government's logic, Congress may criminalize nearly any at-home conduct only because it has the possibility of concealing taxable activity."

I elaborated further in the post criticizing the Sixth Circuit decision:

[T]he Sixth Circuit is badly wrong to conclude that the law is "proper." As explained in  my earlier post, the Supreme Court, in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), ruled that a "proper" power permissible under the Clause is one that is "ancillary" to the implementation of an enumerated power. It cannot be a "great, substantive and independent" power. The power to ban any home-based activity that might serve a substitute for taxable activity outside the home is clearly a "great and independent power." As Judge Edith Jones explains in the Fifth Circuit ruling, "[u]nder the government's logic, Congress may criminalize nearly any at-home conduct only because it has the possibility of concealing taxable activity."

The Sixth Circuit tries to address this point by claiming alcohol is somehow special….

This distinction between alcohol and all other commodities is totally arbitrary. The same reasoning could justify banning home production of anything else that is more easily taxed if produced outside the home. And there is a long history of home production of all kinds of other commodities taxed or severely regulated by the government, ranging from cigarettes to illegal drugs, to pornographic videos.

While Judge Edith Jones (author of the Fifth Circuit decision) is one of that circuit's most conservative judges, the ruling was also joined by liberal Obama appointee Judge James Graves. On the other hand, the Sixth Circuit decision was written by prominent conservative Judge Raymond Kethledge. We shall see if the Supreme Court also divides on this issue in a way that cuts across conventional ideological and jurisprudential lines.

As noted in my post on the Fifth Circuit case, I think Judge Jones is not persuasive in arguing that the home distillery ban isn't "necessary," as well as improper. That argument is unlikely to prevail under the Supreme Court's expansive definition of "necessary, "  dating back to McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), where Chief Justice John Marshall famously ruled that "necessary" includes any measures that may be "useful" or "convenient" for implementing an enumerated power.

As also noted in my posts on the two lower court rulings, I think the government has a better argument that this law is authorized by the Supreme Court's badly misguide precedent on federal power under Commerce Clause (which grants Congress power to regulate interstate commerce). But the Supreme Court is apparently not going to review that issue. The question presented submitted to the Court in McNutt is limited to the Necessary and Proper Clause.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#105. French High School Student Protests Met with Excessive Force

Click to expand Image Students raise their hands in front of police officers as they demonstrate outside Sciences Po during a protest over school overcrowding and decay in Paris, France, October 7, 2026. © 2026 Tom Nicholson/Getty Images

Images from ongoing student protests in France of heavily armed riot police using tear gas, stun grenades, batons, rubber bullets, and rough restraint techniques on children have sparked national and international concern.

High schoolers across France have taken to the streets since September 21 frustrated with the government’s continued under-investment in their education, which has resulted in a shortage of teachers, too large classes, and inadequate school buildings. While schools have been blockaded and some protesters have engaged in violence, the protests have been overwhelmingly peaceful.

Police use of force in response to the protests has resulted in serious injuries to children, including a 15-year-old boy who lost a hand to an explosive police stun grenade and a 14-year-old boy whose jaw shattered from a police tear-gas canister fired at close range. The government announced a temporary suspension of the use of stun grenades.

Police have reportedly detained more than 6,800 people since the demonstrations started; with apparently 86 percent of them, children. Authorities have also reportedly opened 36 internal investigations into allegations of police misconduct. But internal reviews in France rarely translate into real accountability.

Police use of excessive force during protests is not new in France. Human Rights Watch documented severe injuries caused by police during the 2018 “Yellow Vest” movement. And 2023’s pension reform protests and environmental demonstrations were also marked by such use of force. The current student protests began in schools in working-class neighborhoods, where racialized young people constantly experience and fear police harassment and state violence.

Instead of addressing persistent problems with police using excessive force, the government is seeking to strengthen law enforcement’s right to use force. Under consideration since early 2026, a bill proposes to grant officers a “presumption of legality” when using their firearms. Rights groups warn the changes risk lowering the threshold for police to resort to use of firearms and shielding police from judicial scrutiny.

French authorities should stop treating peacefully protesting children as a danger that needs to be neutralized. Instead, the government should uphold its obligations to protect children and their right to protest and listen to the demands of young people on the streets. To restore trust, the government should also thoroughly and promptly investigate all incidents of police use of force and end police tactics and reform the powers that foster police violence.

#106. Judge tosses most of Alec Baldwin’s claims against prosecutors over ‘Rust’ shooting

This aerial photo shows the movie set of “Rust” at the Bonanza Creek Ranch in Santa Fe, New Mexico, in October 2021. (Photo by Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

Citing prosecutorial immunity, a federal judge in New Mexico has dismissed the bulk of actor Alec Baldwin’s lawsuit against the prosecutors who charged him in the fatal 2021 shooting on the set of the movie Rust.

Courthouse News Service reported Thursday that U.S. District Judge Kea Riggs of the District of New Mexico held that prosecutors Mary Carmack-Altwies and Andrea Reeb were entitled to immunity on most of the counts filed by Baldwin. Riggs’ decision came weeks after she dismissed claims against special prosecutor Kari Morrissey on the same grounds.

“Even though the court is concerned by the allegations of misconduct by defendants Carmack-Altwies and Reeb, it recognizes that, as prosecutors, they are entitled to invoke the protection of absolute prosecutorial immunity,” Riggs wrote in her decision.

The case stems from an October 2021 incident on the set of Rust where cinematographer Halyna Hutchins died after a pistol that Baldwin was holding discharged during rehearsal.

Baldwin was charged with involuntary manslaughter in 2023, but the case was dismissed in July 2024 after the judge ruled that prosecutors had engaged in “egregious discovery violations.” Baldwin then sued in early 2025, claiming prosecutorial misconduct, defamation and civil rights violations.

According to Courthouse News Service, Riggs was concerned by the misconduct allegations but found that immunity applied. Riggs, however, ruled that Carmack-Altwies was not immune from claims tied to her alleged role in investigating and destroying the gun, which Riggs said was “too far removed from the judicial process.” Claims over her alleged media statements and involvement in the law enforcement investigation will also proceed because she had not sought their dismissal.

Riggs also found that Reeb violated separation of powers by serving as a state legislator and as a special prosecutor but concluded that she retained authority to prosecute. Riggs declined to dismiss a few “vague and undated allegations” against Reeb, saying it was premature to decide whether not immunity applied.

The prosecutors’ lawyer Luis Robles said his clients were “relieved” and “heartened” in a statement to Courthouse News Service.

Baldwin’s counsel did not respond to a Courthouse News Service request for comment.

Alec Baldwin headed back to trial for ‘Rust’ negligence lawsuit

#107. An immigration-heavy term

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

This week, the second and final one of the October sitting, the justices heard two oral arguments and added three cases to the oral argument docket while continuing to manage emergency applications. We’re expecting an order list on Monday, but, after that, things should be a little quieter at One First Street until the November sitting begins on Nov. 2.

Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EDT.

In an emergency application that was publicly docketed on Thursday, three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants asked the Supreme Court to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that prevents enforcement of a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings. For more on the dispute, see the On Site section below.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court granted a request from the Federal Communications Commission to block a ruling by a federal appeals court that would have required the FCC to rule quickly on a challenge to its “public notice” extending favorable advertising rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees. Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that they would have denied the application.

Also on Wednesday, the justices heard oral argument in Salazar v. Paramount Global, on whether and how the 1988 Video Privacy Protection Act, which was enacted after the Washington City Paper reported on Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork’s video rental history, applies in the internet era. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in Beaird v. United States, on the degree of deference that courts owe to the U.S. Sentencing Commission’s commentary on applying federal sentencing guidelines. Here is the link to our Case Preview.

Also on Tuesday, the court released a list of orders from the justices’ Oct. 9 conference, announcing, among other things, that it had added three new cases to the oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term. The cases address what kinds of orders trial courts can issue in disputes over access to government information from organizations such as the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, whether working as a cook in a camp run by a terrorist group qualifies as providing “material support” for terrorism under federal immigration law, and whether a certificate of appealability may be granted to a prisoner whose claim is foreclosed by his own circuit’s precedent but would be allowed to proceed in a different circuit.

On Sept. 28, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to clear the way for the Federal Bureau of Prisons to implement its new policy on healthcare and accommodations for transgender inmates, which would prevent such inmates from obtaining gender-transition surgeries, hormone therapy, and “social accommodations.” The dispute is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

A dispute over “the use of student IDS to vote” in New Hampshire has arrived on the Supreme Court’s interim docket after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit declined to pause a district-court ruling allowing use of student IDs for establishing a voter’s identity during voter registration, according to InDepthNH. The case addresses New Hampshire’s “House Bill 323 – which made student IDs a no longer valid form of identification to obtain a ballot” – and follow-up guidance from Secretary of State David M. Scanlan on how to implement HB 323, which said “that student IDs cannot be used as proof of ID when registering to vote, requesting an absentee ballot, or checking in to vote in an election.” Scanlan has asked the justices to clear the way for the guidance to take full effect and prevent student IDs from being used during voter registration.

Last month, attorney John Eastman filed a petition for review with the Supreme Court, asking the justices “to review his disbarment over his role in efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election.” On Wednesday, “Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), both lawyers and members of the Senate Judiciary Committee,” filed a friend-of-the-court brief in support of Eastman’s petition, telling the court that “Eastman’s disbarment stemmed from the weaponization of the bar disciplinary process by political activists,” according to Bloomberg Law. “Lee and Cruz wrote that malpractice and court sanctions already protect clients from deficient counsel” and “also argued that ‘ideological attorney discipline’ could have a chilling effect and burden clients’ ability to find willing, independent counsel.” Bloomberg Law noted that, although the Supreme Court “has reversed disbarments in the past, intervention in state bar proceedings is rare.”

In the early 2000s, Edward Williams was twice convicted of driving under the influence. About a decade later, he realized that, as a result of the second of these convictions, he was barred from owning a gun under 18. U.S.C. 922(g)(1), which prohibits firearm possession by anyone convicted of “a crime punishable by imprisonment for a term exceeding one year.” Williams then filed a lawsuit over 922(g)(1), contending it was unconstitutional as applied to him. This week, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed, holding that applying the statute to Williams “was not ‘consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation,’” according to Reason. The ruling deepened a disagreement between the federal courts of appeals over the Second Amendment rights of “people with nonviolent felony records.” Reason noted that “[s]o far, the Supreme Court has declined to accept any of the many petitions asking it to resolve that circuit split.”

In a post for his Substack, Ed Whelan began exploring the unusual circumstances surrounding President Ronald Reagon’s nomination of Sandra Day O’Connor to the Supreme Court. “Chief Justice Warren E. Burger deserves the lion’s share of the credit” for getting O’Connor on Reagan’s radar, according to Whelan, who noted that Burger became her friend and advocate after meeting her during a “houseboat vacation” on Utah’s Lake Powell. Former White House counsel Fred Fielding told Whelan that Burger spoke to him about O’Connor soon after Reagan took office. “He mentioned having met a most interesting state court jurist on a houseboat trip, Sandra O’Connor, and having been with her at a legal conference in London. It was obvious to me he was trying to plant her name in my mind,” Fielding said.

In a post for his Substack, Steve Vladeck pushed back against the idea that “expanding the Supreme Court is the only Court reform worth pursuing,” calling this contention “deeply unhelpful and unfortunate.” Expansion, he contended, “not only won’t do anything to solve the underlying problem (the Court’s complete lack of accountability), but it will almost certainly produce some (to my mind) deeply undesirable, if not disastrous, medium- and long-term effects along the way.” Among other things, Vladeck urged proponents of this type of court reform to consider how to avoid “touching off a race to the bottom, where each time one party controls the House, Senate, and presidency, it expands the Court to ensure an ideologically and politically sympathetic majority.”

Three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants have asked the justices to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that they described as the product of “egregious collusion.” A ruling in the challengers’ favor would temporarily restore a Biden-era regulation that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings – when, for example, a crime victim or witness is seeking immigration relief, such as asylum – while the challengers’ appeal in the lower federal courts is ongoing.

Since late April, the court has granted review in seven immigration-related cases. One of those was dismissed as moot last month, but six remain, meaning that around one-fifth of the cases currently on the oral argument docket involve immigration. What’s more, the justices will soon consider several more high-profile petitions for review in this area.

In his Indigenous Docket column, Matthew L.M. Fletcher offered a brief history of the Tribal Supreme Court Project, which was launched 25 years ago with the goal of establishing “an infrastructure that would allow tribal interests to reach better outcomes in Supreme Court litigation.” As a result of this project, “[t]ribal interests that were floundering, often embarrassed by unanimous decisions untempered by a dissenting opinion, now stand a much more sporting chance before the court.”

In his SCOTUSCrim column, Rory Little highlighted Justice Antonin Scalia’s use of the phrase “in common use at the time” in a major Second Amendment case from 2008, District of Columbia v. Heller, exploring how this potential limitation on gun rights has been abandoned over time and the implications this has for whether possession of AR-15s is constitutionally protected by the Second Amendment.

In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored six petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices at their private conference today, including two addressing the federal ban on home distilling.

In her In the Interim column on Tuesday, Taraleigh Davis shared key takeaways from the Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack for the recently concluded 2025-26 term, highlighting, among other things, the decrease in emergency applications from the Trump administration.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday added three new cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term. The cases include U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, on what types of discovery orders are appropriate in disputes over access to government information.

Sarah Isgur and David French are joined by Vince Chhabria, a judge for the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, and Stanford Law School Professor Nora Engstrom to discuss the incredibly high number of motions granted to seal documents and the line between secrecy and protecting the public interest. They also discuss three new cases that SCOTUS added to its oral argument docket on Tuesday.

The only justice to serve as Speaker of the House and a Supreme Court justice, Justice Philip Barbour served on the court less than five years, a tenure many have deemed too brief to have “a true impact.” We’ll let you be the judge.

Barbour was born in May 1783 in Virginia, though exactly where is disputed – one account places him near Orange County, while Justice Lewis Powell’s account puts him in Williamsburg. (Powell wrote a law review article about all the justices from Virginia, identifying Barbour as the third associate justice from there.) After briefly practicing law in Kentucky, Barbour returned to Virginia in 1802. He and his wife (also his first cousin) had seven children, apparently naming the youngest three boys Quintus, Sextus, and Septimus.

Powell described Barbour’s political ascent as “meteoric,” with Barbour elected to the Virginia House of Delegates in 1812 and to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1814. His older brother, James, served as governor of Virginia while the younger Barbour was in the Virginia House, and served in the Senate when Philip was in Congress. But while James aligned with Henry Clay’s “postwar nationalism,” Philip committed to “agrarian, strict construction, states’ rights.” As part of this, Philip opposed the national bank and protective tariffs, and by one account, was the “first major political figure” to argue that such a tariff was unconstitutional, rather than merely unjust. Both Barbour brothers argued that proposed restrictions on Missouri as a condition of statehood were unconstitutional.

In 1821, Barbour was one of the lawyers for Virginia in Cohens v. Virginia, and argued the position that the Supreme Court had no authority to review a criminal case out of a Virginia state court. Virginia lost on this point; Chief Justice John Marshall held in a unanimous decision that the Supreme Court had appellate jurisdiction to review the Virginia state court’s ruling, writing that “[t]he Constitution and laws of a State, so far as they are repugnant to the Constitution and laws of the United States, are absolutely void.” That December, Barbour replaced the incumbent House Speaker John Taylor of New York, whose antislavery views during the Missouri Compromise debates had cost him support from the South. As the first Speaker of the House from Virginia, Barbour served for the 17th Congress from 1821 to 1823.

When, due to illness, former President James Monroe resigned as president of Virginia’s 1829 convention to revise its constitution, delegates unanimously chose Barbour to succeed him. Barbour was also discussed as a cabinet pick for President Andrew Jackson but was instead given a recess appointment to the federal district court in eastern Virginia in October 1830. Not everyone was a fan of Barbour – former President John Quincy Adams said in 1831 that if Marshall retired, his replacement would be “some shallow-pated wild-cat like Philip P. Barbour fit for nothing but to tear the Union to rags and tatters.”

Southerners, unhappy with Martin Van Buren as Jackson’s vice-presidential nominee, pushed to swap him for Barbour in 1832. Barbour took his name out of the running, allowing Jackson to keep his preferred vice-presidential candidate, Van Buren (while also helping Barbour to get in Jackson’s good graces). Jackson nominated Barbour to the court in December 1835 to take Justice Gabriel Duvall’s seat, and the Senate confirmed him 30-11 on March 15, 1836 – the same day they confirmed Roger Taney as chief justice. Barbour was one of six Jackson appointees to the court, more than any other 19th-century president.

Perhaps Barbour’s most significant opinion came in 1837’s New York v. Miln, which upheld a New York law that regulated ships bringing in immigrants as a valid use of the state’s police power. Barbour used the case to press for a more narrow reading of Congress’ commerce authority and a broader one of state police power, which he described as “unqualified and exclusive.” “[P]ersons,” he wrote, “are not the subject of commerce.”

Barbour dissented only twice on the bench, writing about a dozen opinions and voting most often with his fellow Southerners, Justice John Catron (97.8%) and Taney (97.4%). Joseph Gordon Hylton, who penned Barbour’s encyclopedia entry, wrote that a longer life would almost certainly have made Barbour as fervent a states’ rights champion as his successor, Justice Peter Daniel. (Daniel voted with the majority in Dred Scott v. Sandford.)

Barbour died in his sleep in February 1841 at age 57 from heart disease. This was in the middle of oral arguments in The Amistad Case, which the court decided 7-1 in favor of persons kidnapped illegally from Africa, holding that they were not lawfully enslaved under Spanish law and thus were free individuals.

Justice Joseph Story praised Barbour as “a very conscientious, upright, and laborious judge, whom we all respected for his talents and virtues, and his high sense of duty.” Powell noted that “Barbour’s tenure there was short. ... He wrote few opinions, and consistently voted with Chief Justice Roger B. Taney.”

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “– you've picked some hypotheticals that are particularly helpful for you. Chick-fil-A, you don't think of that as anything other than chicken. But there are a lot of stores that sell a lot of different things, including the type of videos that we're talking about. And so I don't know why we should focus just on the easy hypotheticals.”

MR. CLEMENT: “Well, it's sort of my job to focus on the easy hypotheticals.”

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “I would think your job is to focus on the hard ones –”

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “– at least from our point of view.”
