#108. Jurisprudential Approach of the Six Conservative Justices on the U.S. Supreme Court

When Roger invited me to Dartmouth to discuss the philosophical and jurisprudential differences among the Supreme Court’s six conservatives, I said yes before he could finish the sentence. It is timely—and, for those of us who have spent much of our professional lives thinking about the law and the Constitution, irresistible.

Forty years ago, when I was your age and an undergraduate at Kenyon College, this lecture could not honestly have been given. In 1986, there were not six conservative Justices. More important, the vocabulary you now take for granted—originalism, original public meaning, textualism, and text, history, and tradition—had not yet become the common currency of constitutional debate. Conservative and Republican-appointed Justices existed, but the mature, disciplined, institutionally consequential conservative legal movement did not.

That transformation was neither accidental nor immediate. It was the product of ideas, institutions, litigation, appointments, and principles tested under pressure. The quarterback was Edwin Meese III, President Ronald Reagan’s Attorney General, whom I worked for at Heritage for 18 years.

Throughout my talk tonight, I’m going to give you several book recommendations for those who want to dive deeper into this topic. My first recommendation is The Meese Revolution: The Making of a Constitutional Moment by Professors Steven Calabresi and Gary Lawson.[REF]

Each of today’s six conservative Justices is an originalist and textualist. To understand where they agree, where they diverge, and why it matters, we must begin with the Constitution’s design.

The Intellectual Setting

Early American political thought treated the Constitution as a fixed fundamental law limiting power by separating it horizontally and vertically—even well-intentioned power. Daniel Webster said it was designed “to guard the people against the dangers of good intentions.” Abraham Lincoln made the related point that the American people are the rightful masters of Congress and the courts, not to discard the Constitution, but to remove those who twist it. James Madison, pivotal to the Convention of 1787 and one of the three authors of the Federalist Papers, wrote in Federalist No. 51: “You must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself.”[REF]

My second recommendation is Joseph J. Ellis’s The Quartet: Orchestrating the Second American Revolution.[REF] The understanding reached in this early period endured for a long time, then eroded during the Progressive Era. Progressives began to see fixed meaning, checks and balances, and Article V’s amendment process not as protections but as obstacles to a powerful central government capable of meeting an industrial nation’s demands.

Woodrow Wilson—the poster child of the Progressive Era—rejected the Framers’ image of a balanced machine. Government, he wrote, “is not a machine, but a living thing.” It answers to Darwin, not Newton: “Living political constitutions must be Darwinian in structure and in practice.”[REF] Wilson’s organic metaphor helped justify living constitutionalism—the idea that broad constitutional principles should be applied to contemporary needs rather than constrained by historical understanding.

The Warren Court and, to a significant degree, the Burger Court operated in that climate. In a sense, the Burger Court shows what happens when conservative Justices apply a living Constitution. Progressive lawyers and academics increasingly treated the Constitution as aspirational principles where judges were free—indeed obligated—to update.

Justice William Brennan said it embodied “human dignity,” which for him required abolishing the death penalty. The Court decided consequential cases involving criminal procedure, religion, speech, privacy, and individual rights by applying evolving values to the controversies of the day. Some decisions remain important. But conservatives objected not only to outcomes; they objected to the method.

In Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), Justice William O. Douglas wrote that specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have “penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance.”[REF] From those penumbras and emanations, the Court discovered a right of privacy absent from the text.

Douglas could have extended the family-rights cases Meyer v. Nebraska[REF] and Pierce v. Society of Sisters,[REF] but those cases had been written by the arch-conservative Justice James McReynolds under a theory used against Progressive legislation and the first New Deal. So Douglas reached for penumbras, and Griswold became Exhibit A for extra-constitutional excess.

Eight years later, Roe v. Wade relied on that newly minted right to privacy—grounded in the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause—to create a right capacious enough to include abortion.[REF] The question became less “What does the text mean?” than “What should the text mean in our time?” The result too often resembled policymaking rather than applying law.

To this day, Justice Clarence Thomas keeps a sign in his chambers: “Don’t emanate the penumbras.”

The early conservative answer was judicial restraint: Judges should behave like judges, not legislators, and hesitate before displacing democratic choices. That instinct had wisdom after a Court that sometimes acted like the seniormost house of Congress. But restraint alone was insufficient.

When Congress violates the First Amendment, deference is not meaningful restraint; it is failure to enforce higher law. Conservatives needed a theory that constrained judges while permitting them to enforce the Constitution. Anger at the Warren and Burger Courts could not supply it. Neither could restraint alone.

The Meese Revolution

That was the intellectual setting when Attorney General Meese entered the fray in 1985. He did not invent originalism, but anyone seeking to understand how it became central to the conservative legal movement—and eventually to Supreme Court argument—must begin with the debate he helped launch.

On July 9, 1985, Meese addressed the American Bar Association in Washington.[REF] Most speeches by Attorneys General disappear into archives. This one did not, because he challenged the legal establishment on a fundamental question: What is the proper source of constitutional meaning?

He began with Thomas Paine’s formulation that in America, “the law is king.” Those four words place Congress, the President, and judges beneath the law. Judicial power is constitutional power; therefore, it too must have a source and a limit.

Meese argued that too many opinions had become “more policy choices than articulations of constitutional principle.” The Court “did not yield a coherent set of decisions” but instead had a “jurisprudence of idiosyncrasy” and “continued to roam at large in a veritable constitutional forest.” His criticism was not simply that the Court was liberal. If judges begin with their own conception of justice or good government and reshape doctrine around it, what constrains them?

Meese proposed a “Jurisprudence of Original Intention,” which “would take seriously the admonition of Justice [Joseph] Story’s friend and colleague, John Marshall, in Marbury [v. Madison] that the Constitution is a limitation on judicial power as well as executive and legislative.” He continued: “It has been and will continue to be the policy of this administration to press for a Jurisprudence of Original Intention. In the cases we file and those we join as amicus, we will endeavor to resurrect the original meaning of constitutional provisions and statutes as the only reliable guide for judgment.”

His core principle was memorable: Judges should “judge policies in light of principles, rather than remold principles in light of policies.” Begin with something outside yourself. Begin with the law. Let it constrain what you may do as a judge.

This was also an argument about democracy. The Constitution does not derive authority from judges’ approval; judges derive authority from the constitutional order. Constitutional change remains possible through Article V. Justice Antonin Scalia later put the distinction bluntly: If the Constitution needs updating, amend it; if a statute needs changing, ask Congress. Interpretation and amendment are not the same act.

To the academy and living constitutionalists, this was a radical shift—and a threat. Three months later, Justice Brennan answered at a speech at Georgetown University.[REF] He called original intention, in its doctrinaire form, “little more than arrogance cloaked as humility.” The ultimate question, he said, was what the text means “in our time.” The Constitution’s genius rested not in static meaning from a dead world, but in the adaptability of its great principles to current problems and needs.

Brennan identified difficulties early originalists had to confront, but Meese and later originalists pressed the unanswered question: If constitutional principles adapt to contemporary values, what external legal criterion tells judges which values control? Who identifies them? When does interpretation become revision?

The debate forced refinement. Original intention developed into original public meaning: how constitutional language was publicly understood when adopted. Scalia helped move analysis away from the subjective intentions of particular Framers and toward contemporary dictionaries, state constitutions, the Federalist and Anti-Federalist Papers, newspapers, pamphlets, and other historical evidence. Recovery can be difficult and contested, but the judge still looks for an answer outside himself.

Four decades later, originalism, textualism, original public meaning, and text-history-tradition tests have moved from radical concepts into the mainstream. Success, however, exposed a new problem. Originalism and textualism are not mathematical algorithms. Judges may agree that text, history, and precedent matter yet disagree about what each requires, how much weight precedent deserves, and what to do when a precedent conflicts with the Constitution.

That is where the differences among today’s six originalists become fascinating. Sarah Isgur’s witty Last Branch Standing,[REF] my next recommendation, suggests that we should see not a 6–3 Court but a 3–3–3 Court.

John Roberts, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett are “the deciders”: institutionalists whom critics accuse of sometimes subordinating originalism to protecting the Court amid political controversy. Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch are “the conservative honey badgers,” more willing to apply the Constitution as written without regard to political consequences. The final three—Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor, and Ketanji Brown Jackson—are the liberals on the court.

The categories are useful, but they are not permanent voting blocs. Cases differ, Justices move, and shared methods can point in unexpected directions.

Last term illustrates why simple labels mislead. The Court decided 61 cases. Of those, 43.9 percent were unanimous and 10.6 percent were 8–1; only 10.6 percent were 5–4 and 28.8 percent were 63. Roberts and Kavanaugh were in the majority 95 percent of the time, Barrett 92 percent, Gorsuch 86 percent, and Thomas and Alito 83 percent. Even Justice Jackson, at the bottom, was in the majority 67 percent of the time. Only one in five cases divided 6–3 along ideological lines.

The Institutionalists

Chief Justice Roberts. John Roberts is not merely one of nine Justices; as Chief Justice of the United States, he heads a co-equal branch. His concern for institutional credibility, precedent, continuity, and the scope of judicial intervention is unusually visible.

June Medical Services v. Russo is a clear example.[REF] Four years earlier, Roberts had dissented when the Court invalidated a Texas abortion law in Whole Woman’s Health v. Hellerstedt.[REF] When June Medical presented a materially similar Louisiana law, Roberts still believed the earlier case wrong, but it was now precedent. He supplied the decisive vote to invalidate the Louisiana law, separating two questions: What would I have decided initially, and what should I do after the Supreme Court has decided it? Precedent matters precisely when a judge thinks it wrong, both for predictability and for public confidence that the Court is doing law rather than voting on policy.

Two years later, Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization presented the issue from the other direction. Roberts concluded Mississippi’s 15-week law could stand but declined to overrule Roe and Casey entirely. He wrote:

We granted certiorari to decide one question: “Whether all pre-viability prohibitions on elective abortions are unconstitutional.”… In urging our review, Mississippi stated that its case was “an ideal vehicle” to “reconsider the bright-line viability rule,” and that a judgment in its favor would “not require the Court to overturn” Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pa. v. Casey.[REF]

He continued: “Today, the Court nonetheless rules for Mississippi by doing just that. I would take a more measured course. I agree with the Court that the viability line established by Roe and Casey should be discarded under a straightforward stare decisis analysis. That line never made any sense.” But his bottom line was clear:

But that is all I would say, out of adherence to a simple yet fundamental principle of judicial restraint: If it is not necessary to decide more to dispose of a case, then it is necessary not to decide more. Perhaps we are not always perfect in following that command, and certainly there are cases that warrant an exception. But this is not one of them.[REF]

Justice Alito, by contrast, concluded that once the constitutional foundation failed, the precedent question could not be avoided. The dispute was not whether Mississippi’s law survived but how much the Court had to decide, what it could leave for another day, and what precedent requires when the Court believes an earlier decision wrong. Alito wrote that “Roe was egregiously wrong from the start.”[REF]

Professor Josh Blackman has argued that Roberts’s institutionalism does not always produce minimalism, particularly in separation-of-powers cases. Concern for the Court may lead him toward a narrow decision in one case and a broader one in another. The revealing question is not whether Roberts is simply cautious, but what he believes the Court, as an institution, is entitled—and required—to do.

Justice Kavanaugh. Brett Kavanaugh describes himself as a modern original-public-meaning originalist—what he calls constitutional textualism. The Constitution’s words matter because it is law, not aspiration, and the inquiry differs from reconstructing individual Framers’ private intentions.

Yet his method does not stop there. He ties stare decisis to stability, predictability, reliance, impartiality, and judicial independence and has argued that precedent is constitutionally required. Asked what a judge should do when confronting a Supreme Court precedent from which he previously dissented, Kavanaugh answered that the ordinary course is to follow it—perhaps especially after losing. The law does not reset to zero every morning.

Bostock v. Clayton County shows another aspect of his method.[REF] Kavanaugh and Gorsuch both claimed textualist ground in construing Title VII’s prohibition on discrimination “because of sex.” Gorsuch concluded the text covered discrimination against gay and transgender employees: If changing an employee’s sex changes the employment decision, sex necessarily plays a role, regardless of what the 1964 Congress anticipated.

Kavanaugh distinguished literal meaning from ordinary meaning. Courts should not disassemble a statutory phrase, consult individual definitions, and mechanically reassemble it; they should ask how the whole phrase was ordinarily understood. In his view, ordinary usage treated sex discrimination and sexual-orientation discrimination as distinct concepts.

He connected that linguistic conclusion to separation of powers. His dissent began: “Like many cases in this Court, this case boils down to one fundamental question: Who decides?” He answered: “Under the Constitution’s separation of powers, the responsibility to amend Title VII belongs to Congress and the President in the legislative process, not to this Court.”[REF] He later wrote: “[W]e are judges, not Members of Congress. And in Alexander Hamilton’s words, federal judges exercise ‘neither Force nor Will, but merely judgment.’… Under the Constitution’s separation of powers, our role as judges is to interpret and follow the law as written, regardless of whether we like the result.”[REF]

Gorsuch accepted that premise but rejected its application: Congress did not need to amend a law whose enacted words already resolved the case. This is a genuine jurisprudential disagreement. Is fidelity principally about semantic consequences, or does the ordinary meaning of a phrase as a whole control? Textualism supplies the starting point, not a mechanical finish line.

Justice Barrett. Amy Coney Barrett offers a third variation. My next recommendation is her Listening to the Law: Reflections on the Court and Constitution.[REF]

At the ceremony announcing her nomination, Barrett said of Justice Scalia that “[h]is judicial philosophy is mine, too.”[REF] But she does not merely reproduce Scalia. She begins with the Constitution as a legal text whose provisions retain the meaning they had when adopted.

Originalism does not require mind-reading, guarantee easy answers, or prevent judicial error.

Her deeper conception of judging resists pressure from two directions: outside expectations from political constituencies, friends, critics, and the public and inside temptation to make law conform to the judge’s own preferences. The judge must listen to law rather than master it.

That explains Fulton v. City of Philadelphia.[REF] The Court unanimously ruled for Catholic Social Services, but Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch were prepared to reconsider and overrule Employment Division v. Smith.[REF]

Barrett was not ready without confronting the first sentence of her concurrence: “Yet what should replace Smith?” She found serious textual and structural arguments against Smith, yet resisted replacing one categorical rule with another before addressing the alternatives:

I am skeptical about swapping Smith’s categorical antidiscrimination approach for an equally categorical strict scrutiny regime, particularly when this Court's resolution of conflicts between generally applicable laws and other First Amendment rights—like speech and assembly—has been much more nuanced. There would be a number of issues to work through if Smith were overruled. To name a few: Should entities like Catholic Social Services—which is an arm of the Catholic Church—be treated differently than individuals? Should there be a distinction between indirect and direct burdens on religious exercise? What forms of scrutiny should apply? And if the answer is strict scrutiny, would pre-Smith cases rejecting free exercise challenges to garden-variety laws come out the same way?[REF]

This is more than caution. Barrett asks whether an existing rule is wrong, what principle authorizes its replacement, what the new rule is, and whether the present case requires that move.

Scalia’s originalism was often a theory of dissent—ironically, not in Smith, which he wrote. Using originalism to show why non-originalist decisions are wrong is easier than using it to govern, with concrete legal consequences. Barrett accordingly proceeds carefully.

Her reliance on history poses a similar question. Scholars describe growing use of post-ratification practice—what one writer calls “living traditionalism.” If meaning is fixed at ratification, what work does a practice from fifty, seventy-five, or one hundred years later perform? Later history may confirm an earlier understanding, reveal a settled interpretation, or carry force through precedent. But the judge must explain the bridge from evidence to conclusion. The question is not merely whether history exists, but what it proves.

Roberts, Kavanaugh, and Barrett thus form a recognizable institutionalist grouping without sharing an identical methodology. Roberts emphasizes the Court and the scope of judicial action. Kavanaugh foregrounds precedent, stability, reliance, and continuity. Barrett probes the steps connecting text, history, precedent, and doctrine.

The Conservative “Honey Badgers”

Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch do not simply disregard precedent or consequences. The distinction is comparative weight. When precedent conflicts with their best reading of text and history, they have shown greater willingness to reopen the foundation.

Justice Thomas. Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. provides a vivid example.[REF] A student who failed to make varsity cheerleading and a private softball team, but was offered junior-varsity cheerleading, posted on Snapchat: “F*** school f*** softball f*** cheer f*** everything.” The school suspended her from the team for a year. Eight Justices sided with the student; Thomas dissented alone.

The revealing point is where he began. While the majority developed principles for off-campus speech, Thomas examined schools’ historical authority over students around the Fourteenth Amendment’s ratification. He argued that schools then could discipline comparable conduct and faulted the majority for failing to tether its approach to something stable.

That is Thomas’s instinct.

When modern doctrine rests on premises inconsistent with text or history, he asks whether the Court should keep building on it at all. A precedent’s age does not establish legitimacy. Before asking how to apply a doctrine, he asks where it came from.

My next recommendation is his memoir, My Grandfather’s Son.[REF]

My principal takeaway from the book is that Justice Clarence Thomas’s life—and, in turn, his jurisprudence—is unlike that of any modern Justice, and perhaps any Justice in the Court’s history.

From the beginning, he was an outsider: born into poverty and segregation in a small Georgia community; reared by an exacting, devoutly Catholic grandfather; estranged for a time from the Church; drawn into the fervor of black radicalism; and ultimately returned, by conviction rather than convenience, to conservatism and the Catholic faith.

Along the way, he endured the scorn of leading black liberal intellectuals, who branded him a traitor to his race because he refused to surrender his independent judgment to their ideological demands.

No other Justice has brought to the Court quite this formation of intellect, faith, character, and moral resolve. It is therefore unsurprising that Justice Thomas is most fully himself when he stands alone.

Justice Clarence Thomas’s concurrence in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard College is majestic—an originalist tour de force and utter perfection.[REF] With historical clarity and constitutional conviction, Thomas traces the promise of racial equality from the Thirteenth Amendment through the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the Fourteenth Amendment.

Those enactments, he explains, marked America’s second founding and established a rule at once simple and profound: every citizen, regardless of color, stands equal before the law.

Thomas places the Court’s decision within the long, uneven struggle to honor that command.

The Court betrayed it in Plessy,[REF] restored it in Brown,[REF] and compromised it in Grutter[REF] by allowing universities to sort applicants by race in pursuit of diversity. But the Constitution does not permit government to cure one racial wrong by committing another. Racial discrimination remains unconstitutional whether imposed with hostile motives or benevolent aspirations.

The concurrence’s power lies in its union of text, history, and moral lucidity.

Thomas demonstrates that the Reconstruction Amendments were designed to extinguish legal distinctions based on race—not merely to rearrange their beneficiaries. The Constitution is color-blind because equality before the law admits neither favored races nor disfavored ones. After a regrettable constitutional interregnum, the Court finally returned to first principles: race-conscious admissions cannot survive genuine strict scrutiny, and the promise of equal citizenship belongs to every American.

Justice Thomas is conservative, certainly—but more important, he is the most original, independent-minded, and intellectually fearless conservative jurist of his generation.

That singular formation explains my overriding impression of Justice Thomas: he stands apart from his colleagues in the purity of his originalism and in his willingness to follow the Constitution’s original public meaning wherever it leads, without trimming principle to accommodate precedent, fashion, or institutional comfort. His separate writings in the Commerce Clause cases are illustrative.

He appears uniquely prepared to reconsider the entire doctrinal project that took root in Wickard v. Filburn[REF] and to examine, from first principles, whether the Court’s modern Commerce Clause jurisprudence can be reconciled with the Constitution’s text, structure, and original allocation of sovereign authority.

Perhaps Justice Gorsuch might join him in that undertaking. But Justice Thomas has already demonstrated the rare judicial courage to ask the antecedent question others avoid: not how far an erroneous doctrine may extend, but whether its premises are sound at all.

Were a majority of the Court willing to follow his lead, the result would be nothing less than a constitutional restoration—one that would reestablish the federal government as a government of limited and enumerated powers and renew the States’ rightful place in our constitutional order.

Justice Alito. Justice Alito’s Dobbs majority opinion sharply contrasts with the Chief’s concurrence. Roberts asked whether the Court could uphold Mississippi’s law without completely overruling Roe and Casey. Alito concluded it could not preserve precedents that were “egregiously wrong from the start” merely to produce a narrower opinion. Roberts emphasized the scope of intervention; Alito emphasized the duty to confront constitutional error. Roberts concurred only in the judgment; Alito wrote for the five-Justice majority.

My next recommendation is So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country by Samuel A. Alito.[REF]

In his new book, Alito calls himself a “working judicial originalist,” obliged to decide real cases within an inherited legal system, respect precedent, persuade colleagues, and reckon with consequences for litigants. Using a highway with seven exits, he identifies wrong turns: timidity masquerading as restraint; insisting every constitutional rule appear in black and white; abstraction detached from public meaning at ratification; antiquarian hunts for obscure relics; originalist window dressing attached to non-originalist doctrine; and the claim that the Constitution secretly incorporated Locke or another favored philosopher.

For Alito, originalism begins with text but recognizes structure, necessary implications, and the understanding of informed citizens—not merely discoveries by specialists armed with the judicial equivalent of a pith helmet and trowel.

Chapter Two turns to textualism. Alito honors Scalia for ending the “before Scalia” or “BS” era, when judges elevated committee reports, floor statements, generalized purposes, and policy instincts above enacted words. Overton Park reduced text to a fallback when legislative history failed; Griggs relegated Title VII’s words to a footnote while purpose did the work.

Alito recalls the conveniently manufactured Senate colloquy and Professor Robert Blakey’s immortal declaration, “I am the legislative history of RICO.” Scalia’s corrective was bracingly simple: the text is the law.

Scalia revived canons, sharpened oral argument, cleared judicial prose of professional fog, and demanded rigor even from friends, as his fierce criticism of Alito’s opinion in Hein v. Freedom From Religion Foundation illustrates.[REF] The story honors both: Scalia attacked arguments, not personalities; Alito’s measured recollection distinguishes principled disagreement from disrespect.

Alito’s deeper point is that Scalia’s triumph must not become “hypertextualism”—a wooden method mistaking dictionary entries for meaning and treating context as illicit. Judges are Congress’s faithful agents. Fidelity requires recovering the public meaning communicated by enacted words in linguistic and historical context: not divining hidden motives, but not pretending words stand like tin soldiers in isolation.

His examples involving breakfast, banks, and irony show why semantic meaning alone is insufficient. Context clarifies ambiguity, supplies what speakers reasonably leave unstated, and may show that literal words communicate something different from their bare formulation. This is not purposivism but Scalia’s “objectified intent”: what a reasonable reader, familiar with usage and circumstances, would understand the statute to convey. Canons such as noscitur a sociis, expressio unius, and ejusdem generis depend on contextual inferences.

Alito presses the point in criticizing Bostock. He argues that the majority detached “because of sex” from its 1964 public meaning and dismissed ordinary contextual evidence. His Italian-restaurant hypothetical exposes an agent who obeys literal wording while knowingly defeating the principal’s communicated instruction.

“Objective intent” admittedly raises hard questions about which historical evidence counts and when context becomes a back door for preference. But that difficulty does not defeat Alito’s warning: Scalia’s revolution was never a suicide pact with literalism. Proper textualism binds judges to enacted law, ordinary language, institutional limits, and democratic accountability—neither licensing improvisation nor rewarding studied obtuseness.

Justice Gorsuch. That brings us to Neil Gorsuch and two more recommendations: A Republic, If You Can Keep It and Over Ruled: The Human Toll of Too Much Law.[REF]

Bostock shows why “conservative” tells us little about jurisprudence. Gorsuch did not argue that the outcome was socially desirable; he argued that Congress’s words required it. Method is most revealing when it constrains a judge despite political reaction.

At the National Constitution Center, Gorsuch observed that originalism has a “terrible name,” while living constitutionalism “sounds kinda nice.” Yet he declined to enlist unreservedly in either camp, offering “enduring constitutionalism.”[REF]

Read together, his opinions in Bostock, United States v. Vaello Madero,[REF] and McGirt v. Oklahoma[REF] reveal a coherent method: Enduring Constitutionalism paired with Enduring Textualism. The governing words endure and must be applied as written, even when the result confounds political expectations.

His willingness to side with marginalized litigants is neither ideological apostasy nor accident. It follows from taking text seriously when it places a thumb on the scale for someone government, fashion, or institutional power would rather ignore.

Professors William Baude and Dan Epps captured this on the Divided Argument podcast, observing that Gorsuch defends “some” little guys when they are “being crushed or someone’s trying to crush the little guy.” Baude put it precisely: “[a] little guy with a technical legal argument on his side.”[REF] The modifier matters. Sympathy does not carry the case; law does. When the ostensibly powerless litigant has the stronger legal argument, Gorsuch follows the law to its destination—even when the political gallery expected another route and the consequences are substantial.

What Constrains the Judge?

That returns us to Ed Meese. The most interesting consequence of originalism is not uniformity; it produced none. Meese elevated a question that remains central to American constitutional debate: What constrains the judge? Brennan offered one answer, but for Meese and later originalists, it left the central problem unresolved: If constitutional principles adapt to contemporary values, what external legal criterion identifies which values control?

The challenge is not unique to the left. Some critics of originalism on the right, including advocates of common-good constitutionalism, urge judges and officials to interpret law through substantive principles of the common good. But if living constitutionalism is objectionable because it lets judges translate their values into constitutional law, substituting conservative values for progressive ones does not solve the methodological problem.

Constitutional methodology means little if it constrains only opponents. A method earns its keep when it constrains your own side. That is why Bostock belongs in this story. Whatever one thinks of the outcome, Gorsuch’s opinion shows how interpretive method can lead a Justice to a politically unexpected result. Kavanaugh’s dissent shows something equally important: The label “textualist” does not settle every interpretive question. Judges must still explain what textualism requires.

The arguments following Meese became more sophisticated than either his speech or Brennan’s reply. Original intention became original public meaning. Critics forced originalists to refine their use of history. Originalists forced critics to explain the limits of interpretation. Eventually, judges formed by the same movement began arguing with one another over the answers.

That is a far more useful way to read the Court than counting six conservatives and three liberals. Headlines tell you who won. Someone supplies the vote count. Someone else names each appointing President.

Those facts tell you the score. They do not tell you the method.

Forty years ago, Ed Meese asked, in substance: What constrains the judge? The easy test of the rule of law is when law produces the answer we wanted. The hard test is when it points elsewhere.

So, when the next Supreme Court decision reaches your phone, do not stop at the vote count or the appointing President. Ask what sources the Justice treated as authoritative. Ask what the text contributed. Ask what history established. Ask what happened to precedent. Ask whether the real disagreement concerned the law’s meaning, the method for discovering it, or how much the Court needed to decide.

And ask: Would this method still constrain the judge if it produced a result the judge personally disliked? If you can answer that question, you are no longer merely following the Supreme Court. You are beginning to understand it.

Charles D. “Cully” Stimson is Acting Director of the Legal Policy Center and Senior Legal Fellow, National Security, at The Heritage Foundation. This Heritage Lecture is slightly adapted from an address delivered before the undergraduate chapter of the Federalist Society at Dartmouth College on September 29, 2026.

#109. Libya: Eastern Authorities Carry Out Wave of Executions

Click to expand Image Military leader of Eastern Libya, Khalifa Haftar (center), attends a conference in Sabha, Libya, September 5, 2024.  © 2024 Khaled Nasraoui/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Photo

(Beirut) – The Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), which controls eastern and southern Libya, has executed at least 31 people since late August 2026 following grossly unfair military trials, Human Rights Watch said today. These are the first known executions in Libya since 2010, with at least 50 more people in Gernada military prison at imminent risk of execution.

On August 23, the LAAF military prosecutor announced that 10 people had been executed by firing squad after being convicted of murder and terrorism-related offenses. Human rights groups have documented a total of at least 31 executions as of September 10. The LAAF, led by General Khalifa Haftar, should immediately halt all executions and impose a moratorium on the death penalty, Human Rights Watch said. 

“The Libyan Arab Armed Forces are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya’s own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians,” said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “Every execution carried out under these conditions is an irreversible injustice and every government with influence over the LAAF should be pressing hard to stop the next one.”

Many of those executed had been arrested in the cities of Derna and Benghazi during or after the armed conflict between the LAAF and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018. Between 2018 and 2021, military courts in eastern Libya convicted hundreds of civilians in secret trials targeting real or perceived critics of the LAAF, sentencing at least 22 to death. 

According to Amnesty International, many of the sentences were based on confessions allegedly extracted under torture by the Internal Security Agency, an LAAF-affiliated armed group. At least two death sentences were reduced to life in prison on appeal by a higher military court in 2019, yet the defendants were put to death this year regardless.

The executions also went ahead despite a November 2025 ruling by the constitutional chamber of Libya’s Supreme Court that Law No. 4/2017 is unconstitutional insofar as it grants military courts jurisdiction to try civilians for terrorism and crimes against the state. 

Local human rights groups said that the military trials violated defendants’ due process rights. They were held in secret and without prior notice. Defendants’ families, journalists, and human rights organizations were not allowed to attend. Several defendants were denied lawyers of their choice and those who did have their own lawyers were refused visits before and during trial and could not speak with them privately. They were apparently not allowed to present their cases in court or examine the evidence against them. The verdicts were handed down without providing the defendants or their attorneys with written and reasoned judgments.

Trying civilians in military courts is incompatible with the right to a fair trial under human rights law and such trials violate the right to be tried before an independent and impartial tribunal. In Libya, military prosecutors are often not qualified to investigate civilians and they lack independence. The military prosecutors and judges in eastern Libya are themselves affiliated with the LAAF or allied armed groups. 

Families of defendants were not notified in advance that the executions would take place. The authorities refused to hand over the bodies of those executed, asked relatives to confirm the identities of the dead, then buried them without families present and warned relatives not to hold funerals. Secret executions and denying families a last visit violate international law, including by inflicting severe mental suffering on those executed and their relatives in breach of the absolute prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment.

Libya remains split between two rival authorities. The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU), which is internationally recognized, controls the west, alongside affiliated security agencies and armed groups. The LAAF and affiliated forces and militias control the east and south. Both sides operate with near-total impunity. 

The United Nations and the GNU condemned the executions. Governments that fund, train, and legitimize the LAAF have real leverage, and a responsibility to use it, publicly and privately, to press LAAF leaders to halt all executions, Human Rights Watch said.

Libya’s justice sector is fragmented and deeply polarized. Human Rights Watch has previously documented outdated and repressive legislation, a lack of fair trial rights, and rampant due process violations. Unaccountable militias control prisons that are only nominally under state ministries. 

Libyan authorities in both the east and west should restrict the jurisdiction of military courts to military offenses committed by military personnel and stop trying civilians in military courts altogether. They should promptly review all cases of civilians wrongfully detained and prosecuted before military courts and provide effective remedies, including release, transfer to civilian courts, or retrial in line with international fair trial standards, with acknowledgment of time served. 

Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all countries and under all circumstances because it is inherently inhumane, uniquely cruel and irreversible, and universally plagued by arbitrariness, prejudice, and error. Ninety-two countries have ratified a protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that requires the abolition of the death penalty, recognizing that capital punishment violates the right to life and the prohibition of cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment. Libya should abolish the death penalty and until then enact a moratorium on all executions.

“Libya went more than 15 years without an execution, and the LAAF has shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks,” Khawaja said. “The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar’s forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this.”

#111. America Needs Permitting Reform—With No Gimmicks

America has forgotten how to build, courtesy of a Byzantine permitting process that delays projects for years and often kills them altogether. A new bill could change that, though, and let the U.S. start building again, including badly needed energy infrastructure that would lower prices.

The current paralysis was made painfully evident this year when the Iran war disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and oil jumped from about $70 a barrel to about $100 in a matter of weeks. Prices at the pump skyrocketed while costs for natural gas, fertilizer, electricity, and more all rose as well.

America has weathered the supply shock better than most countries because of our shale production, but the cushion is much thinner than it should be.  Every stalled well, pipeline, port, and power line is a shock absorber missing from U.S. infrastructure. Energy security is national security, and a country that cannot build cannot be secure.

The bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, unveiled September 30 by Senate committee leaders, aims to fix the permitting paralysis with purely commonsense reforms. It sets a one-year deadline for environmental assessments and two-year deadline for full impact statements. It gives opponents 150 days to sue, not six years.

It also narrows Section 401 of the Clean Water Act so states can no longer block pipelines on grounds that have nothing to do with water quality. It lets projects keep moving forward while agencies fix paperwork a court has flagged. And it protects issued permits from being yanked by a later administration. It’s the most serious permitting reform in a generation.

And it’s desperately needed. The Mountain Valley Pipeline, which carries natural gas 300 miles from West Virginia to southern Virginia, took nine years to permit. The National Environmental Policy Act has become the most litigated environmental law in the country, and Section 401 is regularly misused by some states as a veto on any interstate pipelines.

>>> Why Congress Needs to Act Now on Permitting Reform

This is happening while electricity demand is projected to climb 25 percent by 2030 as new factories, data centers, and electric car chargers come online. While this latest bill goes a very long way in fixing the permitting process, it can be better still, and a great place to start is the section expanding the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC’s) power to site interstate transmission lines.

Today, states decide where most power lines go. FERC holds a narrow “backstop” authority that applies only inside corridors designated by the Energy Department, which has never designated one. The bill scraps that step and lets FERC permit lines of 230 kilovolts or more directly, so long as they meet public-interest, consumer-benefit and reliability tests.

Accelerating useful transmission line construction is a worthy goal but the issue here is who pays. The bill says costs of FERC-sited lines must be allocated to customers “roughly commensurate” with benefits they receive, and that customers getting no benefit, or only a trivial one, can’t be charged, which sounds perfectly reasonable.

But “benefits” are calculated by regional grid operators using their own models and assumptions, and those estimates can be stretched.

That’s happened before, like in 2024 when MISO, the grid operator spanning 15 states from Louisiana to North Dakota, approved a $22 billion package of high-voltage lines designed in large part to help states like Minnesota, Illinois, and Michigan meet their “clean” energy targets with remote wind and solar. Because those lines were classified as “multi-value” projects, their costs are shared across the whole region.

>>> The Red-Blue Energy Divide: How Overregulation Inflates Prices

Regulators from Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Dakota, and Montana—states with no renewable mandates—filed a FERC complaint arguing the benefits were inflated and that the setup lets states with aggressive “green” goals shift their higher transmission bills onto neighbors who made different choices. MISO’s own independent market monitor has raised similar concerns.

Now imagine giving FERC power to approve such lines over state objections. Families in red states that rejected expensive and inefficient solar and wind mandates could find the cost of blue-state mandates folded into their monthly electric bills.

The One Big Beautiful Bill rightly phased out the open-ended wind and solar tax credits in Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act. It’d be a shame if permitting reform quietly rebuilt that subsidy through utility prices, where it is harder to see and harder to repeal.

Fortunately, the fixes to protect families are simple. Congress can define “benefits” more tightly and accurately: reliability improvements, congestion relief, and measurable savings for customers being charged, not compliance with another state’s policy mandates. And benefit claims can face independent market-monitor review before FERC signs off.

None of this requires scrapping the bill’s core. Americans would benefit tremendously if Congress took a mend-it-don’t-end-it attitude toward this issue to ensure true energy dominance without gimmicks that risk funding subsidies voters already rejected.

#112. Challengers ask court to pause agreement between Texas and the DOJ on deportation proceedings

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that they described as the product of “egregious collusion.” A ruling in the challengers’ favor would temporarily restore a Biden-era regulation, adopted through notice-and-comment rulemaking, that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings – when, for example, a crime victim or witness is seeking immigration relief, such as asylum – while the challengers’ appeal in the lower federal courts is ongoing.

The Executive Office for Immigration Review, which is part of the Department of Justice, adopted the regulation at the center of the dispute, which provides what is known as “administrative closure,” in 2024.

In 2026, Texas filed a lawsuit in the Wichita Falls division of the Northern District of Texas, where it alleged that the EOIR does not have the power to adopt the administrative-closure rule. The case was assigned to the only federal judge in that division, Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor.

Within hours after the case was filed, the U.S. Department of Justice and Texas filed a motion to have O’Connor enter a final judgment in the state’s favor. The federal government also asked O’Connor both to throw out the rule altogether and to issue an order making clear that the EOIR could not adopt a similar rule in the future. O’Connor granted those requests.

Three cities with substantial immigrant populations – Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – sought to join the case to defend the administrative-closure rule on appeal, along with Centro Legal de la Raza, which provides legal services to immigrants. O’Connor denied their request on the ground that they lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing. In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported.

After the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit turned down their request to block the consent judgment between Texas and the Department of Justice and thereby reinstate the administrative-closure rule while their appeal continued, the challengers came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to intervene.

Lawyer Joshua Salzman of Democracy Forward, representing the challengers, called the consent judgment “indefensible.” “If a judgment procured through such open collusion is allowed to remain in effect,” he wrote, “any agency can avoid the strictures of the” federal law governing administrative agencies “by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief.”

Salzman noted that five years ago, the Supreme Court had granted review to decide a related question – whether states should be allowed to intervene to defend a rule when the federal government has opted not to do so – but ultimately never weighed in on that issue, instead dismissing the case without deciding it. “There is a substantial continuing need,” he said, “for this Court to address whether litigation tactics can be substituted for the … requirement that a federal regulation adopted through notice-and-comment rulemaking may be rescinded only through notice-and-comment rulemaking.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#113. Feds will not retry former Baltimore state’s attorney on mortgage fraud

A mortgage fraud charge against Marilyn Mosby, the former Baltimore state’s attorney—pictured here in 2022—has been dismissed. (Photo by Julio Cortez/The Associated Press)

A mortgage fraud charge against Marilyn Mosby, the former Baltimore state’s attorney, has been dismissed.

A federal jury convicted Mosby of mortgage fraud in 2024 after it found that she submitted a false mortgage application for a home in Florida, the Baltimore Sun reports.

Additionally, in 2023, she was convicted of perjury—related to taking money from the city’s deferred compensation plan. In 2025, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, vacated the fraud charge on the basis that it should have been tried in Florida.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear her appeal earlier this month, and the Maryland U.S. attorney’s office has said it will not retry her, according to CBS News.

Mosby was sentenced to three years of supervised release and served a year of home confinement, according to the Baltimore Sun. Additionally, she will be allowed to keep her Florida home, CBS News reports.

“Despite the attempts to discredit me and dismantle my career, I am still standing. I am deeply grateful to my attorneys for their unwavering advocacy, dedication and commitment to fighting for justice on my behalf,” Mosby said in a statement shared by CBS News.

#114. European Governments Fall Short on Reparatory Justice

Click to expand Image Secretary-General António Guterres addresses the 55th session of the Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland, February 26, 2024. © 2024 Elma Okic/UN Photo

A United Nations Human Rights Council resolution on October 7 calling for concrete action against systemic racism should have been an opportunity for governments to demonstrate their commitment to racial justice.

Instead, the United Kingdom called for a vote, breaking from last year’s consensus on the annually tabled resolution.

Citing concerns about the applicability of international law to establish responsibility and accountability for colonial harm, the UK objected to language on reparations and then abstained from the vote; European Union members of the Council also abstained. Regardless, the resolution passed with 30 votes in favor, 17 abstentions, and none against.

The loss of last year’s consensus reveals the gap between the UK and other European governments’ stated dedication to combat racism and their actual political willingness to address its historical roots.

European governments have present-day obligations to tackle racial discrimination and provide effective remedies. The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination requires states, including the UK, to ensure just and adequate reparation for harm resulting from racial discrimination. The experts who monitor this treaty earlier this year set out clear legal guidance on states’ obligations for such reparation.

Enslavement and colonialism helped establish racial inequalities, the consequences of which persist today. Human Rights Watch has documented systemic racism, including racial profiling and barriers to economic and social rights in Europe. Reparatory justice is essential to confronting these enduring harms.

Jamaica’s pursuit of an advisory opinion from the Judicial Committee of the UK’s Privy Council underscores the importance of examining governments’ legal arguments. Its petition asks whether the enslavement of Africans was lawful under English and international law, and whether the UK owes a reparatory remedy. Next month’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda offers another opportunity to change course. King Charles’s forthcoming Caribbean visit will, apparently, include an acknowledgement of Britain’s involvement in enslavement, although Buckingham Palace says decisions on reparations and formal apologies rest with the UK government.

The UK and other European governments should engage meaningfully with African and Caribbean initiatives and affected communities to develop reparatory measures for the harms they were and are responsible for. These measures can include, according to UN principles, compensation, restitution, rehabilitation, acknowledgment of wrongdoing and reforms to prevent recurrence. Affected communities should shape the process and its outcomes.

The United Nations Human Rights Council resolution calls on governments to move “from rhetoric to reality.” Those that are serious about ending systemic racism should embrace reparatory justice as part of that work.

#115. Philippines-Based American Fraudster Pleads Guilty to Targeting Thousands of U.S. Servicemembers and Veterans

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Robert Wayne Boling Jr., 45, a U.S. citizen who previously resided in the Philippines, pleaded guilty today for his role in an identity-theft and fraud scheme that victimized thousands of U.S. servicemembers and veterans.

According to court documents, Boling operated from the Philippines, and he received and exploited stolen personally identifiable information (PII) of U.S. servicemembers and veterans to compromise their bank accounts and steal money and veterans’ benefits.

“Those who courageously served our nation deserve our gratitude and protection — not to become targets for criminals seeking to profit from their sacrifice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “This defendant betrayed our country by exploiting personal information belonging to thousands of military-affiliated individuals, including elderly and disabled veterans, in a calculated scheme to steal from those who have given so much. Today’s guilty plea demonstrates that the Department of Justice will pursue those who prey on America’s servicemembers and veterans, no matter how sophisticated the schemes may be.”

“We in the Western District of Texas, in partnership with Justice Department’s Criminal Division, have worked for years to get Robert Boling Jr. back from the Philippines and hold him accountable for the crimes he committed against those who serve our nation and their families,” said U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. “This defendant and his fellow fraudsters served themselves by stealing from those who selflessly serve our country. We will always work tirelessly to fully prosecute those who prey on others in this manner, especially when the victims of those crimes are servicemembers.”

“Defrauding the men and women who defended our country is reprehensible,” said Director James R. Ives of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS). “Today’s action demonstrates that DCIS and our partners will relentlessly pursue those who steal from our nation’s service members and veterans.”

Boling’s co-conspirator, Fredrick Brown, who worked as a civilian medical records administrator for the U.S. Army in South Korea, took digital photographs of the PII of thousands of military-affiliated individuals. Brown provided the stolen PII to Boling, who, along with his co-conspirators, used the PII to compromise various accounts belonging to U.S. servicemembers and veterans, including bank accounts and online government-affiliated benefits accounts. Boling and his co-conspirators also worked with a network of money mules in the United States, who provided bank accounts into which stolen funds could be deposited, and helped to remit a portion of the stolen funds to the Philippines. Boling was deported by the Philippines to the United States in May 2026 to face charges related to the scheme.

Boling pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 14, 2027, and faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison for each conspiracy charge. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Boling is the third defendant to plead guilty for his role in the scheme. Co-conspirators, Fredrick Brown and Trorice Crawford, previously pleaded guilty and were sentenced to 151 and 46 months in prison, respectively. Co-conspirators Jongmin Seok and Allan Albert Kerr remain fugitives.

DCIS is investigating the case. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the U.S. Army Criminal Investigation Command, and the Veterans Benefits Administration’s Benefits Protection and Remediation Division provided valuable assistance.

Acting Assistant Chief Lauren M. Elfner and Trial Attorney Carolyn Rice of the Criminal Division’s White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Joseph Blackwell for the Western District of Texas are prosecuting the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided assistance.

This case is part of efforts being undertaken by the Criminal Division’s Cyber-Enabled Scam Initiative (CSI). The CSI is a dedicated team of prosecutors built to find scammers who prey on Americans, disrupt their networks, and hold them accountable. CSI brings together expert prosecutors from across the Criminal Division to accelerate the prosecution of cyber-enabled financial crimes, including complex frauds, government imposter schemes, romance and inheritance scams, financially motivated sextortion, lottery and sweepstakes scams, and other predatory schemes. With nationwide jurisdiction and global reach, CSI leverages every available tool to dismantle criminal operations, pursue bad actors, recover criminal proceeds, and obtain justice for victims. The Criminal Division partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country and is a founding member of the Scam Center Strike Force.

#116. Four Justices Recuse From Petition By Publishing Companies And Court Grants New Case on Disparate Impact

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Many lawyers billed a lot of hours to have a judge affirmed due to a lack of a quorum.

Sophisticated clients develop comprehensive strategies to get a cert petition granted. BMG Rights Management (US) LLC v. Cyril E. Vetter was one of those cases. The question presented concerned limitations on the reversion of copyrights. Paul Clement was retained to represent many of the leading media companies. The Parties to the Proceeding were:

Petitioners are BMG Rights Management (US) LLC; Capitol CMG, Inc. (Parent Company Stock Ticker: UMG); Essential Music Publishing LLC (Parent Company Stock Ticker: SONY); and Warner-Tamerlane Publishing Corp (Parent Company NASDAQ Stock Ticker: WMG).

The Plaintiffs secured top-side amicus brief from heavy-hitters including Paramount (represented by Lisa Blatt), the Motion Picture Association of America, the Recording Industry Association of America, and more. Everything was lined up for a cert grant. Alas, there would be no quorum.

Because the Court lacks a quorum, 28 U. S. C. §1, and since the qualified Justices are of the opinion that the case cannot be heard and determined at the next Term of the Court, the judgment is affirmed under 28 U. S. C. §2109, which provides that under these circumstances "the court shall enter its order affirming the judgment of the court from which the case was brought for review with the same effect as upon affirmance by an equally divided court." Justice Sotomayor, Justice Gorsuch, Justice Barrett, and Justice Jackson took no part in the consideration or decision of this petition.

The lower court judgment survives, and it is hard to imagine another case with the same parties would trigger a different outcome.

What happened here? I have to imagine that these four Justices, who all have lucrative book deals, recused because of either the parties identified, or the issue presented. Curiously, Justice Alito, who is a new publisher, did not step aside.

Going forward, these and other publishing companies need to be aware that they likely do not have a quorum for a cert grant. However, they stand a good chance of having a favorable lower-court judgment affirmed by a quorum-less court.

I've often wondered whether it makes actual good business sense to give lucrative book deals to the Justices. Do they really ever earn back the advance or is it just an interest-free loan? Well, now that media companies may no longer be able to bring cases to the Supreme Court, that value proposition has become far more difficult.

We've seen how significant Justice Alito's recusal was in Suncor. I think these media recusals may prove even more important to the business community. And while Justice Alito could divest those stocks, authors with book deals cannot cure the conflict.

Also in today's order is a cert grant in the racial preferences case from Montgomery County, Maryland. But the Court re-wrote the QP. Here is the Court's version:

The petition for a writ of certiorari is granted limited to the following question: Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.

Here is the question framed in the petition:

Whether a plaintiff alleging that a school district implemented facially-neutral admissions criteria for a racially discriminatory purpose must show that the criteria produced a disparate impact on the targeted racial group before a court may consider evidence of discriminatory intent.

The Court dropped the reference to discriminatory intent and added a focus on "aggregate disparate impact." This case could now reflect an opportunity for the Trump Administration to advance its new policy concerning disparate impact.
