#117. People, Place, Principles: This Is America

Introduction

What does it mean to be an American? Many citizens seem uncertain about what our country stands for, even amid celebrations of its 250th anniversary. Answers often point to a singular element: a people, a place, or an idea. But our country is all that and more. America is defined by the intertwining of people, place, and principles. Each of these elements offers its own contributions, but together they also form an organic reality and an exceptional nation.

James Madison’s theory of separation of powers and checks and balances provides a helpful analogy.[REF] Each of the three branches of the federal government has particular functions and responsibilities, yet they are not strictly cordoned off from one another. Each holds a piece of the others. The President can reach into the legislative process with a veto, the Senate into the executive with its power to confirm.[REF] This ongoing dynamic binds the parts into a coherent whole and ensures that all act with fidelity.

Something similar is true of people, place, and principles. Each component is uniquely valuable even as they cohere.

Americans are a people, united for the most part by a common language, religion, manners, and history. Beyond these are human elements like goodwill and gratitude that foster harmony and come through association. The establishment of civic friendship requires unity in a common cause.

America is also a place, a homeland, and human beings love their home. Its expansive territory as an extended republic supports deliberation and the sovereignty of the people. The qualities necessary to settle the frontier—self-reliance, adventurousness, and grit—still resound as part of the American character. The land has helped to develop America’s people and principles, just as they have developed the land. That land is shared across time, and the building of a civilization upon it has established ties of gratitude linking ancestors, contemporaries, and posterity.

A shared understanding of justice further binds a people. America is a nation grounded in natural law and dedicated to human equality, unalienable rights, and self-government. These principles inform the contours of our political institutions and how we treat each other, thus involving the “people” aspect of our national identity.

People, place, and principles shape one another, and that shaping is what makes America a nation rather than a mere plot of land populated by disparate tribes of varying beliefs.

People

The operative word for a people is “unity.” John Jay’s Federalist No. 2 provides a good starting point to examine how Americans are a “united people.” Jay wrote that the Founding generation was “descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs….”[REF]

Jay’s formulation points to a common culture. Most colonists came from Britain, and the British Constitution supplied some measure of established convention. Early settlers believed in the rule of law in general and the British common law in particular. Concepts familiar from British experience, like separation of powers, would even find their way into America’s Constitution.

A common British culture laid the groundwork for the American culture, yet Americans also grew to distinguish themselves as a distinct people, including through the development of their own form of the English language.[REF] In 1789, America’s “founding lexicographer,” Noah Webster, wrote in Dissertations on the English Language, with Notes, Historical and Critical, that “Now is the time, and this the country, in which we may expect success, in attempting changes favorable to language, science and government…. Let us then seize the present moment, and establish a national language, as well as a national government.”[REF]

Being an independent nation meant developing a national language of America’s very own to “reconcile the people of America to each other, and weaken the prejudices which oppose a cordial union.”[REF] To that end, Webster wrote on the rules of grammar and pronunciation; produced textbooks, a spelling book, and a dictionary; and advocated for the establishment of schools. American English should be distinct from the King’s English but uniform internally and adopted broadly.

Webster is most famous for producing his two-volume American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828.[REF] The dictionary is a valuable resource for scholarship on the Founding and early republic and is still cited by contemporary originalist Supreme Court justices to discern what terms meant in the 18th century. That uniquely American language underlies the Constitution.

A common religion can be as important as a common language in constituting a people. The influence of Christianity on the American Founding is well established.[REF] The Great Awakening swept through America in the 1730s and 1740s; 70 percent to 80 percent of American colonists attended religious services on a regular basis and often listened to sermons about Revolutionary principles; and the most referenced work of the Founding generation was the Bible.[REF]

As a result, Americans were bound by an immense commonality of morality and the virtues born of religious practice. In colonial times, leisure was precious, and deciding to devote that leisure to worship was a revealing choice. (Today, it is a telling decision amid our culture of distraction.) An individual reserving an hour or more of his week to contemplate the divine and morality and to practice humility in bowing and genuflecting has a tremendous effect on the character of his community as well as his own character. Such character formation was open to all, regardless of financial resources or social status.

As George Washington explained in his Farewell Address, it is possible to develop a moral framework through reason alone, but “reason and experience both forbid us to expect that National morality can prevail in exclusion of religious principle.”[REF] Common religious beliefs and practices help to bind and preserve a nation by securing the virtuous citizenry on which a republic depends.

Manners as well as morals contribute to the national character. With the possible exception of George Washington, who copied out a handbook of Rules of Civility at a young age, no Founder thought more seriously about the importance of manners than Mercy Otis Warren.

Everyday practices are the bedrock of individual character, and manners reflect underlying principles and support virtue. Consider the effrontery and discomfort Americans today experience when customers are rude and condescending to waiters: They are not your servants! Aristocracies are characterized by clear distinctions and formalities. The “republican spirit” is more modest, requiring “patience, probity, industry, and self-denial” and a “simplicity of life and manners,” according to Warren.[REF]

As a people, Americans tend to be informal, hardworking, spirited, friendly, and a little bit gritty. Their manners do have characteristic corruptions and vices as well, however. In her History of the Rise, Progress and Termination of the American Revolution, Warren cautioned that “the hurry of spirits, that ever attends the eager pursuit of fortune and a passion for splendid enjoyment, leads to forgetfulness; and thus the inhabitants of America cease to look back with due gratitude and respect on the fortitude and virtue of their ancestors.”[REF]

The degradation of manners is tied to the degradation of virtue, including gratitude. Paraphrasing Xenophon, Warren considered ingratitude to be the “source of all enmities among men,” and an ungrateful man could not “love the gods or even his parents, friends, or country.”[REF] Warren also saw manners as being tied to memory. Her objective in writing a history of the American Revolution was to guard against “forgetfulness,” to sustain the shared story of a people.

Similarly, Jay ends his Federalist No. 2 description of how Americans are one people by writing that “by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war,” they “nobly established general liberty and independence.”[REF] A common history, a national narrative that gives preeminence to the origin story, is part of what unites a people. It reminds us of past sacrifices and acts of heroism and illuminates who we are.

While America as an independent republic was formed in the crucial years between the Declaration and the Constitution, the “peopling” of America began before 1776.[REF] As Christopher DeMuth writes, “In the 150-year colonial period before the American Founding in 1776, the settlers built a prosperous society with strong, independent local governments. It was a world of freedom, enterprise, and productive competition in commerce, religion, speech, and government.”[REF]

For Americans, self-government was both an ideal and a habit. The colonists rebelled against the imposition of the Stamp and Sugar Acts in part because they had been attending to their own affairs for over 150 years. The Mayflower Compact of 1620 was the first governing document of the Plymouth colony, legitimized by the consent of the colonists and grounded in their own authority to govern themselves. Virginia’s elected legislative body, the House of Burgesses, was founded in 1619 and would play a vital role in American independence.

Civic Friendship: Uniting People and Principles

Beyond Jay’s formulation, a people is also sustained by civic friendship. Republican friendship relies on sympathies like benevolence, goodwill, and gratitude and is grounded in a shared understanding and love of the good.

The mechanisms of government are only part of what makes a functioning political order. In practice, civic associations and the habit of robust civic participation are also necessary and help to cultivate friendly sentiments toward fellow citizens. Matthew Mehan, associate dean of Hillsdale College’s Van Andel Graduate School of Government, writes of what “Cicero called the complex of charity (caritates…complexa est), which can be summed up as love of country. Cicero…makes clear that this deep network of loves is the primary source of any and all sense of civic duty to one’s republic.”[REF] Seemingly drawing on Cicero, whose arguments were ubiquitous in the Founding era, John Quincy Adams noted that sympathies between human beings begin with the family and then “spread through the social and moral propinquities of neighbor and friend, to the broader and more complicated relations of countryman and fellow-citizens.”[REF]

The complex of charity is rich and multifaceted, encompassing love, friendship, gratitude, and goodwill. It arises from the less grandiose yet powerful obligations toward family members, everyday interactions with neighbors, and recognition of the sacrifices of ancestors. By gathering in civic associations to resolve a community problem or worship together, for example, citizens come to see themselves as friends united in common cause and belief. Through civic rituals, we commemorate the past and create shared memories that cement our bonds with one another, even across generations.

George Washington believed such bonds to be so essential that he identified them as one of the four pillars on which the American national character and the “existence of the United States as an Independent Power” depended. He hoped that the “prevalence of that pacific and friendly Disposition among the people of the United States” would “induce them to forget their local prejudices and policies, to make those mutual concessions which are requisite to the general prosperity, and, in some instances, to sacrifice their individual advantages to the interest of the Community.”[REF]

In 1783, what was most urgent to Washington was the establishment or ruin of the American national character. Washington believed that “Liberty is the Basis,” the “foundation,” of that character.[REF]

The bonds of civic friendship are made possible by a shared understanding and concomitant love of the good.[REF] Washington so believed this that when he received a copy of the Declaration of Independence on July 9, 1776, he gathered the troops in New York so that the document could be read aloud to them. It expressed the common cause for which, and on which, they staked their all.

Civic friendship existed before the Declaration, but the people’s shared principles of justice were largely tacit. The Declaration articulated them more explicitly, and this allowed for a stronger love of the goods of liberty and justice that it described and thereby further mobilized the American people’s spirit of civic friendship in the cause of independence and the creation of a new republic.

Although civic friendship does not quite rise to the level of Aristotle’s highest form of friendship, which needs to be personal and intimate, friendship among fellow countrymen does depend on commonality of belief. That shared understanding and shared love sets bounds to discourse and behavior and opens the possibility of trust among citizens—the requirement for living a life in common.

Individuals who exist in fear of one another—of their property being stolen or their lives or liberty being infringed upon—cannot be said to be a united people. Only when there is a shared understanding regarding principles such as life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness can a people come together and live in harmony.

As distinguished Washington and Founding scholar Dr. William B. Allen has written, Lincoln and others believed that regimes are guided by “a shared view of justice that makes a people a people. This was a very old idea, one expressed by Plato, and Aristotle, and Cicero, and Aquinas, and even Jefferson.”[REF] That understanding gives rise to noble loves, as loving something begins with knowing it. In turn, what we love reflects who we are, both as individuals and as a people.

Place

The “place” aspect of America has supported its principles and the rugged character and the unity of its people from the beginning.

Before the adoption of the U.S. Constitution, conventional wisdom held that republics needed to be small so that the will of the people could be aggregated and heard and affections among the citizens could be maintained. Yet the world was full of large states, and small ones were in danger of being conquered.

James Madison conceived of the solution to this dilemma of republican scale. A large, secure republic could allow for the voice of the people to be heard, and its very size would repair a characteristic defect of the republics of the past. Factions—groups adverse to the common good—were an endemic problem in republics: indeed, given the nature of man, they are a side effect of human liberty.[REF] The Founders had to find a way to control the effects of faction; Madison’s solution was the theory of the extended republic.

Madison believed that because the American territory is so expansive, the factions it contains would be numerous, and this would make it more difficult for any single one to exert force. Instead, citizens would have to persuade one another in order to direct public opinion and form a legislative majority, and this would make it more likely that justice would prevail and permanently elevate the role of communication in the American regime (something reinforced by the people’s highly literate, participatory Protestant heritage). America’s extended territory would create conditions that demand deliberation, an essential feature of self-government.

The abundance of territory also meant that, in accord with Madison’s and Jefferson’s vision, most Americans could have a physical stake in their country. While serving in the Virginia legislature from 1776 to 1779, Jefferson introduced bills to eliminate primogeniture and entail and, with them, “feudal and unnatural distinctions.”[REF]

Widespread citizen ownership of land promoted self-governing habits, as the populace cultivated their own plots and formed communities. That, in turn, supported America’s principles. As Forrest Nabors, professor of political science at the University of Alaska Anchorage, has written, “Diffused property ownership annexes a material foundation to the legal foundation of the sovereignty of the people.”[REF]

America’s land and climate boast an abundance of natural resources. John Jay observed that America was composed not of “detached and distant territories” but of “one connected, fertile, wide-spreading country” with a “succession of navigable waters” almost made “to bind it together.”[REF] The sheer beauty and bounty of America’s land inspire gratitude, awe, and a love of and attachment to the good. Lincoln likewise would later credit America’s natural resources, as well as distance from Europe, for contributing to its prosperity and national security.[REF]

George Washington, a former surveyor, took care to give the American people coherence by developing the land’s connectedness. He championed the Potomac River Project, an infrastructure initiative that improved waterways and linked roads to those waterways. “The consequences to the Union,” he argued, “in my judgment are immense: more so in a political, than in a commercial view; for unless we can connect the new States which are rising to our view in those regions, with those on the Atlantic by interest…they will be quite a distinct people….”[REF] The project would undoubtedly bolster economic prosperity, but it would also facilitate citizen interaction and the exchange of ideas, thus fostering friendship and unity. This was particularly important for maintaining a common culture with western territories entering the Union as states.

The cultivation of the land builds a civilization over time and unites Americans through ties of gratitude. When Jefferson argued that the Earth belongs only to the living generation, Madison responded that, while that is perhaps true of the Earth in its natural state, “[t]he improvements made by the dead form a charge against the living who take the benefit of them,” and such a debt “can no[t] otherwise be satisfyed than by executing the will of the dead accompanying the improvements. Debts may be incurred for purposes which interest the unborn, as well as the living….”[REF]

The physical world around us is a tangible reminder of the contributions and sacrifices of past generations. We have buildings, roads, monuments, art, cities, and parks that are the product of taming the wilderness and unleashing the human capacity for creation. In some measure, contemporary citizens pay back that debt by adhering to the Declaration and the Constitution and by maintaining America as a free nation.

Taming America’s heartland not only transformed individuals into stewards, attaching them to the land through duty, but also built the American character and cultivated the virtues of a self-governing and resilient people. Those who settled the frontier were robust, simple in their manners, and comfortable taking risks. In fact, Washington believed the rugged manners of Western citizens would have a renewing and moderating effect on the American people. They would help to guard against the avarice that could arise in the more commercial parts of the country.

That at once enterprising and adventurous spirit still endures as part of who Americans are. “Manners” were one of the uniting elements of a people that Jay noted at America’s inception. Those manners have been formed by America the place.

Aside from the “place” supporting “principles” and “people,” America as a place matters simply because physicality matters, because human beings are embodied. With that embodiment come instincts and innate loves. As Alexis de Tocqueville observed, “[t]here exists a love of native country that has its source principally in the unreflective, disinterested, and indefinable sentiment that binds the heart of the man to the place where the man was born.” This instinctive patriotism “does not reason, it believes.”[REF]

This instinct is worth taking seriously. We Americans love our home as our own, delight in its particular beauties and the unique traditions we have planted, and are attached to the soil where family and civic ancestors are interred. As Lincoln so eloquently articulated in the Gettysburg Address, our debt to our forefathers’ sacrifices calls to us most at battlefields, where the physical and intangible intermingle.

Instinctive patriotism, when combined with civic knowledge, evolves into reflective patriotism. America’s foundational documents and free institutions inform our character as individuals and make possible a dignified way of life. Reflective patriotism is a loyalty born of love of homeland but steeled by America’s principles.

Principles

The Declaration of Independence is the most cohesive, though not exclusive, articulation of America’s principles. In an 1825 letter to Henry Lee, Thomas Jefferson noted that he was not aiming at “originality of principle or sentiment,” but rather was trying to articulate an “expression of the American mind.” The “harmonizing sentiments of the day” were “expressed in conversation, in letters, printed essays, or in the elementary books of public right, as Aristotle, Cicero, Locke, Sidney, &c….”[REF] For their intellectual grounding, the Founders relied on Christianity, the natural law tradition, ancient philosophy, British common law, and the Scottish Enlightenment.

Belief in and adherence to the principles of the Declaration were widespread: not just among prominent Founding Fathers, but among the Founding people as a whole. The American people were a deliberative people, and this facilitated the proliferation of a shared view and deep love of justice. They were remarkably literate, in part because of the Protestant insistence that individuals be able to read the Word themselves. America boasted an extensive network of printing presses, and ideas spread through sermons, political pamphlets like Common Sense, and local and state resolves, declarations, and constitutions.[REF]

The principle of human equality was widely discussed and was expressed in nine of the early state constitutions.[REF] Among other things, that maxim served to situate mankind within an ordered universe. In the words of John Adams:

[Equality] really means little more than that We are all of the same Species: made by the same God: possessed of Minds and Bodies alike in Essence: having all the same Reason, Passions, Affections and appetites. All Men are Men and not Beasts…. The blind are Men, and not Insects, the deaf are Men and not reptiles, the dumb are Men and not Trees. All these are Men and not Angells….[REF]

Human beings are not angels free from passions. Yet human beings are capable of reason and speech, equipped with free will and conscience. Such faculties make us responsible for our decisions. They mark us as part of the same species and distinct from animals. As Jefferson wrote, “the mass of mankind has not been born, with saddles on their backs, nor a favored few booted and spurred, ready to ride them legitimately, by the grace of god.”[REF] No person has been born with the right to rule over others absent their consent, notwithstanding the variety of human physical characteristics and talents. Natural right is independent of human will, and individuals are called to discern and obey the dictates of nature rather than to attempt to transform them.

These principles call human beings, and especially Americans, to aspire to self-government, which has a multifaceted meaning. The concept of self-government informs what is fitting for the individual, how we ought to treat one another, and the contours and limits of America’s institutions. We can enslave ourselves through an improper ordering of the soul, by succumbing to addiction or passion, which allows impulse to rule over right reason. Human beings can seek to dominate others or disregard the duties owed to one another that are the reciprocal of unalienable rights.

Self-government on the institutional level means that citizens enjoy a real say in determining their laws and representatives. In Federalist No. 39, Madison explained that “no other form” of government “would be reconcilable with the genius of the people of America; with the fundamental principles of the Revolution; or with that honorable determination which animates every votary of freedom, to rest all our political experiments on the capacity of mankind for self-government.”[REF]

These definitions of self-government are intertwined and mutually reinforcing. As the Founders and the ancients alike contended, a republic depends on a virtuous citizenry. Self-government on the individual level supports a self-governing regime.

Duties and rights are two sides of the same coin: Duties remind citizens of their obligations to the common good and each other, binding a people. By nature, human beings are social and political. As Cicero wrote in De Officiis (On Duties), “the power of reason associates man with man in the common bonds of speech and life” and “prompts men to meet in companies, to form public assemblies and to take part in them themselves.”[REF]

Individuals are made to form families, communities, and institutions. Nature both prompts and demands varying obligations to each, but the appropriate fulfillment of those obligations, on all levels, makes a people.

These principles are eternal, discernible by reason and consistent with Revelation, though recognizing them requires sustained and painstaking citizen formation.

Because of their transcendent nature, the truths of the Declaration are able to bind American citizens even across generations. That includes Americans who have no ancestors among the Founding generation. As Abraham Lincoln said, when Americans of recent vintage turn to the Declaration,

[T]hey find that those old men say that “We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal,” and then they feel that that moral sentiment taught in that day evidences their relation to those men, that it is the father of all moral principle in them, and that they have a right to claim it as though they were blood of the blood, and flesh of the flesh of the men who wrote that Declaration, and so they are. That is the electric cord in that Declaration that links the hearts of patriotic and liberty-loving men together, that will link those patriotic hearts as long as the love of freedom exists in the minds of men throughout the world.[REF]

America’s grounding in these principles makes it an exceptional nation. It is a country deliberately founded on an understanding of what is fitting for human beings. It did not come about through “accident” and “force,” as is usually the case with other nations in history, but by a people deliberating and voluntarily uniting, in habits of the heart and mind, to further the cause of self-government.[REF]

Conclusion

People, place, and principles interact with and reinforce one another in a manner that is organic, reciprocal, and inseparable. Principles reach into the people by supplying the shared view of justice that unites citizens and makes civic friendship possible. Self-government informs how we treat one another, and individual rights come with requisite duties. Fulfilling the aspirations of self-government on all levels unites America as a people and a nation.

Americans are a deliberative citizenry, a characteristic promoted by America’s expansive territory. The settling of the frontier influenced manners, making Americans a robust, resilient, and typically informal people.

America and what it means to be an American are defined by the at once unique and intertwining elements of people, place, and principles. We are a spirited people, forged by a shared history and culture and the cause of self-government enshrined in the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. We steward the land of our predecessors that tangibly evidences their devotion and sacrifices with its monuments, battlefields, and homes. And we defend our rights and bind one another in gratitude, goodwill, and friendship as we accumulate generational debts and fulfill our duties across generations.

This is the America of which we are citizens and that we have the honor and responsibility to preserve for these next 250 years and beyond. America is a particular people, a majestic place, and an experiment that is ever guided by timeless principles.

Brenda M. Hafera is Assistant Director of and Research Fellow in the B. Kenneth Simon Center for American Studies at The Heritage Foundation.

#118. The Second Amendment and AR-15s: an unexplained betrayal of originalism?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Last month, I provided a short discussion of the upcoming AR-15 rifle ban case, Viramontes v. Cook County, noting that the 2008 pathbreaking Second Amendment decision, District of Columbia v. Heller, ended by adding a “Part III” that identified “an important limitation on the right to keep and carry arms.” For a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia wrote that “the sorts of weapons protected were those ‘in common use at the time (emphasis added).’” Scalia said that this limitation is “fairly supported by ... historical tradition” and he provided a lengthy string of citations to demonstrate that proposition.

The Supreme Court has never examined the meaning of the “in common use at the time of the founding” limitation that the Heller majority described and said was supported by history. Instead, as detailed below, federal courts have silently transformed the Second Amendment test to extend it to weapons “in common use today.” Under this transformed test, AR-15 semi-automatic rifles might be protected although its advocates explain that they are a 20th century technological development. Yet if Scalia’s words are given their plain meaning, local governments would seem to have authority to enact bans on such weapons.

Given the consequences of which language applies, I continue to wonder why this is not a centerpiece of the Viramontes debate. (That said, Cook County’s responsive brief on the merits has not yet been filed – it’s due Oct. 21.) Indeed, a week after my column, Professor Jonathan Turley published a short column responding to this point, and calling Scalia’s limitation an “errant qualifier.”

I think that is incorrect. The justices have never expressly examined the Heller limitation I identified (which Scalia wrote), nor has the court ever explained why it does not mean what it appears plainly to say. Transforming a constitutional limitation written as “were in common use at the time” into a test of “are in common use today” is a betrayal not just of words that were essential to the Heller result, but of the originalist soul of its author. It replaces an originalist understanding of the limitations of the Second Amendment with a rootless and manipulable contemporary view of it. If decisional text as well as stare decisis values are to have any integrity when our justices change, but law and precedents still govern, a principled rationale for abandoning Scalia and the court’s “important limitation” must be offered.

Some brief introductory points. First, I consider myself a flaming moderate. I am no firearms expert, but I enjoyed shooting various guns in my rural youth. And on this particular issue, I support reasonable restrictions on modern-day dangerous weapons like AR-15 rifles. I wrote critically about Heller in 2009 (failing to anticipate personnel changes at the Supreme Court a decade later). Whether these things have relevance for you or not, I urge you to not ignore the legal analyses of scholars who disagree with your policy views. But I hope you will agree that any scholar’s policy views should not negate a respectful discussion of the Constitution’s meaning.

Second, I haven’t had the pleasure of meeting Turley and I respect his scholarship. He is a longtime supporter of Second Amendment rights, and I stand in awe of his boundless media energy. Short online essays will never resolve complex legal issues or fully reflect the depth of serious Supreme Court analysis. I’d be pleased to further debate him or others on this constitutional issue.

1. I highly doubt that Scalia’s inclusion of an “important limitation” on the Second Amendment right he championed for 63 pages was “errant.” That is, Scalia did not mean to say “in common use today” but somehow mistakenly wrote “in common use at the time.” Scalia was hardly known as a careless or sloppy writer. He’s been called “the Supreme Court’s greatest writer” by some and is the co-author of a leading treatise on writing and interpretation. The phrase “in common use at the time” appears not once but three times in his opinion (“at the time” appears 10 times, and it plainly means “at the time of the founding” (used four times) in 1791 when the Second Amendment was adopted). Heller was viewed, in 2008 and today, as the most important Second Amendment precedent in our history. There is no doubt in my mind that Scalia understood that and wrote precisely so as to stand the test of time. He did not include this interpretation of the Second Amendment and its “important limitation” by accident.

2. Further evidence that this limitation was not “errant” appears in the next sentence of Heller, where Scalia wrote that “[w]e think that [this] limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” Scalia then included references to eight treatises and four old cases in support of this. Providing deep historical research that “fairly supported” his reading was no error but was perfectly consistent with the originalist method that Scalia effectively embedded at the court today.

3. It was a unanimous Supreme Court almost 90 years ago in United States v. Miller that first employed the “in common use at the time” standard. In that case, the court sustained the federal ban on possessing short-barreled (“sawed off”) shotguns, and by authority of the same statute, “machine guns.” How quickly we forget, or ignore, history (and it’s simply mistaken to say, even as one podcast did, that there “is no history on what the Second Amendment means” before Heller).

Rather than dispute Miller, Heller endorsed and quoted from Miller’s constitutional ruling. According to the Miller court, even if viewed as useful (and commonly used by then-new gangsters like “Machine Gun Kelly”), such weapons could be banned because they were not “in common use” by the militia when the Second Amendment was ratified. That fact is also undoubtedly true about AR-15 rifles, which, as the solicitor general’s brief explains, were not technologically available until the 20th century. Embracing the “in common use at the time” limitation from Miller demonstrated the court’s commitment to the oft-repeated idea that, as Scalia explained in this same paragraph, “[l]ike most rights, the right secured by the Second Amendment is not unlimited.”

4. Turley concluded his essay by saying that “an immediate reversal of Heller” is “unlikely to turn on the word ‘were.’” I completely agree: no “reversal” of Heller is required or even suggested by giving plain meaning to Heller’s statement that “the sorts of weapons protected were those ‘in common use at the time.’” Heller obviously protected the use of handguns, which were in common use in revolutionary times, and at the same time it endorsed the prohibition of modern machine-gun technology in Miller. Thus Heller, and Scalia for the court, drew an unsurprising, constitutional line, a “limitation [which] is fairly supported by ... historical tradition.” Affirming a ban on AR-15 rifles, which as the U.S. solicitor general and the Second Amendment Foundation acknowledge represent new 20th century technology that explains their now-popular use, would honor Scalia’s memory and his careful constitutional consideration, not “reverse” it.

5. Importantly, it is undisputed, and clear from the structure of the Heller opinion, that its Part III, which outlined the “in common use at the time” limitation and other possible restrictions, was included to preserve a shaky five-justice majority. This was explained in detail by a contemporary witness: former Justice John Paul Stevens in 2019, and has been endorsed by other scholars. Now retired Justice Anthony Kennedy was a quiet, but demanding, fifth vote. Without Kennedy’s signing on to this language, Scalia’s opinion might have changed to, at best, a plurality, or a dissent, with Kennedy joining the four Heller dissenters and writing or voting for a more restrictive gun-control doctrine than currently exists. (One wonders what Kennedy’s two prior law clerks now sitting as justices, Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch, might say about this at oral argument.)

6. Given all this, what should we make of a statement made 45 pages earlier in Heller (quoted by Turley without noting that fact), that “the Second Amendment extends, prima facie, to all instruments that constitute bearable arms, even those that were not in existence at the time of the founding”? This was in a different section of Heller, examining what counts as “arms” rather than defining the scope of the right. I think the qualifier (not errant) of “prima facie” further indicates that this was part of a preliminary, “on its face,” discussion of the constitutional text, not (like Part III) a conclusion. Prima facie literally means “on first impression,” that is, before everything else is considered.

Still, there’s no doubt that this early sentence is in tension with the later Part III limitation. But Part III represents the conclusion of the entire opinion. After 45 further pages of consideration – it’s the court’s final word. Other aspects of Part III have been accepted as Second Amendment limitations (such as “sensitive places” and prohibiting possession by dangerous individuals) – so why not this one? If the two statements separated by 45 opinion pages in Heller are in tension, the court needs to explain why Part III does not mean what the majority seemed to plainly rule.

7. If the Part III “in common use at the time” limitation is clear, how then has it been (seemingly successfully) transformed today into a contemporary “are in common use today” idea?

As best I can tell, the problem goes back to a divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a 2011 Heller follow-up case.

After Heller was decided in 2008, the District of Columbia enacted a new ban on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines (both terms have disparate and disputed definitions; interestingly, the Sentencing Commission’s definition of the latter term is the specific issue underlying this term’s first criminal law oral argument, Beaird v. United States). The circuit upheld, 2-1, those bans (while questioning various registration requirements). For the majority, Judge Douglas Ginsburg noted the “in common use at the time” limitation, and that Heller had stated this was “supported by ... historical tradition.” But he then also applied the earlier statement in Heller that weapons “not typically possessed” are unprotected and noted an argument that semiautomatic AR rifles “are commonly possessed” (my emphasis). Frankly, the panel mushed together – or as a lawyer might say “conflated” – the past tense of the limitation, with some present-tense ideas. The panel then noted that the record was “uncertain” regarding whether the weapons at issue “are commonly used” in a relevant sense and upheld the bans on other grounds.

In dissent, then-Judge Kavanaugh immediately adopted the majority’s conflated test, asserting that weapons that “are in common use” are protected (my emphasis). Indeed, Kavanaugh’s 52-page dissent repeated the present-day “are in common use” test over a dozen times, without explaining why he was altering Scalia’s statement.

After Heller (and McDonald in 2010, extending it to the states) numerous scholars have noted that there was a long period of strategic caution or avoidance at the court – effectively 12 years of silence until Kennedy left it. Meanwhile, Scalia’s untimely passing meant he was not around to explain his meaning. (Hats off to Adam Winkler for using the phrase “gun shy” to describe this period).

It is important to note, as Turley pointed out in an earlier column, that the court did file a short unsigned opinion in 2016 on this topic. The Massachusetts Supreme Court had upheld a state ban on stun guns because they “were not in common use at the time of the Second Amendment’s enactment.” In Caetano v. Massachusetts, the court summarily reversed that decision, without full briefing or oral argument. The eight-justice per curiam opinion (Scalia had died a month earlier) said the Massachusetts ruling was “inconsistent with Heller’s clear statement that the Second Amendment “extends . . . to . . . arms . . . that were not in existence at the time of the founding.” Yet Caetano did not mention, let alone address, another obvious inconsistency: that the sentence they quoted appeared to conflict directly with Heller’s “important limitation” of the right, to weapons that “were in common use at the time.” Because the Caetano opinion identified two other reasons for reversing, the force of its per curiam summary reversal is open to debate. But one thing is clear: the Caetano court did not – and the court still never has – discussed or explored the meaning of Heller’s “important limitation” of the Second Amendment to weapons “in common use at the time.”

Finally, in 2022 with a newly constituted court, Justice Clarence Thomas fully adopted (in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen) the contemporary “are in common use” idea that Kavanaugh had used in 2011, omitting “were” and “at the time.” His opinion presented this idea, without further explanation, as a “holding” of Heller. This is, frankly, pick-and-choose selective editing. I am unaware of any further discussion among the justices of the limitation as written by Scalia, its plain meaning, or its semantic transfiguration. Poof – it is as if that paragraph of Heller’s Part III had never been written.

8. There are only three justices left on the court who were there when Heller was written: Chief Justice John Roberts, and Justices Thomas and Samuel Alito. They know the internal history. (Justice Kennedy, now retired, is still with us but remains characteristically circumspect.) Significantly, Thomas and Alito seemed to agree with a statement by Kavanaugh last year questioning a Maryland AR-15 ban and adopting, without explanation, an “are in common use today” test. But Roberts stayed silent, and certiorari was denied in that case. I think Roberts remains an important wild card here.

9. “Wisdom too often never comes, and so one ought not reject it merely because it comes late.” Multiple justices have used variations on this candid mea culpa of Justice Felix Frankfurter, including Scalia himself. Frankfurter further explained that he “would not compound error by pushing [an erroneous decision] further.” Maybe it is “too late” to apply what was a clear majority limitation in Heller. Or perhaps a majority in Viramontes will find wisdom in its later semantic transfiguration. But simply ignoring what the Heller majority found to be an “important limitation,” and failing to engage with Scalia’s historical project, is an application of power rather than judicial integrity.

10. I am unaware of any authority permitting the abandonment of an undisputed textual limitation in a Supreme Court opinion based on the untimely death of its author. “Narrowing” a precedent is one thing – but ignoring its text without analysis seems, to me, to be quite another.

I think the rule of law requires more. The public, at least 50% of which supports modern AR-15 bans, needs to hear why this selective editing, to produce a contemporary rather than originalist test, is consistent with the history-and-tradition approach of Heller and Bruen. Law professor Michael Dorf has written about “a belief in the independent integrity of law” in the context of “predictive” court evaluation. I share that belief (and without, I hope, too much partisan bias). If a historic precedent’s text as well as stare decisis values are to have any real meaning when justices change on the court, a principled rationale for abandoning Heller’s critical language must be offered.

Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

Recommended Citation: Rory Little, The Second Amendment and AR-15s: an unexplained betrayal of originalism?, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 15, 2026, 2:56 PM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/the-second-amendment-and-ar-15s-an-unexplained-betrayal-of-originalism/

#119. Vietnam: Free Abducted Democracy Group Activists

Click to expand Image Nguyen Duc Thuan (left) and Tran Hiep. © Private

(Bangkok) – The Vietnamese authorities should immediately release three activists associated with the overseas Viet Tan organization who went missing in Cambodia, and drop all charges against them, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities should also grant Norwegian and Australian consular officials and family members immediate access to the detained men.

The Vietnamese police claim that Nguyen Duc Thuan, a Norwegian citizen; Tran Hiep (also known as Ho Pham Hiep Huy), an Australian citizen; and Thai Cong Truong Son are members of the outlawed Viet Tan organization and attempted to use fake documents to cross the border from Cambodia to Vietnam on September 18, 2026. The men’s relatives say they never attempted to enter Vietnam.

The police announced that they have charged the three men with “terrorism” under article 299 of the penal code for their association with Viet Tan and with forgery of seals and documents under article 341. Viet Tan is an overseas political organization that advocates for democratic change in Vietnam. It contends that the men were abducted in Cambodia.

“The apparent abduction and detention of the foreign nationals raises many questions about the roles of both the Vietnamese and Cambodian governments,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Norwegian and Australian governments should press the Vietnamese authorities to grant them immediate access to their nationals and to drop baseless charges against them.”

Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep flew to Phnom Penh on September 15 and were reportedly in regular contact with family members outside of Cambodia until the morning of September 18, after which neither could be reached. Both men missed other scheduled appointments in Cambodia and the flight they had booked to leave Cambodia on September 19; they have not been heard from since. Their luggage and other effects except phones and passports were found in their hotel rooms in Cambodia.

Nguyen Duc Thuan requires daily insulin injections for diabetes and medical attention for kidney problems.

As of October 11, neither the Australian nor Norwegian embassy had been granted access to the detained men.

The Vietnamese police claimed that the three men crossed the border into Vietnam at Tay Ninh province, and that “Nguyen Duc Thuan was carrying two fake Vietnamese citizen identification cards” under a fake name and a Norwegian passport under his real name. They said that Ho Pham Hiep Huy “was carrying an Australian passport in the name of Tran Hiep.” The police statement does not describe Thai Cong Truong Son’s identification.

On October 7, Cambodia’s Ministry of Interior issued a statement saying it had confirmed that Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep had entered Cambodia but had not recorded their exit. And said it “categorically” denied any involvement in handing over the men to the Vietnamese authorities.

In the 1980s, Viet Tan had engaged in armed resistance against Vietnam’s communist government. Viet Tan relaunched in 2004 as a political party committed to nonviolent change, but the Vietnamese authorities have arrested and imprisoned Viet Tan members. In 2016, Vietnam officially labeled Viet Tan a “terrorist group.”

In 2019, an Australian member of Viet Tan, Chau Van Kham, and his colleagues Nguyen Van Vien and Tran Van Quyen were arrested in Vietnam and sentenced to 12, 11, and 10 years, respectively, for their involvement with Viet Tan on terrorism-related charges. Their trial lasted only 4.5 hours, suggesting that the verdict was pre-determined. The activities listed in the government’s charges against Chau Van Kham and attributed to Viet Tan, such as making travel arrangements to Vietnam, organizing leaflets for protests, expanding the Viet Tan’s network, writing articles, and sending people abroad for IT training, do not constitute acts of terrorism.

In 2022, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention issued an opinion stating that “the deprivation of liberty of [Viet Tan member] Chau Van Kham … is arbitrary.” Vietnam released Chau Van Kham in July 2023 and repatriated him to Australia. His Vietnamese fellow activists Nguyen Van Vien and Tran Van Quyen are still serving long prison sentences.

In 2018, the Vietnamese police arrested Le Quoc Binh in Binh Dinh province and accused him of participating in Viet Tan and smuggling weapons from Cambodia into Vietnam to “carry out terrorist activities.” Viet Tan rejected the accusation, calling it “a ridiculous fabrication.” The then-public security minister and current Vietnamese president, To Lam, praised the police for arresting Le Quoc Binh. Later accounts in government media of his trial and conviction on charges of terrorism and illegal possession of weapons dropped all mention of Viet Tan.

In May 2026, the Vietnamese police arrested Le Thanh Son and Nguyen Thanh Hung in Dong Thap province for their alleged affiliation with Viet Tan and charged them with “carrying out activities that aim to overthrow the people’s administration” under article 109 of the penal code. Also in May, the police reportedly detained, interrogated and beat a former political prisoner, Huynh Truong Ca, and forced him to admit that he was a member of Viet Tan, which he denied. After Huynh Truong Ca fled, police detained his family members, interrogated them on his whereabouts, and intimidated and pressured them to denounce him.

In recent years, the Vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression—government efforts to silence dissent by targeting dissidents and critics outside their territory. They have pressured other governments, including Thailand and Cambodia, to return Vietnamese citizens who fled Vietnam out of fear of arbitrary arrest, torture, or imprisonment.

Vietnamese security forces have abducted Vietnamese citizens in Germany and Thailand, including Trinh Xuan Thanh, Truong Duy Nhat, and Duong Van Thai. In the past year, courts in Vietnam put on trial in absentia Vietnamese nationals who live overseas, convicting and sentencing them to long prison terms, including Le Trung Khoa, Nguyen Van Dai, Doan Bao Chau, Dinh Yum, Siu Di, and Dang Thi Hue. Since the trials, the police have issued numerous warnings and fined Vietnamese citizens for interacting with those convicted in absentia.

Activists from Vietnam and Thailand have been forcibly disappeared in Cambodia in cases of suspected transnational repression.

“Campaigning for democracy and pluralism is not a crime,” Pearson said. “The Vietnamese government should release Nguyen Duc Thuan, Tran Hiep, and Thai Cong Truong Son and end its practice of transnational repression.”

#121. Global South Wants to Head North and Ceuta Invasion Was Just the Latest Example

Back in August 2023, hundreds of foreign nationals rushed the U.S. border in separate incidents at official crossing points in Brownsville and El Paso, Texas. DHS officers put up physical barriers and stopped traffic over the Gateway International Bridge. On the Mexican side, the military intervened to stop further mass attempts by aliens to enter the U.S. illegally.

For those who have already forgotten, we very recently had hundreds of thousands of inadmissible aliens pouring over our border every month. Why did they come in the millions from 2021-2024 and only a few hundred today? Policy choices. Former President Joe Biden and his Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas were lamentably successful at creating made-up “lawful pathways” and circumventing our laws to parole or release as many aliens into our country as possible. The effects will last decades.

We saw an echo of the Biden border recently in the Spanish city of Ceuta, in North Africa. In July, more than 72,000 non-Spaniards bum-rushed the border while Morocco did little to stop them. The majority were Moroccans, who mostly went home within a few days. But 10,000 or more were from sub-Saharan Africa or claimed to be minors, or both.

Spain is now stuck with processing them under Europe’s insanely soft asylum policies, which will likely result in many being taken to mainland Spain. The success of even a minority of these invaders to access Europe will encourage many more to try.

President Donald Trump ended Biden’s open-borders policies. Since he took office, there have been zero “catch-and-release” cases at the border, the Department of Homeland Security says. Trump also ended Biden’s reckless and illegal mass parole programs. Some aliens still sneak in without being caught, but far fewer now that the Border Patrol has the time and manpower to look for them and the mandate to detain them.

>>> The UN’s Refugee Agency Seems to be Using Weasel Words to Hide Its Open Borders Agenda 

Trump’s prompt action stemmed the manmade disaster that allowed up to 10 million illegal aliens into our country with no vetting and little chance of qualifying for asylum. But Trump can’t change the demand-side of the mass migration equation. The world still has plenty of poor, dysfunctional countries. 

True, there have been some success stories. Elections across Latin America, including Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica and Peru, have replaced leftist leaders with conservative ones, which augers well for security and prosperity in our hemisphere.

In El Salvador, President Nayib Bukele has drastically reduced crime and improved the economy such that the country is desperate for workers. The U.S. taking out Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and replacing him with a more cooperative, if still leftist, leader should improve that country’s economy and allow millions to return home safely.

But elsewhere in Latin America, Africa and Asia, bad governments, weak economies and high fertility continue to make people want to leave. The U.S. remains a favored destination.

So does Europe, where the native population is slowly being supplanted by mass migration from the “Global South.” This is no conspiracy theory; it’s an observable demographic phenomenon.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimated that at least 1,200 migrants in Ceuta could be eligible for asylum in Spain. UNHCR, along with the International Organization for Migration, used millions in U.S. money to channel illegal migration from across the world via Latin America into the U.S.

Claiming asylum so they can get into Spain and the larger EU is what motivates people rushing into Ceuta, just like those who used to rush the U.S. border. They want jobs and better prospects, including generous welfare benefits. But the vast majority are not persecuted at home in the way required to qualify for asylum. They’ll admit as much themselves, at least until the asylum process begins, and they have to make up a story and stick to it.

>>> Trump Has Sealed the Border. Now, Democrats Are Hell-Bent on Ending Immigration Enforcement 

One illegal migrant to Ceuta from Chad, Mohamed Yaqoub, told an AP reporter that “The most important thing for us is to get the papers,” so that he could achieve his goal of studying in France. If he were truly seeking asylum, Yaqoub would have done so in the first safe country he reached outside Chad. He not only didn’t, he admits he won’t even stay in Spain. Once he gets “papers,” he’ll go to France.

Demand to migrate from the Global South to the richer countries is insatiable. But housing, healthcare and welfare benefits are limited. Many EU member countries have structural budget deficits and debt caused by their economies failing to grow while the costs of socialist healthcare and pension systems rise.

The United States is largely in the same boat. Now, like Europe, we have evidence that the typical illegal or low-skilled legal migrant results in a net fiscal loss over his lifetime—thus not saving Social Security, but sinking it.

Let Ceuta and Brownsville be a warning to us to never let the Biden border happen again.

#122. Federal judge balks at lawyer’s $3K hourly rate

A California federal judge has called one lawyer’s hourly rate “patently unreasonable” in a case involving Google’s voice-activated assistant. (Image from Shutterstock)

A California federal judge has called one lawyer’s hourly rate “patently unreasonable” in a case involving Google’s voice-activated assistant.

U.S. District ​Judge Beth Labson Freeman of the Northern District of California approved more than $22.6 million in legal fees in the $68 million privacy settlement but refused to accept a $3,000 rate for David Scott of plaintiffs law firm Scott+Scott, according to a story from Reuters.

“It is not unusual for named partners to charge more than other partners,” Freeman wrote in the Tuesday order. “And the court is cognizant that rates increase year to year. But not to $3,000 an hour.”

Freeman reduced Scott’s fee to $1,600 per hour to calculate the overall class action fee award, Reuters reports.

Reuters also reports that a $3,000 hourly rate is not entirely unusual. The publication has discovered some lawyers at Susman Godfrey charge rates as high as $4,000, while others at Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher and Milbank charge more than $3,000.

“Lawyers operate in a market, and for better ⁠or worse, $3,000 per hour is now very much market rate for top tier partners at large firms,” Adam Levitin, a bankruptcy professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Reuters.

#123. "The AI Data Will Provide an Unrivaled View into the Mind of a Defendant …"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"whose [mental state] is itself the measure of Plaintiff’s [punitive] damages."

That's part of libel plaintiff's argument(filed last week) for subpoenaing defendant's AI queries in Fontainebleau Florida Hotel, LLC v. Botach; the defendant is popularly known as Rabbi Shmuley Boteach. From the introduction:

The Court asked whether Botach's communications with AI platforms fall within the scope of "damages" discovery permitted by ECF No. 261, and specifically how those materials relate to malice and the statutory cap on punitive damages. Precedent from the United States Supreme Court and Eleventh Circuit, as well as Florida law, answers that question directly.

Under Fla. Stat. § 768.73(1)(c), the cap on punitive damages lifts entirely where the fact finder determines that "the defendant had a specific intent to harm the claimant" at the time of the injury. As discussed below, legions of cases from trial courts to the Supreme Court hold that post-defamation conduct is probative of whether defamatory statements were made with intent to harm. Specific intent is therefore not background color to the damages trial or damages discovery. Discovery into Botach's intent to harm Plaintiff is damages discovery, and the AI materials are the most direct evidence of that intent.

Botach did not merely publish an errant falsehood on a blog or make a heated statement in a debate. He methodically engineered his attacks—drafting, refining, and iterating for painful effect through the most potent technologies known to humankind. The prompts and chats are his mental state reduced to writing, and they are probative of damages.

The Court should sustain the objections to the proposed AI-provider subpoenas as drafted and apply the same limits to the overlapping Seventh Request for Production. The issue is whether these demands fall within the scope of "discovery limited to damages." The unresolved punitive amount permits discovery concerning punishment for the adjudicated wrong, not an unrestricted inquiry into Defendant's research or litigation conduct.

The amended complaint already alleges knowing falsity, deliberate fabrication, repeated publication, financial motive, and specific intent to harm. Plaintiff did not pursue AI discovery before the general discovery cutoff. But under the guise of "discovery limited to damages," Plaintiff seeks every responsive AI exchange concerning this litigation, the Hotel, Plaintiff's lawyers, every court order, and the judges. It reaches accounts associated with an expansively defined "Botach," without limiting production to his queries or material used in the actionable publications. The Court should enforce the reopening order before requiring any production and independently preserve substantiated work-product objections.

For more backstory on the case, an excerpt from the long Report and Recommendation issued July 29 by Judge Marty Fulgueira Elfenbein in Fontainebleau Florida Hotel, LLC v. Botach:

This action arises from an encounter between Defendant and then-hotel guest Faiz Akbar … in the lobby of Plaintiff's hotel in December 2024. The Parties sharply dispute the nature of the encounter, who initiated or escalated it, and whether Plaintiff responded appropriately to Defendant's subsequent complaints.

Plaintiff's operative First Amended Complaint alleges that Defendant published false statements concerning the incident and Plaintiff's response to it, including statements that Plaintiff discriminated against Defendant because he is Jewish, knowingly permitted an antisemitic assault to occur on its premises, removed Defendant rather than the alleged aggressor, and refused to cooperate with law enforcement. Based on those allegations, Plaintiff asserts claims against Defendant for defamation and tortious interference with business relationships.

Defendant filed a Counterclaim and Third-Party Complaint asserting claims against Plaintiff and naming Jeffrey Soffer … and Akbar as Third-Party Defendants. Defendant's Counterclaim alleges, among other things, that he was subjected to an antisemitic verbal attack at the hotel, that Plaintiff failed to protect him or adequately cooperate with the ensuing investigation, and that Plaintiff thereafter excluded him from its properties. Defendant asserted claims under federal civil-rights statutes and a claim for tortious interference with business relationships….

The merits of the Parties' competing claims are not directly before the Court in the Motion for Sanctions. Instead, the dispute concerns Defendant's conduct during the litigation, the meaning and scope of the District Court's February 20, 2026 Order …, and whether Defendant's subsequent social-media activity violated that Order in a manner warranting sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(f) or the Court's inherent authority….

On March 11, 2025, Defendant served a subpoena on the Miami Beach Police Department seeking video footage of the underlying incident that Plaintiff previously provided to the department. The Miami Beach Police Department produced responsive surveillance footage to Defendant's counsel on March 26, 2025, and counsel thereafter transmitted that footage to Defendant. On April 2, 2025, before the entry of a protective order, Defendant posted an excerpt of the surveillance footage to his public Instagram account, which had more than 90,000 followers. On April 7, 2025, the Parties jointly moved for entry of a stipulated protective order governing discovery in this action. The Court entered the Parties' Stipulated Protective Order on April 9, 2025.

The Protective Order provides that material produced by a nonparty is automatically treated as "Outside Counsel Eyes Only" for thirty days following production without the need for an affirmative designation by a party. The Protective Order further prohibits the use of discovery material for any purpose unrelated to this litigation, including any public, commercial, business, or personal purpose. The Protective Order restricts access to material designated as "Highly Confidential" or "Outside Counsel Eyes Only" to specified persons and does not permit unrestricted public dissemination of such material….

On April 10, 2025, one day after entry of the Protective Order, Defendant again posted the surveillance footage to his social-media accounts. On April 16, 2025, Plaintiff formally designated the materials produced by the Miami Beach Police Department as "Highly Confidential," and Plaintiff's counsel communicated that designation to Defendant's counsel. Defendant's counsel then informed Defendant of the designation, after which Defendant removed the footage. Defendant contemporaneously published a social-media post acknowledging that he was "required under the rules to remove the video."

Notwithstanding his knowledge of the Protective Order and Plaintiff's confidentiality designation, Defendant again posted the surveillance footage on September 17, 2025…. Although Plaintiff requested severe evidentiary and litigation-ending sanctions [over this], the undersigned concluded that those sanctions were not then supported by the record because a lesser sanction had not previously been imposed for the violation. The undersigned instead awarded Plaintiff its reasonable attorney's fees and costs attributable to the sanctions motion and expressly admonished Defendant that the Protective Order was not optional. The undersigned further warned Defendant that any future violation of the Protective Order would be treated with the utmost seriousness, including case-dispositive sanctions.

After further proceedings concerning the amount of the award, the Court ordered Defendant to pay Plaintiff $15,000.00 no later than April 26, 2026….

Separate from the Protective Order dispute, the District Court addressed Defendant's social-media activity in connection with pretrial scheduling and discovery matters. On February 10, 2026, Plaintiff moved for an extension of time to take Defendant's deposition and represented that Defendant had repeatedly scheduled and cancelled depositions based on asserted physical limitations while simultaneously publishing social-media content showing him engaged in activities including ice skating, kayaking, and bicycling. The District Court granted Plaintiff additional time to take Defendant's deposition and stated that it was "deeply disturbed by this trend." The District Court cautioned Defendant that sanctions, "potentially including the striking of Defendant's pleadings," would be imposed if the conduct continued….

[In a] February 20 Order, the District Court observed that the communications between the Parties had become "toxic," particularly in light of Defendant's online communications, and agreed with Plaintiff that the time had come for the matter to proceed toward resolution. The District Court stated that it was "deeply disturbed by Defendant's conduct," including his "continued social media attacks aimed at Plaintiff and its counsel" and his attempt to effect service at an address he knew belonged to Soffer's child. The District Court then expressly "DIRECT[ED] Defendant to cease such harassing conduct and social media references to Plaintiff and its counsel during the course of this litigation." …

In the Motion for Sanctions, Plaintiff contends that Defendant continued to publish social-media content referencing Plaintiff, Plaintiff's counsel, and this litigation almost immediately after entry of the February 20 Order. Plaintiff identifies multiple occasions between February 26 and May 28, 2026, on which Defendant allegedly violated the Order. [For more details, see the opinion, but here's one example. -EV] …

The May 24, 2026 social media publications constitute perhaps the most egregious violations of the February 20 Order. To recap, in one video, Defendant alleged that a member of his family was confronted and threatened in Jerusalem by an individual who invoked Plaintiff's counsel. Defendant specifically identified Plaintiff's counsel as the attorney representing the hotel in this action and asserted that this lawsuit was filed to "intimidate and silence him" after he publicly alleged that he had been threatened with murder in an antisemitic attack. Defendant further stated that it "remains unknown whether anyone connected to the ongoing litigation had prior knowledge of, encouraged, or otherwise played any role in the confrontation" and that he "has endured nearly two years of legal and public harassment by [Plaintiff's counsel] and the hotel in an effort to financially and personally destroy him after speaking out about the alleged antisemitic attack."

In the other May 24, 2026 post, Defendant referred to Plaintiff, Soffer, and Plaintiff's counsel, Burstyn, by name, and questioned whether Burstyn appeared in materials associated with Jeffrey Epstein. The post also referenced Burstyn's representation of another client, questioned Burstyn's role in events preceding the death of Virginia Giuffre, criticized Burstyn's representation of Plaintiff, and concluded with an assertion concerning public distrust of attorneys, stating that Plaintiff's counsel "is the reason that 84% of Americans believe that attorneys are scumbags."

These posts did not merely allude to Plaintiff—they expressly identified Plaintiff, Plaintiff's counsel, and the upcoming trial. They therefore violated both components of the District Court's directive. They constituted social-media references to Plaintiff and Plaintiff's counsel, and they also plainly continued the very social-media attacks that prompted the District Court's intervention. These publications therefore fall squarely within the conduct the District Court sought to halt and cannot reasonably be characterized as compliance with the February 20 Order….

And the Magistrate Judge therefore recommended sanctions against the Defendant:

The totality of the record demonstrates that Defendant willfully chose to disregard a clear judicial command. It is undisputed that Defendant knew of the District Court's February 20 Order. Nevertheless, Defendant continued making prohibited social-media references over approximately three months.

The violations were not confined to a single publication or a single day. Instead, Defendant repeatedly returned to social media to discuss Plaintiff, Plaintiff's counsel, and the pending litigation. That pattern is inconsistent with negligence or misunderstanding….

Further, Defendant knew the significance of an order, the requirement that he comply with an order, even if he disagreed with it, and the consequences for failing to follow an order. Not only has Defendant already been sanctioned for violating an order of this Court, but Defendant was also warned about the potential for graver consequences if he violates any other orders….

Turning to the issue of whether lesser sanctions would suffice, the record contains multiple warnings of escalating specificity. The District Court first warned Defendant on February 10, 2026 that continued misconduct could result in striking Defendant's pleadings. Then, on February 20, 2026, the District Court directed Defendant to cease social-media attacks and references to Plaintiff and its counsel. Less than one week later, the undersigned warned Defendant that Court Orders are not optional, that Defendant could not take matters into his own hands, and that future violations would be treated with the utmost seriousness, including the potential for Rule 37(b)(2)(A) sanctions. Those warnings did not produce compliance. Another admonition would repeat a measure the record has already shown to be ineffective with Defendant.

Further, the Court previously imposed a sanction in the form of a $15,000.00 fee award based on Defendant's knowing violation of the Protective Order. The violations of the February 20 Order followed that ruling and the accompanying admonition…. [T]he prior monetary sanction did not deter Defendant from again disregarding a pretrial directive….

At his deposition, Defendant admitted under oath that his social-media publications were intended to cause Plaintiff and Plaintiff's counsel to reconsider their conduct and litigation strategy. Consistent with that testimony, Defendant's May 24 and May 28 posts publicly accused Plaintiff of attempting to destroy him through this litigation, attacked Plaintiff and Plaintiff's counsel personally notwithstanding the Court's directive prohibiting such conduct, and attempted to rally public opinion by requesting "your support" in his trial "Against 'that Hotel' in Miami" where he will "absolutely defeat the antisemitism-deniers."

Defendant therefore used repeated violations of the Court's Order as an extrajudicial litigation tactic designed to influence whether, and under what conditions, Plaintiff continued to prosecute its claims against him. That objective directly implicates the integrity of the judicial process. The pattern of Defendant's repeated, willful violations of the February 20 Order when coupled with his stated intention behind his social-media posts and his history of sanctions and admonitions demonstrate that lesser sanctions will not suffice.

Accordingly, the undersigned concludes that striking Defendant's Answer and Affirmative Defenses, dismissing his Counterclaim with prejudice, and entering default judgment as to liability on Plaintiff's well-pleaded claims constitute appropriately tailored remedies that address the institutional harm caused by Defendant's abuse of the judicial process. {This recommendation is not based upon any determination that Defendant's affirmative defenses or Counterclaim lack substantive merit. Rather, it is based upon Defendant's willful violation of this Court's Order, his deliberate use of those violations as a litigation tactic, and the demonstrated inadequacy of lesser sanctions to secure compliance or preserve the integrity of these proceedings.}

With that said, the recommendation of entry of default judgment would not, by itself, establish the amount of Plaintiff's damages. Plaintiff would remain obligated to establish any unliquidated damages through appropriate evidence and further proceedings and Defendant would be able to defend against such damages claims….

[T]he Court [also] finds it appropriate to award Plaintiff its reasonable attorney's fees and expenses incurred as a result of litigating the Motion for Sanctions. The amount should be determined through a separate fee submission with Plaintiff bearing the burden to establish the reasonableness of its counsel's hourly rate along with the reasonableness of the requested fees….

#124. Saudi Arabia: Death Penalty for Facebook Comment

Click to expand Image Anojan Sivarasa. © Private

(Beirut) – A Saudi court has sentenced a Sri Lankan migrant worker to death over a Facebook comment that was deemed blasphemous, Human Rights Watch said today. Saudi authorities should reverse the judgment and release him immediately.

The Saudi Court of Appeal in the Eastern Region handed down the death sentence to Anojan Sivarasa, 24, on September 17, 2026, after two court sessions. An initial ruling had sentenced him to five years in prison.

“Sentencing a migrant worker to death over a Facebook comment that he has publicly apologized for is an outrageous overreaction from Saudi authorities amid a surge in executions,” said Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “No one should face execution for a comment on religion.”

On June 28, Sivarasa replied to a video circulating on Facebook with a comment in Tamil deemed offensive to the Prophet Muhammad by some viewers. The comment quickly gained attention, and a screenshot was apparently sent to Saudi authorities and Sivarasa’s employer, a family member of Sivarasa’s told Human Rights Watch. Sivarasa deleted the comment and uploaded an apology video to his Facebook account. Sivarasa’s employer held him in its office for at least 24 hours and then took him to the Dammam police station, where he was arrested on July 1, the family member said. 

Sivarasa was working in construction and had arrived in Saudi Arabia just 10 months earlier. He is the sole breadwinner for his family in Sri Lanka, the family member said.

The Al-Ahsa Public Prosecution charged Sivarasa with “verbally insulting and offending our Prophet Muhammad” and “producing and disseminating, through the information network, material prejudicial to religious values and public morals, by publishing a comment on a social media program containing words contrary to religious values and public morals,” according to court documents obtained by Human Rights Watch.

On July 27, the Criminal Court of Al-Ahsa issued a judgment convicting Sivarasa under article 6 of the Anti-Cyber Crime Law and sentenced him to five years in prison and a fine of 3 million Saudi riyals (about US$800,000), according to court documents. The court also ordered confiscation of his electronic device and closure of his Facebook account. 

The Al-Ahsa Public Prosecution filed an appeal of the initial judgment. Sivarasa’s lawyer also appealed the initial judgment and sentence. 

On September 17, Sivarasa informed his family that he had been sentenced to death, the family member said. Court documents reviewed by Human Rights Watch show that Court of Appeal in the Eastern Region found Sivarasa guilty of verbally insulting the Prophet Muhammad on a social media post and sentenced him to death.

“We never expected this situation,” the family member said. “This is a funeral house. The family is shocked and they still are recovering from that state of shock.”

On October 5, a prisoner attacked Sivarasa in detention with a small weapon, injuring his head and face. the family member said. He received medical attention and has been moved to a different cell. 

Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people over the last decade, in many cases violating Saudi and international law. Authorities executed at least 356 people in 2025, setting a new record in the country for the highest number of executions in one year since monitoring began.

International human rights law, including the Arab Charter on Human Rights ratified by Saudi Arabia, obliges countries that use the death penalty to only do so for the “most serious crimes” and in exceptional circumstances. Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all circumstances because of its inherent cruelty. 

“Saudi Arabia should immediately quash this sentence and release Sivarasa,” Shea said. “Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections.”
