#125. A Columbus Day Question—Have We Finally Stopped Distorting Our Past?

Dilapidated artwork says a lot about a society. Restoring it can breathe fresh life into a culture. A timely case in point: the Christopher Columbus fountain in front of Union Station in Washington, D.C.

It’s a reminder of our history and of our connection to the old world. Yet it was left to ruin for nearly 20 years. The water didn’t flow, the marble was vandalized and dirty, and the statue was defaced with graffiti during anti-American protests.

This reflects our larger societal problem: the ignorance and hatred of our Western inheritance. We’ve neglected important symbols like the Columbus fountain because we’ve neglected the history behind them. The fountain of the Western intellectual tradition hasn’t flowed for some time, and we must restore it—not just by cleaning up fountains and statues, but by supplementing our own education.

Our intellectual neglect developed over time. In 1952, Robert Maynard Hutchins, an editor of the Great Books of the Western World, warned against education that emphasized vocational training and specialization at the expense of the classics—the great texts of our civilization.

>>> A Guide to Heritage Sites

In true Orwellian fashion, “progressive” education of our own day has proven to be regressive. The energy is toward disdain and criticism. Progress cannot be built on contempt of the past, otherwise each generation would be restarting.

Contempt, abandonment, or just plain neglect of the past is standard fare for many schools. We shouldn’t have been surprised then when 33 Columbus statues were removed or destroyed in 2020: Union Station’s was vandalized, Baltimore’s was thrown into the harbor, Philadelphia’s was temporarily covered with a box, and many more were simply removed.

For the sake of our posterity and Republic, we must make a major change beginning with ourselves. For those of us who went through education detached from history or hostile to our shared inheritance, we can make up for lost time. We need more warriors ready to defend our heritage.

For multiple generations the academy has been infected with critical theory and over-specialization, while K-12 miseducation has contributed to the fact that about a third of American adults are unable to name all three branches of government and 64 percent believe racism is widespread in the United States.

Fortunately, our predecessors left us with a great well to draw from. Hutchins’s collection is a fine place to start; even beyond those volumes, we are blessed with nearly unlimited access to resources.

Our work at the Heritage Foundation is designed for this very purpose. Major projects like our Heritage First Principles series, Guide to Historical Sites, and the Essential Constitution collection, are not designed for the ivory tower, but for the kitchen table. Our work is for everyday Americans with busy lives who want to learn and defend our country.

Beyond these resources, Americans have access to libraries of free books online, free online courses from Hillsdale College, podcasts and YouTube videos, and group programs like the Colson Fellows.

The self-taught life is demanding, yet essential in our efforts to restore the Republic. We should be encouraged by the example of Ben Franklin, the son of a candlemaker with only two years of formal education who became a consequential founding father. It was Franklin who famously quipped that we have a Republic, if we can keep it. Yet we can’t keep what we don’t know.

>>> How Schools Are Remembering—or Forgetting—Sept. 11

The stakes couldn’t be higher. As long as apathy reigns, the radical left will keep ripping apart our history and unity. The revival of the D.C. Columbus statue by President Trump should give us hope that we can reverse the trend.

Beyond the statues, the decades-long campaign against Columbus Day has always had broader civilizational goals. The renaming of Columbus Day and the removal of his statues were framed as “honest discussions about Columbus’s flaws.”

This Columbus Day, we should reflect on the story of his exploration and its significance for our country. We should honor and respect this bridge to the old world. In 534 years, we have a lot to be grateful for, such as how many ventured here in search of freedom, and how true progress eventually eliminated the scourge of slavery that was imported from the old world.

Some 534 years from now, will our posterity look at us as the generation that righted the ship, preserved the Republic, and restored our Western intellectual fountain? Or will they even know the name Christopher Columbus?

There is still hope. It begins with us, with our minds informed by the past, our actions emboldened in the present, and our eyes fixed firmly on the horizon.

Like our fight for “Merry Christmas,” be sure to unapologetically wish those you see a happy Columbus Day.

#127. The Tribal Supreme Court Project

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Native American Rights Fund recently celebrated the 25th anniversary of the Tribal Supreme Court Project, an initiative designed to establish an infrastructure that would allow tribal interests to reach better outcomes in Supreme Court litigation. For decades now, Supreme Court experts sympathetic to tribal interests have advised them to avoid the court if at all possible. Tribal interests face significant structural disadvantages before it, primarily resulting from centuries of precedents arising in what Justice Neil Gorsuch recently called the “atmosphere of their times,” that is, colonialism.

In 2001, in the literal shadow of 9/11, tribal leaders and advocates met to discuss the state of Indigenous advocacy at the Supreme Court. Recent scholarship by leading Indian law scholar David Getches had shown that tribal interests were less likely to prevail in the Supreme Court than even convicted criminals. Worse, tribal interests were typically losing in unanimous or close to unanimous decisions. Indeed, in the year of that very meeting, tribal interests lost five of six cases, four of these losses being unanimous (Nevada v. Hicks; C&L Enterprises v. Shirley; Chickasaw Nation v. United States; and Dept. of the Interior v. Klamath Water Users). Even the United States was losing badly when siding with tribal interests. The fact that the Supreme Court’s roster had not changed since 1994 (and would not change until 2005) also seemed to solidify the court’s skepticism of such interests during this period.

The NARF representatives, as well as representatives of the National Congress of American Indians, several tribal nations, and a handful of experienced appellate advocates came together in Washington D.C. to discuss a strategy on how to respond to these losses. Supreme Court experts and observers identified numerous issues hampering tribal interests. They noted that strategies for defending against petitions for writ of certiorari were lacking, amicus briefs supporting tribal interests tended to be repetitive of the merits briefs, tribal oral advocates struggled before the court during oral argument, and efforts to educate the court about Indigenous history and governance largely failed.

These leaders developed the nugget of a plan to organize collectively whenever an Indian law case reached the Supreme Court at the petition stage and beyond. NARF attorneys would monitor cases (not the easiest work to do in an age where the internet was still in the stone ages and the Supreme Court had not yet made its docket easily accessible to the public). Groups of selected tribal attorneys, appellate litigators, law professors, and tribal leaders would also meet to discuss strategic choices in individual cases, recommending and recruiting Supreme Court specialists at both the petition and merits stage, developing a targeted and focused amicus brief strategy, and creating a plan to educate the court and the federal judiciary about the lived realities of American Indian people, tribal nations, and Indian country generally.

The project (which I have occasionally provided support to) took some time to gain momentum. In 2005’s City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation, for example, the Supreme Court held in an 8-1 opinion from Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that when tribal interests bring claims that are “disruptive” to the “settled expectations” of non-tribal governments and non-Indian citizens they should be barred. But a few years later, in a tribal jurisdiction matter involving nonmembers, Plains Commerce Bank v. Long Family Land and Cattle Co., the court split 5-4 in deciding against tribal jurisdiction. In the three previous tribal jurisdiction cases, the court had ruled unanimously against tribal interests. The dissenters all switched their votes from the previous case.

But in the 5-4 case of Plains Commerce Bank v. Long Family Land, which dealt with whether tribal courts had jurisdiction to decide claims based on suits against non-members voluntarily having conducted business with tribal members, the Tribal Supreme Court Project organized an amicus strategy that has since become a hallmark of the project’s work. First, the affected tribal nation filed an amicus brief that detailed the history of the tribe as well as the tribal court system and its procedures. No more could the court assume facts about the tribal nation, especially those suggested by the tribe’s opponents in their own amicus briefs or those assumed by the court in prior cases. Second, NCAI’s amicus brief strategically enhanced the merits brief with a broader perspective on tribal jurisdiction, as well as providing information about the national policy context. Third, a consortium of tribes and tribal organizations laid down the overall federal statutory framework that supported tribal jurisdiction. Coupled with a brief from the United States in support of tribal jurisdiction that project allies helped in securing by negotiating with the Office of Solicitor General, the court was on notice that if it ruled against tribal jurisdiction it was doing so in contravention of federal policy. Importantly, the merits briefs and several of the amicus briefs were also filed by Supreme Court specialists, names that the justices and their clerks knew and respected.

The project’s strategy came into maturity in 2014 and beyond with a series of decisions favoring tribal interests that would have shocked jaded Indian law observers a decade earlier. Again, the project helped to guide tribal advocates around the county into a comprehensible strategy that helped to answer in advance the questions the court long has asked about tribal nations.

The project is imperfect. For example, 13 Indigenous advocates argued cases on behalf of tribal advocates from the early 1980s through 2001, usually winning their cases. However, since the project prioritizes Supreme Court specialists, who benefit from their mentors guiding them through a pathway that starts for some of them before they even start their career, no Indigenous person has argued a Supreme Court case since the last, James Anaya. Additionally, many of the “victories” have been won on procedural grounds, rather than fundamentally reshaping Indian law.

But given the state of Indian law only a few decades ago, the Tribal Supreme Court Project deserves accolade. Tribal interests that were floundering, often embarrassed by unanimous decisions untempered by a dissenting opinion, now stand a much more sporting chance before the court. After centuries of losses before the nation’s highest judicial body, that is nothing short of remarkable.

Matthew L.M. Fletcher is the Harry Burns Hutchins Collegiate Professor of Law at the University of Michigan Law School.

Recommended Citation: Matthew L.M. Fletcher, The Tribal Supreme Court Project, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 15, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/the-tribal-supreme-court-project/

#128. France Shouldn’t Return Afghans to Taliban Rule

Click to expand Image Afghan refugees board a truck with their belongings as they await deportation at the Pakistan-Afghanistan border in Chaman on October 19, 2025. © 2025 Abdul Basil/AFP via Getty Images

France has confirmed that it has opened a “technical dialogue” with the Taliban authorities regarding forced returns to Afghanistan. The announcement marks a dangerous shift in policy that places Afghans in France at risk of persecution, torture and other grave abuses in contravention of France’s international human rights obligations.

The “technical dialogue” follows in the wake of a Taliban delegation to Brussels in June in which migration and return policies were discussed with European Union officials. Germany has already deported 263 Afghans since last year.

The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that the talks aim “to facilitate the removal of Afghan nationals who are illegally on the national territory and who represent a national security risk.” French officials say the dialogue is narrowly focused but have not set out any guarantees that those at particular risk, including women, would be protected.

Since taking power in August 2021, the Taliban have issued decrees and enacted laws that have deprived Afghans of their fundamental rights. Women and girls are restricted from exercising their rights to education, freedom of movement, and expression. There is also compelling evidence that Taliban forces have detained and tortured people who have been forcibly returned to the country.

French cooperation with the Taliban on a returns process would be with full knowledge of the Taliban’s responsibility for grave human rights violations and systematic oppression. Earlier this month, the International Criminal Court publicly announced the arrest warrants for Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and three other senior officials for the crime against humanity of persecution on gender and political grounds. The warrants, issued in 2025, relate to the persecution of women, girls, and people who do not conform to the Taliban’s expectations of gender, and the political persecution of those viewed as “allies of girls and women.” 

No country should be forcing refugees to return to Afghanistan so long as the Taliban continues to commit widespread human rights abuses. France should suspend any plan for deportations, and any cooperation on migration control should not be used as a vehicle for sending people back to a country where they would face a real risk of persecution or worse.

#130. Civilians Using Guns to Defend Against Multiple Shootings

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

There were apparently at least a dozen such uses in the U.S. in 2025.

News accounts report that the Bend, Oregon school shooting Thursday was stopped in part by an armed civilian. From the N.Y. Times (Anna Griffin, Aaron West, Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs & Chelsia Rose Marcius):

A man in a red pickup truck was driving by and saw the teenager throw his shotgun over the fence and start to climb it, the police said. The driver "verbally confronted" the gunman, who paused to open fire at him, pelting the truck with shots….

Outside, Kaylub Giamanco, a father of two girls at the school, had seen the red pickup get shot while driving by on his lunch break. He swerved onto the sidewalk and ran inside.

He found the gunman wrestling with the teacher who tried to stop him and shot him several times with a .40-caliber handgun that had been legally secured in his truck, the police said. The suspect, who died, was carrying 44 more rounds of ammunition.

Readers might want to know: How often do civilians use guns to help stop shooters who pose ongoing threats to multiple people? (By "civilian," I mean here someone other than a police officer or a security guard; off-duty military members qualify for my purposes.)

Obviously, an exact count is hard to gather, and some cases will be ambiguous. Sometimes, it may not be clear whether the shooter was planning to keep attacking. Sometimes, it may not be clear, at least from press accounts, whether the defender succeeded in stopping the shooter (for instance, by scaring the shooter away). Sometimes a civilian and a security guard or a police officer might step in together. And sometimes news accounts may err. Any count is thus a judgment call, and also likely incomplete because not all incidents make the news.

Still, thanks to a Crime Prevention Research Center spreadsheet, I can say that in 2025 there appeared to have been at least a dozen such incidents. The CPRC report says there were 23; I went through the list, checked the linked news accounts, and tried to exclude ones that seemed just like one-on-one self-defense situations or matters where the defender seemed clearly unsuccessful. (One-on-one self-defense is of course worthy on its own, but it's not what I'm discussing here.) With those exclusions, and trying to be relatively conservative in what I counted, I ended up counting 12 to 14 such incidents in 2025, depending on how you evaluate some of the more ambiguous ones.

Nor does 2025 appear to be unusual. According to the CPRC report, there were roughly the same number of incidents (or in some years, even more) in 2020-2024 as in 2025. I expect that conservative counts for those years would likewise be comparable to my count for 2025.

None of the 2025 defensive gun use incidents were at a school, but gun possession is generally illegal in schools, so it's unsurprising that law-abiding gun owners can rarely stop such shootings. They can of course enter the school after the shooting starts, as the man in the Oregon shooting did, but that involves a higher degree of difficulty.

The 2025 incidents, with the date, state, city (and link to news article), and excerpt from the news article:

According to Kleine, Jones was asked by management to leave the club. Jones angrily left the club. He got a gun, went back to the club, brandished the gun and started firing it while making threats, Kleine said. Kleine added Jones' gunfire hit several people.

The man, whom Kleine declined to identify, returned fire, striking and ultimately killing Jones outside the club, which had a large crowd of people inside….

[T]he supervisor said he was in his upstairs office and heard multiple gunshots, prompting him to grab his firearm and head downstairs to the location of the shooting. He told detectives he got to their workstation and saw Edwards [the shooter] holding a firearm and standing over [one of the victims] while attempting to reload the weapon. The supervisor said he told Edwards to drop the gun while he and other employees pushed the suspect to the ground and called 911.

Deputies say several people in the crowd returned fire, hitting Thompson multiple times…

Vela, who was in the parking lot, allegedly saw the fight, pulled out a handgun, and opened fire on the brawl. A bystander pulled out his own gun and fired back, fatally striking Vela. That bystander was also wounded by Vela's gunfire, and was rushed to the hospital in critical condition.

In total, the bystander, two women, and one man at the scene were all injured by the gunfire.

Two men on a nearby park bench saw what was happening and intervened. Police say Franco then pointed his weapon at the two men, who were also armed, and a gunfight ensued. Franco was shot in the chest, while the two other men weren't hurt…

[Police officer] Babros commended the men who intervened before any other innocent people were hurt…

Two nearby armed residents heard the disturbance and tried to de-escalate the situation. They observed West fire his rifle in the direction of a man …. That is when the neighbors fired their weapons, killing West….

At least two staff members shot the gunman, causing fatal wounds. One staff member, a member of the security team, was shot once in the leg by the suspect. [I included this because it appeared to involve a non-security-guard and a security guard working together; it's impossible to know what would have happened had the security guard been the only armed defender. -EV]

Atlanta police said others who had their concealed carry permit fired back at the man, who was taken to the hospital in critical condition…

Two armed men opened fire at the gathering, injuring five of the guests…. A CCL holder who was present returned fire, killing one of the suspects and injuring the other.

One of the homes struck by bullets belonged to Senior Airman Harrison Friar. Friar said he quickly secured his family inside, then grabbed his personal firearm and confronted the attacker… Investigators say Friar fired two shots, hitting Burnell in the leg and forcing him to retreat.

They credit his actions with giving law enforcement the critical time needed to contain the situation and preventing further loss of life…

After a thorough investigation, it was concluded by authorities that this was a case of self-defense. According to police, Dunn fired a gun at a group of people and gunfire was returned, leading to Dunn's death…

According to the preliminary investigation, the reunion event was ending when Chambers arrived at the park pavilion dressed in black and wearing a ski mask. Police say he fired multiple shots in the direction of four adults and two small children. Two people were struck by gunfire. One of the victims fired back in self-defense. [It is not evident whether the defensive gun use was effective in scaring Chambers away or otherwise distracting him from the shooting. -EV]

Someone in the group returned fire, police said, hitting Montelongo and causing him to crash his car into a fence. He was later pronounced dead on scene…

"It played out like a movie. We believe the citizen bystanders who discharged their firearms acted in self-defense and ultimately saved lives inside of that restaurant," Garcia said. Police say no one was injured in the shooting…

This of course doesn't tells us a lot by itself about the debates about gun control and gun rights. But it is a reminder that multiple shootings are indeed sometimes (and not that rarely) stopped by good guys with guns.

#131. Stop Writing Blank Checks to Campuses That Protect Hate

Ken Griffin just made the largest single gift in the history of American higher education: $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, most of it to launch a new campus in Miami. If the school’s only problem were a shortage of cash, it would be on easy street now. It is not.

Nearly a month after associate professor Uju Anya deleted her X account amid a firestorm over a racist and violent Sept. 11 post, she is still on the faculty website. Donors should not send another dollar to Carnegie Mellon until that changes.

On Sept. 11, Anya wrote, “Die first, white man, then ask yourself why I’m dancing.” This is par for the course for her: She had already celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk. She celebrated the death of Rush Limbaugh. In 2022, she wished Queen Elizabeth an “excruciating” death. Carnegie Mellon called those earlier posts “offensive and objectionable” and said they did not represent the university’s values. Yet, despite proving she’s learned nothing from these reprimands, she’s kept her job.

The same playbook is running now. Officials promised “swift action,” but that action never arrived. The school is instead staging fireside chats and press releases about Griffin’s money, as if the elephant in the room will vanish if they talk loudly enough about computer science and “climate resilience.”

>>> The Great Migration Remaking Higher Ed

Anya herself said on Instagram that Carnegie Mellon never even contacted her about the latest posts. Before she scrubbed her X account, she gloated that her department chairman had texted her that they were just deleting the angry emails. The chairman deleted his own X account shortly afterward.

She also claimed Carnegie Mellon knew exactly what it was getting and that the school had poached her from another institution. Her posts implied the university backed her views, like when she posted that “it should’ve been Trump” after Dolly Parton died. Conservative and white students cannot feel safe in a classroom run by someone who talks that way. She has no business shaping young adults.

Carnegie Mellon’s media relations line now goes straight to a full voicemail. They will not answer any questions.

About 98% of campaign contributions from individuals affiliated with Carnegie Mellon went to Democrats last cycle, according to OpenSecrets. That echo chamber is why Anya felt free to stand firm and claim her boss would trash the complaints.

Carnegie Mellon already receives more foreign money than any American university except Harvard. Federal data put its lifetime haul near $3.9 billion, much of it tied to Qatar. Now it wants a Miami campus that “organizes learning around societal challenges rather than academic majors” and lists “climate resilience” among the organizing themes.

People are free to waste their own money. But we should not cheer when the money flows to institutions that refuse to fire a professor who cheers political murder and racial death threats.

>>> No True Scotsman at St. Andrews: When DEI Goes Too Far

Universities should receive no taxpayer subsidy at all. Factory workers and plumbers should not be forced to underwrite worthless gender studies degrees for Starbucks baristas carrying $100,000 in student debt. Federal student aid and research grants keep the machine running even when the product is indoctrination. Anya’s salary is part of that product. So is the administrative class that issues statements and then goes silent.

Griffin’s gift will rename a computer-science school and plant a flag in Wynwood. Fine. The same institution still lists Anya as an associate professor of second-language acquisition. Carnegie Mellon has issued similar statements about this same professor before. They are hoping the latest public relations disaster blows over the same way the 2022 episode did. Donors who keep writing checks are telling them the strategy works.

Higher education’s refusal to police its own radicals helps explain low levels of confidence in the system. Young people sit in classrooms with faculty who are sympathetic to (or even in favor of) socialism and cash taxpayer-backed paychecks. If elite campuses want private philanthropy, they should end diversity, equity, and inclusion programs and take appropriate action against people who celebrate assassination, telling white men to die first. Until they do, the checkbook should stay closed. And taxpayer money should never have been on the table.

#133. The immigration term

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court added Blanche v. Ozurumba, a case on whether someone who worked as a cook for a terrorist organization is eligible for asylum protections, to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term. Even before that grant, however, the docket was dominated by immigration issues.

Since late April, the court has granted review in seven immigration-related cases. One of those was dismissed as moot (that is, no longer a live controversy) last month, but, including Ozurumba, six remain, meaning that around one-fifth of the cases currently on the oral argument docket involve immigration. What’s more, the justices will soon consider several more high-profile petitions for review in this area, including one that covers the same essential ground as the case dismissed last month.

As I reported last year, it’s not unusual for the justices to hear multiple immigration cases in a single term, because both Republican and Democratic administrations routinely spar with noncitizens and immigrants’ rights groups about how to interpret and apply federal immigration law. However, the second Trump administration’s heightened focus on immigration issues – and reinterpretation of certain detention and deportation policies – has fueled a surge in immigration lawsuits at all levels of the legal system, which explains why the 2026-27 docket has a particularly high number of immigration disputes (that may grow even higher).

Here’s a brief overview of the immigration-related cases already on the oral argument docket, as well as a few pending petitions that may be worth watching.

Perhaps the highest-profile immigration case set for oral argument this term is Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., a challenge by a group of immigrants to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders – a process known as “third-country removals.”

This issue arrived on the oral argument docket via the interim docket, where it has been addressed by the court three times over the past 17 months. The Trump administration first asked the justices to clear the way for third-country removals to continue in May 2025, after a federal judge in Massachusetts barred the government from deporting noncitizens to third-party countries without first providing them with, among other things, a written notice of where they would be sent and an opportunity to raise their concerns about facing torture there. In June 2025, the Supreme Court agreed to put that order on hold. Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote a dissenting opinion, joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.

One day after the court issued that decision, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer returned to the interim docket, asking the justices to allow the administration to remove a group of immigrants being held on a U.S. military base in Djibouti to South Sudan, a move that had been blocked by the same federal judge. On July 3, the Supreme Court granted the administration’s motion for clarification, explaining that its June order allowed the deportations to South Sudan. Sotomayor and Jackson again dissented. Kagan wrote a concurring opinion, reiterating her opposition to the court’s June decision but adding that she did “not see how a district court can compel compliance with an order that this Court has stayed.”

Last month, after the federal judge in Massachusetts issued a final judgment blocking its third-country removal policy, the Trump administration brought the issue back to the interim docket yet again, asking the justices to put the new decision on hold. On Sept. 29, the court – over objections from Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson – agreed to temporarily pause the lower court’s ruling. However, it also took up the dispute for oral argument in December. The justices asked the litigants to brief several questions, including whether the administration’s third-country removal policy is unlawful.

Another closely watched case on the Trump administration’s approach to deportations is Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha. It addresses the administration’s policy of detaining noncitizens who have been apprehended within the United States under 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A), a section of federal immigration law that mandates detention of applicants for admission into the country who are “not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted” and does not provide for bond hearings.

Past administrations have applied Section 1225 only to noncitizens who were apprehended crossing the border or soon after they entered the country; noncitizens who were apprehended within the U.S. years or decades after they arrived in the country had been detained under a different statute, Section 1226, which does authorize bond hearings or conditional parole. By shifting to Section 1225 detentions, the Trump administration has sought to detain noncitizens apprehended within the country without bond while they await removal proceedings.

In recent months, judges across the country have delivered thousands of rulings against these detentions, and most federal appeals courts to address the issue have decided that Section 1225 does not apply to noncitizens apprehended within the country. On Oct. 1, the justices took up Rhoney, agreeing to clarify the scope of Section 1225.

Genalo v. Black, the case that was dismissed from the oral argument docket last month, also addressed access to bond hearings. Specifically, it asked whether immigrants detained under a law targeting noncitizens who commit certain crimes have a due process right to a bond hearing once their detention becomes “unreasonably prolonged.” The Trump administration had also asked the justices to determine what the government must show to justify continued detention if such a hearing is indeed required.

The case was dismissed after Sauer notified the court that the administration agreed with the immigrant, Keisy G.M., that the case no longer presented a live controversy because he had been pardoned by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and was therefore no longer eligible to be detained under the law at issue. In his letter requesting dismissal, Sauer said that the Justice Department aimed to soon bring a new case presenting the same questions to the court so that the justices could still answer them during the 2026-27 term. (More on that later.)

As noted above, the justices granted review on Tuesday in Blanche v. Ozurumba, agreeing to clarify what type of support an immigrant must have provided to a terrorist organization to be ineligible for various immigration benefits, including asylum protections.

The case involves Izuchukwu Ozurumba, a Nigerian man who worked as a cook in a camp run by a separatist organization called the “Unknown Gunmen” “for about six months” before escaping, according to the government’s petition. He traveled to Venezuela and then to the United States, where he applied for asylum, but an immigration judge and the Board of Immigration Appeals concluded that his work in the camp amounted to “material support” for terrorism and that he was, therefore, ineligible for asylum and subject to removal under a provision of federal law that deems anyone who provides “material support” for a “terrorist organization” ineligible for a visa or entrance into the United States.

Ozurumba appealed his case to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, which agreed with him that his work as a cook in the camp did not represent “material support” for a terrorist organization. “Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have ‘sustained’ the organization in the broadest possible sense ... but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities,” concluded Judge James Wynn in the majority opinion. The Supreme Court will now review the 4th Circuit’s ruling.

Asylum policy is also at the center of Wassily v. Blanche, which is set to be argued on Nov. 30. The case asks whether a noncitizen whose asylum protections have been terminated remains eligible to become a lawful permanent resident, also known as a green card holder.

Wassily was appealed to the Supreme Court by two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of multiple crimes. They assert that they remain eligible for adjustment to a green card, because the text of the law addressing such adjustments refers only to someone who has been “granted asylum” and does not explicitly address what is to happen if this grant is later terminated.

In the government’s response to the petition, Sauer did not oppose Supreme Court review. He defended the lower court’s decision, arguing that it was correct when it held that immigration law “allows only noncitizens with current asylum status to adjust to lawful permanent resident status.” But, after highlighting a conflict between the federal courts of appeals on the issue, Sauer described the case as a “suitable” one with which to resolve “the disagreement on an important and recurring legal question.”

In an August column for SCOTUSblog, Duncan Fulton contended that “Wassily is of considerable significance,” because “recent policy changes by the Trump administration have” put more asylum beneficiaries at risk of losing their asylum protections. And columnist César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández recently wrote that the case “highlights the tension between a law enacted half a century ago that seems to let people who had been granted asylum, only to lose it later, obtain a green card despite a conviction for a long list of crimes, and today’s prevailing political sentiment that can’t contemplate doing anything of the sort.”

The justices will also hear argument in two cases that stem from immigration disputes but don’t raise what we would typically think of as immigration questions.

The first, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, addresses the H-2A program, which enables U.S. employers “to bring foreign nationals to the United States to fill temporary agricultural jobs.” The justices agreed to decide whether the Department of Labor has the power to hold hearings to collect money from employers who violate the terms of this visa program.

The second, Montoya Palacios v. Liggins, asks whether a habeas petition challenging civil immigration detention qualifies as a “civil action” under the Equal Access to Justice Act. If it does, a detainee who prevails in such a case could be eligible for attorney’s fees if the government’s position was not “substantially justified.”

In the coming weeks and months, the justices will have several more opportunities to add immigration-related cases to the oral argument docket, when it weighs petitions for review addressing other aspects of the Trump administration’s policies on asylum, immigration detention, and deportation.

A petition typically needs to be granted by late January to make it onto the oral argument docket for the current term. And even if none of these pending petitions are taken up for argument, the 2026-27 term will likely be remembered for its immigration-related rulings.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#134. Japan’s Commitment to Sport Needs to Include Athlete Protection

Click to expand Image Photo montage of the Tokyo Olympic Stadium and youth in Japan training and playing popular sports. © 2019 imagenavi/Aflo; 2005 Doable/a.collectionRF/amanaimages; 2020 Human Rights Watch; 2015 Satoru Kobayashi/a.collectionRF/amanaimages; 2016 RYO/amanaimages; Trevor Williams/Getty Images; 2020 Human Rights Watch; 2016 Matsuo/Aflo; AdobeStock

Every October, Japan celebrates Sports Day, a public holiday established to commemorate the 1964 Tokyo Olympic Games and Japan's longstanding commitment to sport as a national priority.

There has been much to celebrate in recent years. For more than six decades, Japan has had dedicated legislation – now known as the Basic Act on Sports – to advance sports on a national level. By investing in facilities, athletes’ development, and public participation—and hosting mega-events like the 2020 Olympics—Japan has become a leading sports nation.

Yet, one critical issue has received too little attention: protecting athletes and children from sports-related abuse. Human Rights Watch has documented the widespread physical, sexual, and verbal abuse many Japanese children and athletes experience when they participate in sports. A professional athlete described suffering abuses from his coach: “I was hit so many times, I can’t count ... the coach … hit [me] in the face in front of everyone. I was bleeding, but he did not stop.”

Under public pressure from athletes and survivors to reform, the Japanese parliament passed in 2025 amendments to the Basic Act on Sport requiring the national government to prevent abuse in sport. So far, however, the government has not adequately implemented the law—largely relying, instead, on individual sports federations and organizations to handle complaints of abuse.

But, as Human Rights Watch has reported, athletes and children are often hesitant to report abuse to these institutions because they fear retaliation and because federations often protect their leaders rather than athletes. Reporting mechanisms also vary widely by sport, creating unequal access to protection.

The Japan Sports Agency is now drafting the government's five-year blueprint for sports policy, which will be implemented in 2027. This plan should better address abuse in sport, including by establishing an independent Safe Sport Center to receive complaints, investigate abuse allegations, and support those who have been harmed.

Sport Day should be an opportunity not only to celebrate Japan’s athletes but to make them safer. Japan’s government should ensure that everyone can participate in sport safely, without abuse, and can report harm through a trusted system.

A New Orleans attorney who pleaded guilty in a scheme to stage truck crashes has been sentenced to more than two years in prison.

#138. SCOTUS considers new take on old law

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Justice Clarence Thomas was confirmed to the Supreme Court 35 years ago today. In May, he became the second-longest-serving justice in Supreme Court history.

On Wednesday, the justices heard oral argument in Salazar v. Paramount Global, on whether and how the 1988 Video Privacy Protection Act, which was enacted after the Washington City Paper reported on Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork’s video rental history, applies in the internet era. It was the final argument of the October sitting.

Later on Wednesday, the Supreme Court granted a request from the Federal Communications Commission to block a ruling by a federal appeals court that would have required the FCC to rule quickly on a challenge to its “public notice” extending favorable advertising rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees. Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that they would have denied both requests. For more on the decision, see the On Site section below.

Tomorrow, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EDT.

On Sept. 28, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to clear the way for the Federal Bureau of Prisons to implement its new policy on healthcare and accommodations for transgender inmates, which would prevent such inmates from obtaining gender-transition surgeries, hormone therapy, and “social accommodations.” The dispute is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#142. Justices grant Trump administration’s request to pause lower court ruling in political ad rate dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday cleared the way for political parties and joint fundraising committees to continue to receive favorable advertising rates in the run-up to the 2026 election. In a five-page, unsigned opinion, the justices extended a pause on a ruling by a federal appeals court in Virginia that had instructed the Federal Communications Commission to act quickly on a petition by four Democratic candidates for Congress for review of a notice that the parties and committees are entitled to those advantageous rates.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that they would have denied the requests.

Wednesday’s opinion by the Supreme Court means that the FCC no longer has any obligation to rule on the availability of the favorable rates, which are currently in place, on any particular timetable – and in particular, it does not have to do so before the November election.

This was the second time since late August that the court has been drawn into the dispute over the discounted rates, which under federal election law are available to candidates for federal office during the 45-day-period before the primary election and the 60-day-period before the general. In March, the FCC’s Media Bureau issued a “public notice” indicating that political parties and joint fundraising committees should also receive the favorable rates.

Three candidates for U.S. Senate seats – Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, and former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina – as well as Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, who is running for reelection in Michigan, went to the full FCC in late April, asking it to review the notice. In early June, with their request still pending before the FCC, the candidates went to federal court, where they argued that the public notice was inconsistent with federal election laws.

A divided panel of the 4th Circuit agreed. In his opinion for the majority, Judge Robert King deemed federal law “unambiguous”: it gives the preferential rates only to a “candidate” for his or her personal use, which does not extend to a candidate’s “mere authorization of someone else’s use.”

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee, which had joined the case, went to the Supreme Court in late August, asking the justices to put the 4th Circuit’s ruling on hold. They contended (among other things) that the 4th Circuit lacked the power to consider the candidates’ challenge because the public notice was not the kind of final agency action that the court of appeals has the authority to review.

On Sept. 4, the justices temporarily paused the 4th Circuit’s decision, with only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissenting. In a four-page, unsigned opinion, the court emphasized that the committees were likely to prevail on their argument that the 4th Circuit cannot review the public notice before the FCC does.

The case then went back to the lower court, where the candidates sought an order instructing the FCC to act on their petition for review of the public notice. A divided panel granted that request on Wednesday, Oct. 7, and directed the FCC to issue its decision by noon on Friday, Oct. 9.

Before that deadline, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to intervene again. Sauer told the court that the 4th Circuit had “seriously erred in trying to short-circuit the Commission’s deliberations.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee and National Republican Congressional Committee filed their own application the same day, seeking to pause the 4th Circuit's order. They told the justices (among other things) that, "[i]f the case for a stay was strong the first time around, it's open and shut now."

Later on Thursday, Oct. 8, Chief Justice John Roberts, who handles emergency applications from the 4th Circuit, immediately paused the 4th Circuit’s order to give justices time to consider the request – a procedure known as an administrative stay. Roberts also took the relatively rare step of instructing the challengers to respond on Saturday.

In their Saturday filing, the candidates urged the justices to leave the 4th Circuit’s ruling in place. They blamed the FCC for the dispute now before the court, accusing the agency of seeking to “engage in blatant procedural trench warfare to stave off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is too late to matter.”

In its opinion, the court explained that although the FCC must “act on every application it receives,” it is not required “to act within a particular timeframe. The Commission may exercise its discretion to set its own procedures and schedule for resolving such applications.” Therefore, it reasoned, the 4th Circuit’s order instructing the FCC “to issue a final decision on the candidates’ application just five months after it was filed and within just 48 hours—all while the Commission’s deliberation process was still ongoing”—violated the “system of separation of powers.”

If allowed to stand, the court continued, the 4th Circuit’s order would also cause irreparable harm, another factor that courts consider in deciding whether to grant emergency relief, by requiring the FCC to “triage its ongoing deliberation process and prepare a final order on an extremely expedited timeline.”

The Supreme Court granted the FCC’s request and put the 4th Circuit’s order on hold while the appeals process plays out. It dismissed the Republican groups’ request as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy – in light of its grant of the FCC’s request.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#145. "The Supreme Court Should Not Have to Keep Trimming the Same Poison Ivy One Tiny Branch at a Time"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A nice line from Ninth Circuit Judge Lawrence VanDyke.

The broader context, from Judge VanDyke's opinion dissenting from denial of rehearing en banc in Whitfield v. Mullin, joined by Judges Patrick Bumatay and Eric Tung; the question Judge VanDyke is confronting is when a Ninth Circuit precedent stops being binding on future panels because it's inconsistent with intervening Supreme Court precedent:

[T]his case illustrates (yet again) a more fundamental problem within our circuit: Miller v. Gammie's improper demand that our own circuit's precedent be privileged over the Supreme Court's more recent instructions unless our precedent is "clearly irreconcilable" with what the Supreme Court has subsequently told us. 335 F.3d 889, 893 (9th Cir. 2003). This prevents three-judge panels of our court from applying more recent Supreme Court authority whenever it is merely inconsistent with our own. The effect of this rule is both obvious and obviously wrong—we systematically hold the Supreme Court's instructions about the right answer to any number of legal questions in lower regard than our own wrong precedents….

The reality is that our en banc court is often unable or unwilling to fix things at odds with Supreme Court precedent. Sometimes, the obstacle is simply institutional inertia; the costs of en banc review make correction burdensome enough that erroneous precedent persists by default. We are a very busy court, and we can't be expected to take every case en banc that presents a legal issue where subsequent Supreme Court authority is inconsistent with, but not "clearly irreconcilable" with, our own.

But that is not the only problem with Miller's rule. The effect of that inverted rule is especially insidious (and no doubt intentional) when our precedent involves one of the many contested legal questions where our circuit's ideological commitments are at odds with what the Supreme Court has recently told us. In those instances, it is very unlikely a majority of our court would ever vote to take a case en banc to abandon the majority's own preferred doctrinal approach, even after the Supreme Court has undermined its foundation. Judge Reinhardt famously announced the Ninth Circuit's motto: the Supreme Court can't "catch 'em all."

Miller's strictures ensure that the Supreme Court's guidance will, for the most part, be limited in this circuit to only those instances where the Court actually "catches" a specific case—that is, where it actually grants review and issues a binding opinion in that case. And even in that rare instance, Miller ensures that whatever guidance the Supreme Court provides will have little spillover effect beyond the very narrow issue actually decided by the Court in that case. Everything else is not "clearly irreconcilable" (judges and lawyers alike are, after all, pretty good at distinguishing), so three-judge panels of this court that would very much like to follow the Supreme Court's recent guidance can't. And those who would very much like to avoid the Supreme Court's guidance can do so simply by not voting to take a case en banc.

The consequence is perverse. To correct our circuit's many erroneous precedents and ensure litigants can benefit from intervening Supreme Court decisions, the Supreme Court will have to take case after case after case and reverse them all, slowly, over the course of decades, one by one by one, as it has done so many times before.

The Supreme Court should not have to keep trimming the same poison ivy one tiny branch at a time. There are many judges on our circuit who would be glad to do the right thing and apply the Supreme Court's guidance in three-judge panel decisions whenever that guidance is inconsistent with our circuit's own earlier precedents. By overturning Miller in this or some future case, the Supreme Court would remove a perverse rule that entrenches erroneous precedent in this circuit, enabling three-judge panels to help hack away at the overgrowth. Help us help you.

The Supreme Court should take up this case to correct our circuit's erroneous "serious questions" rule [that's the debate in the underlying case, which has to do with the standard for granting preliminary injunctions]. But while it's at it, why not also correct Miller's "clearly irreconcilable" standard? Addressing the former will eliminate one of many legal doctrines in our court that are inconsistent with subsequent Supreme Court authority. But also addressing the latter would do much more to conform the Ninth Circuit's law to the Supreme Court's—without the Supreme Court's needing to exhaustively address every single error seriatim.

#146. Court appears likely to allow internet suit based on decades-old video privacy law to go forward

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday seemed likely to let a lawsuit brought by a Tennessee man alleging that a website owned by entertainment giant Paramount Global violated a 1988 video privacy law when it shared information with Facebook go forward, at least for now. After nearly 90 minutes of oral argument in Salazar v. Paramount Global, the justices appeared poised to agree with Michael Salazar that the law, the Video Privacy Protection Act, applies to any consumer of the products sold by a company that provides videos. Although some members of the court expressed concerns about the possibility that allowing Salazar’s suit to proceed could open the door to lawsuits against a broad swath of U.S. companies, those concerns appeared to be assuaged in part by the prospect that other provisions of the law could serve as a check on such suits. Moreover, some justices suggested that companies could easily avoid suits in the future by obtaining their customers’ consent to share their personal information.

The law before the court on Wednesday has its origins in the 1987 battle over the nomination of Judge Robert Bork to fill the vacancy left by the retirement of Justice Lewis Powell from the Supreme Court. A Washington journalist, Michael Dolan, obtained and published a list of the videos that Bork had rented from his local video store.

Bork’s nomination failed, with 58 senators voting against him and only 42 for him. That likely had little to do with his taste in movies, which included (as Dolan later recounted) “whodunits and Brit films, costume drama and otherwise.” But Dolan’s article spurred Congress to enact the Video Privacy Protection Act, which bars a “video tape service provider” from “knowingly disclos[ing], to any person, personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider.”

Salazar filed a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Nashville, Tennessee, alleging that Paramount’s disclosure of his video-viewing history without his consent violated the VPPA. He asked the court to award $2,500 in damages (the maximum available under the law) for the alleged violation of the VPPA to him and the other members of the class, as well as (among other things) punitive damages and attorney’s fees.

A divided U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit upheld that ruling. Writing for the majority, Judge John Nalbandian wrote that although, standing alone, “the expression ‘goods or services’ is not limited, its association with surrounding words cabins its meaning. The full definition of ‘consumer’ in the statute does not encompass consumers of all ‘goods or services’ imaginable, but only those ‘from a video tape service provider.’”

Salazar came to the Supreme Court last fall, asking the justices to weigh in, which they agreed in late January to do.

On the one hand, although the question was not actually before them, some justices were skeptical that Paramount Global fell within the definition of “video tape service provider” at all. Justice Clarence Thomas was the first to make this point. He told Joshua Hammack, who represents Salazar, that the statute only applies to an entity that rents, sells, or delivers “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.” How, Thomas asked, would that extend to videos streamed over the internet?

When Hammack countered that the law does not require a tangible object, but instead also covers videos that someone plays on their phone or at their house, Thomas suggested that streaming a movie on TV might be closer to traditional television (which is not covered by the VPPA) than picking a video up from a movie rental store.

Thomas made the same point with Paul Clement, who represents Paramount Global, asking how 247Sports.com qualifies as a video tape service provider. It does not naturally seem, Thomas said, to be in the business of providing videos.

But Clement also indicated that the definition of “video tape service provider” sweeps more broadly than companies whose sole business is selling or renting video tapes. When Congress enacted the VPPA, he noted, it “did make it pretty clear” that a department store that sold videos would be considered a video tape service provider.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett echoed Thomas’ question, asking Hammack why the videos that 247Sports.com played on its site made it analogous to a 1980s-era movie-rental store and therefore a “video tape service provider.” She appeared unpersuaded by Hammack’s contention that when 247Sports.com plays videos on its site, it has a “profit motive,” telling him that “basically every other business” with a website has a profit motive. “[I]f I’m on Nordstrom’s website,” she said, “and I click to … see the model show me what the shoes are going to look like … that’s a profit motive.”

Justice Samuel Alito also appeared doubtful at times that Paramount Global was a “video tape service provider,” telling Hammack that the VPPA was a “law that is based on the technology of the 1980s.” He questioned whether Paramount was selling or renting videotapes, and what it meant for a product to be “similar” to videotapes. “[I]t is not similar,” he noted, “in the sense that you go to a Blockbuster store and get a VHS tape.”

Chief Justice John Roberts, who was relatively quiet during Wednesday’s argument, suggested that Salazar’s interpretation of the VPPA was inconsistent with Congress’ goal of protecting a consumer’s video-viewing history. He harkened back to what he described as a favorite hypothetical of retired Justice Stephen Breyer, involving a sign that proclaims “no pets in a park.” Does that mean, Roberts queried, that someone who has a pet snail in his pocket can be prosecuted, or does it mean that we should look at the purpose of the rule?

Justice Brett Kavanaugh pressed both lawyers on a key argument made by Paramount Global: whether allowing Salazar’s lawsuit to move forward would open the floodgates to lawsuits against all kinds of businesses that stream videos on their websites.

Hammack stressed that federal trial courts have ruled that businesses such as, say, Chick-fil-A are not “video tape service providers” and therefore not subject to suit under the VPPA.

That response prompted Kavanaugh to ask Clement how the court should think about what Kavanaugh characterized as the “sky-is-falling concern” when Paramount Global could still prevail on two separate questions that are not actually before the court – what constitutes a “video tape service provider” and whether the kind of information that Paramount disclosed to Facebook qualifies as “personal identifiable information.”

Kavanaugh then suggested that a “very easy solution” to the problem facing Paramount Global and other similarly situated companies would simply be to obtain their customers’ consent before disclosing any information obtained from them.

Justice Elena Kagan made the same point, telling Clement that a company could avoid liability under the VPPA in two ways: first, by getting consent; and, second, by ceasing the practice of selling people’s personal information.

Kagan also indicated that, in her view, this case was precisely the kind of case that Congress intended to cover in the VPPA. She described a scenario in which a judge watched many videos of women wrestling on a sports website like 247Sports.com, with the potential for embarrassment if that video-viewing history were disclosed. “[C]ouldn’t this case kind of be the paradigmatic” example, she asked, of a case to which the VPPA would apply?

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared sympathetic to Salazar’s position. She told Clement that he had “a line-drawing problem.” The point of the VPPA, she said, “was the unlawful disclosure without consent of personally identifying information.” But under Paramount Global’s interpretation, she continued, the application of the statute would hinge on “what particular item the consumer purchased” from the video tape service provider. “And I don’t understand why that should be the dividing line or why that makes any sense in this concept.”

Barrett also questioned whether Salazar has a legal right to sue, known as standing. She emphasized that Salazar’s information had not actually been disclosed to a person, no matter “what this Pixel thing is.”

Hammack pushed back, responding that Salazar’s video-viewing history had gone to Facebook, the world’s largest social-media company.

Barrett raised the question again with Clement, asking whether Paramount Global conceded that Salazar has a right to sue.

Characterizing the information that had been disclosed to Facebook as “gobbledegook,” Clement offered to provide additional briefing on the question of whether Salazar could bring his lawsuit at all.

A decision in the case is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#147. Hiring disparities among new lawyers grew wider for 2025 graduating class

White law school graduates found jobs at a higher rate than their Black, Hispanic and Asian classmates in 2025, widening a long-standing employment gap. (Image from Shutterstock)

White law school graduates found jobs at a higher rate than their Black, Hispanic and Asian classmates in 2025, widening a long-standing employment gap, according to new figures from the National Association for Law Placement.

Reuters reported Wednesday that according to the NALP’s study, more ​than 94% of white law graduates had work within 10 months of graduation, while the share for graduates of color decreased to less than 91%. Black graduates fared worst, at 87%, a decline from close to 90% in 2024. Hispanic graduates experienced a small decrease, from more than 92% the previous year to slightly over 91% in 2025. Asian graduates stayed flat at about 92%. Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander graduates, a small group, did the best, topping more than 96%.

Positions requiring a bar license, the most prized kind of legal work, followed a similar pattern. Only graduates of Middle Eastern or North African background kept pace with or beat white graduates there. Students who were first in their families to attend college also trailed those with college-educated parents.

“A law degree should open doors, but NALP’s latest report shows that those doors are not equally open to everyone,” said Nikia Gray, the executive director of the NALP, in a statement.

The class entered the workforce as the White House pressed an aggressive push against diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. Federal regulators have questioned large law firms about how they hire, and one prominent diversity-focused organization, Diversity Lab, closed its doors in June after drawing scrutiny from antitrust enforcers.

Roughly 50 firms that once supplied the NALP with data on their attorneys’ demographics chose not to this year, which the group blamed on the pressure campaign.

Separately, federal education officials are looking at whether to strip the council of the ABA Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar of its role overseeing law school accreditation, citing in part what they view as sluggishness in dropping diversity requirements.
