#151. Hooch, hardball, and Halloween

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

The Supreme Court has disposed of four of last week’s 14 relists and appears to be holding a fifth. As is frequently the case, the government did especially well. The justices granted review in U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, the separation-of-powers fight over discovery into whether DOGE is an “agency” subject to FOIA, and Blanche v. Ozurumba, the case asking whether cooking for a terrorist organization counts as “material support” only if it advances the organization’s actual commission of terrorism. And summer holdover Berry v. United States finally got its grant: The court will decide whether a certificate of appealability may issue when binding circuit precedent forecloses a prisoner’s claim, but another circuit has accepted it. Clark v. United States, which raises the same certificate-of-appealability question (plus a separate issue involving collateral challenges to financial penalties), lost the fight to be the court’s vehicle of choice and now appears to be held for Berry.

Lastly, the court denied review in Herrera-Salazar v. United States, the double-jeopardy challenge to successive prosecutions for being “found in” the United States without an intervening departure. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch, filed a statement respecting the denial. Although they agreed that Herrera-Salazar’s removal made review unwarranted, and hoped his repeated prosecution was unusual, they wrote to “underscore” that his prosecution presented “serious constitutional problems” and urged courts to avoid the “constitutional absurdity” they believed had occurred here. The other nine relists are making a return appearance this week.

As for the pro se petitions I labeled “lost causes” last week – none had drawn a response, or even a request for one – the label held up: None was granted. The court denied certiorari in some and denied leave to proceed in forma pauperis in the others.

Now on to new business. Friday’s conference docket once again features exactly 100 cases and applications, including six first-time relists.

With Halloween approaching, it seems only fitting to begin with spirits – of the distilled variety. The first two relists, Department of Justice v. McNutt and Ream v. Department of the Treasury, involve a subject near and dear to American hearts: the right to make your own whiskey. Federal law has taxed distilled spirits since the days of Alexander Hamilton, helping to spark the Whiskey Rebellion. After the Civil War, Congress banned distilling in a “dwelling house” or in “any shed, yard, or inclosure connected with” one, 26 U.S.C. § 5178(a)(1)(B). The government defends the ban as a necessary and proper means of enforcing federal excise taxes on liquor, arguing that it channels distilling into places where tax collectors can keep an eye on it. Two federal appeals courts considered challenges to the same law less than two weeks apart and reached opposite conclusions.

In Department of Justice v. McNutt, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held that the ban exceeds Congress’ enumerated powers. Scott McNutt received a letter from the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau after he bought distilling equipment, warning him that unlicensed distilling is a crime. He and the Hobby Distillers Association sued, and a federal district court in Texas enjoined enforcement of the ban against McNutt, the association, and its members. The 5th Circuit affirmed the injunction, reasoning that a ban on distilling reduces taxable activity rather than helping to collect the tax and so is not “plainly adapted” to the taxing power under McCulloch v. Maryland. The court denied rehearing en banc without noted dissent. The government’s petition reminds the justices that the court “usually grants review when a court of appeals has invalidated a federal statute.”

Eleven days later, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit went the other way in Ream v. Department of the Treasury. John Ream, a former aerospace engineer and brewery and taproom owner in Newark, Ohio, wants to distill whiskey at home. He has picked out the alcohol recipes he desires to use and a $600 copper pot still but hasn’t bought it. The district court dismissed his suit for lack of standing. A divided 6th Circuit panel reversed on standing but upheld the ban on the merits, reasoning that it shifts consumption toward commercial spirits that are less prone to tax evasion. Judge Andre Mathis dissented on standing. Ream’s petition adds a second question asking the court to overrule or clarify Gonzales v. Raich. Ohio and 14 other states have weighed in on his side.

Here is a rarity: Everyone agrees the court should take a case. The solicitor general concedes the split and the importance of the question, but argues that the court should grant McNutt and hold Ream. In the government’s view, McNutt is the cleaner vehicle because the judges agreed that at least one plaintiff had standing, while standing is disputed in Ream. Here’s another noteworthy thing: The government no longer defends the ban under the commerce power, making this, in its view, a taxing-power split and nothing more. The McNutt respondents likewise ask the court to grant both cases. Ream, for his part, says the government is just trying to keep the court away from Raich. A grant in McNutt seems likely; whether Ream gets invited along is a tougher question.

Third time’s the charm for school admissions challenges?

For the third time in three years, the justices are being asked whether parents challenging ostensibly race-neutral admissions policies must show a disparate impact before courts may consider evidence of discriminatory intent. In Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a group of Montgomery County, Md. parents represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation argue that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit conflicts with other circuits by requiring challengers to allege that the targeted group’s share of admissions fell below its share of the applicant pool. The court denied the earlier petitions, Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County School Board and Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence v. School Committee for the City of Boston, both times over dissents by Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas. In the Boston case, Justice Neil Gorsuch also wrote separately to echo their concerns. Alito warned that the 4th Circuit’s rule would become a “blueprint for evading” constitutional limits on consideration of race in admissions under Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College.

This case involves Montgomery County’s four selective magnet middle school programs. After a 2016 consultant’s report found Black and Hispanic students underrepresented, the district changed its admissions criteria, using “peer grouping” and “local norming” that favored students from higher-poverty schools. According to the complaint, Asian-American students’ share of invitees dropped sharply, falling by half at two of the programs. The district court initially refused to dismiss, finding it plausible that the board acted with discriminatory motive. But when the district switched during the COVID-19 pandemic to a lottery open to students at or above the 85th percentile on locally normed tests, the parents amended their complaint to challenge the lottery as a successor to the earlier plan. This time the district court dismissed, concluding, among other things, that the parents had not plausibly alleged that the lottery itself was adopted with discriminatory intent. The 4th Circuit affirmed in a short per curiam order, relying on circuit precedent in the TJ case that requires a challenger to show an aggregate disparate impact.

The parents’ petition argues that the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st and 4th Circuits are now on one side of a 2-2 split requiring a showing of aggregate disparate impact. On the other side, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit held in 2024 that challenges can proceed based on other evidence of intentional discrimination, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed this year. The Montgomery County Board of Education responds that the case is “an exceptionally poor vehicle” and that the lottery, which is difficult to “even conceptualize” as “intentionally discriminat[ing] on the basis of race,” was adopted for different reasons, by different officials, than what the parents mainly attack. It argues that the case would come out the same way in every circuit. We’ll soon learn whether the more developed split changes the court’s mind – or merely produces another dissent from denial.

The family of legendary Pittsburgh Pirates outfielder Roberto Clemente says his native Puerto Rico has appropriated the slugger’s trademarks. In 2022, the commonwealth began offering commemorative license plates and registration tags bearing Clemente’s image, jersey number, and the words “3000 hits.” The program allegedly raised roughly $15 million for a sports district named in Clemente’s honor. Clemente’s family, who say they never authorized it, sued under the takings clause and the Lanham Act in Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit held that the alleged infringement of the family’s trademarks did not constitute a per se taking comparable to a physical appropriation of property. It also held, bound by circuit precedent, that Puerto Rico enjoys the same sovereign immunity as a state and that the Lanham Act doesn’t abrogate it.

The Clementes ask the Supreme Court to decide whether intangible property is exempt from per se takings claims, and whether Puerto Rico is entitled to sovereign immunity in federal court. The justices expressly reserved the immunity question in a 2023 case concerning Puerto Rico’s financial oversight board, and Justice Thomas has expressed doubt that the commonwealth enjoys it. Although the petition identifies no square circuit split, it has attracted support from several property-rights organizations. Puerto Rico responds that the 1st Circuit decided only the narrow theory the Clementes chose to press. Puerto Rico also argues that the 1st Circuit had no occasion to announce a sweeping rule about intangible property. And it emphasizes the absence of a split and argues that the Lanham Act doesn’t unequivocally abrogate its immunity.

That’s a lot of constitutional law for a license plate.

Next up is Bauer v. Marks, a qualified-immunity case arising from the unrest in Minneapolis following George Floyd's death in 2020. During a confrontation between protesters and police, Minneapolis SWAT officer Benjamin Bauer fired a projectile at 19-year-old Ethan Marks, striking him in the eye and causing severe injuries. Marks sued, alleging excessive force. Bauer argued that he was entitled to qualified immunity because his conduct did not violate clearly established law.

A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit disagreed, concluding that disputed facts about whether Marks still posed a threat precluded qualified immunity. Bauer sought Supreme Court review, arguing that the appeals court had improperly focused on the moment Bauer fired rather than considering the entire encounter. Last year, the justices sent the case back to the 8th Circuit for reconsideration in light of their decision in Barnes v. Felix, which rejected the so-called “moment-of-threat” rule and required courts to consider the totality of the circumstances in evaluating excessive-force claims.

But a divided panel of the same court reached the same result on remand. The majority maintained that it had already considered the entire encounter, while Judge David Stras dissented, writing that, given the chaos during the unrest, no precedent clearly established that Bauer’s actions were unlawful. Bauer has now returned to the Supreme Court, arguing in his petition that the 8th Circuit both defied the justices’ remand order and failed to identify sufficiently similar precedent clearly establishing that his conduct was unlawful. Marks’ mother, who was substituted as plaintiff following his death earlier this year, responds that the panel faithfully applied Barnes and that factual disputes preclude qualified immunity.

Our final relist has impeccable timing. In Hanaway v. Sanderson, Missouri is asking the justices to decide whether the First Amendment gives convicted sex offenders a right to refuse to display a government-mandated Halloween sign. Missouri law requires registered sex offenders to remain indoors during trick-or-treating hours, turn off their outside lights, avoid Halloween-related contact with children, and post a sign stating, “No candy or treats at this residence.” Violations are misdemeanors.

Thomas Sanderson, a registered sex offender who traditionally decorated his home for Halloween and handed out candy, was arrested in 2022 for violating the law. He challenged the sign requirement, arguing that forcing him to display the government's message on his property violated his First Amendment right against compelled speech. The district court agreed, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit affirmed on the merits, holding that the sign requirement was subject to strict scrutiny and that Missouri had failed to demonstrate that it was narrowly tailored to protect children. It did, however, vacate the broader injunction and remand for relief limited to Sanderson under Trump v. CASA.

Missouri argues that the sign is a factual disclosure incidental to its conduct restrictions, so at most intermediate scrutiny applies under Rumsfeld v. FAIR. It claims a split between the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 8th and 11th Circuits, which struck down Halloween signs, and the 5th Circuit, which upheld disclosure requirements associated with federal sex-offender registration. A group of states led by Iowa supports Missouri, arguing that the decision threatens other public-safety disclosure requirements. Sanderson responds that the only other federal appeals court to consider a similar Halloween sign requirement – the 11th Circuit – struck it down too.

The justices may be reluctant to intervene without a square circuit split, but the timing could hardly be better. I will leave it to our readers (both of you) to make the “trick or treat” jokes.

That’s all for this week! After next Monday’s orders, the relists take a break until November. Enjoy the time off – I know I will.

Issue: Whether the law clearly established that the officer’s use of a less-lethal projectile, under the totality of the circumstances, constituted an unreasonable use of force in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia, 25-1426

Issues: (1) Whether the Fifth Amendment exempts intangible property from the per se rules that govern takings of tangible property; and (2) whether Puerto Rico enjoys any form of immunity from suit in federal court and, if so, whether the Lanham Act abrogates that immunity.

Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, 26-12

Issue: Whether a plaintiff alleging that a school district implemented facially-neutral admissions criteria for a racially discriminatory purpose must show that the criteria produced a disparate impact on the targeted racial group before a court may consider evidence of discriminatory intent.

Issue: Whether Missouri’s Halloween sign-posting requirement, which requires factually accurate disclosures, unconstitutionally compels the speech of convicted sex offenders.

Ream v. Department of the Treasury, 26-93

Issue: Whether the prohibition on the production of distilled spirits in particular locations, including “in any dwelling house” or “in any shed, yard, or inclosure connected with any dwelling house,” 26 U.S.C. 5178(a)(1)(B), is necessary and proper for carrying into execution Congress’s enumerated power to lay and collect taxes.

Issue: Whether the prohibition on the production of distilled spirits in particular locations, including “in any dwelling house” or “in any shed, yard, or inclosure connected with any dwelling house,” 26 U.S.C. 5178(a)(1)(B), is necessary and proper for carrying into execution Congress’ enumerated power to lay and collect taxes.

Issues: (1) Whether the City of Chicago’s practice of impounding and selling a driver’s vehicle upon three unpaid parking tickets – keeping all sale proceeds without offsetting the ticket debt or refunding the surplus, and extending this to all vehicles registered to the driver, including those never ticketed and those purchased after any infraction – constitutes an unconstitutional taking; and (2) whether the takings clause places any limit on the ability of a local government to confiscate property under its police power.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether the takings clause has a police-power exception, making no compensation due when the government damages private property under its police power outside of eminent domain – or not; and (2) whether the government is exempt from liability under the takings clause when law enforcement officers intentionally destroy an innocent person’s property while trying to apprehend a fugitive.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether the government is exempt from liability under the takings clause when law enforcement officers intentionally destroy an innocent person’s property in the course of attempting to apprehend a fugitive; and (2) whether the doctrine of “public necessity” is an exception to the takings clause.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

Issue: Whether private instruction in courses required for state licensure constitutes government speech.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether, in a use-of-force case which involves multiple instances of force, Barnes v. Felix requires that each use-of-force be analyzed progressively from before the first instance of force used through the last instance of force used, considering the information known to the officer, the suspect’s prior actions (including any compliance, non-compliance, resistance, and reaching or grabbing for a weapon), and the suspect’s reactions to those prior use(s)-of-force, and, if so, whether Officers Moore and Kurtz violated Stephen Romero’s constitutional rights under this standard; and (2) whether, when analyzing a defendant law enforcement officer’s motion brought under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), in a use-of-force case where body camera video clearly depicts the entire lead-up to and application of force by a law enforcement officer, whether the lower courts may analyze the clearly established prong of qualified immunity at a more general, plaintiff-friendly, level than at the motion for summary judgment stage of litigation and, if not, whether Officer Moore and Officer Kurtz are entitled to qualified immunity under the facts of this case.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a violation of a clearly established constitutional right; and (2) whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a complete lack of training on the constitutional right in question.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

Issue: Whether the principles of Hope v. Pelzer are limited to Eighth Amendment claims or extend to free speech and free exercise clause claims such that petitioner’s constitutional claims should not be barred by qualified immunity.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

StandWithUs Center for Legal Justice v. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 25-1404

Issues: (1) Whether the harassers’ subjective discriminatory intent is an element of a hostile environment claim under Title VI; and (2) whether the First Amendment bars a plaintiff from pleading a Title VI hostile environment claim based on “protected speech.”

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

Issue: Whether, and under what circumstances, a bankruptcy court may override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor a valid arbitration agreement with respect to Section 362(k) claims.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28 and Oct. 9 conferences.)

John P. Elwood is a partner at Arnold & Porter in Washington, D.C., specializing in appellate litigation and administrative law.

#152. New White House press secretary calls confusion over legal credentials misunderstanding

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia joins President Donald Trump as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Updated: President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary has said the confusion over her legal credentials has been a misunderstanding, according to a story by the New York Times.

When Katie Zacharia was asked in which state she passed the bar, she “assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” Zacharia told the New York Times.

She noted Tuesday that this was “all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she told the New York Times.

That day, Zacharia had twice responded with, “When I moved to China,” to the question about the bar.

There is long-standing debate over the terms “lawyer” and “attorney”—often used interchangeably. Some use “lawyer” to describe a person with a JD, and some use “attorney” to refer only to those who have passed the bar exam.

But both terms require licensure by a state or other jurisdiction’s supreme court, says Sophie Martin, the senior managing director of operations and administration for the Helix Bar Review at the AccessLex Institute. And California code says a candidate must have passed the bar exam to be called a lawyer.

Zacharia did graduate from the Pepperdine University Rick J. Caruso School of Law in 2011.

While the New York Times reporter didn’t have the chance to ask her directly whether Zacharia passed a bar exam, the Wall Street Journal reports that she took but did not pass the California bar exam after law school graduation.

On Wednesday, the Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit ethics watchdog group, filed a complaint with the State Bar of California calling for a probe into Zacharia’s credentials.

“Ms. Zacharia has repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime,” according to the complaint.

Is she or isn’t she? Trump’s new press secretary claims she took the bar—in China

Updated Oct. 19 at 10:07 a.m. to include additional information about Katie Zacharia’s bar exam performance.

#154. Michigan Woman Pleads Guilty to Employment Tax Conspiracy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A Michigan woman pleaded guilty today to conspiring to defraud the United States for more than a decade, and to causing a tax loss of approximately $1.7 million.

According to court documents and statements made in court, Roxanne L. Huneycutt, of Fenton, owned and oversaw a series of full-service staffing companies since 2012. The staffing companies recruited temporary employees to perform manual labor, office administration, and other tasks for clients. The staffing companies were responsible for handling payroll and employment taxes associated with the employees.

From 2012 through 2024, the staffing companies failed to pay approximately $1.7 million in employment taxes to the IRS. In 2015, the Internal Revenue Service assessed penalties against Huneycutt for willfully failing to pay over certain employment taxes, but Huneycutt did not pay the penalties nor start complying with the law. To support the conspiracy and avoid detection of it, Huneycutt changed the names and physical locations of the staffing companies and filed paperwork with the State of Michigan indicating that she was not an owner of the staffing companies. Huneycutt spent proceeds from the staffing companies on personal expenses including but not limited to travel, clothing, jewelry, housing, and home decoration.

Huneycutt pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States. She is scheduled to be sentenced on February 18, 2027, and faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison. Huneycutt’s co-conspirator previously pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and is awaiting sentencing.

A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division made the announcement.

IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case.

Unit Chief Jorge Almonte and Trial Attorney Hayter L. Whitman of the Fraud Division are prosecuting this case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

#155. Witnessing a reorientation of the First and Second Amendments on the Roberts court

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

This is the third part in a series for SCOTUSblog recounting two decades of constitutional change through the five editions of our casebook, the first published in 2008 and the latest to be published this December.

Twenty years ago, the Supreme Court strictly enforced the separation of church and state, deferentially reviewed restrictions on free exercise rights, and played no role in enforcing the Second Amendment. This was the state of the law when one of us began law school in the fall of 2006.

What a difference two decades has made for the First and Second Amendments.

In 2006, shortly after the Roberts court’s inception, the modern concept of “religious liberty” was nascent. The conservative justices on the court, led by Justice Antonin Scalia, were skeptical of religious litigants who were seeking exemptions from neutral and generally applicable laws; that is, laws that did not target a particular religion. Nor did the free exercise of religion doctrine seem particularly controversial. In the first edition of our casebook, the entire chapter stretched only 20 pages. We included, for example, the 1878 case of Reynolds v. United States, which distinguished belief from conduct. There, the Supreme Court had protected a religious belief in polygamy but allowed the prosecution of a person who engaged in polygamy.

For modern cases, we began with Sherbert v. Verner. This Warren court ruling held that even neutral laws burdening religion would be reviewed under strict scrutiny; that is, the government needed to make a strong showing that impositions on religious practices were necessary. But Scalia’s decision in Employment Division v. Smith arguably rolled back Sherbert and reviewed such laws only with rational basis scrutiny; that is, any regulations on religion which were “reasonable” would hold. For the remainder of the Rehnquist court, Smith seemed set in stone, with no prospects of reversal. Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah provided an exception to the Smith rule where a particular faith is targeted, but that was generally the extent of it. In the first edition of our casebook, the scope of free exercise doctrine thus seemed both settled and limited.

During the early Roberts court, government policies that reflected a growing societal secularism began to clash with not only minority faiths, like Jehovah’s Witnesses and Seventh-day Adventists, but also mainstream Catholic and Protestant beliefs. Slowly but surely, protections for religious liberty expanded. The second edition of our casebook introduced the so-called ministerial exception with Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church and School v. EEOC. This doctrine exempted some religious employers from discrimination laws. The third edition, in 2017, previewed future clashes over funding of religious schools in Trinity Lutheran Church v. Comer. This narrow case held that the state could not deny funding for a playground at a church because of the church’s religious status. We also included Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., which granted an exemption from the Obamacare contraceptive mandate to a religious corporation. By the fourth edition in 2021, the court's trajectory on taxpayer funding for religious schools seemed clearer with Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue. This ruling held that the state could not deny educational tax credits for parents to use at a religious school. At this point, the free exercise clause chapter stretched about 40 pages – about double what it was only a few editions earlier.

In recent years, the court has become even more protective of religious liberty. We now begin with People v. Philips, an 1813 New York case that exempted a priest from testifying about incriminating information he learned during a confession. This interesting case stands in sharp tension with Smith, which refused a religious exemption from an otherwise neutral law, and reflects where the current court has been heading.

We also added the district court precursor to the landmark Supreme Court case of Barnette v. West Virginia State Board of Education. Before the Supreme Court, Justice Robert Jackson’s canonical decision ruled that requiring students to salute the flag was a form of compelled speech that violated the free speech clause of the First Amendment. But the lower court actually ruled that the flag law burdened Jehovah’s Witness students’ free exercise rights. After Sherbert, we added Wisconsin v. Yoder, which exempted Amish children from compulsory education laws. After Smith, Yoder seemed like a dead letter, as Scalia’s majority opinion effectively limited Yoder to the unique Amish context. But a new case, Mahmoud v. Taylor, reinvigorated Yoder, holding that the decision applies more broadly to grant opt-outs to parents who object to instruction that interferes with the right to direct the religious upbringing of their children.

1971’s Lemon v. Kurtzman prohibited entanglement between church and state. In 2008, the Lemon test was the law of the land, except when it wasn’t. Two cases in our book did not invoke the test: Marsh v. Chambers, which upheld a chaplain prayer before the meeting of the Nebraska legislature, and Lee v. Weisman, which halted a rabbi’s benediction before a middle school graduation ceremony. But the leading case in 2006, McCreary County, Kentucky v. A.C.L.U. of Kentucky, expressly applied Lemon to block a Ten Commandments display in a courthouse. Then again, the companion case, Van Orden v. Perry, upheld a Ten Commandments stone statue on the grounds of the Texas Capitol. The latter ruling stood as something of an outlier, perhaps because Justice Stephen Breyer thought it was imprudent for the court to mandate the destruction of an old monument. In any event, all of these precedents seemed settled.

By the third edition in 2017, however, there was change in the air. Marsh v. Chambers was augmented by Town of Greece v. Galloway, which followed a “history and tradition” approach to uphold a legislative prayer. And in the fourth edition, American Legion v. American Humanist Association upheld a public display of a Latin Cross, which served as a World War I memorial. This precedent suggested Lemon was on shaky ground. But all of the above cases remained good law.

Then, in 2022, came Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, which upheld the right of a football coach to pray on a 50-yard line after games. This precedent deemed Lemon to be, if not reversed, then “abandoned.” The first section of our textbook now includes three cases in which the Supreme Court purported to separate church and state: Everson v. Board of Education of Ewing Township, Engel v. Vitale, and Lemon v. Kurtzman. We previously did not include Everson and Engel, which concerned transportation to religious schools and school prayer, but thought it useful to show how the now-defunct “separationist” Lemon came to be.

We also focus on five cases from the Roberts court: Town of Greece v. Galloway and Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, discussed above; Our Lady of Guadalupe School v. Morrissey-Berru, which expanded the ministerial exception; Carson v. Makin, which barred the government from denying tax credits to religious schools; and Catholic Charities Bureau, Inc. v. Wisconsin Labor & Industry Review Commission, which prevented the government from denying a tax exemption to a religious nonprofit. These new cases would have been unthinkable in 2008, a time when the Lemon test reigned, but now define the contours of the establishment clause.

The court’s recent understanding of the Second Amendment has been transformative as well. The court heard oral argument in District of Columbia v. Heller in March 2008, the same month our book’s first edition was published. But Scalia’s majority opinion was still three months away. The first edition could only include a short excerpt from the Supreme Court’s majority opinion in United States v. Miller from 1939, which upheld a conviction for carrying a sawed-off shotgun. The entire chapter stretched about five pages. At the time, the Second Amendment – much less Second Amendment doctrine – was not yet a thing.

The Second Amendment chapter would begin to take shape by the time of our second edition in 2013. The excerpts of District of Columbia v. Heller and McDonald v. City of Chicago each stretched about 20 pages. The former case established that the Second Amendment guaranteed an individual right to keep and bear arms, and the latter case incorporated that right to the states. We also included two circuit court decisions that began the process of developing doctrines to implement the Second Amendment. Blue states legislated as if the holdings of Heller and McDonald were limited to the possession of guns inside the home. For whatever reason, as circuit courts upheld virtually every novel gun measure, the Supreme Court went for more than a decade without deciding a major gun case. Indeed, the leading support for gun rights from the Supreme Court came from dissents from denials of certiorari, which condemned treating the right to arms as a “second class” constitutional right.

The third edition, published in 2017, maintained Heller and McDonald, but added eight lower court decisions concerning gun ranges, gun stores, safe storage laws, “assault weapons,” and the right to carry.

Once again, our latest edition shows a continued shift in constitutional law, even if doctrinal certainty remains lacking. In their place, four new Supreme Court decisions now have full coverage. The court decided two cases about where the right to bear arms applies. New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen held that the Second Amendment protects a right to carry arms outside the home. Wolford v. Lopez invalidated a Hawaii law that presumptively ban carrying firearms in all places to the public. The court also decided two other cases about who can bear arms: United States v. Rahimi ruled a person subject to a domestic violence restraining order could not bear arms, while United States v. Hemani held that a user of marijuana could bear arms.

Alas, this developing jurisprudence is proving difficult to apply and even understand. In 2008, we thought Heller could bring to the right to keep and bear arms what First Amendment decisions in the 20th century brought to the freedom of speech. Any such movement has developed slowly. But more recently appointed justices appear to have broken the logjam. This term, the court will decide whether the Second Amendment guarantees the right to possess AR-15 and similar semi-automatic rifles, which (hopefully) will address the important but neglected question of which arms are protected by the Constitution.

But the bottom line is that, even if the right to possess a firearm has expanded dramatically, the contours of what that means is strikingly undeveloped.

The next installment in this series considers the changes to Congress’ enumerated powers, the president’s executive powers, and the separation of powers between those branches.

Josh Blackman is a professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston. He holds the Centennial Chair of Constitutional Law. Josh is also an Adjunct Fellow at the Manhattan Institute.

Randy E. Barnett is the Patrick Hotung Professor of Constitutional Law at the Georgetown University Law Center, where he founded the Georgetown Center for the Constitution.

Earlier this year, SCOTUSblog published the first Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack, a statistical portrait of the Supreme Court’s interim/emergency/shadow docket for the 2024-25 term. Now that the 2025-26 term has concluded, Taraleigh Davis produced a second edition of this stat pack, which we released on Tuesday.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court released a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Oct. 9, announcing, among other things, that it had added three new cases to the oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term. The cases include U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, on what types of discovery orders are appropriate in disputes over access to government information. For more on Monday’s order list, see the Morning Reads and On Site sections below.

Also on Tuesday, the justices heard oral argument in Beaird v. United States, on the degree of deference that courts owe to the U.S. Sentencing Commission’s commentary on applying federal sentencing guidelines.

Today, the justices will hear argument in Salazar v. Paramount Global, on whether and how the 1988 Video Privacy Protection Act, which was enacted after the Washington City Paper reported on Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork’s video rental history, applies in the internet era.

On Sept. 28, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to clear the way for the Federal Bureau of Prisons to implement its new policy on healthcare and accommodations for transgender inmates, which would prevent such inmates from obtaining gender-transition surgeries, hormone therapy, and “social accommodations.” The dispute is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

The court is currently weighing requests from the Federal Communications Commission and two Republican groups to block a ruling by a federal appeals court that would require the FCC to rule quickly on a challenge to its “public notice” extending favorable advertising rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees. These interim docket cases are also fully briefed.

#159. Libertarianism and Democracy Revisited - A Rejoinder to Matt Zwolinski

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

We agree on many key points, but have a few notable differences.

On October 4, I published a post on "Libertarianism and Democracy," critiquing political philosopher Matt Zwolinski's earlier Liberalism.Org article on the same topic. Earlier today, I posted Matt's response to me. The present post is my rejoinder:

I would like to thank Matt for his interesting and insightful response. We agree on several key points, including that democracy is generally superior to authoritarianism, that libertarian critiques of democracy have great merit, and that - in much of the world - the most serious threats to liberty now come from the nationalist right, rather than the the political left. But we still differ on a few key points related to libertarianism and democracy.

The Nature of Libertarian Critiques of Democracy

Perhaps the most crucial disagreement is about the nature of libertarian critiques of democracy. Matt suggests that "[m]ost of what Ilya calls the libertarian critique of democracy is really a critique of big government." If so, libertarians can just focus on criticizing big government generally, while simultaneously extolling democracy.

There are indeed flaws of big government that arise regardless of whether it is democratic or authoritarian. But those outlined in my earlier Liberalism.Org article are in fact specific to democracy. They include tyranny of the majority, voter ignorance, and the tendency of democracy to create opportunities for illiberal forces to seize power and - in the worst case scenario - even destroy democracy itself.  Tyranny of the majority is obviously a problem distinctive to democracy. The same goes for rational voter ignorance, which arises from the perverse incentive structure  of individual voters, who have only an infinitesimally small chance of influencing electoral outcomes. And, while illiberal forces can and do seize power under authoritarian systems, the pathways democracies (usually involving the electoral process) create for them are distinctive.

Authoritarian systems have their own distinctive flaws, which are generally even worse. But the distinctive nature of democracy's flaws means they cannot simply be folded into a generic critique of big government. In addition, as noted in my response to Matt, these distinctive flaws of democracy are at the heart of many of today's most serious threats to liberty and justice in many democratic systems, including the threats posed by the nationalist right. Thus, it is important for libertarians to emphasize the nature and gravity of these weaknesses, and the value of our proposals for dealing them (which in many cases are different from and better than those advanced by other types of liberals). As emphasized in my earlier response, this is an area where libertarians often have a comparative advantage over other liberals. On the other hand, we generally do not have a comparative advantage when it comes to explaining why democracy is better than authoritarianism.

Along related lines, Matt suggests that libertarian critiques of the state aren't "an argument against democratic control of whatever the state does do." But once we recognize that democracy has significant distinctive flaws, there is actually a case for insulating some functions of government from democratic control. Obvious examples include the judiciary and monetary policy (unless we want to cut government out of the latter entirely, and adopt free banking). Indeed, even most non-libertarian liberals recognize that such insulation is desirable in some cases, most notably the courts.

The Problem of Libertarians Tempted by Authoritarianism

Matt argues that we should, nonetheless devote extensive energy to extolling democracy, because doing so is likely to have an impact on fellow libertarians who may otherwise be tempted to embrace authoritarianism. It is likely true that libertarians tempted in this way are more easily dissuaded by other libertarians than by non-libertarians. But such people are a tiny minority within an minority. Libertarians are a small group (probably around 5-10% of the US population or even less, depending on how you draw the line). Those sympathetic to authoritarianism are much fewer still. Thus, it makes little sense to devote more than a modest amount of time and effort to dealing with them, as opposed to addressing the much larger group of non-libertarian liberals who need to be more cognizant of the dangerous shortcomings of democracy.

Moreover, when we look at libertarians who have shifted to the "alt right" or otherwise become advocates of illiberal ideas, the problem in most cases is not excessive skepticism of democracy, but insufficient commitment to liberty - particularly, the liberty of people from different ethnic, racial, or religious backgrounds, that of migrants, and those with unconventional lifestyles. That is pretty obviously the case with Curtis Yarvin and Hans-Hermann Hoppe, both mentioned by Matt. The former's advocacy of a "post-liberal" ideology of repression (which is really based on pre-liberal models) is pretty obviously not the product of a man who thinks authoritarianism is a better way to protect liberty than democracy. Indeed, his concern is exactly the opposite (that democracy allows for way too much liberty). The same goes for Hoppe's advocacy of repression of immigrants, gays and lesbians, and people with various non-traditional lifestyles. Peter Thiel, the third case mentioned by Matt, is that of a person who has abandoned libertarianism for "national conservatism," an ideology focused on exalting the interests of ethnic and culture majorities and using the state to punish perceived "enemies." To the extent we want to focus on dissuading such people, it should be to reemphasize the value of liberty for all, not extolling the virtues of democracy. People who value democracy more than liberty are generally unlikely to become libertarians in the first place.

Matt and I also have a modest disagreement over whether there can be situations where some form of authoritarianism can be a lesser evil compared to democracy. I think such cases are extremely rare, but not nonexistent. Matt's position is less clear, and perhaps I misunderstand him. But he does seem to want to deny this possibility. In response to my examples of the allied occupations of Germany and Japan after World War II, he seems to think these don't really count because "those occupations were run by democracies answerable to their own voters, and they ended." But they were still cases where non-democratic government was imposed on a population, and that population itself did not have control over when and if it would end.

In these cases, a non-democratic occupation government was a lesser evil than immediate establishment of democracy, because of the highly illiberal nature of German and Japanese majority public opinion at the time.  Similar circumstances can potentially arise in other countries. And, in some cases, a domestically generated authoritarian regime might still be a lesser evil than any democracy that is feasible at the time.

In some situations, the problem can be dealt with by limiting democracy, rather than abjuring it completely. For example, as noted in my earlier response, post-occupation West Germany long banned Nazis and communists from competing in elections, but otherwise committed to free electoral competition. But there could be situations where such constraints are not enough. Because such cases are highly unusual, this is not a particularly important disagreement. But it does have relevance in situations where we consider how to deal with a society where majority public opinion is deeply illiberal.

Finally - and least important - Matt differs with me about the use of the terms "libertarian" and "classical liberal," arguing that the former are more likely to be democracy-skeptics than the latter. We can, if we want, define the two terms in such a way that people we label with one are generally more suspicious of democracy than those we label with the other one. But that is not the way the terms are typically used. That said, different people use these terms in different ways. To my mind, they are mostly just alternative labels for the same general ideology. But I don't have much of a beef with people who prefer to use them differently than I do, so long as they make clear what they mean.

Ultimately, Matt and I agree on much more than we differ. But a few of the issues we differ have real significance. I am grateful for the opportunity to consider them.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#160. Personal injury lawyer disbarred after pleading guilty in stolen accident report scheme

A Georgia personal injury attorney was disbarred after pleading guilty for his part in a scheme to use stolen accident reports for finanial gain. (Image from Shutterstock)

The Georgia Supreme Court has disbarred a personal injury lawyer who pleaded guilty for his part in a scheme using stolen accident reports to find clients and financially benefit from settlement money.

The state’s high court on Wednesday disbarred William Taylor Payne, who was convicted in a scheme involving a police department employee and others who illegally accessed law enforcement accident reports over 30,000 times between Jan. 1 and Aug. 12, 2015, for financial gain, Law360 reports.

Payne used the data to solicit and obtain clients for personal injury cases for the William Taylor Payne PC law firm, according to records from the DeKalb County Superior Court in Georgia. The data was stolen from the Georgia Electronic Accident Reporting System, a secure computer website and database of police accidents created and maintained by LexisNexis on behalf of the state’s Department of Transportation, according to court documents.

In a statement to Law360, Miles Stephen Cowan, counsel for Payne, said his client was a dedicated lawyer who raised a daughter as a single parent.

“Since Bill is now in his early 80s, I can attest to what was a very fine career as a litigator who could be relied on to cite statutory authority on a wide range of matters, by rote memory, particularly the evidence code and civil practice act,” Cowan said.

#162. Who Should Defend Democracy?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Matt Zwolinski responds to my critique of his earlier article on libertarianism and democracy.

On October 4, I published a post on "Libertarianism and Democracy," critiquing political philosopher Matt Zwolinski's earlier Liberalism.Org article on the same topic. Matt has written a response to me, which I have agreed to post at this site. The remaining paragraphs of this post were written by Matt Zwolinski, not me (Ilya Somin). I have posted a rejoinder to Matt's thoughtful response here.

My recent Liberalism.org essay, "Democracy Belongs on the List," made the case that classical liberals should count democracy among their core commitments, alongside private property, free markets, and the rule of law. And it belongs there for the same reason. Like property rights and markets, democracy is a crucial way of keeping power in check.

Ilya Somin has written a generous and thoughtful reply to that piece. And I think he actually agrees with me more than the framing of his post might suggest. Ilya grants that democracies are generally freer and more prosperous than the alternatives, that democracy is "a valuable check on power," that libertarians should arguably stress these points "more often," and that "in much of the world today, right-wing nationalists pose a greater threat to libertarian values and priorities than the political left does." What's left mainly comes down to two questions: what counts as a libertarian critique of democracy, and whose job it is to defend democracy.

Before turning to those substantive issues, though, there's one terminological matter that's worth clearing up. Ilya says that nothing of significance hinges on whether we call our view "libertarian" or "classical liberal." And on most questions I'd agree. On this one, though, I think the difference matters. In The Individualists, John Tomasi and I draw a distinction between strict libertarians and classical liberals. The former group tends to treat liberty as a moral absolute and to derive their politics from a single overarching principle like the non-aggression axiom. Think Murray Rothbard or Ayn Rand. The latter treat liberty as a strong but defeasible presumption and are more empiricist and pluralistic in their approach to politics. Think Friedrich Hayek or Richard Epstein.

My sense is that these two camps within the broader "liberty movement" have taken pretty different stances toward democracy, with strict libertarians being much more critical than their classical liberal brethren. Even back in the 19th century, you could find Benjamin Tucker insisting that voting is always a form of aggression, and Lysander Spooner arguing that women "have just as good a right to make laws as men have, and no better: AND THAT IS JUST NO RIGHT AT ALL." Herbert Spencer was even willing to walk back his support of women's suffrage once he decided that women would probably use their vote to support bigger government. That's a pretty different take than anything you're likely to find in Ludwig von Mises or Friedrich Hayek (more on whom later), let alone in John Stuart Mill.

That brings us to the first of the two substantive issues under dispute. Ilya argues that recent events have made libertarian critiques of democracy more important than ever, and that the libertarian solutions to democracy's flaws are "primarily to limit and decentralize government power." I'm with him on that, but I don't think this settles, or even really addresses, the debate about democracy. Limiting and decentralizing government power is a claim about the scope of the state, about how much government should do. It's a principle that would apply to any government, whether democratic or not. And, crucially, it isn't an argument against democratic control of whatever the state does do.

That distinction was at the heart of my essay. Following Jacob Levy, I argued that classical liberals have let a perfectly sound critique of too much government slide into a skepticism about democracy itself, treating democracy, in Levy's words, "as if the contrast to 'democratic' were 'economic' rather than 'autocratic.'" One can be a radical about reducing the scope of the state and still insist that its agents must be answerable to the people they govern. Most of what Ilya calls the libertarian critique of democracy is really a critique of big government. That's an argument I largely agree with, as far as it goes. The trouble comes when we file it under the wrong heading. When we ourselves blur the line between critiques of state power and critiques of democracy, we shouldn't be surprised when people come away thinking libertarians are against democracy.

That brings me to comparative advantage, which is where I think Ilya's argument is most interesting but also most mistaken. Libertarians are a small minority, he says, and "we have no comparative advantage when it comes to extolling the virtues of democracy relative to authoritarianism. Other types of liberals can do this work just as well as we can, perhaps better." So we should stick to what we do best, which is analyzing democracy's flaws.

This argument might make sense in some contexts. But as a general principle, I think it misfires, and it misfires most badly when the audience is classical liberals and libertarians themselves. That, after all, is where the turn against democracy has actually happened. Hans-Hermann Hoppe's Democracy: The God That Failed argued that monarchy was preferable to democracy, and complained that "habitual democrats" had been tolerated rather than "isolated, excluded and expelled from civilization." Curtis Yarvin, who came to neoreaction by way of libertarianism, credits Hoppe with opening "a kind of door to the pre-revolutionary world" for him. And in 2009, Peter Thiel wrote in a Cato Institute publication that "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible." None of this follows from the libertarian critique of voter ignorance, and nothing Ilya has written points in this direction. But it grew in a movement where, as Janet Bufton recently put it in Liberal Currents, "even liberal libertarians were taught arguments about why democracy fails," and hardly anyone was making the case for democracy on libertarian terms. Any old liberal can explain to the public why democracy beats dictatorship. But a libertarian drifting toward Hoppe or Yarvin isn't going to listen to them. Only libertarians can tell libertarians that democracy is theirs.

So if democracy is a libertarian value, what kind of libertarian value is it? Ilya argues that democracy shouldn't be "a first-order libertarian priority, on par with liberty, constraining coercion, property rights, and increasing human happiness," because its value is instrumental rather than intrinsic. I agree that the value of democracy is instrumental. In that way, it's in precisely the same position as a number of items on the classical liberal list. Free trade, federalism, judicial review, and the rule of law are instrumental too. What I want to resist is the claim that because democracy is only instrumentally valuable it's therefore dispensable – something that can be traded away whenever we can imagine something better. What we can imagine, though, is a poor guide to what works. The better question, as David Schmidtz argues, is what has "an observable history of leading self-interested agents to act in ways that are useful and agreeable to the people around them," and by that test democracy has very few rivals.

Which leaves us with Hayek. Ilya defends Hayek's preference for "a liberal dictator to a democratic government lacking liberalism" as a claim about rare hypothetical cases, and suggests that transitional non-democratic rule "may be necessary" in places like Russia and China, citing the Allied occupations of Germany and Japan. But those occupations were run by democracies answerable to their own voters, and they ended. Russia and China, in contrast, have no outside power that could impose a transition and then hand power back. The only realistic candidate for transitional power in those countries is a domestic strongman, which is exactly the case Hayek had in front of him. Hayek wasn't musing about hypotheticals; he was talking about Chile.

Ultimately, Ilya and I want the same thing. We both advocate a form of libertarianism that resists concentrated power wherever it appears, including when it arrives through the ballot box. Where we differ is on the need to say out loud that democracy is one of the ways we resist it. I think we should, and I think libertarians are better placed to say it than anyone, since the people who most need to hear it are our own.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. #163. Court grants cases on DOGE data dispute, prisoners’ rights, and what qualifies as “material support” for terrorism

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday added three new cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, agreeing to decide, among other things, what kinds of orders trial courts can issue in disputes over access to government information and whether working as a cook in a camp run by violent separatists qualifies as providing “material support” for terrorism under federal immigration law.

President Donald Trump created the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE, in January 2025 to advance his agenda by “modernizing Federal technology and software to maximize governmental efficiency and productivity.” Although it is not a cabinet-level department, DOGE was widely involved in Trump’s efforts to reduce the size of the federal government.

The dispute now before the court, U.S. Doge Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, began after a government watchdog group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, filed a request under the Freedom of Information Act for (among other things) communications between the DOGE administrator, Amy Gleason, and DOGE staff, as well as financial disclosures submitted by DOGE personnel.

CREW went to federal court in Washington last year, asking DOGE to disclose documents that it said it wanted before Congress passed a bill to fund the federal government.

CREW also sought to fast-track discovery – the process of exchanging information in litigation – to determine whether DOGE is a federal “agency” that must comply with FOIA. It asked for a list of current and former DOGE employees, a list of employees and positions for which DOGE had recommended termination, a list of government contracts and grants that DOGE had recommended be canceled, and the opportunity to depose Gleason.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper granted most of CREW’s discovery requests, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit turned down DOGE’s plea to pause that order.

U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer then came to the Supreme Court in May 2025, asking the justices to intervene. He told the justices that the discovery required under Cooper’s order “offends the separation of powers by compromising the ‘necessity’ for confidentiality that allows presidential advisors to provide ‘candid, objective’ advice and communication.”

In a two-page, unsigned order in early June 2025, the court – over the objections of Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson – sent the dispute back to the D.C. Circuit for another look. The majority wrote that the portions of Cooper’s discovery order that required the government to disclose the content of DOGE’s recommendations within the executive branch, as well as whether those recommendations were followed, were too broad. Moreover, it added, concerns about the separation of powers between the branches of government “counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal Executive Branch communications.” The court put Cooper’s discovery orders on hold while the litigation continued.

When the case returned to the lower courts, CREW modified its discovery requests so that it no longer sought information about “recommendations” made by U.S. DOGE employees. The lower courts then declined to block CREW’s requests.

DOGE came to the Supreme Court in March, asking the justices to weigh in. Sauer told the court that the D.C. Circuit “has continued to approve intrusive discovery against a presidential advisory body without adequate consideration for the separation of powers, the FOIA statute, and” the Supreme Court’s order last year on the interim docket. Among other things, he argued, that order “required the courts below to reassess all remaining discovery—not just requests for USDS recommendations—with the ‘deference and restraint’ applicable to presidential advisors under Cheney v. U.S. District Court,” a 2004 case in which the justices held that when considering requests for information directed at the vice-president and other senior executive branch officials, “special considerations” should “control when the Executive Branch’s interests in maintaining the autonomy of its office and safeguarding the confidentiality of its communications are implicated.”

CREW urged the justices to deny review. It argued that in formulating the new discovery order, the D.C. Circuit had “followed this Court’s instructions” in its earlier ruling on the interim docket “to the letter.” Instead, it contended, the government was seeking “to transform this Court’s carefully crafted stay-stage order into a sweeping ruling that Cheney effectively forecloses discovery in this case. That is not what this Court said,” CREW insisted, “and, especially after remand, this case looks nothing like Cheney.”

On Tuesday, the court agreed to address the D.C. Circuit’s ruling.

The immigration case granted on Tuesday, Blanche v. Ozurumba, was also brought to the court by the Trump administration. In a petition for review filed in May, Sauer asked the justices to clarify what type of support an immigrant must be shown to have provided to a terrorist organization in order to be “removable and ineligible for various immigration benefits” under a federal immigration law that states that an individual who “affords material support” to such a group is “ineligible to be admitted to the United States.”

Blanche v. Ozurumba involves Izuchukwu Ozurumba, “a native and citizen of Nigeria,” who worked as a cook in a camp run by a separatist organization known as the “Unknown Gunmen” “for about six months” before escaping, according to the government’s petition. He made his way to Venezuela and then the United States, where he applied for asylum, but an immigration judge and then the Board of Immigration Appeals concluded that his work in the camp amounted to “material support” for terrorism and that he was, therefore, ineligible for asylum.

Ozurumba appealed his case to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, which held that “the record does not support the conclusion that Ozurumba provided material support” to the Unknown Gunmen. “Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have ‘sustained’ the organization in the broadest possible sense—by converting raw groceries into meals they enjoyed—but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities,” concluded 4th Circuit Judge James Wynn in the majority opinion.

The Supreme Court will clarify what qualifies as "material support" of a terrorist organization such that an immigrant is ineligible for asylum and removable from the United States.

The justices also granted review on Tuesday in Berry v. United States, on whether a certificate of appealability – a prerequisite for appealing a decision that denies a request for post-conviction relief – may be granted to a prisoner whose claim is foreclosed by his own circuit’s precedent but would be allowed to proceed in a different circuit. In his petition for review, Corey Berry emphasized that the federal courts of appeals were split over this question on circuit splits.

The court on Tuesday declined to take up the case of Jesus Herrera-Salazar, who was sentenced to 15 months in prison, followed by two years of supervised release, after he pleaded guilty to being “found in” the United States after having been deported. While on supervised release, Herrera-Salazar was instructed not to leave eastern Oklahoma; after he was pulled over in a traffic stop there, he was again indicted and convicted on a charge of being “found in” the U.S. after having been deported. After his second conviction, he was sentenced to 21 months in prison and three years of supervised release.

Herrera-Salazar argued that the second indictment violated the Constitution’s double jeopardy clause, which provides that “[n]o person shall ... be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.” He contended that both sets of charges and convictions stemmed from the same offense – being present in the United States after deportation. After the lower courts rejected that argument, Herrera-Salazar asked the Supreme Court to weigh in.

The justices on Tuesday denied that request. Justice Sonia Sotomayor penned a statement, joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch, regarding the decision not to weigh in on the case. She wrote that “[b]ecause I hope the facts of this case are anomalous and because Herrera-Salazar has since been removed from the United States, I concur in the Court’s decision not to grant review in this case. I write, however, to underscore the serious constitutional problems that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar.”

“When a defendant is convicted of a crime that involves continuous, uninterrupted conduct,” Sotomayor stated, the court’s cases “and the logic of the Double Jeopardy Clause strongly suggest that the Government is barred from charging that defendant with the same continuous crime for a second time simply by focusing on a different time marker.” Otherwise, she posited, the government could bring multiple indictments against a defendant for each month of a continuous crime. “There is even more force to this double jeopardy objection,” she added, “where the Government itself effectively forbids the defendant to cease his unlawful conduct.”

The court did not act on several high-profile petitions for review, including a challenge to a Maryland suburb’s admissions policy for selecting students for magnet middle schools and a pair of challenges to the federal ban on home distilleries. The justices will consider those cases and others at their Oct. 16 conference.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#164. Finding right fit is more important in judicial clerkship hiring than politics, new study says

Law students often assume that politics decide who wins a judicial clerkship, but judges say otherwise. (Photo by Peter Dazeley/Getty Images)

Law students often assume that politics decide who wins a judicial clerkship, but judges say otherwise, according to a new study based on interviews with 194 federal and state judges.

According to a story published Monday by Reuters, the judges surveyed placed greater importance on finding candidates who can meet the demands of the job, get along with everyone in a small chambers, and stay connected afterward.

Titled What Judges Want, the study—which was written by Tracey George, a professor at the Vanderbilt University Law School; Mitu Gulati, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law; and Albert Yoon, a professor at the University of Toronto Faculty of Law—found that experience and maturity ranked among the top factors for judges, along with recommendations from trusted law professors and other judges.

According to the study, only 39% of the judges raised politics or ideology as a hiring factor, and no judges surveyed said they hired clerks expressly for shared politics. Additionally, no judge surveyed said they would hire only members of the right-leaning Federalist Society or the left-leaning American Constitution Society.

The study also found that law school grades were not as important for some judges, who found that they could be misleading or unreliable metrics for building strong relationships with clerks. Instead of stockpiling a bunch of strong students, the study found that many judges are looking for people they can develop lifelong bonds with.

“In many cases, judges are choosing ​confidants for life,” the report said, according to Reuters.

#165. $65K Settlements with EEOC Over Failure to Accommodate Muslim and Christian Employees' Religious Days Off

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From a press release last month, just posted on Westlaw:

N.C. Detective Agency, a Durham-based security company, will pay $65,231 in compensatory damages and back pay, and take other corrective actions to voluntarily resolve a religious discrimination investigation by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), the federal agency announced today.

The EEOC's investigation found reasonable cause to believe that an employee requested to be excused from work due to a Muslim religious holiday, but the request was denied. The company was aware of the employee's need for a religious accommodation but did not engage in the legally required interactive process, and instead terminated her in June 2025 when she did not report for duty.

And from another press release two weeks later, also just posted on Westlaw:

Reynolds IGA Foodliner, Inc., owner and operator of a chain of grocery stores, will pay $65,000 and provide other equitable relief to settle a religious discrimination and retaliation lawsuit filed by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), the federal agency announced today.

According to the suit, shortly after she was hired as a deli clerk at the Piggly Wiggly store in Hazlehurst, Georgia, the employee requested Sundays off to observe her Sabbath. The employee's supervisor denied the request, claiming that, if the store gave the employee Sundays off, it would have to do the same for all other employees. The employee continued to request the accommodation, and the company fired her in January 2025.

"Employers cannot deny religious accommodation requests simply for fear of upsetting other employees," said Marcus G. Keegan, regional attorney for the EEOC's Atlanta District. "The EEOC remains committed to enforcing federal anti-discrimination law and protecting employees' rights to religious freedom."

Darrell E. Graham, director of the EEOC's Atlanta District, said, "Employers must thoughtfully consider each request for religious accommodation on an individual, case-by-case basis and otherwise make good-faith efforts to accommodate their employees' religious beliefs. Employers must be aware of their obligations under federal law to provide reasonable religious accommodations absent undue hardship."

Finally, from a third press release from last month (it was published in between the first two, but was again just posted on Westlaw); this one involves a lawsuit and not a settlement:

Blue Bell Creameries, Inc., a Brenham, Texas-based frozen snack manufacturer and distributor with a production facility in Sylacauga, Alabama, unlawfully terminated a Jewish body shop technician soon after he requested a beard‑related religious accommodation, the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) charged in a lawsuit announced today.

Even supporters of bans on religious discrimination by private employers might debate whether employers should be required to give religious exemptions from generally applicable rules (exemptions that could themselves be seen as discrimination in favor of religious observers). But Congress has indeed mandated such exemptions: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, as amended in 1972, generally requires employers to accommodate religious objectors' requests for exemptions from generally applicable work rules, unless doing so would pose an "undue hardship" for the employer.

That extends to time off for religious holidays: Indeed, the leading recent case on the subject, Groff v. DeJoy, involved a Christian employee's request for an exemption from having to work Sundays. And of course it extends, as it must, to all religions.
